# *The Life of St. BARNABAS the Apostle.*

<margin>
ᵃ Theodore Lector, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 2, page 557. Alexander the Monk, in the location cited above, number 31.
ᵇ Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 16, chapter 37, page 716, Volume 2.
ᶜ Alexander, as above, numbers 29, 30.
</margin>

They threw his body into the fire with the intent to consume it, but the flames had not the least power over it. His kinsman Mark privately buried him in a cave not far from the city, while his friends mourned the loss with solemn lamentation. I will omit the miracles reported to have occurred at his tomb. The remains of his body were discovered in the year 485 AD, during the reign of Emperor Zeno (though Nicephorus mistakenly dates this to the twelfth year of Anastasius). He was dug up under a carob tree <note>original: "Bean or Carob Tree"</note>, and upon his breast was found a copy of St. Matthew’s Gospel written in Barnabas’s own hand. Bishop Anthemius took the Gospel with him to Constantinople, where the Emperor received it with great reverence and laid it away with great care and diligence.

As a testimony of his joy, the Emperor honored the Episcopal See of Salamis with a special prerogative: it was to be an "autocephalous" see <note>original Greek: sedes αὐτοκέφαλος</note>, meaning it was independent of any foreign jurisdiction. This privilege was later ratified by Emperor Justinian, whose wife, Theodora, was a Cypriot. The Emperor also greatly enriched the Bishop upon his return, commanding him to build a church dedicated to St. Barnabas over the place of his burial, which was accordingly erected with more than ordinary stateliness and magnificence. 

It is added to the story that these remains were discovered because St. Barnabas himself appeared to Anthemius three separate times. However, I view this as a mere addition to the story, designed only to serve a contemporary purpose. At that time, Peter (nicknamed "the Fuller"), the Patriarch of Antioch, claimed jurisdiction over the Cypriot churches as if they were subject to his see. Anthemius would not agree to this and stubbornly asserted his own rights. How easy it would have been to take the occasion of finding St. Barnabas's body and add the detail of the visions to gain credit for the cause and advance it with the Emperor. Accordingly, it had its intended effect. Whoever reads the whole story and the circumstances of the appearances, as related by my author, will see that they seem plainly calculated for such a purpose.

<margin>
ᵈ Ibid. number 18.
ᵉ *On Modesty*, chapter 20, page 582. See also Philastrius, *On Heresies*, chapter 60.
ᶠ *Against Celsus*, book 1, page 49.
ᵍ *Ecclesiastical History*, book 3, chapter 25, page 97.
</margin>

XIV. As for his outward form and shape, he is described by the ancients in this way: He was a man of a handsome countenance and a grave, venerable appearance. His eyebrows were short and his eyes were cheerful and pleasant, expressing a sense of majesty without any bitterness or harshness. His speech was sweet and obliging. His clothing was simple <note>original: "mean"</note>, as became a man of a disciplined and self-denying life; his gait <note>original: "gate"</note> was composed, natural, grave, and decent. 

This elegant physical structure was but the lodging of a more noble tenant: a soul richly furnished with divine graces and virtues. He possessed profound humility, overflowing charity, firm faith, an immovable constancy, and an unconquerable patience. He had a mighty zeal and unwearied diligence in propagating Christianity and working for the good of souls. He so entirely devoted himself to a traveling life, constantly moving from place to place, that he could find little or no time to leave any writings behind for the benefit of the Church—at least none that have certainly reached us. Indeed, in ancient times, there were some—Tertullian in particular—who supposed him to be the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, an opinion that is now generally rejected. There is also an epistle still in existence under his name, of great antiquity, which is frequently cited by Clement of Alexandria and his student Origen (to name a few). Origen even styles it the "Catholic Epistle of Barnabas," but it was placed by Eusebius among the "spurious" <note>original Greek: νόθα; meaning books of disputed or illegitimate apostolic origin</note> works...

The structure and composition of it are intricate and obscure, consisting of unusual allegories and forced, improbable interpretations of Scripture, though its main purpose is to show that the Christian religion has replaced the rites and customs of the **Mosaic Law**. The latter part of it contains a useful and excellent exhortation framed around the concept of **two ways**: one of **light** and the other of **darkness**. The first is under the guidance of the **Angels of God** (illuminating ministers <note>original Greek: φωταγωγοὶ ἄγγελοι</note>, as he calls them), while the other is under the direction of the **Angels of Satan**, the prince of the iniquity of this age. In describing the way of **light**, he encourages most of the specific duties and examples of the **Christian** and **spiritual** life, which are listed there with admirable **accuracy** and **conciseness**. In the way of **darkness**, he represents those specific sins and vices we are to avoid. I am confident that the **pious reader** will not think it a waste of time, nor regret the effort to read through such an ancient and useful discourse. He expresses himself in this way:

<margin>Epistle of Barnabas, page 248. Vossius Edition.</margin>

XV. THE **way of life** is this: **Whoever travels toward the appointed place will hasten by their works to reach it. The knowledge given to us on how to walk in this way is this: You shall love your Creator. You shall glorify him who redeemed you from death. You shall be simple in heart and, being rich in spirit, you shall not join yourself with those who walk in the way of death. You shall hate to do anything displeasing to God. You shall hate all kinds of hypocrisy. You shall not forsake the commandments of the Lord. Do not exalt yourself, but be of an humble mind. You shall not take glory for yourself, nor shall you take evil counsel against your neighbor. You shall not add boldness to your soul. You shall not commit fornication, nor be guilty of adultery or sexual perversion <note>original: "buggery"—a term historically used for various sexual acts then considered "unnatural" or criminal</note>.**

**You shall not neglect God’s command in correcting the impurity of others, nor shall you show favoritism when you rebuke someone for their faults. You shall be meek and silent, and stand in awe of the words you hear. You shall not hold a grudge against your brother. You shall not be of a double and unstable mind, doubting whether this or that is true.**

I have nothing more to say regarding this excellent person than to add the description given of him by an inspired author <note>Referring to St. Luke, the author of the Book of Acts.</note> who could not err: *“He was a good man, full of faith, and of the Holy Spirit.”*

I. <image-desc>A large decorative initial 'S' set within a square frame, embellished with intricate floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>ST. TIMOTHY was, as we may probably assume, a *Lycaonian*, born at *Lystra*, a noted city of that province. He was a person in whom the *Jew*, the *Gentile*, and the *Christian* all met together. His father was by birth a *Greek* and by religion a *Gentile*—or if he was a convert, he was at most only a "sojourning proselyte" <note>original Hebrew: גר תושב, *Ger Toshav*</note> or *Proselyte of the Gate*. These were converts who did not obligate themselves to circumcision and the rites of *Moses*, but only to the observance of the seven laws of the sons of *Noah*. His mother, *Eunice*, daughter to the devout and pious *Lois*, was a *Jewess*, who nevertheless did not hesitate to marry this *Greek*.

<margin>"Do you see how the Law was gradually set aside when such intermarriages began to occur?" <note>original Greek: Ὁρᾶς πῶς ἤρετο ὁ νόμος καταλυθείς, τῆς ἐπιμίξεων οὕτως γινομένων. Chrysostom, Homily 1 on 2 Timothy, p. 1627.</note></margin>
This is an argument that the "partition wall" was now tottering and ready to fall, seeing that *Jew* and *Gentile* began to marry in this way. His mother and grandmother were women of eminent virtue and holiness, and they seem to have been among the first converted to the Christian faith. It was no small instance of their piety that they took great care in his education, instructing him in the knowledge of divine things and seasoning his tender years with virtuous and sober principles,

<margin>2 Timothy 3:15.</margin>
so that *from a child he was acquainted with the Holy Scriptures*. By this, he was admirably prepared to receive Christianity and equipped to lead a strictly pious life.

<margin>"The source and root of goodness is to receive a proper education." <note>original Greek: Πηγὴ καὶ ῥίζα καλοκαγαθίας, τὸ νομίμως τυχεῖν παιδείας. Plutarch, On the Education of Children, p. 4.</note></margin>
And indeed, religion never thrives more naturally than when it is planted early and its foundations are laid in youthful piety. For the mind being then soft and tender, it easily receives the best impressions. These degrees of influence gradually work their way into the soul and imperceptibly reconcile it to the difficulties of a holy life. Thus, what must necessarily feel harsh and severe to a man who tries to rescue himself from a lifelong habit of sin, the youth is unacquainted with; he proceeds smoothly in a way that has become pleasant and delightful. None start with greater advantages, nor usually persevere with more vigorous constancy, than those who *remember their Creator in the days of their youth*. They sacrifice the first fruits of their time to God and to religion before corrupt affections have placed a bias upon their inclinations, and before a series of vices has depraved and largely put to sleep the natural instincts of good and evil.

II. PREPARED by such excellent cultivation in the *Jewish* religion, God was pleased to transplant him into a better soil. *St. Paul*, in pursuing his commission to preach the Gospel to the *Gentiles*, had come as far as *Antioch*...

*Antioch* in *Pisidia*, then to *Iconium*, and so to *Lystra*, where the miraculous cure of a paralyzed cripple made way for the acceptance of the Christian doctrine.
<margin>a St. Simeon Metaphrastes, Life of St. Timothy, in Laurentius Surius, Jan. 24, section 11, page 411.</margin>
Among others converted there, we are $^a$ told, were *St. Timothy’s* parents, who courteously treated and entertained the Apostle at their house, wholly resigning their son to his care and guidance. About two years later, during his review of these recent church plantings, Paul came again to *Lystra*, 
<margin>Acts 16:1, 2, 3.</margin>
where he chose *Timothy*—who was recommended to him by the universal testimony of the Christians in that area—to be an *Evangelist* <note>original: "Evangelist"; here meaning a traveling missionary assistant to the Apostles</note>, serving as his assistant and traveling companion. Paul wanted someone always with him whom he could entrust with important matters and dispatch for any extraordinary business or urgent need of the Church. 

Indeed, *Timothy* was not circumcised, for since this was a part of paternal authority, it did not lie within his mother's power to perform. This was well known to all the *Jews*, and *St. Paul* knew this would be a significant prejudice against Timothy’s ministry wherever he went. Because the *Jews* were extremely zealous for circumcision, they would not patiently endure any man preaching to them—or even speaking with them—who was himself uncircumcised. To remove that obstacle, Paul had him circumcised, becoming in lawful matters *all things to all men, that he might gain the more*. 

<margin>b Homily 34 on the Acts of the Apostles, page 684.</margin>
*St. Chrysostom* says $^b$ the wisdom and prudence of *St. Paul* was admirable in this design: "He circumcised him, so that he might take away circumcision" <note>original Greek: Περιέτεμεν, ἵνα περιτομὴν καθέλῃ</note>. By this, he meant that Timothy would be more acceptable to the *Jews* and, by that means, better able to correct their mistaken opinion regarding the necessity of those legal rites. At other times, we find Paul sharply arguing against circumcision when it was treated as a justification for following *Mosaic* institutions, which he saw as effectively undermining the great goals of Christianity. 

In this instance, he did not contradict his own doctrine or practice an unauthorized conformity with the *Jews*. Rather, it was
<margin>c Stromata (Miscellanies), book 7, page 730.</margin>
only (as $^c$ *Clement* of *Alexandria* observes regarding this passage) a prudent concession to the current mood of the *Jews*. Paul was unwilling to offend them or cause them to completely reject the faith by too suddenly and violently tearing them away from the circumcision of the flesh, as he hoped to bring them over to the "circumcision of the heart." Therefore, someone who accommodates himself for the salvation of another cannot be charged with dissimulation or hypocrisy. He does this purely for the benefit of others—something he would not do for any other reason or because of the rites themselves. This is "the part of a wise and kind instructor, who is a true lover of God and the souls of men" <note>original Greek: τοῦ φιλανθρώπου & φιλοθέου παιδαγωγοῦ</note>.

III. Once *ST. PAUL* was equipped with such a suitable companion, they set forward in their evangelical progress. Having passed through *Phrygia* and *Galatia*, they came down to *Troas*. From there they set sail for *Samothrace*, then to *Neapolis*, and then to *Philippi*, the capital of that part of *Macedonia*. After being mistreated by the magistrates and people there, they departed for *Thessalonica*, where the fury and malice of the *Jews* forced them to flee to *Berea*. Here they met people of a more generous and noble character who were ready to embrace the Christian doctrine, but only after they had first compared it with the predictions the Prophets had made concerning the *Messiah*. Yet even here they could not escape the relentless spirit of the *Jews*, so the Christians were forced to privately escort *St. Paul* to *Athens*, while *Silas* and *Timothy*

...who were not so much the immediate objects of their spite and cruelty, stayed behind to instruct and confirm the converts of that place. Whether they came to him during his stay at *Athens* is uncertain; *St. Luke* takes no further notice of them until they came to him at *Corinth*, his next stop. Upon their arrival there (if it was not earlier at *Athens*), *St. Paul* dispatched *Timothy* to *Thessalonica* to inquire into the state of Christianity in that city and to confirm them in the belief and profession of the Gospel. Paul seems to have had a particular kindness for that church; since his last visit there, he had resolved more than once to return to them, but the great Enemy of Souls <note>meaning Satan</note> had repeatedly thrown some hindrance <note>original: "rub"</note> in his way.

1 Thessalonians 3:6, 7, and following.
</margin>
IV. FROM *Thessalonica*, *Timothy* returned with the welcome news of their firmness and constancy despite the persecutions they endured, their mutual charity to each other, and their particular affection for *St. Paul*. This news pleased the good man infinitely, as certainly nothing can provide greater joy and satisfaction to a faithful guide of souls than to behold the welfare and prosperity of his people. Nor did his care for them end here; he immediately wrote his first Epistle to them to encourage them in their sufferings. He urged them not to desert the Christian religion just because the Cross <note>symbolizing suffering and persecution</note> accompanied it, but rather to adorn their Christian profession by living a life consistent with its holy designs and precepts. In the opening of this Epistle, he included not only his own name but also those of *Silas* and *Timothy*, partly to give greater honor to his fellow-workers, and partly so that their united authority and agreement might have a stronger influence and force upon the readers. He did the same in a *second* Epistle, which he sent to them not long after to make up for his lack of personal presence—something he had given them hope for in his previous letter and which he himself seemed to desire so passionately. They remained at *Corinth* for at least eighteen months when *St. Paul* resolved to travel to *Jerusalem*. He did not stay there long but went to *Antioch*. After traveling through the regions of *Galatia* and *Phrygia* to establish the Christianity recently planted in those parts, he came to *Ephesus*. Although he met with great opposition there, he preached with even greater success. He became so completely occupied with the concerns of that city that, although he had intended to go into *Macedonia* himself, he was forced to send *Timothy* and *Erastus* in his place. Having completed their mission, they returned to *Ephesus* to assist him in promoting the affairs of religion in that city.

V. AFTER ST. PAUL had resided at *Ephesus* and the surrounding areas for three years, he determined to take his leave and depart for *Macedonia*. He was the *first Bishop* (says <sup>a</sup> *Eusebius*) of the province or diocese of *Ephesus*. He was the "first to act as Bishop of Ephesus" <note>original Greek: πρῶτος Ἐφέσου Ἐπισκοπῆσαι</note>, says the <sup>b</sup> author in *Photius*. In the <sup>d</sup> *Apostolical Constitutions*, he is explicitly said to have been ordained Bishop of Ephesus by *St. Paul*. VI. **THIS** extraordinary and miraculous way of choosing bishops and ecclesiastical officers, besides other advantages, created <note>original: "begat"</note> a great reverence and respect <note>original: "veneration"</note> for the governors of the church. They were looked upon as God’s choice, bearing the immediate mark <note>original: "character"</note> of Heaven upon them. This method seemed especially necessary for *St. Timothy* more than others, to protect him from the contempt that his youth might otherwise have invited. That he was quite young at that time is evident from *St. Paul’s* counsel to him to conduct <note>original: "demean"</note> himself so that *no man might despise his youth*. The governors of the church in those days were <margin>Elders <note>original: Πρεσβύτεροι</note></margin>, in terms of their age as well as their office. Indeed, they were called *Elders* because those admitted into the orders of the church were usually persons of a significant age. *Timothy* had not yet reached this age. And yet the word <margin>youth <note>original: νεότης</note></margin>, *youth*, allows for a broader meaning than we usually give it in ordinary speech. ᵍ *Cicero* tells us of himself that he was <term>adolescentulus</term> <note>original Latin: a very young man or youth</note>, a mere youth, when he pleaded *Roscius*'s cause; yet ʰ *Aulus Gellius* proves him to have been no less than 27 years old at that time. *Alexander*, the son of *Aristobulus*, is called ⁱ <margin>a youth <note>original: νεανίσκος</note></margin>, *a youth*, at the time of his death, even though he was over thirty. *Hiero* in ᵏ *Polybius* is styled <margin>a very young man <note>original: κομιδῆ νέος</note></margin>, *a very young man*, whom ᵏ *Casaubon* proves to have been 35 years of age. The same historian, speaking of *Titus Flamininus* <note>original: "T. Flaminius"</note> making war upon *Philip* of *Macedon*, says he was <margin>a very young man <note>original: νέος κομιδῆ</note></margin>, *a very young man*, for he was not over thirty years old. As *Casaubon* observes, it was the custom of both *Greek* and *Latin* writers to extend the *juventus*, or youthful age, from the thirtieth until the fortieth year of a man's life.

To which we may add what *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch legal scholar and theologian.</note> observes: that the Greek word for youth <note>original: "νεότης"</note>, answering to the Hebrew word for a young man <note>original: "בחור" (Bachur)</note>, denotes the military age—that is, all the active and mature part of a man’s life that is opposed to old age. <margin>Acts 20:2, 3, etc.</margin>VII. St. *TIMOTHY*, having been thus settled at *Ephesus*, did nonetheless accompany St. *Paul* for some part of his journey into *Greece*. At the very least, he went to him there regarding some urgent affairs of the Church and then returned to his charge. Not long after this, St. *Paul* wrote his *First Epistle* to him to encourage him in his duty and to direct him how to behave himself in that eminent position in which he had placed him. Because the success of the ministry depends in large measure upon the people employed in it, Paul gives him more particular rules on how to proceed in this matter, and how those people ought to be qualified whom he admitted to that honorable and important office. As *Nicephorus* <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, a 14th-century church historian.</note> speaks, <margin>* Ecclesiastical History, book 2, chapter 34, page 189.</margin>"vividly detailing, as in a model, the life and teaching of a church leader" <note>original: "ὡς ἐν τύπῳ ⛬ ἱεραρχικὸν βίον & λόγον ἀναζωγύρως διεξιὼν"</note>. In that Epistle, he excellently represents, as if in a brief sketch, the life and conduct of the sacred governors of the Church, describing the tempers and manners of those who are appointed to be the guides and ministers of religion. He also knew well that crafty teachers and false apostles were creeping into the Church; he remarks upon their principles and practices, warning Timothy to beware of them and to stand continually on his guard against them. The holy man followed his instructions and was, no doubt, faithful to his trust, which he managed with all care and diligence. About six years later, St. *Paul*, being then a prisoner at *Rome*, wrote a *Second Epistle* to him <margin>Apostolic Antiquities, Life of St. Paul, Section 7, number 5; 2 Timothy 4:9.</margin>(for we have shown elsewhere that this Epistle was written during his first arrival in *Rome*) to excite him to great care and fidelity in his business, and in undermining the false and subtle insinuations of deceivers. In it, he orders *Timothy* to come to him with all speed to *Rome*. Timothy accordingly came and joined with Paul in several Epistles written from there to the *Philippians*, *Colossians*, and to *Philemon*, as his name at the beginning of those Epistles clearly declares. During his stay at *Rome*, he was for some reason cast into prison, and then released <margin>Hebrews 13:23, 24.</margin>and set at liberty about the time of St. *Paul’s* enlargement <note>original: "enlargement"; meaning release from confinement.</note>, as Paul clearly suggests at the close of his Epistle to the *Hebrews*. After this, he came back to *Ephesus*, nor is it probable that he ever moved from there again until his translation into Heaven. Among their many idolatrous festivals, they had one called *Katagogion* <note>original: "ΚΑΤΑΓΩΓΙΟΝ"; a festival involving the "bringing down" of images or a homecoming celebration.</note>, which was celebrated in this manner: dressing themselves in grotesque <note>original: "antic"</note> costumes and covering their faces with ugly masks <note>original: "Vizors"</note> so that they might not be recognized, they carried clubs in their hands and moved idols in a wild and frantic manner through the most prominent places of the city, singing certain songs and verses to them. <margin>
a. On the Martyrdom: *Timothy the Apostle according to Photius, Code 254, columns 1401, 1404. Commentary on St. Timothy by Symeon Metaphrastes in Surius, January 24, numbers 9, 10. This cursed and detestable custom gave just offense to all pious and good men, especially *St. Timothy*, whose spirit was grieved to see God so openly dishonored. He saw human nature sunk into such a deep degeneracy and so arbitrarily driven to the most savage barbarities by the great murderer of souls <note>A reference to the Devil.</note>. The good man often endeavored to reclaim them by gentle and mild entreaties; but alas, gentle medicine <note>original: "Physic"</note> works little upon a stubborn constitution. When that would not do, he came out to them in the middle of the street during one of these fatal ceremonies and reproved them with necessary sharpness and severity. 

But cruelty and licentiousness are too headstrong to tolerate opposition. Impatient at being controlled in their wild extravagances, they fell upon him with their clubs, beat and dragged him up and down, and then left him for dead. Some Christians, finding him still breathing, took him up and lodged him outside the gate of the city, where he expired three days later. He suffered martyrdom on the 30th day of the fourth month according to the *Asian* computation, or on the 22nd of *January* by the *Roman* account (the date the *Greek* Church celebrates his memory), or the 24th according to the *Latin* Church. This happened (as some believe) in the time of the Emperor *Nerva*, while others more probably refer it to the reign of *Domitian*, as it occurred before *St. John’s* return from his banishment on *Patmos*, which was about the beginning of *Nerva's* reign. 

After he died, the Christians of *Ephesus* took his body and decently buried it in a place called *Pion*—or *Piron* according to *Isidore*, who adds that it was a mountain. There it rested securely for several ages until *Constantine* the Great (or as others say, his son *Constantius*) caused it to be translated <note>The formal ritual of moving a saint's relics from one location to another.</note> to *Constantinople*. It was laid to rest together with the remains of *St. Andrew* and *St. Luke* in the great Church of the Holy Apostles, erected by *Constantine*.

X. These excellent virtues infinitely endeared him to *St. Paul*, who seems to have had a very passionate kindness for him, never mentioning him without great tenderness and titles of reverence and respect. Sometimes he styles him his *son*, his *brother*, or his *fellow-laborer*: *Timothy our brother, and Minister of God, and our fellow-laborer in the Gospel of Christ*. Sometimes he adds expressions of particular affection and honorable regard: *Timothy, my dearly beloved son*; and *Timothy, who is my beloved son, and faithful in the Lord*. To the Church at *Philippi* he wrote even more expressly: *I trust to send Timothy shortly to you, for I have no man like-minded* (<term>isopsychon</term> <note>original: "ἰσόψυχον"; meaning "of equal soul" or "of the same mind"</note>, equally dear to me as myself) *who will naturally care for your state. <margin>1 Corinthians 16:10, 11.</margin>
easily affected by harsh and unkind impressions, Paul entered a particular caution on his behalf with the Church of *Corinth*: *If Timothy comes, see that he may be with you without fear, for he works the work of the Lord, as I also do. Let no man therefore despise him, but conduct him forth in peace, that he may come unto me.* These are instances of great care and tenderness, which plainly suggest that *Timothy* was an extraordinary person.
<margin>b. Homily 1 on 2 Timothy, page 1626.</margin>
*Chrysostom* thinks that Paul merely calling him his "dearly beloved son" is a sufficient argument for Timothy’s virtue. For such affection, not being based on biological nature, can flow from nothing but virtue and goodness—the lovely and essential ornaments of a divine and holy soul. We love our children not only because they are witty, handsome, kind, or dutiful, but because they are ours, and very often for no other reason; nor can we do otherwise as long as we are subject to the impressions and laws of nature. However, true goodness and virtue have no other arts but their own naked worth and beauty to recommend them, nor can they challenge regard and veneration from us by any other argument.

This is a story which, as I cannot disprove it, so I am not overly eager to believe; nor is it important enough for my purpose to investigate it more particularly.

I. <image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' within a square frame featuring floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc><margin>\* Homily 1 on Titus, page 1693.</margin> The ancient writers of the church make little mention of this holy man; who he was and where he came from is not known, except by uncertain probabilities. <margin>Acts 18:7.</margin> St. Chrysostom conjectures <note>original: "conjectures": guesses based on incomplete information</note> him to have been born at Corinth, for no other reason than because in some ancient copies (as is still found in several manuscripts today) mention is made of St. Paul going into the house of one [Titus] <margin>Florus, Roman History, book 3, chapter 7, page 65.</margin> named Justus, a worshiper of God, while at Corinth. Writers of later ages generally claim he was born in Crete—better known by the modern name of Candia. It is a noble island (as the historian <note>referring to Lucius Annaeus Florus</note> calls it, adding that the only reason the Romans went to war there was their desire to conquer such a fine country) in the Aegean Sea. In ancient times, it was no more famous for being the birthplace of Jupiter (the sovereign of the pagan gods) and for the Labyrinth of Daedalus <note>original: "Dædalean Labyrinth"</note> said to be located there, than it has been in recent times for being the site of long wars between the Ottoman <note>original: "Turkish"</note> Emperor and the Republic <note>original: "State"</note> of Venice. History <note>original: "Antiquity"</note> has not certainly passed down to us any specific details about his parents. # The Life of ST. TITUS.

---

He was inspired again to hear the voice. A year later, he was again commanded in a vision to study the volume of the Jewish Law. He opened the book and cast his eye upon the words of the prophet:
<margin>Isaiah 41:1</margin>
> *Keep silence before me, O Islands, and let the people renew their strength: let them come near, let them speak: let us come near together to judgment, etc.*

Whereupon his uncle, who was at that time the Proconsul <note>A provincial governor in the Roman Republic and Empire.</note> of Crete, having heard the fame of our Lord’s miracles in Judea, sent him to Jerusalem. He stayed there until Christ’s ascension, when he was converted by that famous sermon of St. Peter, through which he gained three thousand souls at once. I cannot guarantee the truth of this story, though it is claimed to be derived from the *Acts* said to have been written by Zenas the Lawyer (mentioned by St. Paul). I confess that without better evidence, I dare not encourage the reader to place too much trust in it. Let us, therefore, move on to something more certain and unquestionable.

III. Having arrived in Judea or the surrounding areas, and being convinced of the truth and divinity of the Christian faith, he became St. Paul’s convert and disciple, though we do not find when or where he was converted. It is likely either that he followed St. Paul as a companion and assistant, or that he joined the Church of Antioch. It was there that the famous controversy arose concerning circumcision and the Mosaic laws <note>The religious laws and rituals established by Moses.</note>, and whether they were as necessary to observe as the belief and practice of Christianity.
<margin>Acts 15:1, 2, etc.</margin>
The church determined that *Paul and Barnabas, and certain others of them, should go up to Jerusalem to the Apostles and Elders about this question.*
<margin>a Codex Bezae MS on Acts 15:2. <note>original: "Cod. Bezæ MS. ad Act. 15. 2."</note></margin>
In fact, a very ancient manuscript <gloss>a</gloss> adds that when Paul earnestly persuaded them to remain in the doctrine they had been taught, those very Jewish zealots who had come down to Antioch and first caused the doubt were the ones who requested that Paul, Barnabas, and some others go and consult with the Apostles and Elders at Jerusalem and abide by their judgment and determination of the case. Among those sent on this Gospel embassy was our St. Titus,
<margin>Galatians 1:2, etc.</margin>
whom St. Paul (encouraged to take this journey by a particular revelation) was willing to take along with him. No sooner had they come to Jerusalem than spies were at hand. Some zealous Jews, pretending to be Christian converts, worked their way into St. Paul’s company and acquaintance, narrowly observing what liberties he took regarding legal rituals so they might find an accusation against him. They charged him with preaching to and associating with the Gentiles <note>Non-Jewish people.</note>, noting that at this very time, Titus—an uncircumcised Greek—was his close companion. They claimed this was a scandal that could only be avoided by circumcising him, so that it might appear Paul had no intention of undermining the rites and customs of the Law. St. Paul (who knew when to give ground and when to maintain his position) would by no means consent to this. Although at another time he was willing to circumcise Timothy (a Jew on his mother's side) to please the Jews for their own education and to have a better chance to win them over, he refused here to circumcise Titus, a Gentile. He did this so he would not seem to betray the freedoms of the Gospel, harden the Jews in their unreasonable and deep-seated <note>original: "inveterate"</note> prejudices against the non-Christians <note>original: "Heathens"</note>, or give the Gentiles a just reason to feel offended or discouraged and drive them further away from Christianity. Accordingly, he resisted their demands with unbreakable resolution, and his practice in this matter was immediately justified by the formal decision <note>original: "decretory Sentence"</note> of the Council called to settle this matter.

I. Ancient Church writers mention little of this holy man; his identity and origins are known only through uncertain probabilities. <sup>a</sup> St. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople and Church Father.</note> suggests that he was born in Corinth, for no other reason than that in some ancient copies of the Bible (as is still seen in several manuscripts today), mention is made of St. Paul visiting the house of one [Titus] named Justus, a worshiper of God, while in Corinth. # The Life of ST. TITUS.

He was eager once more to hear the voice. A year later, he was again commanded in a vision to study the scrolls of the Jewish Law. He opened the book and his eyes fell upon the words of the Prophet:

<margin>Isaiah 41:1</margin>
> "Listen in silence before me, you islands, and let the people renew their strength; let them come near, and let them speak; let us come together for judgment." 

Whereupon his uncle, who was the Proconsul <note>original: Proconsul; a governor of a Roman province.</note> of Crete at the time, having heard the reports of our Lord’s miracles in Judea, sent him to Jerusalem. He remained there until Christ’s ascension, when he was converted by the famous sermon of St. Peter, which won three thousand souls at once. I cannot guarantee the truth of this story, though it is claimed to be derived from the *Acts* said to have been written by *Zenas the Lawyer*, mentioned by St. Paul. This is an authority that, I confess, I dare not encourage the reader to rely on too heavily without better evidence. Let us therefore turn to something more certain and unquestionable.

<margin>
Acts 15:1, 2.
ª Manuscript of the Codex Bezae <note>original: Cod. Beze MS; an important 5th-century manuscript of the New Testament containing a unique version of the text of Acts.</note> regarding Acts 15:2.
Galatians 1, 2, etc.
</margin>
III. Having arrived in Judea or the surrounding areas and become convinced of the truth and divinity of the Christian faith, he became St. Paul’s convert and disciple, though we do not know exactly when or where he was converted. It is likely either that he followed St. Paul as a companion and assistant, or that he joined the Church at Antioch. It was there that the famous controversy arose concerning circumcision and the Mosaic Institutions <note>The religious laws and rituals established by Moses.</note>, which some argued were just as necessary to observe as the belief and practice of Christianity. They decided that *Paul, Barnabas, and certain others of them should go up to Jerusalem to the Apostles and Elders about this question.* Furthermore, a very ancient manuscript adds that when Paul earnestly persuaded them to remain in the doctrine they had been taught, those very Jewish zealots who had come down to Antioch and first started the argument *themselves requested Paul, Barnabas, and some others to go and consult with the Apostles and Elders at Jerusalem, and to abide by their judgment and decision on the case.*

In the group sent on this mission for the Gospel was our St. Titus, whom St. Paul (encouraged to take this journey by a specific revelation) was willing to take along with him. No sooner had they arrived in Jerusalem than spies were at hand—certain zealous Jews pretending to be Christian converts—who worked their way into St. Paul's company and acquaintance. They closely watched how much liberty he took regarding the religious laws so that they might find grounds for an accusation against him. They charged him with preaching to and associating with the Gentiles, and pointed out that at that very time Titus, an uncircumcised Greek, was his close companion. This was a scandal that could only be avoided by circumcising him, which would show that Paul had no intention of undermining the rites and customs of the Law. 

St. Paul (who knew when to yield and when to stand his ground) would by no means consent to this. Although at another time he was willing to circumcise Timothy—who was Jewish on his mother’s side—to please the Jews for their own spiritual growth and to better win them over, he refused to circumcise Titus, a Gentile. He did this so that he would not seem to betray the freedom of the Gospel, harden the Jews in their unreasonable and deep-seated prejudices against the Heathens <note>Non-Jewish people.</note>, or give the Gentiles a just reason for offense and discouragement, which might cause them to turn away from Christianity. Accordingly, he resisted their pressure with unshakable resolution, and his actions were immediately justified by the final ruling of the Council summoned to decide this matter.

III. The business for which they were sent being settled in the Synod <note>The Council of Jerusalem.</note>, he undoubtedly returned with St. *Paul* to *Antioch*. From there, he accompanied him in his travels until, after visiting the Churches of *Syria* and *Cilicia*, they set sail for *Crete*. I believe, along with ^a^ *Capellus*, that this period is the most likely time for their journey to that island. I find this more probable than the dates suggested by ^b^ *Baronius* and others, who place it during St. *Paul's* journey from *Macedonia* into *Greece* (which Baronius assumes was a sea voyage through the *Cyclades* islands in the *Aegean* Sea). I also disagree with ^c^ *Grotius*, who refers it to Paul's later voyage to *Rome*. Grotius bases his theory on a double mistake: first, that St. *Paul* and his company stopped and stayed at *Crete* on that trip, when the text only says they sailed *under it* and passed *by it*; and second, that *Titus* was even in the company at that time, of which there is no evidence or mention in the history. 

Sailing, therefore, from some port in *Cilicia*, they arrived at *Crete*. There, St. *Paul* diligently set himself to preach and spread the Christian Faith. He delighted, as much as possible, in being the first messenger of the joyful news of the Gospel in every place he visited, refusing to plant in *another man’s territory* or build upon *foundations already laid by others*. However, because the care of other Churches called for his attention, he could not stay long enough to see Christianity reach full maturity and perfection there. Consequently, he appointed *Titus* as Bishop of that island, so that he might nurture that infant Church, oversee its growth and prosperity, and manage its government and administration.

IV. This is not merely an interpretation made up by ancient writers; it seems clearly based on St. *Paul's* own words. He tells *Titus*, *For this reason I left you in Crete, that you should set in order the things that are lacking, and ordain elders in every city, as I had commanded you*. This means: "I appointed you governor of that Church, so that you might organize and manage its affairs according to the rules and directions I gave you." *Ordain Elders*] he means Bishops (says ^l^ *Chrysostom*), as I have often explained elsewhere. *Elders in every city*] Paul was not willing (as Chrysostom adds) for the entire administration of such a large island to be managed by one person. Instead, he wanted every city to have its own governor to oversee and care for it. In this way, the burden would be lighter by being shared among many, and the people would be served with greater diligence. Indeed, *Crete* was famous for having more cities than any other island in the world; for this reason, it was called <term>Hecatompolis</term> <note>From the Greek 'hekaton' (hundred) and 'polis' (city), meaning "The Island of a Hundred Cities."</note> in ancient times. V. For several years, *St. Titus* continued his duties in *Crete* until he received a summons from *St. Paul*, who was then preparing to leave *Ephesus*. The Apostle had asked *Apollos* to accompany *Timothy* and others whom he had sent to *Corinth*. However, *Apollos* chose instead to go to *Crete*. By him and *Zenas*, Paul wrote an Epistle <note>A formal letter; specifically the biblical Book of Titus.</note> to *Titus* to encourage him to be active and vigilant, and to teach him how to conduct himself in the position where Paul had placed him. Indeed, he needed all the advice *St. Paul* could provide, as he had a very unruly and difficult group of people to manage. The country itself was no more fruitful and abundant than the people's behavior was corrupt and immoral. <margin>Titus 1:12.</margin> *St. Paul* reminded *Titus* of the bad reputation one of their own poets (who certainly knew them best) had given them:

They were so famous for lying that "to act like a Cretan" <note>original: Κρητίζειν</note> and "to act like a Cretan against a Cretan" <note>original: Κρητίζειν πρὸς Κρῆτα</note> became proverbs meaning "to lie like a Cretan" and "to out-cheat a cheater." ## VI.

In the Epistle itself, the main body consists of rules and directions for the various ranks and relationships of men. Because spiritual and church affairs are more significant than all others, he first instructs Titus on the qualifications of those he should appoint to be Bishops and Guides of Souls. They must be holy and harmless, innocent and inoffensive—men who had not divorced their first wife to marry a second <note>This refers to the biblical requirement that a bishop be the "husband of one wife."</note>, whose children were sober, orderly, and raised in the Christian faith. They must be approachable <note>original: "easie and treatable"</note>, mild-mannered, and not prone to anger. They must be free from a love of wine and any desire for riches through dishonest <note>original: "sordid"</note> and greedy designs. They should be kind and hospitable, lovers of goodness and good men, modest and prudent, just and honest, strict and temperate. They must be firm and constant in owning and defending the Christian doctrines that have been delivered to them, so that they may be able both to persuade and comfort others, and mightily convince those who resist and oppose the truth.

It was certainly not without great reason that the Apostle required the guides and governors of the Church to be thus able to refute opponents <note>original: "gainsayers"</note>. For whatever authors report of *Crete*—that it bred no serpents or venomous creatures—it is certain that the poison of error and heresy had crept in there along with the acceptance of

<margin>
Titus 1:10.
Verse 14.
Titus 3:9.
</margin>

Christianity. There were many unruly and vain talkers, especially those of the "Circumcision" <note>Jewish converts to Christianity who maintained that followers of Jesus must still follow Jewish Law.</note>, who endeavored to corrupt the doctrine of the Gospel with Jewish fables, groundless and unauthorized traditions, mystical and Cabalistic <note>Referring to the Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism.</note> explanations, and foolish questions and genealogies. For the Jews, borrowing their notions from the schools of *Plato*, had fallen into a habit of deriving things from an imaginary generation: first *Binah* or "Understanding," then *Achmoth* or *Cochmah* "Wisdom," and so on until they came to *Milcah* "the Kingdom," and *Shekinah* or "the Divine Presence." This was much the same way the poets of old traced the family trees <note>original: "pedigrees"</note> of their gods. They first had their several conjunctions <note>original Greek: Συζυγίαι—the coupling and mixing of things together</note>, and from there proceeded their genealogies <note>original Greek: γενεαλογίαι—their generations</note>. Out of Chaos came *Erebus* <note>A personification of darkness.</note> and the dark Night; their union produced the *Ether* and the Day. From there, <sup>a</sup> *Hesiod* proceeds to explain the whole pagan theology concerning the origin of their gods.

<margin>

## VII.

In imitation of all this, and from a mixture of it all, the *Valentinians*, *Basilidians*, and the rest of the *Gnostic* <note>Early Christian heretics who claimed to possess secret, "higher" knowledge.</note> crowd formed the senseless and unintelligible systems of their "Fullness" <note>original Greek: Πλήρωμα (Pleroma)</note> and thirty *Aeons* <note>Divine beings or "ages" in Gnostic mythology.</note>, divided into three classes of conjunctions. In the first were four couples: *Profundity* and *Silence*, *Mind* and *Truth*, the *Word* and *Life*, and *Man* and the *Church*. In the second were five, namely: *Profound* and *Mixture*, *Unaging* <note>original: "Ageratus"</note> and *Union*, and so forth. In the third were six: the *Advocate* <note>original: "Paraclete"</note> and *Faith*, *Paternal* <note>original: "Patricos"</note> and *Hope*, and so forth. Of all this, if anyone desires to know more, they may find enough in the works of *Irenaeus*, *Tertullian*, and *Epiphanius* to this purpose—if they can understand it.

VIII. After St. Paul departed from Ephesus, he came to Troas. Although he had a good opportunity to preach the Gospel offered to him there, yet (as he himself tells us) he had no rest in his spirit because he did not find his brother Titus. Paul had been impatiently expecting Titus to bring him an account of the state of the Church at Corinth. Whether Titus had already been with Paul and was sent on this errand, or had been commanded by him to stop at Corinth on his way from Crete, is not known. Not meeting him there, Paul went on to Macedonia, where at length Titus arrived. He comforted Paul in the midst of all his other sorrows and difficulties with the joyful news of the happy condition of the Church at Corinth. He reported how readily they had reformed those failings <note>original: "miscarriages"</note> which Paul had charged them with in his first Epistle. This fully proved the great character Paul had given of them to Titus, and they provided significant evidence of it in the kind and welcoming entertainment Titus found among them. Soon after, St. Paul—having received the collections from the Macedonian Churches for the poor <note>original: "indigent"</note> Christians at Jerusalem—sent Titus and St. Luke back to Corinth. He sent them to encourage their charity and prepare their contributions before his own arrival there, and through them, he wrote his second Epistle to that Church.

IX. TITUS faithfully carried out his mission to the Church of Corinth and, having finished the services for which he was sent, we may suppose he returned back to Crete. We do not hear any further news of him until St. Paul's imprisonment at Rome. Titus went there (if my <gloss>a</gloss> author speaks truly) about two years after Paul and stayed with him until his martyrdom. He was reportedly present at the execution and, together with St. Luke, committed Paul to his grave. This is an account which I confess I am less inclined to believe, because I am assured by St. Paul himself that before his death, Titus had left him and gone into Dalmatia—a province of Illyricum—to plant the "Gospel of Peace" among that fierce and warlike nation, probably visiting there on his way back to Crete. This is the last notice we find of him in the Holy Scriptures, and the records of the Church from that point on do not furnish us with any certain records or remarks <note>original: "Memoirs or Remarques"</note> concerning him.

Indeed, if the story some people tell were true, one thing alone would be enough to make him memorable to posterity: I mean his converting Pliny the Younger, that learned and eloquent man who was Proconsul of Bithynia and an intimate close advisor <note>original: "Privy Counsellor"</note> to the Emperor Trajan. For they tell us <gloss>b</gloss> that while returning from his province in Bithynia, Pliny landed in Crete, where the Emperor had commanded him to build a temple to Jupiter. This was done, but no sooner was it finished than St. Titus cursed it, and it immediately tumbled to the ground. The man, as you may guess, was strangely troubled and came with tears to the holy man to request his counsel. Titus advised him to begin the building again in the name of the God of the Christians, and it would not fail to prosper. He did so, and having finished it, he was baptized along with his son. Furthermore, some—to make the story "perfect"—add that he suffered martyrdom for the Faith at Novocomum, a city of Insubria in Italy, where he was born. I presume the reader will not expect me to take the pains to disprove this story, which is sufficiently improbable in itself, and which I view as being made of the same material <note>original: "Metal"</note> and coined in the same...

# The Life of ST. DIONYSIUS.

I.
<image-desc>Decorative initial 'S' depicting a landscape with hills, plants, and small buildings, possibly a stylized monastery or hermitage.</image-desc>
DIONYSIUS was born at Athens, the "Eye of Greece," and the fountain of learning and culture <note>original: "Humanity"</note>. It was the only place that, without competition, had for so many ages maintained an undisputed reputation for arts and sciences. There was a universal gathering of people from all parts of the world to Athens to perfect themselves in the more refined and useful studies. Though we find nothing particularly concerning his parents, we may safely conclude them to have been people of noble status, or at least of a higher rank than common, seeing that none were admitted to be judges of the Areopagus <margin>a *Isocrates, Orat. Areopag. p. 147.* *See also Maximus, Prologue to the Works of St. Dionysius, Preface, p. 34.*</margin> (as one who knew very well informs us) <term>unless they were nobly born, and had gained a good reputation for great virtue and moderation in their lives</term> <note>original: "Πλὺν οἱ καλῶς γεγόνοτες, ὃ πολλῶ ἀρετῶ ἐ ῷωφροσύνω ὃν τῇ βίω ἐυδοκίμησι"</note>. Being born in the very midst of arts and civility, his education could not have been anything but learned and honorable, especially considering the advantages of his birth and fortune. Accordingly, he was <gloss>b</gloss> <margin>b *Suidas, under the word "Stoud," p. 744.*</margin> instructed in all the learned sciences of Greece, wherein he made such vast improvements that he easily surpassed any of his time. There was scarcely any sect or school of philosophy then in fashion which he had not considered and tested. It does not indeed appear to which of them he particularly devoted and applied himself; those who suppose him to have joined the school of *Plato* do so, I believe, for no other reason than because the doctrine contained in the books that bear his name seems so closely related to the principles of that noble sect.

II. BUT it was not a domestic education, nor all the advantages which *Athens* could afford, that could satisfy the vast potential of his mind. He therefore resolved to refine and improve himself through foreign travel. He studied with their philosophers and wise men so that he might perfect himself in the study of **mathematics** and the more mysterious and obscure parts of learning. Egypt had in all ages been looked upon as the primary school not only of astrology, but of the more deep and uncommon speculations of theology. The great masters of wisdom and divinity among the non-Christians <note>original: "Gentiles"</note> never thought they had learned enough until they had crowned their studies by conversing with the Egyptian sages. For this reason, it was frequented by Orpheus, Homer, Solon, and Thales, as well as by Pythagoras and Plato—and who not? Indeed, regarding Pythagoras, <margin>a</margin> Clement of Alexandria reports that he even allowed himself to be circumcised so that he might be admitted into the secret shrines <note>original: "eis ta adyta"</note>—to the concealed rites and notions of their religion—and become acquainted with their secret and mystical philosophy. The place Dionysius settled in was Heliopolis, a city between Coptos and Alexandria, where the Egyptian priests mostly resided. It was a place excellently suited for the contemplation of the heavenly bodies and the study of philosophy and astronomy. There, <margin>b</margin> Strabo (who lived around this same time) tells us he was shown the dwellings of the priests and the apartments of Plato and Eudoxus, who lived there for thirteen years. Furthermore, a very ancient <margin>c</margin> historian assures us that Abraham himself lived there and taught the Egyptian priests astronomy and other branches of learning.

III. Dionysius no doubt applied himself to his studies in this place, during which stay one memorable event is reported. The Son of God about this time was delivered up at Jerusalem to a painful and shameful death by the hands of violence and injustice. At that moment the Sun, as if ashamed to behold such great wickedness, hid its head and put on mourning to attend the funeral of its Maker. This eclipse was contrary to all the known rules and laws of nature, happening during a Full Moon, when the Moon is at its greatest distance from the Sun and consequently cannot be in conjunction with it. The Moon moved itself under the Sun from its eastern <note>original: "Oriental"</note> to its western <note>original: "Occidental"</note> point, and then back again by a reverse <note>original: "retrograde"</note> motion, causing a strange loss of light for three hours together. That there was such a wonderful and supernatural darkness over all the Earth for three hours at the time of our Savior's suffering, by which the Sun was darkened, is unanimously attested by the Gospel historians. It is mentioned not only by them, but <margin>d</margin> Phlegon of Tralles (who was once a servant to the Emperor Trajan) speaks of an eclipse of the Sun that happened about that time, "the greatest of any that had been ever known" <note>original: "Megistē tōn egnōsmenōn proteron"</note>, by which the day was turned into night and the stars appeared at noon. An earthquake also accompanied it, by which many houses at Nicaea in Bithynia were overturned. Apollophanes, beholding this strange eclipse, cried out to Dionysius that these were changes and revolutions of some great importance, to whom the other replied, **"Either God is suffering, or at least he feels sympathy and shares the suffering of the one who is."** I confess these passages are not to be found in the most ancient writers of the Church, but that should not be a fair objection when we consider how little care was then taken to record things in writing, and how a great many of those few ancient records that were written were quickly lost, as Eusebius frequently complains. This is not to mention that a great many writings might have—and did—escape his notice. # The Life of St. DIONYSIUS.

He himself had met with several writings of the ancient authors, of which there is no trace in *Eusebius* <note>original: "Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian known as the 'Father of Church History'."</note>. But however that may be, it does not argue against the facts. Many things, though never formally recorded, are preserved in their substance by constant tradition and report. I do not deny that the various authors who report this event might have derived it directly from the epistles said to be written to St. *Polycarp* and *Apollophanes*. However, I cannot suppose that the author of these epistles simply invented the facts out of his own head, but rather delivered what tradition had passed down to his time. Indeed, what would more strongly shake the foundation of the story, if true, is what <margin>a Tract. 35 on Matthew, folio 89, column 1.</margin> <sup>a</sup> *Origen* supposes: that this darkness which was over all the earth, and the earthquake that attended our Lord's Passion, extended no farther than *Judea*, just as some of the other omens extended no farther than *Jerusalem*. But as to what degree of truth or probability that opinion may hold, I leave to others to inquire.

IV. DIONYSIUS, having finished his studies at *Heliopolis*, returned to *Athens*, incomparably fitted to serve his country. Accordingly, he was promoted to be one of the judges of the *Areopagus*, a position of great honor and renown. The *Areopagus* was a famous senate-house built upon a hill in *Athens*, where their great court of justice assembled. <margin>b Aristid. Volume 1, page 331.</margin> <sup>b</sup> One author calls it "the most honored and most sacred of the courts among the Greeks" <note>original: "τῆς ἐν τοῖς Ἕλλησι δικαςηρίων τιμιώτατον & ἁγιώτατον"</note>. Under their jurisdiction came all the greater and more capital cases, and especially matters of religion, blasphemy against the gods, and contempt of the holy mysteries. Therefore, St. *Paul* was brought before this court as a proclaimer of strange gods when he preached to them concerning *Jesus* and *Anastasis* <note>Greek: "Anastasis" means Resurrection</note>. No one could be a member of this council except persons of high birth and quality, wise and prudent men of very strict and severe manners. This solemn and grave assembly struck such great awe and reverence into those who sat in it that <sup>c</sup> *Isocrates* tells us that in his time—even when they had somewhat degenerated from their ancient virtue and men were otherwise irregular and excessive—once chosen into this senate, they immediately ceased their vicious inclinations. They chose instead to conform to the laws and manners of that court <margin>c In the place cited above.</margin> "rather than to persist in shameful vice" <note>original: "ἢ τῇ αἰσχρῇ κακίᾳ ἐμμένειν"</note>. They were exactly upright and impartial in their proceedings and heard cases at night or in the dark, so that the person of the plaintiff or the lawyer <note>original: "Pleader"</note> might have no undue influence upon them. Their sentence was final and decisive, and from their determination there was no appeal. Their number was uncertain; some say it was limited to nine, others say it was thirty-one, others fifty-one, and some say even more. Indeed, the "Nine Men" <note>original: "Novemviri"</note>—who were the King <note>original: "Basileus"</note>, the Archon, the General <note>original: "Polemarchus"</note>, and the six Lawgivers <note>original: "Thesmothetæ"</note>—were the constant source and nursery of this great assembly. Having discharged their various offices, they annually passed into the *Areopagus*. <margin>d Diogenes Laertius, Book 2, in the Life of Socrates, page 115.</margin> <sup>d</sup> Therefore, when *Socrates* was condemned by this court, we find no fewer than two hundred and eighty-one people giving their votes against him, besides those whose "white stones" <note>In ancient Greek courts, a white stone represented a vote for acquittal, while a black stone was for conviction.</note> were for his acquittal. In an ancient inscription upon a column in the *Acropolis* at *Athens*, erected to the memory of *Rufus Festus*, Proconsul of *Greece* and one of these judges, mention is made of the *Areopagite* Senate of three hundred.

<margin>

V. Our **St. Dionysius** <note>original: "S. Denys"</note> sat in this grave and respected court when **St. Paul**, around the year 49 or 50 AD, came to **Athens**. There, Paul resolutely defended the cause of **Christianity** against the attempts of the **Stoic** and **Epicurean** philosophers, who were the main voices against it. The **Athenians**, who were deeply curious and religious <note>original: "superstitious" - in this context, it refers to an intense or excessive concern with religious matters</note> concerning matters of faith, did not know what to make of this new and strange doctrine he taught. They soon brought him before the **Senate of the Areopagus**, which had the proper authority over such cases. 

Here, in a concise and eloquent speech delivered with great freedom of mind and strength of reason, Paul plainly demonstrated the folly and absurdity of the many worthless gods they blindly worshipped. He explained to them that infinite Being who made and governed the world, and described the binding obligations He had placed upon all mankind to worship and adore Him. Paul also showed how God had strengthened all former calls to gratitude, obedience, repentance, and reformation through this final and greatest era—by sending His Son to reveal such an excellent religion to the world. 

While some treated his speech with scorn and laughter, and others politely dismissed it, the discourse still had a successful influence on many. It convinced them of the reasonableness and divinity of the Christian faith. Among these was our **Dionysius**, one of the judges who sat in judgment of him, and **Damaris** his wife (as <sup>a</sup> **St. Chrysostom** and others identify her), and likely his entire household. 

One <sup>b</sup> author (though I confess I do not know by what authority) tells of a specific debate between **Dionysius** and **St. Paul** concerning the **Unknown God**, who, as both God and man, was to appear in later ages to reform the world. The Apostle showed this to be the Holy **Jesus**, who had recently come down from heaven. This so satisfied **St. Dionysius** that he prayed Paul to intercede with heaven so that he might be fully confirmed in this belief. The next day, after **St. Paul** had restored sight to a man born blind, he told the man to go to **Dionysius** and, by that sign, claim his promise to become a convert. Dionysius, amazed by this sight, readily renounced his idolatry and was baptized into the faith of Christ along with his household. 

However, I know the reputation of this author too well to place much weight on this story, especially since I find that **Baronius** <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607) was an influential Catholic historian.</note> himself is unwilling to trust it. To this I might add <sup>c</sup> **St. Chrysostom's** observation that the **Areopagite** was converted <term>solely by public speech</term> <note>original: ἀπὸ δημηγορίας μόνης (apo dēmēgorias monēs)</note>, as there was no miracle we know of that might have prompted it.

VI. Once baptized, we are <sup>d</sup> told he was placed under the care and instruction of **St. Hierotheus** to be further taught in the faith. Hierotheus is a person not even mentioned by any of the ancient writers, which creates in me a strong suspicion that it is only a fictional name and that no such person ever actually existed. Indeed, the *Greek Menaion* <sup>e</sup> <note>A liturgical book of the Eastern Orthodox Church containing services for the saints.</note> claims he was one of the nine senators of the **Areopagus** and was then appointed as tutor to **St. Dionysius**. <sup>f</sup> Others claim he was a **Spaniard** by birth, the first Bishop of **Athens**, and that he later traveled to his own country to be the Bishop of **Segovia** in **Spain**. I believe both accounts are equally true—which is to say, not at all. Such a person would likely never have been thought of if there had not been some mentions of such a teacher in **Dionysius’s** own works, which were later confirmed by the <term>scholiasts</term> <note>Ancient commentators or grammarians who wrote explanatory notes on classical texts.</note> who wrote about him, and eventually developed by others into a formal legend. It was there that he suffered martyrdom. Among the infinite other miracles reported of him, he is said to have picked up his head after it had been cut off by the executioners and to have carried it in his hands for two miles—with an angel going before him and a heavenly choir attending him all the way—until he came to the place of his burial. IX. **HILDUIN**, encouraged by his powerful patron, partly to exalt the honor of **France** and partly to advance the reputation of his own monastery, found an obscure **Dionysius** who had been Bishop of **Paris**. He moved him back in time by an age or two and claimed he was the same person as the **Dionysius** of **Athens**, a person of much greater honor and veneration. Using a mix of records and the traditions current among his own people, he drew up a formal account of him from start to finish—likely adding whatever he thought appropriate of his own invention to complete the story. We may suppose these commentaries of his were quickly carried to **Rome**. There, they were found by the **Greeks**, who frequently came on embassies to the Roman See during that time, and were taken to **Constantinople**. From these, **Methodius** (who had himself been an <term>Apocrisiarius</term> <note>A high-ranking ecclesiastical representative or ambassador</note> or ambassador from **Nicephorus**, the **Greek Patriarch**, to **Pope Paschal** at **Rome**, and who was later promoted to the Patriarchate of **Constantinople** after infinite troubles) gathered the materials to write the life of **Dionysius**. It is clear he did not get these details from the records of his own Church; when **Hilduin** began composing his *Areopagitics*, he explicitly says<sup>b</sup> that the **Greeks** had written nothing concerning the martyrdom of **St. Denis**, because they could not obtain the details from such a great distance. Therefore, **Methodius** must have derived his information from **Hilduin**, or at least from some reports of that time. It is most probable he used **Hilduin's** work, because there is such an exact agreement between their accounts—not only in specific passages, but often in the very same words—as **Monsieur Launoy** has demonstrated by a detailed comparison.<sup>c</sup> This work by **Methodius** was quickly brought from **Constantinople** back to **Rome** by **Greek** ambassadors, where<sup>d</sup> **Anastasius** confesses he found it. He translated it into **Latin** and then sent it to **France**, where it was read, owned, and published by<sup>e</sup> **Hincmar**, as appears by his letter to **Charles the Bald**, the Emperor. In that letter, he plainly states that as soon as he read this *Life* written by **Methodius**, he found it to agree admirably with what he had read in his youth (meaning, I have no doubt, the writings of **Hilduin**). He explains by whom and how the *Acts* of **St. Denis** and his companions came to the knowledge of the **Romans**, and from there to the notice of the **Greeks**. This is the most likely origin and progression of the story that I can think of. From this point, how easy was it for later writers in both the **Western** and **Eastern** Church to swallow a story so plausibly tailored to their tastes? Nor did the **Greeks** have any reason to over-critically examine or reject something that brought so much honor to their Church and nation, and which seemed to put not only **France** but the entire **Western** Church under an obligation to them for furnish-

X. Although we cannot doubt that he conducted himself with all diligence and faithfulness in the discharge of his office, yet because the ancient writers have passed down no specific details to us, we shall not rely on reports that are false or, at best, of doubtful credibility. Nothing certain can be recovered about him beyond what **Aristides**, the Christian philosopher (who lived and was likely born at **Athens** not long after **Dionysius**), relates in the <margin>a</margin> **Apology** <note>A formal defense of the faith</note> which he published for the Christian religion: that after a most resolute and prominent confession of the faith, and after enduring several of the severest kinds of torture, he gave the final and greatest testimony to it by laying down his life. This most likely occurred during the reign of **Domitian**, as is admitted (perhaps prompted by a secret instinct of truth) by Abbot **Hilduin**, **Methodius**, and their followers. Others, however, extend his life to the times of **Trajan**, and some even to the reign of **Hadrian**, who began his rule of the Empire in AD 117. They do this partly to allow enough time for the accounts they give of him, and partly to preserve the authority of his writings, in which a passage is quoted from the letters of **Ignatius**, written just before his martyrdom in AD 107.

I hope the reader will not expect from me an account of the miracles said to have been performed by him either before or after his death, or of the fierce disputes between various places in the Roman Church regarding his relics <note>Physical remains or personal effects of a saint</note>. One story, however, I shall not omit. In a village in **Luxembourg**, not far from **Trier** <note>original: "Treves"</note>, there is a church dedicated to **St. Denis**, where his skull (or at least a piece of it) is kept. On the crown of the skull there is a white cross, while the other parts of the bone are black. According to local tradition, supported by <margin>b</margin> some authors, this mark was made when **St. Paul** laid his hands upon him during his consecration <note>The formal act of ordaining someone as a bishop</note>. If this is true, I have nothing more to say except that "Holy Orders" (which the Roman Church considers a sacrament) did here, in a literal sense, confer an "indelible character" <note>A theological term for a permanent spiritual mark left on the soul by certain sacraments</note> and mark upon him.

XI. His bodily appearance <note>original: "τυπῶς Σωματικὸς"</note> is described by the <margin>c</margin> **Greek Menaion** <note>A liturgical book of the Eastern Orthodox Church containing the lives of saints</note> in this way: he was of middle height, slender, and fair-skinned but pale. His nose was gracefully curved, his eyes deep-set with short eyebrows, his ears large, his hair thick and white, and his beard was moderately long but very thin. As for the character of his mind expressed in his speeches and the excellent conduct of his life, the Greeks—according to their tendency to exaggerate in both attitude and language—bestow the most extravagant praises and commendations upon him. They call him the "Sacred Interpreter" <note>original: "ἱεροφάντορα"</note> and "contemplator of hidden and unspeakable mysteries" <note>original: "τῶν ἀποῤῥήτων θεωρὸν"</note>, and an unsearchable depth of heavenly knowledge. They call him the "Theologian of the Trinity" <note>original: "τριαδικὸν θεόλογον"</note> and the "God-bearing instrument of those life-giving graces that are beyond all understanding" <note>original: "τῶν ὑπὲρ ἔννοιαν ζωοποιῶν χαρισμάτων θεοφόρον ὄργανον"</note>. They say of him that his life was wonderful, and his speech even more so; his tongue was full of light, and his mouth breathed holy fire; but his mind was most perfectly god-like <note>original: "ἀκριβῶς θεοείδεστατον"</note>. They include many more such descriptions throughout their liturgical services. And certainly, if the ideas he gave us about the celestial hierarchy, the orders of angels, and the nature of that otherworldly state were as clear and certain as some would have us believe, he might deserve that title which others...

XII. We are told<sup>b</sup> that the great and clear evidence of his wisdom and eloquence are the works he left behind. The ideas and language in which they are expressed are so lofty and sublime that they seem barely possible for a mere mortal to have produced. These books are infinitely intricate and complex—as our countryman <sup>c</sup> **Johannes Scotus** <note>Johannes Scotus Eriugena, a 9th-century scholar who translated these works from Greek into Latin</note>, who first translated them into Latin, tells us. They are far beyond the reach of modern understanding, and few are able to penetrate them, both because of their antiquity and the sublimity of those heavenly mysteries they discuss. It is a work so pleasing to all speculative seekers into the nature of things and the more hidden and secret parts of learning, that (if **Suidas** <note>The author of a massive 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> speaks truly) some of the Heathen philosophers—and particularly **Proclus**—often borrowed not only his ideas, but his very words and phrases. Because of this, Suidas suspects that some of the philosophers at **Athens** stole those books of his mentioned in the dedicatory letter to **St. Timothy** (which are now lost) and published them under their own names. 

But if I were to make a guess, I would rather suspect that this **Pseudo-Dionysius** <note>The name given by scholars to the anonymous 5th or 6th-century author who wrote under the name of Dionysius the Areopagite</note> fetched his speculations and a good part of his expressions from **Plotinus**, **Iamblichus**, and the rest of the later **Platonists**. For certainly, one egg is no more like another than this man's divinity is like the theology of that school, especially as explained by the philosophers who lived in the early ages of Christianity. I will not bother to prove here that our **Dionysius** was not the actual author of the books currently attributed to him. For although many people argue for his authorship with all possible zeal and stubbornness, there are many others—even notable men within the Roman Church—who clearly disown and deny it. Among the Reformed <note>Protestant</note> churches, it has been extensively disproved by many, and by none with greater learning and industry than **Monsieur Daillé** <note>Jean Daillé (1594–1670), a French Huguenot minister</note>, who has said everything necessary (if not more than enough) on this subject. However, regarding the date of their birth and first appearance, when he dates them as late as the sixth century, he takes away somewhat from the antiquity that might probably be allowed to them.

XIII. Identifying the specific author of these books is not easy to determine. Among the various guesses about this matter, none seems more worthy of consideration than what <sup>d</sup> **Lorenzo Valla** <note>A famous 15th-century Italian humanist</note> tells us some learned Greeks of his time believed: that it was **Apollinaris**. Whether it was the father or the son does not matter much, as both were men of great talent and shared the same style and character. "Both were masters of Greek learning" <note>original Greek: ἀμφότεροι ἑλληνικῶν λόγων διδάσκαλοι</note><sup>e</sup>, though of the two, the son was the most likely candidate. It is certain that **Apollinaris** was "trained in all sorts of knowledge and skilled in the styles and forms of speech," as <sup>f</sup> **Sozomen** describes him. And <sup>g</sup> **St. Basil** says of him that, being gifted with a facility for writing on any subject, joined with a great readiness and fluency of language, he filled the world with his books. Even in his theological tracts, he did not seek to establish them by proof from Scripture, but from human arguments and ways of reasoning; "he established his doctrine not from any specific text, but from his own intellect," as <sup>h</sup> another also says of him. He was born and raised at **Alexan-**

Resenting this as a major insult, and <margin>a Socrates, page 161.</margin> "relying on the abundance of his sophistical eloquence" <note>original Greek: τῇ εὐφορίᾳ τοῦ Σοφιστικοῦ λόγου θαῤῥῶν</note>, he was prompted by a bold confidence in his own sophistical wit and subtle ways of arguing. He began to introduce new ideas in matters of doctrine and established a sect named after himself. 

Certainly, anyone who thoroughly considers the principles of **Apollinaris**, as they are represented by <sup>b</sup> **Socrates**, <sup>c</sup> **Sozomen**, <sup>d</sup> **Theodoret**, <sup>e</sup> **Basil**, and <sup>f</sup> **Epiphanius**, will find that many of them have a close affinity with Platonic ideas. Some are even similar to those found in the books attributed to **Dionysius**. Regarding the doctrine of the **Trinity**, they were generally correct; <sup>g</sup> **Socrates** particularly tells us the Apollinarians confessed the Trinity to be "consubstantial" <term>consubstantial: sharing the same essence or substance; a key term in the Nicene Creed</term>. To this, I add what a learned <sup>h</sup> man of our own nation has observed: that Apollinaris and his followers were guilty of forging church writings, which they falsely attributed to **Gregory Thaumaturgus**, **Athanasius**, and **Pope Julius**, as <sup>i</sup> **Leontius** proves in great detail. Thus, it is quite probable that these works were forged in the school of Apollinaris, either by himself or by some of his disciples.
