XIV. The theory seems even more likely when we consider that there was a certain <sup>k</sup> **Dionysius**, who was probably a friend of **Apollinaris**. Apollinaris is said to have written a famous letter to him that was circulated under the name of **Pope Julius**. Furthermore, among his own students, he had a man named **Timothy** (who was condemned along with his master by <sup>l</sup> **Pope Damasus** and the Synod at **Rome**). This gave them an easy opportunity to publish their own ideas under the more venerable names of those ancient and apostolic figures. 

Or, more likely, Apollinaris himself—being so well-versed in the art of counterfeiting—took the opportunity to compose and publish these works under the name of the ancient Dionysius. He could hardly have chosen a name more suited to his purpose: a man born in the very center of learning and eloquence <note>Athens</note>, who could easily be imagined to have been educated in all the schools of philosophy and to be specifically familiar with the writings and theories of **Plato** and his followers, which were so famous and widely accepted in that place. 

There is even more reason to believe this when we consider that <sup>m</sup> Apollinaris rewrote the Gospels and the writings of the Apostles into the form of dialogues, imitating Plato’s style among the Greeks. As for the style of the Dionysian works, which is very high-flown and affected, we previously noted how uniquely qualified Apollinaris was, possessing a talent for inventing new words and a complex way of speaking. The <sup>n</sup> historian observes that the primary tool he used to spread his heresy, and in which he had a singular talent, was his "art of words" <note>original Greek: τέχνη λόγων</note>—meaning artificial word structures and subtle ways of expressing himself. Besides this, he was an incomparable poet (both the father and the son). He was deeply devoted to the study of poetry and wrote poems in imitation of—and to the envy of—the best among the...

In imitation of **Homer**, he wrote *Epic Poems* <note>original: "Heroic Poems"</note> based on the history of the Old Testament up until the reign of **Saul**. He also wrote *Comedies* in the style of **Menander**, *Tragedies* imitating **Euripides**, and *Odes* following **Pindar**. He composed *Divine Hymns* that were publicly sung in the churches of his breakaway sect, as well as *Songs* that men sang at feasts and during their work—even women sang them while spinning wool <note>original: "at the Distaff"</note>. Through these exercises, he was perfectly prepared for lofty and poetic styles of writing. He might easily have been tempted—especially since the subject matter allowed it—to indulge in an unrestrained and excessive imagination <note>original: "wanton and luxuriant fansie"</note> in his choice, composition, and use of words. Certainly, there was never a stranger collection—a "multitude of words" <note>original Greek: *λέξεων πολυκληθίαν*, Maximus himself calls it</note>—of sublime, affected, inflated, and poetic phrases than what is found in these books attributed to **St. Denis** <note>Saint Dionysius</note>.

XV. If one were to ask why a man, after so much effort, would choose to publish his works under another person’s name rather than his own, there is a simple answer: this has been an old practice. Some men have adopted it either because it was their whim to credit their own work to others, or to avoid the criticism that their ideas might provoke. Most often, however, it was done to gain greater respect and value for their writing by sending it out under the name of someone for whom the world already had a just regard and veneration. 

As for the theory of **Monsieur Daillé** <note>Jean Daillé (1594–1670), a French Protestant scholar known for his work on the early Church Fathers</note>: he suggests that the reason several learned volumes were written and falsely attributed to the Fathers of the ancient Church was to defend them from a common accusation made by the pagans <note>original: "Gentiles"</note>. The pagans used to charge Christians with being an unrefined and uneducated generation whose books were filled with nothing but plain, simple doctrines and who were strangers to all types of learning and eloquence. To counter this objection, several writers took it upon themselves to compose books full of learning and philosophy, which they published under the names of the first preachers and spreaders of the Christian faith. Daillé argues that this was specifically the case for the *Recognitions* attributed to **Clement**, and the writings attributed to **Dionysius**. 

I grant that the first case is very likely and rational. The *Recognitions* were probably written around the second century, when this objection was most common (as seen in **Celsus’s** book against the Christians) and when few learned discourses had been published by them. However, I can by no means agree with this regarding the second case. Dionysius’s works were written long after the learning and eloquence of Christians had sufficiently proven itself to the world—to the shame, conviction, envy, and admiration of its greatest enemies. There was far less need for them for this purpose, especially if it is true (as Daillé himself so confidently asserts and argues) that they were not written until the beginning of the sixth century, around the year 520. By that time, there were few learned pagans left to make such an objection, as paganism had been almost entirely banished from the civilized world.

But whoever the true author was, or for whatever reason he wrote them, it is clear that he laid the foundation for a mystical and incomprehensible theology <note>original: "Divinity"</note> among Christians. From this source came all those wild **Rosicrucean** notions <note>A reference to the Rosicrucians, a secret society claiming esoteric wisdom; the author views these mystical ideas as non-traditional</note> that some people are so fond of, and whose life and practice they praise as the very soul and perfection of the Christian state. The fact that this author directly serves this purpose can be judged by the reader from a single instance, and I assure

Therefore, God is known in all things and apart from all things; God is known through knowledge and through ignorance. There is of him thought, and word, and knowledge <note>original: "science"</note>, and touch, and sense, and opinion, and imagination, and name, and all other things; and yet he is not thought of, nor spoken of, nor named. He is not any of the things that exist, nor is he known in any of the things that exist. *God (he says) is known in all things, and without all things: he is known by knowledge, and by ignorance: there is both a thought <note>original: "cogitation"</note> of him, and a word, and a knowledge <note>original: "science"</note>, and a touch, and a sense, and an opinion, and an imagination, and a name, and all other things; and yet he is neither thought, nor spoken of, nor named. He is not any thing of those things that are, nor is he known in any of the things that are; he is both all things in all, and nothing in nothing; out of all things he is known to all, and out of nothing to nothing. These are the things which we rightly discourse concerning God. And this again is the most divine knowledge of God, that which is known*

More of this and similar material <note>original: "stuff"</note> is plentifully scattered throughout these books. And if this is not mystical and profound enough, I do not know what is; certainly, anyone but one well-versed in this sort of theology would look upon it as a strange jargon of nonsense and contradiction. And yet this is the height of devotion and piety which some men earnestly strive for and in which they glory. It is as if a man could not truly understand the mysteries of religion until he had resigned his reason, nor be a Christian without first becoming an enthusiast <note>original: "Enthusiast" — in the 17th century, this referred to someone claiming direct, often irrational, divine inspiration</note>, nor be able to speak sense unless in a language which no one can understand.

# The Life of Saint Clement.

*Rome. The great confusion regarding the first Bishops of that See. A probable account attempted concerning the order of Saint Clement’s succession and reconciling it with the timelines of the other Bishops. The account given of him in the ancient Epistle to Saint James. Clement’s appointment of Notaries to record the **Acts of the Martyrs**, and his dispatching of messengers to spread the Gospel. The Schism in the Church of **Corinth**, and **Clement’s Epistle** to that Church. An inquiry into when that **Epistle** was written. The persecution under **Trajan**. His proceedings against the **Fellowships** <note>original Latin: "Heteriæ"</note>. A short account of **Saint Clement's** troubles from the writings of **Simeon Metaphrastes**. His banishment to **Cherson**. **Condemnation to the mines** <note>original Latin: "Damnatio ad Metalla"</note>, and what that entailed. The great success of his **Ministry** in his place of exile. **Saint Clement’s Martyrdom**, and the manner of it. The anniversary miracle reported on his feast day. The date of his **Martyrdom**. His genuine Writings. His **Epistle** to the **Corinthians**: the praise given to it by the **Ancient Church fathers**. Its **Style and Character**. The great modesty and humility that appears in it. The fragment of his second **Epistle**. **Spurious Writings** <note>original: "Supposititious Writings"</note>. The **Recognitions**; their various titles and different editions. Their **Antiquity**. A theory concerning their **Author**. The opinions of the **Ancient Church fathers** regarding the corruption of these texts. The **Epistle to Saint James**.*

I. <image-desc>Decorative initial T with mermaids and foliage</image-desc> It adds significantly to the honor of this venerable **Apostolic Man** (for all antiquity understands the reference to be to him) that he was a **fellow laborer** with Saint **Paul**, and one of those whose names were written in the **Book of Life**. He was born in **Rome**, on the **Caelian Hill** <note>original: "Mount Cœlius"</note>, as we are informed by the **Pontifical** <note>The *Liber Pontificalis* or "Book of the Popes," a record of early bishops of Rome</note> attributed to the name of **Damasus**, among other sources. His father's name was **Faustinus**, but who he was, and what his profession or way of life might have been, is not recorded. Indeed, in the **Book of Recognitions** and the **Clementine Homilies** <note>original Greek: "мі πλάσια" (Homiliae)</note> (mentioned by the ancients and lately published), we find more specific accounts of him. Although these books are falsely attributed to **Saint Clement** and are in some cases subject to valid criticism, they are of great antiquity in the Church—written not long after the **Apostolic Age** (as we shall show hereafter). Therefore, we shall draw a few details from them for our purpose, though we cannot absolutely guarantee their historical certainty. In those texts, **Saint Clement** is depicted as giving this account of himself:

<margin>a. Life of Clement, Council Records, Vol. 10, col. 74.</margin>

II. He was descended from a noble line, born of the family of the **Caesars**. His father, **Faustinian** (or **Faustas**), was a close relative of the **Emperor** (likely **Tiberius**) and was educated alongside him. Through the Emperor's arrangement, he was married to **Mattidia**, a woman from a prominent Roman family. Clement was the youngest of three sons; his two elder brothers were **Faustinus and Faustus**, who later changed their names to **Nicetas and Aquila**. His mother, who was apparently a woman of exquisite beauty, was relentlessly pressured by her husband’s own brother to engage in unchaste behavior. To avoid these troublesome advances, yet reluctant to reveal the truth to her husband for fear it would cause a scandal or dishonor their family, she devised a plan. Saint Clement grew up engaged in all manly studies and virtuous actions, until he fell into a state of great mental dissatisfaction concerning the immortality of the soul and the state of the afterlife. He applied himself to search more narrowly into the nature and the truth of things. After having frustrated all his own ideas, he turned to the schools of the philosophers, where he met with nothing but fierce contentions, endless disputes, and deceptive and uncertain methods of reasoning. From there, he resolved to consult the Egyptian **Hierophants** <note>original: "Hierophantæ"; high-ranking priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note> and to see if he could meet with anyone who, by the arts of magic, was able to summon back someone who had departed to the invisible world. He hoped the very sight of such a person might satisfy his curious inquiries about this matter. While he was in this state of suspense, he heard of the Son of God appearing in the world and the excellent doctrines he had published in Judea. He was further instructed in these by the ministry of Saint Barnabas, who came to Rome. He followed Barnabas first to Alexandria, and from there, after a little time, to Judea. Arriving at Caesarea, he met with Saint Peter, by whom he was instructed and baptized; he continued as Peter’s companion and disciple for a great part of his life.

III. This is the summary of what I thought good to borrow from those ancient writings. As for his relatives—the various misfortunes his father, mother, and two brothers separately encountered, and the strange accidents by which they all afterwards met, were converted, and were baptized into the Christian faith—I omit those details. I do so partly because they are less relevant to my purpose, and partly because the story looks more like a dramatic scene of fiction than a true and real history. Regarding the account of his being related to the Imperial family: although it is more than once confidently asserted by Nicephorus (who transcribes a good part of the story) and by others before him, I cannot help but see it as an evident mistake. This error likely arises from no other source than the story of **Flavius Clemens** the **Consul** <note>A Roman aristocrat and relative of Emperor Domitian who was executed, possibly for Christian sympathies</note>, who was a first cousin to the Emperor Domitian, and whose wife, Flavia Domitilla, was also a near relative of the Emperor. We have elsewhere given an account of their conversion to and martyrdom for the faith of Christ, based on the writers of those times. It is probable that Saint Clement mostly followed Saint Peter’s travels and came with him to Rome, where he eventually had the government of that Church committed to him. Dorotheus tells us that he was the first of the **Gentiles** <note>Non-Jewish people</note> who embraced the Christian faith, and that he was first made Bishop of Sardica (a city in Thrace, afterwards called Triaditza) and then of Rome. But in this claim, I think he stands alone; I am sure he has none of the ancient writers to join him, unless he refers to another Clement, whom the *Alexandrian Chronicle* also identifies as one of the **Seventy Disciples** <note>original: "LXX Disciples"</note> but seems to confuse with our Saint Clement. That he was Bishop of Rome is a point of unanimous and unquestionable agreement among all ancient writers, though they strangely vary regarding the time and order of his appointment. IV. It is clear both from <sup>a</sup>Irenaeus and <sup>b</sup>Epiphanius, as well as before them from <sup>c</sup>Caius, an ancient writer, and from <sup>d</sup>Dionysius, Bishop of Corinth, that Peter and Paul jointly laid the foundations of the Church of Rome. Therefore, they are equally styled "Bishops" of it: one acting as the Apostle of the Gentiles (as we may probably suppose), taking care of the Gentile Christians, while the other, as the <term>Apostle of the Circumcision</term> <note>A title for Saint Peter, referring to his primary mission to the Jewish people.</note>, applied himself to the Jewish converts at Rome. We cannot imagine that—given such deep-seated and long-standing prejudices between Jews and Gentiles, especially in matters of religion—they would suddenly lay these aside and both join together in one public society. We know that in the Church of Jerusalem, until the destruction of the Temple, no one was admitted except Jewish converts. It might have been the same at first in Rome, where vast numbers of Jews resided at the time; they might have kept themselves for some time in distinct assemblies, the one under Saint Paul, the other under Peter.

There seems to be some foundation for such a conjecture even in Apostolic history. Saint Luke tells us that Saint Paul, upon his <margin>*Acts 28: 23, 24, 25, 28, 30, 31.*</margin> first coming to Rome, was rejected by the Jews and turned to the Gentiles, declaring to them the "salvation of God." The Gentiles gladly heard and accepted it, and Paul continued preaching the "Kingdom of God" and receiving all who came to him for two years together. I look upon this as the first settled foundation of a Gentile Church at Rome. The further care and presidency of this church Saint Paul might have passed down to Linus (whom the <term>interpolated Ignatius</term> <note>Referring to versions of the letters of Ignatius of Antioch that were later expanded or altered by other writers.</note> identifies as his deacon or minister). Meanwhile, Saint Peter, having established a church of Jewish converts, might have turned it over to Saint Clement. <sup>e</sup>Tertullian <margin>e *On the Prescription of Heretics, chapter 32, page 213.* f *Apostolic Constitutions, book 7, chapter 47, folio 451, 601.*</margin> expressly says that Peter ordained Clement as Bishop of Rome. Accordingly, the compiler of the <sup>f</sup>*Apostolic Constitutions* records that Linus was ordained Bishop of Rome by Saint Paul, and Clement by Saint Peter.

He says, indeed, that Linus was the first, and that may very well be true, seeing as Saint Paul was in Rome for a considerable time before Saint Peter arrived (regardless of what modern writers of that Church say to the contrary). When Linus died, he was probably succeeded in his distinct role by Cletus or Anacletus (for the Greeks—likely most correctly—generally consider them to be the same person). At that time, Clement, whom Saint Peter had ordained to be his successor, continued to act as the president over the church of Jewish converts. Things remained this way until the death of Cletus, at which point the difference between Jew and Gentile had quite worn off. The entire presidency and government of the whole Church of Rome then devolved upon Saint Clement as the survivor. From this period of time, the years of his episcopacy (according to the common calculation) are said to begin.

By this account, not only the records of <sup>g</sup>Optatus <margin>g *On the Schism of the Donatists, book 2, page 38.* h *Bucherian Catalogue; edited commentary on Victorinus’s Paschal Canon, chapter 15, page 269.*</margin> and the <sup>h</sup>*Bucherian Catalogue* may be true—which place Clement after Linus—but also the accounts of Baronius and many of the ancients, who place both Linus and Cletus before him. We can accept that they did indeed precede him as bishops and pastors of the Gentile Church. As for a more distinct and particular account of the dates, I calculate them as follows: Peter and Paul suffered martyrdom in the Neronian persecution (as we have likely shown elsewhere) in **AD 65**. After this, Linus held office for twelve years, four months, and twelve days. Cletus followed for twelve years, one (or as Baronius says, seven)...

The good man declined the honor with all possible modesty, but Saint Peter urged it upon him in a long discourse. The exact time this Epistle was written is not known, as its date cannot be certainly determined by any ancient records or any hints within the Epistle itself. VII. Simeon the Metaphrast <note>A 10th-century Byzantine author known for compiling the lives of saints.</note>, in the account of Clement's martyrdom <margin>See note B.</margin> (which is much the same as the *Life of Saint Clement* said to be written by an uncertain author and published long ago by Lazius at the end of the work by Abdias of Babylon), describes the beginning of his troubles as follows. Saint Clement, having converted Theodora, a noble lady, and afterwards her husband Sisinnius—a kinsman and favorite of the late Emperor Nerva—found that winning over such a prominent man quickly influenced others of high rank and status to embrace the Faith. Such is the power of religious example among the Great to sway people toward piety and virtue. But envy naturally resents the good of others and hates the person who brings it about. This success brought upon Clement the particular hatred <note>original: "odium"</note> of Torcutianus, a man of great power and authority in Rome at that time. Torcutianus used the city's lower magistrates to incite the people to riot against the holy man, charging him with magic and sorcery, and for being an enemy and blasphemer of the gods. They cried out that he must either offer sacrifice to the gods or pay for his impiety with his blood. Mamertinus, the Prefect of the City, a moderate and prudent man, wishing to quiet the uproar, sent for Saint Clement and mildly persuaded him to comply. But finding Clement’s resolution unshakable, he sent word to the Emperor to inform him of the case. The Emperor returned a short <term>rescript</term><note>An official written reply or edict from a Roman emperor.</note> stating that Clement should either sacrifice to the gods or be banished to Cherson <note>A city in the Crimea.</note>, a desolate city beyond the Black Sea <note>original: "Pontic Sea"</note>. Mamertinus, having received the imperial command, unwillingly complied and ordered that all things be made ready for the voyage. Accordingly, Clement was transported there to dig in the marble quarries and labor in the mines. "Condemnation to the mines" <note>original: "Damnatio ad Metalla"</note> is a punishment frequently mentioned in Roman laws, where it is described as a punishment next to death <margin>See note C.</margin> <note>original: "proxima morti pœna"</note>. Indeed, the treatment under this sentence was extremely harsh and rigorous. Besides the severest labor and most intolerable hardship, the condemned person was treated with every kind of inhumanity: whipped and beaten, chained and fettered, and stripped of his estate <margin>See note D.</margin>, which was forfeited to the imperial treasury. The person himself was permanently degraded to the status of a slave and consequently rendered incapable of making a will. Not only this, but they were further subjected to the most public marks of infamy and dishonor <margin>See note E.</margin>: their heads were half-shaved, their right eyes gouged out, their left legs disabled, and their foreheads branded with a mark of shame. This particular disgrace was first used in these cases by Caligula <margin>See note F.</margin> (the historian notes it as an instance of his cruel temper) and continued from his time until the reign of Constantine, who abolished it by law in the year of Christ 315 <margin>See note G.</margin>. This is to say nothing of the hunger and thirst, the cold and nakedness, and the filth and squalor they were forced to endure in those miserable places.

Simeon the *Metaphrast* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine author known for compiling and rewriting the lives of saints.</note>, in his account of Clement's martyrdom—which is much the same as the *Life of Saint Clement* said to be written by an unknown author and published long ago by Lazius at the end of the works of *Abdias of Babylon*—sets down the beginning of his troubles as follows. *Saint Clement* had converted *Theodora*, a noble lady, and later her husband *Sisinnius*, a kinsman and favorite of the late Emperor *Nerva*. Gaining such a prominent man quickly drew others of high rank and quality to embrace the Faith. Such is the power of the example of religious greatness in swaying people toward piety and virtue. 

But envy naturally resents the good of others and hates the person who achieves it. This success brought upon him the particular hatred <note>original: "odium"</note> of *Torcutianus*, a <margin>c Same source, page 832.</margin> man of great power and authority at that time in *Rome*. By influencing the city's lower magistrates, he incited the people to riot against the holy man, charging him with magic and sorcery, and with being an enemy and blasphemer of the gods. They cried out that he should either offer sacrifices to the gods or pay for his impiety with his blood. *Mamertinus*, the Prefect of the city—a moderate and prudent man—wishing to calm the uproar, sent for *Saint Clement* and mildly persuaded him to comply. But finding Clement's resolution inflexible, he sent word to the Emperor about the case. 

The Emperor returned this short imperial decree <note>original: "Rescript"</note>: that he should either sacrifice to the gods or be banished to *Cherson* <note>Modern Sevastopol in Crimea.</note>, a desolate city beyond the *Black Sea* <note>original: "Pontic Sea"</note>. *Mamertinus*, having received the imperial mandate, unwillingly complied with it and ordered everything to be prepared for the voyage. Accordingly, Clement was transported there to dig in the marble quarries and labor in the mines. 

"Condemnation to the mines" <note>original: "Damnatio ad Metalla"</note> is a punishment frequently mentioned in *Roman Law*, where it is described as "a punishment very close to death" <note>original: "proxima morti pœna"</note> <margin>d Law 28, Digest concerning punishments, Book 48, Title 19.</margin>. Indeed, the treatment under this sentence was extreme and rigorous. Besides the severest labor and most intolerable hardship, the condemned person was treated with every kind of inhumanity: whipped and beaten, chained and fettered, and deprived of his estate <margin>e Law 36, as cited above; Law 12, Digest on the rights of the treasury; Law 49, Title 14; Law 1, on the goods of the condemned; Law 8, Who can make a Will, Section 4. Cyprian, Epistle 77 to Nemesianus, page 155; Eusebius, Book 8, chapter 12, page 307.</margin>, which was forfeited to the government treasury. The person himself was permanently reduced to the status of a slave and consequently rendered unable to make a will. Not only this, but they were further exposed to the most public marks of infamy and dishonor: their heads were half-shaved, their right eyes bored out, their left legs disabled, and their foreheads branded with a shameful mark. This piece of disgrace was first used in these cases by <margin>f Suetonius in the Life of Caligula, chapter 27, page 428.</margin> *Caligula* (and the historian notes it as an instance of his cruel temper), and it continued from his time until the reign of *Constantine*, who abolished it by a <margin>g Law 2, Theodosian Code on punishments, Book 9, Title 40.</margin> law in AD 315. This is to say nothing of the hunger and thirst, the cold and nakedness, and the filth and squalor which they were forced to struggle with in those miserable places.

VIII. Arriving at the place of his uncomfortable exile, he found vast numbers of Christians condemned to the same miserable fate. Their spirits were greatly lifted under all their pressures at the sight of such a good man. Through his constant preaching and the frequent miracles he performed, their enemies were converted to a better opi-

The inhabitants of those countries daily flocked to the Faith, so that in a short time Christianity had driven Paganism out of the region, and all monuments of idolatry thereabouts were defaced and overturned. The news of this was quickly carried to the Emperor, who dispatched Aufidianus the President <note>original: "President"; a term for a Roman provincial governor or prefect.</note> to put a stop to this growing sect. He attacked them with methods of terror and cruelty, putting great numbers of them to death. But finding how readily and resolutely they stepped forward for execution, and that today's martyrs only prepared others for tomorrow's torments, he gave up contending with the multitude. Instead, he resolved to single out one person of note above the rest, whose exemplary punishment might strike dread and terror into the others. To this purpose Saint Clement was chosen. After all temptations to renounce his faith were tried on him in vain, the executioners were commanded to take him aboard a ship and throw him into the bottom of the sea, where the Christians would have no hope of finding him. This kind of death was called *katapontismos* <note>original: "καταποντισμὸς"; a Greek term for execution by drowning.</note>, and was used not only among the Greeks—as seen in the instance mentioned by <sup>a</sup> Diodorus Siculus—but also by the Romans, as we find several criminals condemned to be thrown into the sea by both <sup>b</sup> Tiberius and Avidius Cassius. To this our Lord refers when, in the case of willful scandal, he pronounces it *better for the man that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and he cast into the bottom of the sea.*

Although <sup>c</sup> Saint Jerome tells us that this punishment was common among the ancient Jews in cases of more severe crimes, I do not remember that any such capital punishment ever actually prevailed among them. I shall not relate here what I find concerning the strange and miraculous discovery of Saint Clement’s body, nor the particular miracle of a little child preserved for an entire year in the church erected to him in the middle of the sea (though solemnly asserted by <sup>d</sup> Ephrem, Bishop of the place). I doubt people would ever have a belief wide enough to swallow such stories, or the infinite other miracles said to have occurred there. It shall only suffice to mention one: that upon the anniversary of his martyrdom, the sea retreats on each side into heaps and leaves a clear, dry passage for three miles to the martyr's tomb. This tomb was located within a church built (as it must be supposed, by angels) within the sea. Once the people’s devotions are ended, the sea returns to its place; "God by this means doing honor to the martyr," <note>original: "τιμῶντος τοῦ Θεοῦ κἀνταῦθα τὸν μάρτυρα"</note> says <sup>e</sup> one of my authors. I only add that these traditions were current before the time of Gregory, Bishop of Tours, <sup>f</sup> who speaks of them with great reverence and devotion.

This was a little more than two years after his banishment, after he had been the sole Bishop of Rome for nine years, six months, and several days, according to Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius, a 16th-century Cardinal and historian.</note> and others. However, the catalogue of Bucherius <note>Gilles Bucher, a Jesuit scholar who published ancient Roman chronologies.</note> is more reliable, as it was composed before the death of Pope Liberius in the year 354; it lists his reign as nine years, eleven months, and twelve days. His martyrdom happened on the 24th of November, according to Baronius and the ordinary Roman computation, but on the ninth of that month, says the small Martyrology published by <sup>k</sup> Bucherius, which was unquestionably one of the authentic calendars of the ancient...

IX. THE writings which at this day bear the name of this apostolic man are of two sorts: genuine or supposititious <note>original: "supposititious"; meaning falsely attributed or forged.</note>. In the first class is that famous *Epistle to the Corinthians*, so much praised by the ancients. Irenaeus calls it "the most sufficient writing" <note>original: "ἱκανωτάτη γραφὴ"</note>; <sup>b</sup> Eusebius says it is a "truly great and wonderful" <note>original: "μεγάλη τε καὶ θαυμασία"</note> Epistle; and Saint Jerome <sup>c</sup> adds that it is "very useful." Photius <sup>d</sup> titles it "noteworthy" <note>original: "ἀξιόλογος"</note>, worthy of all esteem and veneration; and Eusebius <sup>e</sup> assures us it was "universally acknowledged" <note>original: "ἀνωμολογημένη ὡς καὶ πᾶσα"</note>, received by all, and indeed reverenced by them next to the Holy Scriptures. Therefore, it was publicly read in their churches for some ages, even until his time, and perhaps for a long time after. The style of it (as <sup>f</sup> Photius truly observes) is very plain and simple, imitating an ecclesiastical and unaffected way of writing, which breathes the true spirit and character of the Apostolic Age. 

It was written on the occasion of a great schism <note>original: "Schism"; a formal division or split within a church.</note> and rebellion in the Church of Corinth, started by two or three factious persons against the governors of the church. These individuals, envying either the spiritual gifts or the authority and esteem of their guides and teachers, had attempted to depose them and had drawn the greatest part of the church into the conspiracy. Clement, therefore, endeavors by soft words and strong arguments to reduce them back to peace and unity. 

His modesty and humility in this letter are particularly noticeable—not only in that he writes it entirely in the name of the Church of Rome without ever mentioning his own name, but also in that he treats the Corinthians with such gentle and mild persuasions. Nothing of sourness or an imperious "lording it over God’s inheritance" <note>A reference to 1 Peter 5:3, criticizing leaders who rule by force.</note> is to be seen in the whole Epistle. Had he known himself to be the infallible judge of controversies, to whose sentence the whole Christian world was bound to submit—invested with a supreme, unaccountable power from which there was no appeal—we might have expected to hear him argue in a very different manner. But these were the infringements and usurpations of later ages, when a spirit of greed and worldly ambition had stifled the modesty and simplicity of those first and best ages of religion. 

There is so great a similarity in many things, both in words and matter, between this and the *Epistle to the Hebrews*, that it tempted Eusebius, Saint Jerome, and some others before them to conclude that Saint Clement was at least the translator of that Epistle. This *Epistle to the Corinthians*, after it had been generally mourned as lost for many ages, was published here in England about forty years ago <note>This refers to the 1633 publication of the *Codex Alexandrinus* by Patrick Young, which contained the text of Clement's epistle.</note>—a treasure not sufficiently to be valued, serving to the benefit of the church in general and the honor of our own church in particular. 

Besides this first letter, there is a fragment of a second Epistle, or rather a homily <note>original: "Homily"; a sermon or religious discourse.</note>, containing a serious exhortation and direction to a godly life. It is ancient indeed, and many would persuade us that it is his and was written many years before the first, as it shows no signs of troublesome and unquiet times. However, Eusebius, Saint Jerome, and Photius assure us that it was rejected and never obtained the same level of approval among the ancients as the first. Therefore, though we do not strictly rule against it being his, we think it safer to agree with the judgment of the ancients than with a few recent writers on this matter.

...fictitious and disowned (as Eusebius says) because they did not "preserve the pure character of apostolic orthodoxy" <note>original: "καθαρὸν τὸν ἀποστολικῆς ὀρθοδοξίας ἀποσώζειν χαρακτῆρα"</note>. Although, the truth is, he says this only of the *Dialogues of Peter and Appion*, not even mentioning the *Decretal Epistles* <note>Letters of early Popes later found to be forgeries.</note> as being not worth noticing. There are four works extant today that are attributed to him: the *Apostolical Canons* and the *Constitutions* (said to be written by him, though dictated by the Apostles), the *Recognitions*, and the *Epistle to St. James*. Regarding the first two, the *Apostolic Canons and Constitutions*, I have expressed my opinion on them elsewhere, to which I shall add nothing here. The *Recognitions* follow, which were passed down to us under different titles by the ancients: sometimes styled *St. Clement's Acts, History,* or *Chronicle*; sometimes *St. Peter’s Acts, Itinerary, Periods,* or *Dialogues with Appion*. All of these are unquestionably just different titles (or perhaps portions) of the same book. It is true, as **b** Photius suspected and **c** Rufinus (who translated it) expressly tells us, that there were two different editions of this book, differing in some things but the same in most. It deserves to be considered whether "the Clementines" <note>original: "τὰ Κλημέντια"</note> mentioned by **d** Nicephorus—which he says the Church received, denying they were the ones meant by Eusebius—and those *Clementine Homilies* lately published under that very name, are not that other edition of the *Recognitions*, since they exactly match Rufinus’s description, differing in some things but mostly agreeing with them. There is yet a third edition, or rather an abstract of them all, styled *Clement’s [work] concerning the Acts, Travels, and Preachings of St. Peter* <note>original: "Κλημέντος περὶ τῶν πράξεων"</note>, agreeing with the former, though keeping closer to the *Homilies* than the other. I suspect this was compiled by Simeon the Metaphrast, for several reasons, but especially because the addition joined to it by the same hand concerning Clement’s martyrdom is identical, word-for-word, with that of Metaphrastes, except for the conclusion, which is taken out of St. Ephrem’s homily on the miracle performed at his tomb.

XI. The *Recognitions* themselves are undoubtedly of very great antiquity, written about the same time and by the same hand (as Blondel likely conjectures) as the *Constitutions*, around the year 180 AD or not long after. I am certain they are cited by **f** Origen as the work of Clement in his *Periods* (or Travels), and his large quotation is found word-for-word in them today. Furthermore, before him, we find a very long **h** fragment of Bardesanes the Syrian (who flourished around 180 AD) concerning *Fate*, which is word-for-word the same as what we find in the *Recognitions*; it seems just as reasonable to suppose that Bardesanes took it from there as it is to think the other author borrowed it from him. Indeed, what if Bardesanes himself was the author of these books? It is certain that he was a man of great talent and learning, quick and eloquent, "and a most skilled debater" <note>original: "καὶ διαλεκτικώτατος"</note>. He was heretically inclined, for he came out of the school of Valentinus, whose strange notions he had so deeply absorbed that even after his recantation, he could never fully clear himself of their remnants, as Eusebius informs us. However, Epiphanius tells us he was originally Orthodox and later fell into the errors of that sect, like a well-loaded ship that, after performing its voyage, is shipwrecked in the very sight of the harbor. He was a great mathematician and astrologer, "having reached the height of Chaldean knowledge" <note>original: "ἐπ’ ἄκρον τῆς Χαλδαϊκῆς ἐπιστήμης ἐληλακώς"</note>, meaning he was accurately versed in Chaldean learning, and wrote incomparable *Dialogues* concerning Fate...

And surely no one can have looked into the *Recognitions* without seeing that a significant portion of the dialogues and discourses between St. Peter and St. Clement involves doctrines concerning *Fate*, the *Genesis* <note>original: "Genesis" — here referring to the astrological influence of one's birth</note>, the influence of the stars and heavenly constellations, and similar notions. The great variety of learning found within them plainly shows their composer to have been a master of all human learning and the study of philosophy. I might further remark that Bardesanes seems to have had a peculiar genius for books of this nature, as it was specifically noted **a** of him that, besides the Scriptures, he dealt in certain apocryphal writings. He wrote many compositions **b** <note>original: "πλεῖστα Συγγράμματα"</note>, which St. Jerome translates as "infinite volumes." These were written for the most part in Syriac, but his students translated them into Greek, though he himself was sufficiently skilled in that language, as Epiphanius notes. Among these books might have been the *Recognitions*, plausibly attributed to St. Clement, who was well known to be St. Peter's companion and disciple. If more of Bardesanes' many books were extant today, I have no doubt that a much greater similarity in both style and ideas would appear between them. However, I propose this only as a probable conjecture and leave it to the reader's pleasure to either reject or accept it. 

I am not ignorant that both **c** St. Jerome and **d** Photius charge these books with heretical opinions, especially some that are derogatory to the honor of the Son of God. It may be that Rufinus (who **e** confesses the same thing and supposes them to have been inserted by some heretical hand) concealed these in his translation. Indeed, **f** Epiphanius tells us that the Ebionites <note>A Jewish Christian sect that emphasized Jewish law and often held a non-divine view of Jesus</note> so extremely corrupted the books that they left almost nothing of St. Clement's sound and true teachings in them. He observes this from their contradiction to Clement's other writings, those "Encyclical Epistles" <note>Letters intended for general circulation among churches</note> of his (as he calls them) which were read in the churches. But it is plain he means only those copies which were in the possession of those heretics, which are probably no longer extant. None of those particular alterations he says they made appear in our current books; nor in those large and certainly uncorrupted fragments of Bardesanes and Origen is there the slightest significant variation from the books we have today. But enough of this.

### XII.
The Epistle to St. James, the brother of our Lord, is undoubtedly of the same date as the rest. In its conclusion, the author pretends that he was commanded by St. Peter to give James an account of his travels, discourses, and the success of his ministry, under the title of *Clement’s Summary of Peter’s Popular Preachings*, to which he says he would next proceed. So, this Epistle was originally nothing but a preface to St. Peter's *Acts* or *Periods* (which are effectively the same as the *Recognitions*). Accordingly, in the recent edition of the *Clementine Homilies* (which bear the very title mentioned in that Epistle), it is found prefixed before them. This Epistle (as Photius tells us) varied according to different editions: sometimes claiming that it, and the account of St. Peter's *Acts* attached to it, were written by St. Peter himself and sent by him to St. James; and sometimes claiming they were written by Clement at St. Peter’s request and command. From this, Photius conjectures that there was a twofold edition...

There were editions of *Saint Peter’s Acts*, one said to be written by himself and the other by Clement. When, over time, the first was lost, the one attributed to Saint Clement remained. It would have been better if this were the only instance where certain men have tampered with the writers of the ancient Church to support a failing cause.

...the nature of the Rechabites. His *conversion* to *Christianity*. The relatives and family of our Savior met to discuss a fit successor to take his place. No one was thought suitable to be a candidate for the office except for one of our Lord's own relations. Accordingly, with one consent, they bestowed the honor upon **Simeon**, our Lord's next kinsman, whom they all judged most worthy of the position. I am aware that **Eusebius** <note>A 4th-century historian known as the "Father of Church History."</note> seems to suggest that this election was made not only after **St. James’s** death, but after the destruction of **Jerusalem**. Between those two events, there was a gap of no less than eight or nine years. 

However, it is very unreasonable to suppose that so famous and eminent a Church—a Church newly established and planted in the midst of the most bitter and deep-seated enemies—should be left without a guide and pastor for so long. This is especially true since the Apostles had all long since dispersed into various remote quarters of the world. Not to mention that most of the Apostles were dead before that time; or if they had not been, they could not have easily returned and met together for this business in such a gloomy and distracted state of things as the **Roman Wars** and the utter ruin and overthrow of the **Jewish Nation** had then created in those parts. 

<margin>* *Chronicle*, for the Year of Christ 62. <note>original: "Chron. ad Ann. Chr. LXII."</note></margin>
<margin>b Year 1 of the 212th Olympiad, 11th Indiction, 2nd year of Vespasian, p. 580. <note>original: "Ann. 1. Olympiad. CCXII. Indict. XI. Vespas. 2. p. 580."</note></margin>

Furthermore, **Eusebius** himself elsewhere places **Simeon’s** succession immediately after **St. James’s** martyrdom. Nor is any vacancy in that See <note>The office or jurisdiction of a bishop.</note> mentioned by any other writer. The <superscript>b</superscript> ***Chronicle of Alexandria*** places his succession in the year 69 AD. It tells us that in this year, **St. James** the Apostle and Patriarch of **Jerusalem** died, and **Simeon** (or **Simon**) was made Patriarch in his place. The *Chronicle* claims that **St. Peter**, at the time of his departure for **Rome** to establish his own See, had ordained **James** to that position. It is plain that the publisher of that text, for want of distinguishing the facts correctly, did not understand this passage. This account goes against the testimony of all the ancient writers, who state that **St. James** suffered martyrdom several years earlier. Nor do any of them say that he was ordained by **St. Peter**; many of them expressly affirm that he received his consecration directly from the hands of our Lord himself.

IV. How he managed the affairs of that Church is not distinctly known, as few particular accounts have been passed down to us. We may be confident that his presidency was filled with sufficient trouble and difficulty, not only from the malicious and turbulent temper of the people to whom he was continually exposed, but because it coincided with the darkest and most fatal period of the **Jewish** Church. For the sins of that nation were now ripe for vengeance. They had filled up the measure of their iniquities by their cruel usage of the Apostles and messengers of our Savior: their barbarous treatment of **St. Stephen**, and afterward of **St. James the Great** <note>James the son of Zebedee, one of the first apostles martyred.</note>, and their last bloody murder of **St. James the Less** <note>James the Just, the brother of the Lord and first Bishop of Jerusalem.</note>. But above all, they were judged for their insolent and merciless behavior toward the Son of God and the Savior of the world. Therefore, *the wrath of God came upon them to the uttermost*, and the **Romans** broke in upon them and *took away both their place and nation*. Because this history contains such remarkable examples of Providence—instances of severe displeasure toward a people who for so many ages had enjoyed the unique favor of God—and because their destruction so clearly justified the predictions of our Savior and paved the way for the honor and advancement of Christianity, we shall relate the summary of it here.

The Jews resented the tyranny of the **Roman Yoke** <note>A metaphor for the oppressive weight of Roman imperial rule.</note>, which seemed heavier on their necks than on those of other nations. This was because they considered themselves a more free-born people and were prideful of the great charters and immunities which Heaven had directly granted them. This made them willing to seize any opportunity to reclaim their ancient liberty. They attempted this most unitedly under the government of **Cestius Florus**, whom **Nero** had sent to be the Procurator <note>A Roman provincial governor, usually focused on financial and judicial management.</note> of that province. For two years straight, Florus practiced intolerable oppression and arrogant cruelties. Despite the people’s prayers and the pleas of powerful negotiators, he did not relent. Their patience was finally exhausted, and they broke out into open rebellion.

<margin>
b *ibid.* <note>original Latin for "in the same place," referring to Josephus.</note> chapter 15, page 809.
</margin>
The fatal conflict began first at **Caesarea**, and like lightning, it instantly spread across the whole nation until every place was full of blood and violence. Florus, unable to handle them himself, called for assistance from **Cestius Gallus**, the Governor of **Syria**. Gallus came from **Antioch** with an army, captured **Joppa** and some other places, and laid siege to **Jerusalem**. However, after all that effort, he was forced to retreat, and indeed to flee with his entire army, leaving all his military equipment and supplies behind him.

<margin>

d *ibid.* chapter 14, page 850. *Hegesippus* book 3, chapter 18, page 351.
e *ibid.* book 5, chapter 1, page 892.

The news of this failure was soon carried to Nero, who was then staying in **Achaia** (Greece). He immediately dispatched **Vespasian**—a man of wise conduct and proven courage, and the best commander of his time—to be General of the army. Arriving in Syria, Vespasian united the Roman forces and invaded **Galilee**. He burned **Gadara** and destroyed **Jotapata**, where the historian **Josephus** himself was taken prisoner. Vespasian pursued his conquests with tireless diligence, with victory following his sword everywhere. He was preparing to besiege Jerusalem when he heard of the chaos in **Italy** following the death of Nero and the illegal seizures of power by **Galba**, **Otho**, and **Vitellius**. He decided to return to **Rome** to free it from the unhappy troubles that burdened it. His decision was so highly praised by the army that they immediately proclaimed him Emperor. He then hurried to **Egypt** to secure that country, which was a location of vital importance to the Empire.

VI. From **Alexandria**, Vespasian sent his son **Titus** back into **Judea** to continue the war. Titus thought no way was quicker to bring the war to an end than to attack the capital city, to strike at Jerusalem itself. Accordingly, he made everything ready to begin the siege.

<margin>
g *ibid.* book 6, chapter 1, page 904. chapter 12, page 910.
h *ibid.* book 6, chapter 13, page 936.
</margin>
The state of Jerusalem at this time was very grim. That place, whose honor and security once rested on being a *city at unity within itself*, was now torn to pieces by internal factions. How unlikely is a kingdom to stand for long when it is divided against itself? **Simon, the son of Giora**, a bold and ambitious man, had taken control of the Upper City. **John**, who headed the **Zealots** (an arrogant and unruly group), commanded the lower parts and the outer areas of the **Temple**. The inner parts of the Temple were secured by **Eleazar, the son of Simon**, who had won over a considerable number of soldiers to his side. All of these groups were constantly quarreling with and opposing one another. As Titus’s army approached just before the **Passover festival** <note>original: "Paschal Solemnity"</note>, he surrounded the city. Gradually drawing it into a tighter siege, he strictly blocked all exits and paths of escape. He built a wall thirty-nine furlongs long <note>Approximately 4.8 miles or 7.8 kilometers.</note>, which he reinforced with thirteen forts. The Christians universally withdrew themselves and seasonably retreated there, as if to a little *Zoar* <note>In the Bible, Zoar was the small town where Lot found refuge from the fire that destroyed Sodom.</note> from the flames of *Sodom*, and so not one of them perished in the common ruin. It likely derived its name from *Pella*, a city in *Macedonia*, having been founded and peopled by the *Macedonians* from *Alexander the Great's* army who settled in *Asia*. It is plain that its inhabitants were *Gentiles* <note>Non-Jews</note>, because the ᵃ *Jews* under their king, *Alexander Jannaeus*, sacked the city because the residents would not adopt the rites of the Jewish religion. It seems that God purposefully directed the Christians here so they would be out of the reach of the *besom of destruction* <note>original: "Besom of Destruction" (a broom used for sweeping; a metaphor for total cleansing or divine judgment)</note> that was to sweep away the *Jews* wherever it came. 

Nor was it a less remarkable instance of the care and tenderness of Divine Providence over them that when *Cestius Gallus* had besieged *Jerusalem*, he unexpectedly broke off the siege. This gave them both a warning of their danger and an opportunity to escape. How long *Simeon* and the Church continued in this little sanctuary, and when they returned to *Jerusalem*, is not known. If I might venture a guess, I would place their return at the beginning of *Trajan's* reign, when the fear had sufficiently subsided and the hatred and severity of the *Romans* had eased, allowing them to return with more safety. 

It is certain that they returned before the time of ᵇ *Hadrian*, who—forty-seven years after the devastation—came to *Jerusalem* to oversee its repair. He found there a few houses and a small Christian church built upon *Mount Sion*, in the very place where that *Upper Room* was located, into which the disciples went after they returned from our Lord’s Ascension. Here, the Christians who had returned from *Pella* held their solemn assemblies. They were so renowned for the flourishing state of their religion and the prominence of their miracles that *Aquila*, the Emperor's kinsman (whom Hadrian had made governor and overseer of the city's rebuilding), was convinced and embraced Christianity. However, because he continued to pursue his old magical and astrological studies despite frequent warnings, he was cast out of the church. He resented this as such a great insult that he abandoned the faith <note>original: "apostatized"</note> for *Judaism* and afterwards translated the Bible into *Greek*. 

But to return to *Simeon*: we may be confident that he administered his province with all diligence and faithfulness. In the discharge of his duties, God was pleased to preserve him as a person highly useful to His church until a very great age, late into the middle of *Trajan's* reign. At that time, he was brought to give his last testimony for his religion, based on a very thin pretense.

I. FINDING nothing recorded concerning the country or parentage of this holy man, I shall not build upon mere fancy and conjecture. He is ordinarily styled, both by himself and others, *Theophorus*. Although, like *Justus*, it is often no more than a common epithet, it is sometimes used as a proper name. It is written according to different accents: either *Theophóros* <note>original: Θεοφόρος</note>, which denotes a divine person—a man whose soul is full of God and all holy and divine qualities ("one who carries Christ in his soul" <note>original: ὁ τὸν Χριστὸν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ περιφέρων</note>, as Ignatius himself is said to explain it); or *Theóphoros* <note>original: Θεόφορος</note>, which in a passive sense implies one who is carried by God. In this latter sense, he is said to have derived the title from our Lord taking him up into His arms.

<margin>
Mark 9:36.
Matt. 18:2, 3, 4.

^b Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 2, ch. 35, p. 192.
^c [Note missing in margin]
^d Annotations on the *Acts of Ignatius*, p. 37.
^e Chrysostom, *Homily on St. Ignatius*, p. 506, Vol. 1.
</margin>
For we are told that he was that very *child* whom our Savior took into His arms and set in the midst of His disciples as the most vivid example of innocence and humility. This is affirmed (if numbers were enough to prove it) not only by the ^a Greeks in their public rituals, by ^b Metaphrastes, Nicephorus, and others, but also (as the Primate of Armagh <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), a famous scholar and Archbishop.</note> ^c observes from the manuscripts in his own possession) by two ^d Syriac writers more ancient than they. ...more secret and uncommon mysteries. While it is probable that he refers to his private conversations with St. Peter and Paul, some of the aforementioned authors—and not only they, but also the <margin>a Acts of Ignatius, p. 1, ch. 5. Edited by Ussher.</margin> *Acts of his Martyrdom* (supposedly written by those present)—further assure us that he was St. John's disciple. 

Being fully instructed in the doctrines of Christianity, his eminent talents and the great piety of his life led to him being chosen as Bishop of Antioch, the capital <note>original: "Metropolis"</note> of Syria and the most famous and renowned city of the East. Antioch was no more remarkable among secular <note>original: "Foreign"</note> writers for being the Eastern seat of the Roman Emperors and their governors than it is in church history for its early embrace of the Christian faith. It was here that the venerable title of *Christians* was first given to the disciples of the Holy Jesus, and it was St. Peter's first and special residence. For these reasons, the Synod of <margin>b According to Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History, book 5, ch. 9, p. 211.</margin> Constantinople, assembled under Nectarius, deservedly called it the *most ancient and truly Apostolic Church of Antioch, in which the honorable name of Christians first began* in their synodical letter to the Western bishops. In all these respects, it is frequently styled in church writings by the honorary title of <term>Theopolis</term> <note>original Greek: Θεόπολις</note>, or the *City of God*. 

That Ignatius was appointed Bishop of this church is universally accepted, though regarding the time and order of his arrival, almost the same difficulties arise as did with the succession of Clement to the See of Rome. These may not be easily resolved except by the same explanation readily granted in this case by <margin>* At the year 45, no. 14. See Roman Martyrology, February 1, p. 88.</margin> Cardinal Baronius himself and other notable writers of that Church. I do not need to prove what is evident in itself and clearly acknowledged by the ancients: that Peter and Paul established Christianity in this city, and both contributed to the foundation of this church—one reaching out to the Jews, the other to the Gentiles. The "vineyard" was certainly large enough to require the joint efforts of these two great planters of the Gospel, as it was a vast and populous city containing, according to St. Chrysostom's estimation, no fewer than 200,000 souls. But because the Apostles could not stay in one place forever, as they were called to the ministry of other churches, they found it necessary to appoint others in their place; one resigned his trust to Euodius, and the other to Ignatius. 

Therefore, in the <margin>c Book 7, ch. 47, p. 451.</margin> *Apostolic Constitutions*, Euodius is said to have been ordained Bishop of Antioch by St. Peter, and Ignatius by St. Paul. Upon the death of Euodius, and as the Jewish converts became better reconciled with the Gentiles, Ignatius took over the sole care and presidency of that church, in which he might possibly have been later confirmed by Peter himself. This is likely what the author of the <margin>d At the year of Tiberius XIX, p. 526.</margin> *Alexandrine Chronicle* meant when he stated that Ignatius was appointed Bishop of Antioch by the Apostles. In this way, he can be said to both immediately succeed the Apostle (as <margin>e Origen, Homily 6 on Luke, p. 214. f Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, ch. 36, p. 106. g Athanasius, On the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia, p. 922. h Chrysostom, in the location cited, p. 500. i Jerome, On Illustrious Men, regarding Ignatius. k Socrates, Ecclesiastical History, book 6, ch. 8, p. 313.</margin> Origen, Eusebius, Athanasius, and Chrysostom affirm) and also to be the one following Euodius (as St. Jerome, Socrates, Metaphrastes, and others place him). Regardless, since Euodius died and Ignatius was established by the hands of the Apostles, he might justly be said to succeed St. Peter. It is in this sense that some of the ancients expressly claim he received his consecration from St. Peter; "he received the grace of the high priesthood through the right hand of the great Peter," says <margin>m On the Unchangeable, Dialogue 1, p. 33, Vol. 4.</margin> Theodoret <note>original Greek: διὰ τῆς τοῦ μεγάλου Πέτρου δεξιᾶς τῆς ἀρχιερωσύνης τὴν χάριν ἐδέξατο</note>. III. For over forty years, **St. Ignatius** continued in his charge at **Antioch**. (Nicephorus, the Patriarch of Constantinople, assigns him only four years, but the Greek figure "μ" <note>The Greek letter 'mu' (μ) represents the number 40; the author suggests a scribe's error turned 40 years into 4.</note> for forty was probably omitted from the account through the carelessness of transcribers.) He served in the midst of very stormy and tempestuous times. Yet, like a wise and prudent pilot, he sat at the helm and avoided the dangers that threatened them through his prayers and tears, his fastings, the constancy of his preaching, and the tireless pains he took among his people. He feared that any of the more weak and unsettled Christians might be overwhelmed by the storms of persecution. Whenever a brief period of calm and quiet occurred, he rejoiced in the prosperity of the Church. As for himself, however, he somewhat impatiently expected and longed for martyrdom. Without it, he believed he could never perfectly attain the love of Christ, nor fulfill the duties and measures of a true disciple—a martyrdom which, accordingly, later became his portion.

Indeed, regarding the specific acts of his government, nothing memorable is recorded of him in the ancient records of the Church, other than what $^b$ Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century church historian</note> relates (by what authority, I confess, I do not know). Socrates says that Ignatius saw a vision in which he heard the angels celebrating the honor of the Holy Trinity with alternate hymns. In imitation of this, he instituted the practice of **antiphonal** <note>original: "Antiphonal" — a style of singing where two groups or choirs respond to one another</note> hymns in the Church of Antioch, which then spread throughout the entire Christian Church. Whether this story was made up on purpose to compete with the **Arians** <note>original: "Arrians" — followers of a theological doctrine deemed heretical that prompted many early church debates</note>—who used to sing alternating hymns in their congregations on the Saturdays and Sundays with sharp reflections against the Orthodox, so much so that Chrysostom was forced to introduce the same way of singing into the Orthodox assemblies—or whether it was really instituted by Ignatius but later fell out of use, I will not say. 

It is certain that Flavianus, later Bishop of Antioch in the reign of Constantius, is $^a$ said to have been the first to establish the choir in this way and to appoint David’s Psalms to be sung by turns, a practice which then spread to other churches. **St. Ambrose** was the first who brought it into the Western Church, reviving (says the $^d$ historian) the ancient institution of Ignatius that had long been disused among the Greeks. But to return to the story.

<margin>$^e$ Acts [of Ignatius], in the same place, page 2.</margin>
<margin>$^f$ Acts of Ignatius, section 3.</margin>

IV. IT was about the year of Christ 107 when **Trajan** the Emperor, swelled with pride from his recent victory over the **Scythians** and the **Dacians**, came to Antioch in the ninth year of his reign to prepare for the war he was resolved to wage against the **Parthians** and **Armenians**. He entered the city with the pomp and ceremony of a Roman triumph. As his first care was usually for religious matters, he immediately began to inquire into that affair. Indeed, he $^e$ looked upon it as an insult to his other victories to be conquered by Christians. Therefore, to make this religion submit, he had already begun a persecution against them in other parts of the Empire, which he resolved to carry on here. **St. Ignatius** (whose concern for the good of his flock made him continually stand on his guard) thought it more prudent to go himself than to stay and be sent for. Of his own $^f$ accord, he presented himself to the Emperor. A long and detailed conversation is said to have passed between them, with the Emperor wondering how he dared to transgress his laws, while the good man asserted his own innocence...

...innocency, and the power which God had given them over evil spirits, and that the gods of the **Gentiles** <note>Non-Christians, specifically those practicing Greco-Roman polytheism.</note> were no better than **demons** <note>original: "Dæmons"</note>, there being but one supreme deity, who made the world, and his only begotten Son **Jesus Christ**, who though crucified under **Pilate**, had yet destroyed him that had the power of sin, that is, the Devil, and would ruin the whole power and empire of the demons, and tread it under the feet of those who carried God in their hearts. The result was that he was cast into prison, where (if what the <margin>On the 27th day of the month of August.</margin> **Greek** Rituals and some others report is true) he was, for the constancy and resolution of his profession, subjected to the most severe and merciless torments. He was whipped with *plumbatæ* <note>original: *Plumbatæ*; scourges with leaden bullets at the end of them</note>, forced to hold fire in his hands while his sides were burnt with papers dipped in oil, his feet stood upon live coals, and his flesh was torn off with burning pincers. Having by an invincible patience overcome the malice and cruelty of his tormentors, the Emperor pronounced the <margin>Acts of the Martyr, page 4.</margin> final sentence upon him: that being incurably consumed by superstition, he should be carried bound by soldiers to **Rome**, and there thrown as a prey to wild beasts. The good man heartily rejoiced at the fatal decree. "I thank you, O Lord," said he, "that you have condescended thus perfectly to honor me with your love, and have thought me worthy, along with your Apostle **Paul**, to be bound with iron chains." With that, he cheerfully embraced his chains, and having fervently prayed for his Church, and with tears recommended it to divine care and providence, he delivered himself into the hands of his keepers, who were appointed to transport him to the place of execution.

V. It may justly seem strange, and it was something that puzzled the great **Scaliger** <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a leading scholar of the Renaissance known for his work on historical chronology.</note>, why he should be sent such a vast distance from **Antioch** in **Syria** to <margin>Observations on the Chronicle of Eusebius, page 207.</margin> be martyred at **Rome**. Of this, several probable accounts may be given. First, it was usual for the governors of provinces, where the criminals were more than ordinarily eminent—either for the quality of their persons or the nature of their crimes—to send them to **Rome**, so that their punishment might be made an example in the eyes of the world. Secondly, his enemies were not willing that he should suffer at home, where he was already too much honored and esteemed, and where his death would only raise him to a higher veneration among the people and settle their minds in a firmer belief of that faith which he had taught them, and which they then saw him sealing with his blood. Thirdly, by such a long journey, they hoped that in all places where he went, men would be more effectively terrified from embracing that religion which they saw so much disliked and resented by the Emperor, and the profession of which could not be bought but at such a heavy price. Additionally, there was the probability that by this treatment the constancy of **Ignatius** himself might be broken and he might be forced to yield. Fourthly, they designed to make the good man’s punishment as severe and heavy as they could, and therefore so contrived it that there might be a combination of circumstances to render it bitter and grievous to him: his great age (being then probably over eighty years old), the vast length and tediousness of the journey (which was not a little increased by "the longer circuits of the route" <note>original Greek: μακρότεροι δίαυλοι τοῦ δρόμου</note>, as <margin>Homily cited, page 504.</margin> **St. Chrysostom** observes, for they did not take the direct passage to **Rome**, but by infinite windings diverted from place to place), and the trouble and difficulty of the passage—bad at all times, but much worse...

His situation was made worse now in winter by the lack of all necessary conveniences and accommodations for such an aged and infirm person. He also faced the rude and merciless treatment of his keepers, who treated him with total harshness and inhumanity. As he himself complained: *"From Syria even to Rome, both by sea and land, I fight with beasts; night and day I am chained to ten leopards (meaning my military guard), who, the kinder I am to them, the more cruel and fierce they are to me."* Besides what was dearer to him than all this, his credit and reputation might be in danger of suffering. At such a great distance, the **Romans** were generally more likely to believe he suffered as a criminal for some notorious crime, rather than as a martyr for religion. <margin>b Acts of the Martyrdom, as cited above, page 995.</margin> **Metaphrastes** <note>original: *Metaphrastes*; referring to Symeon Metaphrastes, a 10th-century Byzantine author who compiled the lives of saints.</note> assures us this was one particular reason for his being sent there. 

Furthermore, Divine Providence—which knows how to bring good out of evil and overrule the plans of bad men for wise and excellent purposes—might have permitted it to be so for several reasons. First, that leading him so far in triumph might make the Faith more remarkable and illustrious. Second, that he might <margin>See Chrysostom's Sermon, cited page 505.</margin> have a better opportunity to establish and confirm the Christians who flocked to him from all parts as he traveled along. By giving them the example of a generous virtue, he armed them with a stronger resolution to die for their religion. Especially, it allowed him to seal the truth of his religion at **Rome**, where his death might be <margin>Ibid.</margin> a "teacher of piety" <note>original: *didaskalos tēs eusebeias*</note> (as **Chrysostom** <note>St. John Chrysostom, an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> speaks), and teach the city that was so famous for arts and wisdom a "new and better philosophy" <note>original: *kakeinō philosophian*</note> than they had learned before. 

To all this may be added that this was not done by the provincial governor—who did indeed have the power of executing capital punishments within his own province (which seems to have been the main ground of **Scaliger’s** <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a 16th-century scholar who questioned the historical details of Ignatius's journey.</note> doubt)—but immediately by the Emperor himself. It was his pleasure and command that Ignatius should be sent to **Rome**, where we must now follow him to his martyrdom. In this account, we shall mainly follow the *Acts of the Martyrdom*, written in all probability by **Philo** and **Agathopus**, the companions of his journey who were present at his death. Two ancient versions of these records were first recovered and published to the world by the incomparable Bishop **Usher** <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh and a famous scholar of church history.</note>.

VI. Being consigned to a guard of ten soldiers, he took his leave of his beloved **Antioch**. There was no doubt a sad parting between him and his people, who were to see his face no more. He was conducted on foot to **Seleucia**, a port town of **Syria** about sixteen miles away—the very place from which **Paul** and **Barnabas** set sail for **Cyprus**. No sooner were they set on shore than he went to greet **St. Polycarp**, the bishop of that place and his old fellow-pupil under **St. John** the Apostle. Joyful was the meeting of these two holy men. **St. Polycarp** was so far from being discouraged that he rejoiced in the other's chains and earnestly urged him to a firm and final perseverance. People from the surrounding country came here, especially the bishops, priests <note>original: "Presbyters"</note>, and deacons of the **Asian** churches, to behold such a venerable sight, to receive the holy martyr's prayers and blessing, and to encourage him to hold on to his final sacrifice <note>original: "consummation"</note>. VII. His guards, becoming somewhat impatient with their stay at **Smyrna**, set sail for **Troas**, a well-known city in **Lesser Phrygia** not far from the ruins of ancient **Troy**. Upon arrival, he was greatly refreshed by the news that the persecution had ended in the Church of **Antioch**. However, some very learned men believe—though certainly without any good reason—that this was not a separate letter from the previous one, but was addressed to both **St. Polycarp** and his Church of **Smyrna** together. Regardless, they conclude it is certain that the version of the Letter to **St. Polycarp** currently in existence is not the original, as it lacks the true character and spirit of **Ignatius**, while others of great reputation argue quite convincingly that it is genuine and authentic. From there, they directed their course through the **Tyrrhenian Sea** to **Puteoli**. **Ignatius** wished—if it could have been granted—to have traveled from there by land so that he could follow the same path **St. Paul** took to **Rome**. After staying a day and a night at **Puteoli**, a favorable wind quickly carried them to the **Roman** port near **Ostia** at the mouth of the **Tiber River**, about sixteen miles from **Rome**. This was the great harbor and station for the Roman navy. The holy martyr longed to arrive there, as eager to reach the end of his life's race as his guards—weary of the voyage—were to reach the end of their journey.

Hoping that the people might be discouraged from desiring his death, he expressed a pious indignation, entreating them to place no obstacles <note>original: "rubs"</note> in his way, nor do anything that might hinder him, now that he was hastening toward his crown of martyrdom. So that his punishment might be more spectacular and public, one of their solemn festivals—the time of their **Saturnalia** <note>An ancient Roman festival in honor of the god Saturn, held in December</note>, and specifically the part of it when they celebrated their **Sigillaria** <note>The final days of the Saturnalia, characterized by the giving of small figurines as gifts</note>—was chosen for his execution. Accordingly, on the 13th of the **Kalends** of **January** (that is, **December 20**), he was brought out into the **Amphitheater**. Following his own fervent desire that he might have no other grave but the bellies of wild beasts, the lions were let loose upon him. He met the alarm of their roaring with no other concern than this: that as God's own grain, he should now be ground between the teeth of these wild beasts to become **pure bread** <note>original: "White Bread"</note> for his heavenly Master. The lions were not long in doing their work; they quickly finished their meal and left nothing behind but what they could not easily devour—a few hard and solid bones.
