X. Around this time, or a little before, while **Trajan** was still at **Antioch**, he stopped, or at least lessened, the persecution against Christians. This occurred because he had received an account from **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Younger, a Roman lawyer and author</note>, the Proconsul of **Bithynia** (whom he had employed for that purpose), concerning the innocence and simplicity of the Christians. Pliny reported that they were a harmless and inoffensive people. Trajan also recently received a letter from <margin>b *Extant in John Malalas, as cited above. See Ussher, Appendix to Ignatius, page 9; and Excerpts from John of Antioch, edited by Valesius, page 818.*</margin> $^b$ **Tiberianus**, the Governor of **Palestina Prima**, in which he stated that he was exhausted from enforcing the laws against the **Galileans** <note>A common derogatory term for Christians in the early Roman Empire</note>. Tiberianus noted that they crowded themselves in such large numbers for execution that he could not, through either persuasion or threats, keep them from identifying as Christians; he further requested His Majesty's advice in the matter. Consequently, Trajan gave a command that no search <note>original: "inquisition"</note> should be made for Christians, though if any of them offered themselves up, they should be executed. Thus, the fire that had previously blazed and burned openly began to die down, and only smoldered in private corners.

There are those who tell <margin>c *Symeon Metaphrastes, Martyrdom of Ignatius, cited in Cotelerius, page 1002.*</margin> $^c$ us that **Trajan**, having heard a full account of **Ignatius** and his sufferings, and how fearlessly he had undergone that bitter death, repented of what he had done and was particularly moved to soften and relax the persecution. Because of this (as **Metaphrastes** <note>Symeon Metaphrastes, a 10th-century Byzantine author and hagiographer</note> observes), not only Ignatius's life, but his very death became "the bringer of many good things" <note>original Greek: πολλῶν πρόξενος ἀγαθῶν</note>—namely, the cause of great peace and prosperity, and the glory and establishment of the Christian faith. Some suggest, quite plausibly, that the severe judgments which occurred not long after may have influenced the Emperor's mind toward more tenderness and pity for the remainder of his life. For during his stay at **Antioch**, there <margin>d *Dio Cassius, Roman History book 68; and Xiphilinus, Life of Trajan, pages 249-251. John Malalas, Chronographia book 10, as cited above.*</margin> were dreadful and unusual $^d$ earthquakes, fatal to other places, but which hit **Antioch** hardest. At that time, the city was filled more than usual with a vast army and a gathering of people from all parts of the world. Among thousands who died, and the far greater numbers who were maimed and wounded, **Pedo** the Consul lost his life, and **Trajan** himself would have met the same fate had he not escaped through a window. These accidents undoubtedly prepared his mind for a more serious consideration and regard of things, though these calamities did not happen until several years after **Ignatius's** death.

XI. Whether these judgments were immediate instances of divine displeasure for the severity used against the Christians, and particularly for their cruelty to **Ignatius**, I will not say. What is certain is that the Christian Church suffered a massive loss in such a useful and excellent person. For he was a good man, one in whose breast the true spirit of religion clearly lived. He was a man of very moderate and restrained <note>original: "mortified"</note> desires, and it was in this sense that he surely intended that famous saying, so celebrated by the ancient writers: "My Love is crucified" <note>original Greek: Ο ΕΜΟΣ ΕΡΩΣ ΕΣΤΑΥΡΩΤΑΙ</note>.

"...my *Love is crucified*," <note>This famous phrase from Ignatius's Epistle to the Romans is often interpreted as referring to Christ, though Ignatius clarifies here he means his worldly desires.</note> that is (as he explains in the very words that follow) his appetites and desires were crucified to the world, along with all its lusts and pleasures. We may, with ᵃ **St. Chrysostom**, consider him in a threefold capacity: as an *Apostle*, a *Bishop*, and a *Martyr*. As an *Apostle*—in the larger sense of the word, he being "the successor to the thrones of the Apostles" <note>original Greek: θρόνων διάδοχος τῶν Ἀποστόλων</note>, as the ᵇ **Greek** Church offices style him, the immediate successor of the Apostles in their See—he was careful to spread and propagate the genuine doctrine which he had received from the Apostles. He took a kind of universal care of all the churches; even on his journey to **Rome** he surveyed "the dioceses or churches belonging to all the cities" <note>original Greek: τὰς κατὰ πόλιν παροικίας</note> where he arrived, as ᶜ **Eusebius** tells us, confirming them by his sermons and exhortations, and directing Epistles to several of the principal ones for their further order and establishment in the faith. As a *Bishop*, he was a diligent, faithful, and industrious pastor, infinitely careful of his charge. Although it was exceedingly vast and numerous, he prudently instructed, governed, and supervised it for over forty years, even in the midst of uncertain and troublesome times. He had a true and unchangeable love for his people, and when he was forcibly taken from them for his martyrdom, there was no church to which he ᵈ wrote where he did not particularly beg their prayers to God for his church at **Antioch**. To some of them, he expressed a desire that they would send "a divine ambassador" <note>original Greek: θεοπρεσβευτήν</note> there specifically to comfort them and to congratulate them on their happy deliverance from persecution. Because he knew that the prosperity of the church and the good of souls were undermined as much by heresy from within as they were assaulted by violence and persecution from without, he kept a watchful eye on that threat. He took every opportunity to warn the church to beware of heretics and seducers—"beasts in the shape of men" <note>original Greek: τὰ θηρία τὰ ἀνθρωπόμορφα</note>, as he styles ᵉ them—whose wild notions and brutish manners began even then to debase religion and corrupt the simplicity of the faith. Indeed, he fully met all the requirements of a wise governor and an excellent guide of souls. ᶠ **St. Chrysostom** reviews the particular characteristics of a Bishop described by **St. Paul** and finds them all accomplished and fulfilled in him. With such generous care (says ᵍ he), and such exact diligence, did he preside over the flock of Christ, even to the point of fulfilling what our Lord describes "as the highest standard and rule of the office of a bishop" <note>original Greek: ὡς μέγιστον ὅρον καὶ κανόνα τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς</note>: to lay down his life for the sheep. This he did with all courage and fortitude, which is the last point we shall remark concerning him.

## XII.

AS a *Martyr*, he gave the highest testimony to his fidelity and to the truth of that religion which he both preached and practiced. He gloried in his sufferings as his honor and his privilege, and looked upon his chains—he calls ʰ them "spiritual pearls" <note>original Greek: τοὺς πνευματικοὺς μαργαρίτας</note>—as his jewels and ornaments. He was raised above either the love or fear of his current state and could, with as much ease and freedom (says ⁱ **Chrysostom**), lay down his life as another man could take off his clothes. The truth is, his soul was strangely inflamed with a desire for martyrdom; at every step of his journey, he wished to meet the wild beasts that were prepared for him. He tells the ᵏ **Romans** that he desired nothing more than for them to quickly do their work—that he would invite and court them to devour him speedily. And if he found them reluctant, as they had been...

If they [the wild beasts] had been hesitant toward others, he would provoke and force them. And though the death he was to undergo was most savage and barbarous, and presented in the most horrid and frightful forms—enough to startle even the firmest resolution—yet they could make no impression <gloss>a</gloss> because of his firm and adamantine soul <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἐπὶ στεῤῥᾶν & ἀδαμάντινον ψυχὴν</note> (as the **Greeks** say of him), any more than the crashing of a wave upon a rock of marble. "Let the fire," he said <gloss>*</gloss>, "and the cross, the assaults of wild beasts, the breaking of bones, the cutting of limbs, the battering of the whole body into pieces—yes, and all the torments which the Devil can invent—come upon me, so long as I may reach **Jesus Christ**." He professed that he thought it much better to die for Christ than to live and reign as the sole monarch of the world. These were certainly expressions of a mighty zeal and a divine passion raised to its highest pitch.

And yet, after all this, this excellent person was humble to the lowest level of abasement <note>original: "abasure"</note>. He often <gloss>b</gloss> professed that he looked upon himself as one born out of due time <note>original: "Abortive," a reference to St. Paul's self-description in 1 Corinthians 15:8</note>, and the very least of the faithful in the whole church of **Antioch**; and that although it was his greatest ambition, he did not know whether he was worthy to suffer for his religion. Finally, I might enter into a discussion concerning his *Epistles* (the true indicators <note>original: "Indices"</note> of the piety and divine temper of his mind). I mean those seven listed and quoted by **Eusebius** and collected by **Saint Polycarp**, as <gloss>c</gloss> Polycarp himself explicitly testifies. But I shall refrain, despairing to offer anything significant after so much has been said by learned men about them. I will only observe that, regarding the objections to the evidence from **Saint Polycarp's** testimony, little more is said even by those who have argued against it than what might be urged against the most genuine writing in the world. I add **Saint Polycarp's** description of these Epistles, by which he recommends them as highly useful and beneficial: that they contain "instructions and exhortations regarding faith and patience, and whatever is necessary to build us up in the religion of our Lord and Savior."

# I.

<image-desc>Decorative drop-cap 'S' set within a square woodcut border featuring floral and leafy patterns.</image-desc>POLYCARP was born toward the end of Nero's reign, or perhaps slightly earlier; his advanced age at the time of his death, along with other circumstances, makes this highly probable, if not certain. It is uncertain where he was born, and I see no sufficient reason why we may not place his birth <note>original: "Nativity"</note> at Smyrna, an eminent city of Ionia in Asia Minor. It was the first of the seven cities that claimed to be the birthplace of the <margin>a *Strabo, Geography, book 14, page 646.* <note>original: "Strab. Geograph. l. 14. p. 646."</note></margin> famous Homer. In his memory, they had a library and a square portico called the *Homereum*, with an adjacent temple and statue of Homer. They even used a type of bronze coin named the *Homereion* after him, which was likely stamped with his image. It was a place of great honor and <margin>THE MOST POWERFUL SENATE OF THE FIRST CITY OF ASIA, IN BEAUTY AND GREATNESS, AND THE MOST SPLENDID METROPOLIS OF ASIA, AND THE ORNAMENT OF IONIA, THE CITY OF THE SMYRNAEANS. <note>original Greek: "Η ΚΡΑΤΙΣΤΗ ΒΟΥΛΗ ΤΗΣ ΠΡΩΤΗΣ ΤΗΣ ΑΣΙΑΣ ΚΑΛΛΕΙ ΚΑΙ ΜΕΓΕΘΕΙ ΚΑΙ ΛΑΜΠΡΟΤΑΤΗΣ ΚΑΙ ΜΗΤΡΟ- ΠΟΛΕΩΣ ΤΗΣ ΑΣΙΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΚΟΣΜΟΥ ΤΗΣ ΙΩΝΙΑΣ ΣΜΥΡΝΑΙ- ΩΝ ΠΟΛΕΩΣ Marmor. Oxon. II. p 47. Eadem habet Marm. LXXVIII. p. 129. CXLIII. p. 277. Append. The Greeks, in their *Menæon* <note>A liturgical book used in the Eastern Orthodox Church containing the services for the fixed festivals of the year.</note>, report that he was educated at the expense of a certain noble matron named *Callisto*. She was a woman of great piety and charity. It is said that when she had emptied all her granaries in relieving the poor, they were suddenly filled again by Saint *Polycarp’s* prayers. The circumstances of this event are related more particularly by *Pionius* (who suffered martyrdom under the *Decian* persecution, though I strongly doubt it was the same man mentioned here) to this <gloss>*</gloss> effect: *Callisto*, warned by an angel in a dream, sent for and redeemed *Polycarp* (then only a child) from some men who were selling him. She brought him home, took care of his education, and finding him to be a youth of ripe and promising intellect, she made him the steward <note>original: "Major-domo"</note> of her house as he grew up. His charity, it seems, was dispensed with a very liberal hand, so much so that during her absence, he emptied all her barns and storehouses to serve the poor. For this, he was accused by his fellow servants upon her return. Not knowing at the time why he had used the supplies, she called for the keys and commanded him to resign his trust. No sooner was this done than she entered and found all the storehouses full, and in as good a condition as she had left them; his prayers and intercession with Heaven had replenished them. Indeed, Heaven is sometimes content to perform a miracle rather than let charity suffer for its own kindness and bounty. In his younger years, he is said to have been instructed in the Christian faith by *Bucolus*, whom the same <gloss>b</gloss> *Menæon* elsewhere informs us Saint *John* had consecrated as Bishop of *Smyrna*. However, <gloss>c</gloss> authors of more unquestionable credit and ancient date tell us that he was Saint *John’s* disciple. Not only that, but as <gloss>d</gloss> *Irenaeus*—who was his own student—assures us (and is followed in this by Saint *Jerome*), he was taught by the Apostles and spoke familiarly with many who had seen our Lord in the flesh.

II. BUCOLUS, the vigilant and industrious Bishop of *Smyrna*, having died (by whom Saint *Polycarp* was, as we are told, made a Deacon and Catechist <note>A teacher of the basic doctrines of the faith.</note> of that church, an office which he discharged with great diligence and success), <gloss>e</gloss> *Polycarp* was ordained in his place. This followed *Bucolus’s* own prediction; for, as the <gloss>f</gloss> *Greeks* report, he had foretold during his lifetime that Polycarp should be his successor. The <gloss>g</gloss> ancients generally say he was appointed by Saint *John*, though <gloss>h</gloss> *Irenaeus*, followed by the <gloss>i</gloss> *Chronicle* of *Alexandria*, affirms it was done by the *Apostles*. It is unclear whether he means any of the Apostles besides Saint *John* were then alive, or whether he means "Apostolic persons" (commonly styled Apostles in the early writings of the Church) who joined with Saint *John* in the consecration. <gloss>k</gloss> *Eusebius* says that *Polycarp* was familiarly acquainted with the Apostles and received the government of the Church of *Smyrna* from those who had been eyewitnesses and ministers of our Lord. It adds much to the honor of Saint *Polycarp*, and demonstrates his great diligence and concern for the good of souls, that (as we shall note more later) *Ignatius*, while passing to his martyrdom, wrote to him. *Ignatius* particularly recommended to him the inspection and oversight of his own Church at *Antioch*, knowing him, says <gloss>l</gloss> *Eusebius*, to be truly an Apostolic man, and being assured that he would use his utmost care and faithfulness in that matter. The <gloss>m</gloss> author of the *Alexandrian Chronicle* tells us that it was the Bishop of *Smyrna* (who could not well be any other than Saint *Polycarp*) to whom Saint *John* committed the care and education of the young man he took under his wing during his visitation. This was the same youth who later ran away and became the captain of a company of lawless and corrupt highwaymen, but was afterwards brought back and

# The Life of St. POLYCARP.

...and reclaimed by that Apostle <note>This refers to a famous story by Clement of Alexandria about a young man who became a bandit and was later "reclaimed" by the Apostle John. Some traditions associated the negligent bishop in that story with Polycarp.</note>. However, since **Clement of Alexandria**, who relates the story, <margin>a *In Eusebius, Book 3, chapter 23, page 92.* <note>original: "Ap. Euseb. l. 3. c. 23. p. 92."</note></margin> mentions neither the name of the bishop nor the city—though he confesses there were some who spoke of it—and since this circumstance is not noted by any other ancient writer, nor does such a neglect of duty seem consistent with **St. Polycarp’s** known care and industry, I shall leave the story as it is. 

Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that **Smyrna** was near **Ephesus** (as Clement says that city was) and that **St. John** seems to have had a more than ordinary regard for that Church. It was, next to Ephesus, the first of those seven famous **Asian Churches** to which he directed his Epistles <note>The letters to the seven churches in the Book of Revelation.</note>, and St. Polycarp was at this time its Bishop. It is not only highly probable, but according to a <margin>b *James Ussher's Introduction to the Letters of Ignatius, chapter 2, page 9.* <note>original: "Usser. Prolegom. ad Ignat. Epist. c. 2. p. 9."</note></margin> learned man, it is beyond all question, that he was the "**Angel of the Church of Smyrna**" <note>In the Book of Revelation, "Angel" is traditionally interpreted as the Bishop or presiding messenger of the church.</note> to whom that **Apocalyptic Letter** was sent. 

Indeed, the character and circumstances ascribed by St. John to the "Angel" of that Church seem to agree exactly with Polycarp, and with no other Bishop of that Church we read of in history from those times. Anyone who compares the account of **St. Polycarp’s Martyrdom** with the notices and hints the **Apocalypse** gives regarding that person’s sufferings and death will find that the prophecy and the actual events match perfectly. The strongest argument against this is the long duration of his presidency over that See <note>A "See" refers to the jurisdiction or diocese of a bishop.</note>. By this account, he must have served as Bishop for at least 74 years—from the end of **Domitian’s** reign (when the Apocalypse was written) to the persecution under **Marcus Aurelius**, when he suffered. The only solution needed for this is that his great, even extreme age at the time of his death makes it not at all improbable; especially considering that several centuries later, **Remigius**, Bishop of **Reims**, served as Bishop of that place for 74 years.

III. It was not many years after **St. John’s** death that the persecution under **Trajan** began to intensify, in which the **Eastern** regions suffered greatly. In AD 107, **Ignatius** was condemned by the Emperor at **Antioch** and sentenced to be transported to **Rome** for his execution. On his voyage there, he stopped at **Smyrna** to greet and speak with **Polycarp**. These holy men mutually comforted and encouraged each other, discussing the affairs of the Church. From Smyrna, Ignatius and his company sailed to **Troas**, from where he sent back a letter to the Church of Smyrna. 

In this letter, he attempted to strengthen them against the errors of the times that had crept in among them—especially against those who undermined our Lord’s humanity and denied his coming in the flesh, claiming instead that he suffered only in an imaginary and ghostly <note>original: "phantastic"</note> body <note>This refers to the heresy of Docetism, which claimed Christ only "seemed" to have a physical body.</note>. He severely censures and strongly refutes this opinion, as it deserved. Furthermore, he urged them to show proper respect and regard for their Bishop and the spiritual guides and ministers set over them. He also requested that they send a messenger specifically to the Church of **Antioch** to congratulate them on the peace and tranquility that was then beginning to be restored there. Besides this, he wrote specifically to **St. Polycarp**, whom he knew to be a man of apostolic character and singular faithfulness. He recommended the care and supervision of his grieving Church of Antioch to him. In the letter itself, which still exists today, there are many short and useful rules and precepts for living, especially those concerning the pastoral and episcopal office.

# The Life of St. POLYCARP.

And here again he renews his request concerning **Antioch**, asking that a messenger be sent from **Smyrna** to that church, and that **St. Polycarp** would write to other churches to do the same. This is something he would have done himself, had his hasty departure from **Troas** not prevented him. We find nothing more concerning Polycarp for many years after this, until some unfortunate differences in the Church brought him onto the public stage.

IV. It happened that the **Quartodeciman** controversy <note>From the Latin word for "fourteenth," this dispute concerned whether Easter should be celebrated on the 14th day of the Jewish month of Nisan, as in the East, or always on a Sunday, as in the West.</note> about the observation of **Easter** began to grow very intense between the **Eastern** and **Western** Churches. Each side stood very firmly upon its own way, justifying themselves by **Apostolic** practice and tradition. So that this fire might not break out into a greater flame, **St. Polycarp** <gloss>a</gloss> undertook a journey to **Rome** to intervene with those who were the main supports and champions of the opposite party and who gave life and spirit to the controversy. 

Though the exact time of his arrival cannot be precisely defined, it depends in great measure upon the succession of **Anicetus** to that See <note>The "See" refers to the jurisdiction or office of the Bishop of Rome.</note>, as it was during his time that Polycarp arrived. It is evident that almost all the ancient catalogs place Anicetus before **Soter** and next to **Pius**, whom he succeeded. **Eusebius** <gloss>b</gloss> places this succession in 154 AD—a calculation certainly much more accurate than that of **Baronius**, who places it in the year 167. Consistent with this, the **Chronicle of Alexandria** <gloss>c</gloss> places **St. Polycarp’s** arrival in **Rome** in 158 AD, during the 21st year of the Emperor **Antoninus**. 

It is true indeed that in two ancient catalogs of the **Bishops of Rome**, set down by **Optatus** <gloss>d</gloss> and **St. Augustine** <gloss>e</gloss>, Anicetus is listed before Pius and is made to immediately succeed **Hyginus**. By that account, his arrival must be moved fifteen years earlier, for Eusebius positively says that Pius held office for that long. And it seems to lean somewhat in this direction, because Eusebius, having given an account of the Emperor **Antoninus Pius’s** official decree <note>original: "Rescript" — a formal written reply from a Roman emperor.</note> in favor of the Christians (granted in his third consulship, around 140 AD), immediately adds <gloss>f</gloss> that around the time of the events spoken of, Anicetus governed the Church of Rome and Polycarp came there on this errand. The recent peace and indulgence granted to the Christians likely provided both the opportunity and encouragement for his journey. 

However, since this timeline contradicts Eusebius’s plain and positive account in other places, and since the most ancient catalogs—especially those of **Irenaeus** <gloss>g</gloss> and **Hegesippus** <gloss>h</gloss> (who both lived and were at Rome in the time of Anicetus himself)—constantly place Anicetus next after Pius, I dare not disturb this ancient and almost undisputed record of things until I can find better evidence. But whenever it was, he came over to Anicetus to confer with him about this affair. 

This makes me wonder all the more at the learned **Monsieur Valois** <gloss>i</gloss>, who with such stubborn confidence denies that Polycarp came to Rome for this purpose, claiming it was not the difference about the **Paschal** <note>Relating to Easter or Passover.</note> festival but some other controversies that brought him there. Yet the express words of **Irenaeus** <gloss>k</gloss> (if Eusebius represents them correctly) are that he came to Rome to confer and discourse with Anicetus, "because of a certain controversy concerning the day on which Easter was to be celebrated." <note>original: "διὰ δὲ ζήτημα περὶ τῆς τοῦ πάσχα ἡμέρας"</note> It is true he says <gloss>l</gloss> that they differed a little "about certain other things," <note>original: "περὶ ἄλλων τινῶν"</note> but this did not prevent the former from being the main errand and motivation for his voyage there—though even about that (as he adds), there was no great contention between them. # The Life of St. POLYCARP.

These holy and blessed souls knew that the essential and vital parts of religion were not tied to rituals and external practices, and so they mutually greeted and embraced each other. They could not convince one another to abandon their established customs; instead, they were content to hold their own views while maintaining the spirit of charity, which was the supreme and common law of their faith. To show this unity, they shared the Holy Sacrament together. As a mark of great honor, **Anicetus** allowed **St. Polycarp** to consecrate the Eucharist in his own church. Afterward, they parted in peace; though both sides retained their ancient rites, they maintained the peace and communion of the Church.

<margin>
a *The Synodicon, edited by Pappus; Greek edition, page 3. Councils, Volume 1, column 583, latest edition.*

The ancient *Synodicon* <note>A historical collection of the decrees of church councils.</note> tells us that a provincial synod was held at **Rome** regarding this matter by **Anicetus**, **Polycarp**, and ten other bishops. At this meeting, it was decreed that **Easter** should not be kept at the same time or following the rites and manners of the **Jews**, but should be celebrated "on that very glorious and great Lord’s day" <note>original: "αὐτῇ τῇ πανδόξῳ & μεγάλῃ κυριακῇ"</note> that followed it. However, it is improbable that **St. Polycarp** would have voted for such a decision, as we know he could not agree with **Anicetus** in this controversy and left **Rome** with the same judgment and practice he had when he arrived.

<margin>
b *Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 3, chapter 3, page 233; and in Eusebius, Book 4, chapter 14.*

V. During his stay at **Rome**, he mainly applied himself to convincing those who spoke against the faith, testifying to the truth of the doctrines he had received from the Apostles. Through this, he brought many back to the communion of the Church who had been infected and overcome with errors—especially the destructive heresies of **Marcion** and **Valentinus**. <note>Marcion and Valentinus were prominent 2nd-century leaders of Gnosticism, a movement the early Church condemned as heretical.</note>

When **Marcion** happened to meet him one day in the street, he resented the fact that Polycarp did not greet him. He called out, "**Polycarp**, recognize us!" The good man replied with righteous indignation, "I recognize you as the first-born of Satan."

<margin>

*A man who is a heretic, after the first and second admonition, reject; knowing that such a person is perverted and sinful, being self-condemned.*

Indeed, **St. Polycarp's** pious and devout mind was filled with a powerful zeal and a deep hatred for the poisonous and harmful principles that corrupted the simplicity of the Christian faith in those times. Whenever he heard anything of that nature, he was accustomed to immediately stop his ears and cry out:

He would immediately flee from the place where he had heard such talk. He showed the same dislike in all the letters he wrote to neighboring churches or individuals, warning them of errors and urging them to remain steadfast in the truth.

# The Life of St. POLYCARP. 117

<margin>a *Letter to Florinus, as cited above.*</margin>
He tells us elsewhere that in his youth, when he was with *St. Polycarp* in *Asia Minor* <note>original: "lesser Asia"</note>, he took such particular notice of things that he perfectly remembered the very place where he used to sit while he spoke, his movements, his physical appearance, his way of life, his sermons to the people, and the account he used to give of his close friendship with *St. John* and others who had seen our Lord. He rehearsed their sayings and whatever they had told him concerning our Savior, his miracles, and his teachings—all of which they had either seen or heard themselves, agreeing exactly with the accounts of the Holy Scriptures. *Irenaeus* tells us he took special notice of all this, faithfully treasured it in his mind, and made it part of his constant meditation. These are all the significant remarks found among the ancient writers concerning *Polycarp* during his time governing the Church at *Smyrna*. Indeed, several miracles and particular episodes of his life are related by the previously mentioned *Pionius*, which greatly exalt the honor of this holy man. But since that author is obscure and we have no reasonable assurance of who he was or where he got his information, I prefer to suspend my belief rather than entertain the reader with those (at best, uncertain) stories he has given us.

VI. In the reign of *Marcus Antoninus* <note>Better known today as Marcus Aurelius.</note> and *Lucius Verus*, a severe persecution began (whether it was the fourth or fifth, let others investigate) against the Christians. *Melito*, Bishop of *Sardis*, who lived at that time and dedicated his Apology to the Emperors, mentioned <margin>b *In Eusebius, Book 4, chapter 26, page 147.*</margin> "new edicts and decrees throughout Asia" <note>original: "καινὰ κτ’ Ἀσίαν δόγματα & διατάγματα"</note> which the Emperors had issued through *Asia*. By virtue of these, impudent and greedy informers harassed and robbed the innocent Christians. But the storm grew into a more violent tempest around the seventh year of their reign, AD 167, when the Emperor *Marcus Antoninus*, planning an expedition against the *Marcomanni* <note>A powerful Germanic tribal confederation that threatened the Roman Empire.</note>—the fear of whom had significantly <margin>c *Julius Capitolinus in the Life of Marcus Antoninus, chapter 13, page 181.*</margin> alarmed those in *Rome*—summoned the priests together and began more solemnly to celebrate their religious rites. No doubt he was told there was no better way to appease and reconcile the gods than to treat the Christians harshly, as they were generally viewed as the most open and hateful enemies of the gods. It was at this time that *St. Polycarp*, after a long and diligent performance of his duties in his episcopal office, received his crown of martyrdom. Later <margin>d *Greek Menology, February 23rd.*</margin> Greek writers are vastly wide of the mark, stating in their public services that he suffered martyrdom during the *Decian* persecution <note>Under Emperor Decius, c. 250 AD.</note>. Nor is *Socrates* <margin>e *Ecclesiastical History, Book 5, chapter 22, page 284.*</note> any closer to the truth (however he fell into the error) when he tells us that he was martyred under *Gordian*. Such mistakes are so extravagant that they need only be mentioned to be refuted. Regarding his sufferings and martyrdom, we have a full and detailed account in a letter from the Church of *Smyrna*, written not long after his death to the Church of *Philomelium* (or more correctly, *Philadelphia*). It was written as a circular letter to all the dioceses <note>original: "παροικίαις" (parishes)</note> of the Holy Catholic Church. The vast majority of it was included by *Eusebius* in his History, leaving out only the beginning and the end, although the entire letter, along with its ancient translation (or rather paraphrase), has since been published by Bishop *Ussher*. It was written by *Euaristus* and later (as seen by the various signatures at the end) transcribed from *Irenaeus’s* copy by *Caius*,

<margin>

VII. THE persecution grew intense at <margin>b</margin> *Smyrna*, and many had already sealed their faith with their lives. The general outcry was, "*Away with the godless!*" <note>original: "impious," meaning those who did not worship the Roman gods</note> (or the "*atheists*," as they commonly called and considered the Christians); "*let Polycarp be found!*" The good man was not disturbed by the news but resolved to face the danger. However, his friends—knowing his exceptional usefulness and that our Lord had allowed his disciples to flee to another city when persecuted in one—prevailed upon him to withdraw to a neighboring village. There, with a few companions, he continued day and night in prayer, earnestly interceding with Heaven (as had always been his custom) for the peace and tranquility of all the churches in the world. Three days before his arrest, while praying at night, he fell into a trance and dreamed that his pillow was on fire and burned to ashes. When he woke, he told his friends this was a prophetic sign that he would be burned alive for the cause of Christ. Meanwhile, he was being hunted everywhere. Upon learning this, his friends persuaded him to retreat to another village. He had no sooner arrived than his enemies were nearby; they seized a couple of youths and, by beating one of them, forced a confession of Polycarp's location. They were then led to his lodging. Entering the house in the evening, they found him in bed in an upstairs room. Although he had received advance notice of their coming and could have easily saved himself by slipping into another house, he refused, saying, "*The will of the Lord be done*." Understanding his persecutors were there, he came down and greeted them with a very cheerful and gentle expression. Those who had not known him before were astonished to see such a venerable person of such great age, with so grave and composed a presence; they wondered why there was so much effort to hunt and capture this poor old man. Not at all concerned, Polycarp ordered a table to be spread and food to be set out, inviting them to eat. He requested only that he might have one hour for prayer. Permission being granted, he stood and began his devotions. He was so powerfully assisted by divine grace that he continued praying for nearly two hours, heartily recommending to God the cases of all his friends and acquaintances—whether great or small, honorable or humble—and the state of the universal <note>original: "Catholic"</note> Church throughout the world. All who heard him were astonished, and many of them now repented that such a divine and venerable old man should be put to death.

This *Herod* was an <term>Irenarcha</term> <note>A "Peace-keeper" or "Justice of the Peace" in the Roman provincial administration.</note>, one of those "to whom the vigilance of protecting the public peace belonged," <note>original: "ad quos tuendæ publicæ Pacis vigilantia pertinebat"</note> as <sup>a</sup> *St. Augustine* describes them. Their office was mostly the same as that of our modern *Justices of the Peace*, as they were appointed to guard the provinces and to secure public peace and quiet within their several jurisdictions. They were tasked with preventing and suppressing riots, disturbances, robberies, and thefts; they also inquired into the associates and accomplices of such persons and transmitted the examinations and notices they received to the magistrates.

They were appointed either by the Emperor himself, the <term>Praetorian Prefects</term> <note>High-ranking administrative and military officials.</note>, or the <term>Decurions</term> <note>City councilors.</note>. At this time, the custom in the provinces of *Asia Minor* was for every city to annually send ten names of their principal citizens to the Governor of the Province, who then chose one to be the <term>Irenarcha</term>, the Keeper or Justice of the Peace.

Because they were later found to be oppressive and troublesome to the people, the office was abolished by a law of the younger <sup>c</sup> *Theodosius*, though the position remained under another name. This office at *Smyrna* was at this time managed by this *Herod*, whom <sup>d</sup> *Baronius* conjectures to be *Herodes Atticus*, a man of consular dignity and of great learning and eloquence who had been a tutor to the current Emperor. <sup>e</sup> It is certain that this *Herod* governed in the free cities of <sup>f</sup> *Asia* and resided sometimes at *Smyrna*. However, it weakens the conjecture that the name of that *Herod's* father was *Atticus*, while this man's was *Nicetes*, unless we suppose him to have had two names. But whoever he was, he was a great enemy to *Polycarp*. Meeting him on the way, he took him up into his chariot, where both he and his father sought to undermine his constancy with persuasive suggestions. They asked him what great harm there was in saying, "*Caesar is Lord*," and in sacrificing, by which means he might escape. This was a common way of testing Christians; it was not that they had any hesitation to acknowledge the Emperor as their *Lord* (none were more eager to show all due subjection and reverence to princes), but because they knew that the *Romans*, too prone to flatter the ambition of their Emperors into a foolishly claimed divinity, usually understood that title to mean God, as <sup>g</sup> *Tertullian* tells them. In any other sense of the word, they could as freely as anyone call him *Lord*, though, as he adds, even <sup>h</sup> *Augustus* himself modestly forbade that title to be applied to him.

IX. ST. POLYCARP returned no answer to their demand until they importunately urged him; then he replied that he would not comply with their persuasions at any price. Having failed in their goals, they now laid aside the *mask* of their pretended friendship and turned their kindness into scorn and insults. They thrust him out of the chariot with such violence that he bruised his thigh in the fall. Undaunted by this, as if he had received no injury, he cheerfully hastened on to the place of his execution under the conduct of his guard. </margin>
A shout was made, with everyone rejoicing that he had been captured. The <term>Proconsul</term> <note>A governor of a Roman province.</note> (whose name was *L. Statius Quadratus*)—who served as the Proconsul of *Asia* this very year, as *Aristides* the Orator, who lived at this time in *Smyrna*, informs us (having not long before been a Consul at *Rome*)—asked him whether he was *Polycarp*. When he confessed that he was, the Proconsul began to persuade him to recant. "Consider," said he, "your great age; swear by the <term>genius of Caesar</term> <note>The guardian spirit or divinity of the Emperor, which Romans were required to worship as a sign of loyalty.</note>, repent, and say with us, 'Away with the impious!'" These were "what was customary for them," <note>original: "ἃ συνήθες αὐτοῖς"</note> as my authors truly observe: their usual terms and proposals to Christians. The Christians stoutly refused to swear by the Emperor’s *genius*; upon this account, the Heathens generally slandered them as traitors and enemies to the State. To clear themselves of that charge, they openly professed <sup>a</sup> that although they could not swear by the *fortune* of the Emperor (as his "geniuses" were accounted deities, whom the Christians knew to be but <term>demons</term> <note>In this context, malevolent spirits or false gods.</note> and cast out at every opportunity), they nonetheless did not hesitate to swear by the Emperor’s *safety*—a thing more grand and sacred than all the *geniuses* in the world.

<margin>
<sup>b</sup> *Letter to the Emperor Trajan*, Letter 97, Book 10. <note>original: "Epist. ad Trajan. Imp. Ep. 97. l. 10."</note>
</margin>
X. THE Holy Martyr, looking about the stadium and beholding the crowd with a severe and angry countenance, beckoned to them with his hand, sighed, and looked up to Heaven, saying (though in quite a different sense than they intended), "Away with the impious!" <note>The Romans used "impious" to refer to Christians who did not worship their gods; Polycarp used the term to refer to the pagan crowd.</note> The Proconsul still persuaded him to swear, promising to release him and urging him to blaspheme *Christ*. They were accustomed to assault Christians with that temptation to test the sincerity of those who had supposedly abandoned their faith—a course which <sup>b</sup> *Pliny* tells us he observed toward apostate Christians, though he also confesses that none who were truly Christians could ever be brought to do it. The suggestion was met with a noble scorn and drew from *Polycarp* this generous confession: *"Eighty-six years I have served him, and he never did me any harm; how then shall I now blaspheme my King and my Savior?"* But nothing will satisfy a malicious, misguided zeal; the Proconsul still pressured him to swear by *Caesar’s genius*. To him, Polycarp replied, "Since you are so vainly ambitious that I should swear by the Emperor’s genius, as you call it, as if you did not know who I am, hear my free confession: I am a Christian. If you have a mind to learn the Christian Religion, appoint me a time, and I will instruct you in it." The Proconsul advised him to persuade the people; he answered, "To you I rather choose to address my discourse, for we are commanded by the laws of our religion to give to princes and the powers ordained of God all that due honor and reverence that is not prejudicial or contrary to the precepts of religion. As for them" (meaning the common crowd), "I think them not competent judges to whom I should defend or give an account of my faith."

XI. THE Proconsul now saw it was in vain to use any further persuasion and entreaties, and therefore turned to harsher arguments. "I have wild beasts at hand," said he, "to which I will cast you, unless you recant." "Call for them!" cried the Martyr, "for we are immutably resolved not to change the better for the worse, accounting it fit and proper only to turn from vice to virtue." "Since you make so light of wild beasts," added the Proconsul, "I have a fire that shall tame you, unless you repent." "You threaten me with a fire," answered *Polycarp*, "that burns for an hour and is soon extinguished; but you are ignorant, alas, of the fire of eternal damnation and the judgment to come, reserved for the wicked in the other world. But why do you delay? Bring forth whatever you have a mind to."

...and he spoke much more with a pleasant and cheerful confidence, and a divine grace was visible in his very expression; he was far from sinking cowardly under the great threatenings made against him. Indeed, the <term>Proconsul</term> himself was astonished by it. However, finding that no progress could be made with him, he commanded the Crier in the middle of the **Stadium** to make an open proclamation three times (as was the Roman custom in all capital trials): "**Polycarp has confessed himself a Christian.**" When this was said, the entire multitude of both Jews and Gentiles who were present gave a mighty shout. It is probable that the "Common Council" or Assembly of Asia <note>original Greek: "τὸ Κοινὸν τ’ Ασίας"</note> might have been held at Smyrna around this time for the celebration of their public shows and sports; that it was sometimes held here is evident from an ancient inscription mentioning it. They cried out aloud, "**This is the great Teacher <note>original: "Doctor"</note> of Asia, and the Father of the Christians; this is the destroyer of our gods, who teaches men not to offer sacrifice or worship the deities.**"

<sup>a</sup> See Book 6, Section 14, regarding exemptions, Title 1; and Book 8, Section 1, regarding vacancies, Title 5; see also Aristides, *Sacred Orations*, Book 4. <note>These are citations from Roman legal digests and the orator Aristides regarding the duties and exemptions of public officials.</note>

XII. Once the shouting had subsided, they immediately addressed themselves to Philip the <term>Asiarch</term> <note>A high-ranking official and priest who presided over the religious games and festivals in the Roman province of Asia.</note>. These ᵃ **Asiarchs** were Gentile priests belonging to the community of Asia, chosen yearly at the Common Council or Assembly of Asia. There were about ten of them (one being the Principal) chosen from names submitted by the various cities. It was an office of great honor and credit, but also of great expense and cost, as they were obliged to entertain the people with shows and sports during the festival solemnities; therefore, the position was only given to the most wealthy and substantial citizens. Philip was in this position at the time, and the people clamorously requested him to set a lion upon the criminal. He told them he could not do so, as he had already completed the **beast-hunting shows** <note>original Greek: "τὰ Κυνηγέσια"</note>—the hunting of wild animals with men, which was one of the famous spectacles of the **Amphitheater**. Then they unanimously demanded that he should be burnt alive; a fate which he himself had prophetically foretold would be his portion, based on the vision in his dream. The thing was no sooner said than done. Everyone vied to play a part in this fatal tragedy, fetching wood and bundles of sticks <note>original: "Faggots"</note> from various places with incredible speed. The Jews, in particular, were especially active in this service; malice toward Christians was almost as natural to them as it is for fire to burn. The fire being prepared, **Saint Polycarp** untied his belt, laid aside his garments, and began to take off his shoes—tasks he was not usually required to do himself, as the Christians eagerly competed for the chance to do them for him, and happy was the person who could first touch his body. Such was the great reverence everyone had for him, even from his younger years, because of the admirable strictness and regularity of his holy life.

XIII. The officers employed for his execution, having prepared everything else, came according to custom to nail him to the stake. However, he requested that they omit this, assuring them that he who gave him strength to endure the fire would enable him to stand immovable in the hottest flames without being nailed down. So they only tied him. Standing like a sheep ready for the slaughter, intended as a grateful sacrifice to the Almighty, he clasped his hands behind his back and poured out his soul to Heaven in the following prayer: "**O Lord God Almighty, the Father of your well-beloved and ever-blessed Son Jesus Christ, through whom we have received the knowledge of you; the God of Angels, Powers, and of every creature, and of the whole race of the righteous, who...**"

### XIV. 

How blind and stubbornly obstinate is unbelief! The pagans <note>original: "Infidels"</note> were so far from being convinced that they were instead exasperated by the miracle. They commanded a spearman—one of those who used to kill wild beasts when they became outrageous—to go near and run him through with a sword. He had no sooner done this than such a vast quantity of blood flowed from the wound that it extinguished and put out the fire. Along with this, a dove was seen to fly from the wounds of his body, which some suppose to have been his soul, clothed in a visible shape at the time of its departure; though it is true that this circumstance is not mentioned in Eusebius's account, and probably was never in the original. 

Nor did the malice of Satan end here. He knew by the innocent and blameless course of Polycarp's life, and the glorious constancy of his martyrdom, that he had certainly attained the crown of immortality. Nothing was now left for his spite to work on but to deprive the Christians even of the honor of his remains <note>original: "bones"</note>. For many were desirous to give his body a decent and honorable burial, and to assemble there for the celebration of his memory; but they were prevented by some who prompted Nicetes, the father of Herod and brother to Alce, to advise the Proconsul not to give his body to the Christians, lest, abandoning their crucified Master, they should henceforth worship Polycarp. This suggestion, though managed by the pagans, was first devised and prompted by the Jews, who narrowly watched the Christians when they tried to take away his body from the place of execution:

> "whole world, or that we should worship any other. Him we adore 
> "as the Son of God, but martyrs, as the disciples and followers of our 
> "Lord, we rightly love for their eminent kindness toward their 
> "own...

XV. The Centurion, seeing the stubbornness and obstinacy of the **Jews**, commanded the body to be placed in the center and burned to ashes in the usual manner. The Christians gathered up his bones as a choice and priceless treasure and buried them with dignity. They resolved to meet in that place, if possible (and they prayed God that nothing might hinder it), to celebrate the "birthday" of his martyrdom. This was done both to honor the memory of the departed and to prepare and encourage others to give a similar testimony to the Faith in the future. Both of these considerations gave rise to the *Memoriæ Martyrum* <note>Latin: "Memories of the Martyrs"</note>, those solemn annual commemorations of the martyrs which, as we have shown more fully elsewhere, were generally kept in the Primitive Church. Thus died this apostolic man in the year of Christ 167 <note>original: "Ann. Chr. CLXVII"</note>, in about the hundredth year of his age. The **eighty-six years** he spoke of, during which he had served Christ, cannot be said to begin from his birth, but from his baptism or "new birth." At that time, we cannot easily suppose him to have been younger than sixteen or twenty years old. Furthermore, his conversation with the Apostles and his consecration by **Saint John** reasonably suggest he was of a mature age; we cannot think that John would ordain a youth or a very young man as a Bishop, especially of such a large and populous city. The incomparable <gloss>a</gloss> Primate <note>This likely refers to Archbishop James Ussher, a prominent 17th-century scholar</note>, based on a passage in Polycarp's epistle, conjectures that he lived (though not yet converted to Christianity) at the time when **Saint Paul** wrote his epistles. If this is so, it would mean he was even older. This is no more improbable than what <gloss>b</gloss> **Quadratus**, the Christian apologist—who lived under **Hadrian** and dedicated his defense to that Emperor—reports: that some of those whom our Lord had healed and raised from the dead were still alive even in his own time. Regarding **Simeon**, the successor to **Saint James** in the bishopric of **Jerusalem**, <gloss>c</gloss> **Hegesippus** explicitly relates that he was 120 years old at the time of his martyrdom. I am certain that <gloss>d</gloss> **Irenaeus** particularly notes of our **Saint Polycarp** that he lived for a very long time and had reached an exceedingly great age when he underwent a most glorious and illustrious martyrdom for the Faith.

<margin>e *Thomas Smith, Epistle concerning the Seven Churches of Asia, page 164.*</margin>

XVI. He suffered on the second day of the month **Xanthicus** <note>A Macedonian month roughly corresponding to April</note>, the seventh day before the Kalends of **May**. However, it is difficult to determine whether this was a mistake for the seventh day before the Kalends of **April** (referring to March 26), or for the seventh day before the Kalends of **March** (referring to February 23). It is enough to note that his memory is celebrated by the **Greek Church** on February 23 and by the **Latin Church** on January 26. The amphitheater where he suffered is still largely standing (as a recent <gloss>e</gloss> eyewitness and diligent researcher into antiquity informs us). On its two opposite sides are the dens where the lions were once kept. His tomb is in a little chapel on the side of a mountain in the southeast part of the city, solemnly visited by the **Greeks** on his festival day. To maintain and repair it, travelers usually throw a few *aspers* <note>a small Turkish silver coin</note> into an earthen pot that stands there for that purpose. How miserable the state of this city is under the **Turkish** yoke...

To look a little earlier at the times we are writing about: although I do not like to make harsh or unkind interpretations of the actions of Divine Providence, yet I cannot help but observe how heavily God’s displeasure fell not long after **Polycarp’s** death—on other places, but more particularly upon this city—through plague, fire, and earthquakes. By these means their city, previously one of the glories and ornaments of **Asia**, was turned into rubbish and ashes; their stately houses were overturned, and their temples ruined. This included one temple in particular which, as it elevated **Asia** above other countries, gave **Smyrna** honor and precedence above other cities of **Asia**. Their trade was ruined, and their marketplaces and ports were laid waste, besides the great numbers of people who lost their lives. XVII. I cannot better conclude the story of **Polycarp’s** martyrdom than with the preface which the Church of **Smyrna** includes at the beginning of it, as it so excellently presents the illustrious faith and patience of those primitive Christians.

> "It is clear (they say) that all those martyrdoms are great and blessed
> which happen by the will of God; for it becomes us Christians, who have
> a more divine religion than others, to ascribe the sovereign disposal of
> all events to God. Who would not stand and admire the noble greatness
> of their minds, their singular patience, and admirable love for God?
> When their flesh was so torn off their backs with whips that the whole 
> structure and composition of their bodies, even to their innermost veins 
> and arteries, could be seen, they still patiently endured it. This was 
> to such an extent that those who were present pitied and grieved at the 
> sight of it, while the martyrs themselves were endowed with such 
> invincible determination that none of them gave even one sigh or groan.
> The holy martyrs of Christ let us see that, at the time they were being

XVIII. As for his writings: besides the fact that ᵇ *Saint Jerome* mentions the volumes of *Papias* and *Polycarp*, and the previously mentioned ᶜ *Pionius* mentions his *Epistles* and *Homilies*, ᵈ *Irenaeus* clearly indicates that he wrote several *Epistles*. Of all of these, none are extant today except the *Epistle to the Philippians*. This is an epistle peculiarly celebrated by the ancients; it is "very useful," says ᵉ *Saint Jerome*, and "most wonderful" <note>original Greek: "πάνυ θαυμαστὴ"</note> as ᶠ *Suidas* and ᵍ *Sophronius* style it—a most admirable epistle. ʰ *Irenaeus* gives it this tribute <note>original: "Elogium"</note>: that it is a *most perfect and absolute Epistle, from which those who are concerned for their salvation may learn the character of his faith and the truth which he preached*. To this, *Eusebius* adds that in this epistle, he makes use of some quotations from the First Epistle of *Saint Peter*. This is an observation that holds true for the epistle as we have it today, as there are many places in it cited from the first, but not one from the second epistle.

*Photius* passes this just and true judgment of it: that it is full of many admonitions, delivered with clearness and simplicity, according to the ecclesiastical way and manner of interpretation. It seems to hold a great affinity, both in style and substance, with *Clement's* epistle to the *Corinthians*, often suggesting the same rules and making use of the same words and phrases; so it is not to be doubted that he had that excellent epistle particularly in mind when writing it. Indeed, it is a pious and truly Christian epistle, furnished with short and useful precepts and rules of life, and penned with the modesty and simplicity of the Apostolic times. It was valued by the ancients next to the writings of the Holy Canon; <margin>as cited above.</margin> and *Saint Jerome* tells us that even in his time it was read in the public assemblies of the Asian church <note>original: "in Asia conventu"</note>. It was first published in Greek by *P. Halloix* the *Jesuit* in the year 1633, and not many years after by Bishop *Ussher*. I presume the pious reader will think it no useless digression if I here append such a venerable monument of the ancient Church.

I am, therefore, brothers, greatly troubled for Valens and for his wife; may the Lord give them true repentance.

I. <image-desc>A large decorative drop-cap initial 'W' featuring intricate vine-work and a central figure's face or mask within the letter's framework.</image-desc>WHETHER St. *Quadratus* was born at *Athens*, no records of Church antiquity enable us to determine; though the thing itself is not improbable, as his education and residence there, and his governance of that church, seem to give some weight to the idea. And as Nature had furnished him with incomparable abilities ("excellent talent" <note>original Latin: "excellens ingenium"</note>, as *a St. Jerome* says of him), so the place gave him great advantages in his education. He was thoroughly trained in the finest parts of learning and the most excellent institutions of philosophy, on which account the *b* Greeks truly style him "a man of great learning" <note>original Greek: "ἄνδρα πολυΐστορα"</note>. He became acquainted with the doctrines and principles of Christianity by being brought up under the instruction of the Apostles; for *c* *Eusebius* and *d St. Jerome* tell us more than once that he was a student and a disciple of the Apostles. This must be understood to mean the apostles who lived the longest, and particularly *St. John*, whose scholar he was in all probability, as were also *Ignatius*, *Polycarp*, *Papias*, and others. Therefore, *e Eusebius* places him among those who were of "the first rank" <note>original Greek: "τὴν πρώτην τάξιν"</note>—that is, those who were of the very first order among the Apostles' successors. There are those who claim that he was appointed by *St. John* as the Bishop of *Philadelphia* (one of the seven famous churches of *Asia*) at the time when *St. John* sent his epistle to that church. However, I confess I know of no authority for this, as the ancients are entirely silent on the matter. I pass it by as an unsupported and uncertain assertion, seeing they might with equal justification have made him Bishop of any other place.

<margin>
*f Eusebius, book 4, chapter 23, p. 143.*
*g Letter to the Athenians, quoted in Eusebius, as cited above.*
</margin>

II. UNDER the reign of *Trajan*, as is probable (though *Baronius* places it under *Hadrian*, in the sixth year of his empire), *f Publius*, the Bishop of *Athens*, suffered martyrdom. He is thought by some to have been the very same *Publius* whom *St. Paul* converted on the island of *Malta* <note>original: "Melita"</note> during his voyage to *Rome*, and who afterwards succeeded *Dionysius the Areopagite* in the See <note>A "See" refers to the seat of authority or the jurisdiction of a bishop.</note> of *Athens*. To him succeeded our *Quadratus* (as *g Dionysius*, Bishop of *Corinth*, who lived not long after that time, informs us), who found the state of that church

<meta>This page continues the biography of Saint Quadratus, focusing on his efforts to reform and revitalize the Church in Athens after a period of persecution and decline.</meta>

# The Life of St. QUADRATUS.

<margin>
*a Greek Menology, as cited above.*
*b Origen, Against Celsus, book 3, p. 128.*
</margin>
The Church was in a bad condition at his arrival. Upon the martyrdom of *Publius* and the persecution that followed it, the people were generally dispersed and fled. It is no wonder that when the *Shepherd is struck, the sheep are scattered* <note>A reference to Zechariah 13:7 and Matthew 26:31</note> and go astray. Their public and solemn assemblies were deserted, their zeal had grown cold and weak, their lives and manners were corrupted, and they were very close to a total apostasy from the Christian faith. This good man, therefore, set himself with great zeal to restore the ancient spirit of religion. He re-established order and discipline, brought the people back to the public assemblies, and rekindled their faith into a holy flame. Nor did he content himself with merely reforming what was wrong; with infinite diligence, he preached the faith and, through daily converts, enlarged the borders of his Church. As the *Greek Rituals* <note>The liturgical books of the Eastern Orthodox Church</note> express it, the sages and wise men of *Greece* were convinced by his doctrines and wise discourses. They embraced the Gospel and acknowledged Christ to be the Creator of the world and the great wisdom and power of God. In a short time, he brought the Church to such an excellent character that *Origen* (who lived some years later), while demonstrating the admirable power of the Christian faith over the minds of men and its triumph over all other religions in the world, cited this very Church of *Athens* as an example. He noted its good order and constitution, its meekness, quietness, and constancy, and its care to prove itself to God—qualities infinitely beyond the common civil assembly at *Athens*, which was divisive and disorderly. Origen argued that the civil assembly could not be compared with the Christian Church in that city; that the Churches of Christ, when examined alongside the pagan gatherings, shone like lights in the world. He stated that everyone must confess that even the worst parts of the Christian Church were better than the best of their popular assemblies. He added that the "Senators of the Church" (as he calls the church leaders) were fit to govern in any part of the Church of God, while the common Senate had nothing worthy of that honorable dignity, nor were they raised above the manners of the common people.

<margin>
*c Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 37, p. 109.*
*d Cited in Eusebius, book 5, chapter 17, p. 183.*
*e Valesius's Annotations on Eusebius, book 4, chapter 23, p. 81.*
</margin>
III. The *Athenian* Church was thus excellently established, primarily due to the tireless industry and the prudent care and leadership of its current Bishop. His success in this was greatly aided by those extraordinary supernatural powers which God had granted him. That he was endowed with a spirit of prophecy—the ability to speak suddenly on great and urgent occasions, to interpret obscure and difficult Scriptures, and especially to foretell future events—we have the express testimony of *Eusebius*. Eusebius affirms that he lived at the same time as *Philip’s* virgin daughters <note>Four sisters mentioned in Acts 21:8–9 known for their prophetic gifts</note> and possessed the prophetic gift <note>original Greek: "προφητικὸν χάρισμα" (prophetikon charisma)</note>. Another author, much older than Eusebius, who was disproving the errors of the *Cataphrygians* <note>Followers of Montanism, a movement that claimed new prophetic revelations</note>, also reckons him among the prophets who flourished under the era of the Gospel. I know a learned man who would like to persuade us that the *Quadratus* who had the prophetic gifts was a different person from our *Athenian* Bishop. However, the grounds he proceeds upon seem to me very weak and unconvincing. For instance, he says that *Eusebius* does not call that *Quadratus* a Bishop. But who does not know that people are not mentioned by all their titles in every instance? There was even less need for it here; when *Eusebius* first speaks of *Quadratus*, he was not yet the Bishop of *Athens*, so it would not have been proper to mention him in that capacity. Nor is his other objection of greater

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Saint Quadratus's identity, specifically whether he is the same person as the "prophetic" Quadratus, and transitions into the historical context of the persecutions under Emperor Hadrian.</meta>

# The Life of S. QUADRATUS.

<margin>
* As cited in Eusebius, book 4, chapter 23, page 143.
</margin>
<margin>
O most holy Quadratus, by your awe-inspiring wonders, you led the faithless to the divine faith like a God-inspired Apostle and a venerable hierarch. <note>original: Τῶν τὰ φοβερά, Κοδράτε, θαύματα, ἀπίσεις εἰς πίσιν θείαν ἐνῆγες, ὡς Ἀπόστολοͼ θεόληπτοͼ, ὡς σεπτὸς ἱεράρχης, ἱερώτατε.</note> Greek Menaion, in the location cited above.
</margin>
...weight, that the prophetic *Quadratus* did not survive the times of *Hadrian* <note>original: "Adrian"</note>, whereas our Quadratus lived at the same time as *Dionysius*, Bishop of *Corinth*. Dionysius lived under *Marcus Antoninus* <note>Marcus Aurelius</note> and speaks of Quadratus as his contemporary and the recently ordained Bishop of *Athens*. But whoever looks into that passage from *Dionysius* will find no foundation for such an assertion. Rather, the opposite is true: he speaks of him as if he had died before his own time, as I believe anyone who impartially considers the passage must confess. Furthermore, St. Jerome <note>original: "S. Hierom"</note> and all writers after him unhesitatingly consider them to be the same person. 

So, we may still attribute to him his gift of prophecy, which earned him so much reverence while he lived and so much honor to his memory since his death. To this may be added what the Greeks, in their *Menaion* <note>original: "Menaeon"; a liturgical book of the Eastern Orthodox Church</note>, quite probably say of him: that he was granted the power to work miracles, and that through his prayers, he ruined the idolatrous temples of the heathens. By these means, he greatly confounded the infidels and brought great numbers to the faith.

<margin>
a Jerome, Letter to Magnus, as cited above.
* Sulpitius Severus, Sacred History, book 2, page 142.
b See Roman Martyrology for September 20, page 583.
c Tertullian, Apology, chapter 6, page 6.
d Eusebius, book 3, chapter 33, page 105.
e Marius Maximus, cited by Aelius Spartianus in the Life of Hadrian, chapter 20, page 88; see also Dio Cassius, book 69, near the beginning.
f Spartianus, Ibid, chapter 14, page 69.
</margin>
IV. BUT the fair weather and prosperity of the Church usually did not last long in those days. They had enjoyed a short period of peace toward the end of *Trajan's* reign. But now, unfortunately, under *Hadrian*, his successor, the weather changed. There arose (as ᵃ St. Jerome calls it) a most grievous and heavy persecution, which * *Sulpitius Severus* explicitly calls the "fourth persecution." Indeed, how grievous it was is clear from the many thousands of martyrs who suffered then, as mentioned in the ancient martyrologies of the Church. 

Even at ᵇ *Rome* itself, *Eustachius* and his wife *Theopistis*, along with their two sons, are said to have been thrown to the lions by the Emperor’s command. When the mercy of those savage beasts spared them, they were ordered to be burned to death inside the belly of a brazen bull. It is true that ᶜ *Tertullian* says *Hadrian* published no new laws or edicts against the Christians; however, since the laws enacted by *Trajan* remained unrepealed and were not set aside, there were many who were willing to put them into execution. 

We find ᵈ that although *Trajan* had commanded a stop to the persecution of Christians, the people and provincial governors continued their accustomed cruelties anyway. While there was no general persecution, there were specific provincial ones. No doubt this increased after his death when *Hadrian* came to the empire, whom they knew too well to think he would oppose such proceedings. 

Despite what some have said regarding the clemency and good nature of that prince, there are ᵉ others who plainly state that his kindness was merely feigned <note>original: "personated"</note>. They argue that he was naturally cruel and that (following the true spirit of superstition) any acts of piety he performed were done out of fear that the same evil fate that befell *Domitian* might happen to him. Instances of his cruelty are common in the writings about his life. In short, he was a strange mixture <note>original: "contemperation"</note> of vice and virtue. The ᶠ historian gives a true characterization of him: he was severe and cheerful, grave and affable, deliberate and yet impulsively <note>original: "eagerly"</note> wanton, covetous and liberal, cruel and merciful, a great deceiver <note>original: "dissembler"</note>, and perpetually inconstant in all his actions.

# The Life of S. QUADRATUS.

...foreign religions, and especially Christianity. Indeed, how he felt about the Christians is sufficiently clear from his <margin>a This exists in the works of Flavius Vopiscus, in *The Life of Saturninus*, page 959.</margin> letter to the consul Servianus, written shortly after his return from Egypt. In this letter, he gives the Christians there such a wicked and base character, not hesitating to claim that the people—even their priests, bishops, and their very Patriarch himself—would worship both Christ and Serapis <note>a Graeco-Egyptian deity</note>, and that they were a most disruptive, conceited, and harmful generation. From this letter, it seems clear to me that while he was there, he had severely persecuted the Christians and forced some weak or false believers to worship the local deities, which probably gave him the grounds for his criticism and for applying the accusation to all of them. Since he viewed the Christians as such a vile sort of people, it is less surprising that he would overlook or even encourage their persecution in other parts of the Empire.

He <margin>b Spartianus, chapter 1, page 4.</margin> primarily dedicated himself to Greek studies, which he was so unusually fond of that he was commonly nicknamed *Graeculus*, or the "Little Greek." This led him to take great delight in those regions and to engage with the learning and philosophy of those countries. In about the sixth or seventh year of his reign, he came to Athens, where he took on the position and honor of an *Archon* <note>a chief magistrate in Athens</note>. He celebrated their traditional athletic games and granted many specific laws and privileges to that city. Most notably, he was initiated into their Eleusinian Mysteries, which were considered the most sacred and venerable in the entire pagan world and were specifically known simply as "The Mysteries."

These were solemn and religious rites performed in honor of Ceres <note>the Roman name for Demeter, goddess of the harvest</note> in memory of the great benefits received from her. Those seeking entry were called *mystai* <note>original: μύσται; initiates</note>, and they were often not admitted to full participation until after a five-year trial period. This trial consisted of several stages, each with its own specific rites: first, there were the "common purifications" <note>original: πάνδημοι καθαρμοί; *pandēmoi katharmoi*</note>; then the "secret rites" <note>original: ἀπόρρητοι; *aporrhētoi*</note>; next the "stations" <note>original: συστάσεις; *systaseis*</note>; then the "initiations" <note>original: μύησις; *myēsis*</note>; and finally—the highest level of all—the "inspections" or "visions" <note>original: ἐποπτεία; *epopteia*</note>. 

Others categorize them this way: first, the "purifications" <note>original: τὰ καθάρσια; *ta katharsia*</note> and atonements; then followed the "Lesser Mysteries" <note>original: τὰ μικρὰ μυστήρια; *ta mikra mystēria*</note>, when they were solemnly initiated and admitted; and lastly, after some time, they reached the "Greater Mysteries" or the "visionary rites" <note>original: τὰ ἐποπτικά; *ta epoptika*</note>. These were the most secret ceremonies of all, where they were allowed to see the entire mystic scene. From then on, they were called "Inspectors" <note>original: Επόπται; *Epoptai*</note> and were bound by a solemn oath never to reveal these mysterious rites to anyone. 

We cannot reasonably suppose that the Emperor Hadrian was forced to follow these tedious methods of initiation; their mystical laws were undoubtedly waived for such an extraordinary person. He likely became both a candidate and an "Inspector" <note>original: Επόπτης; *Epoptēs*</note> at once, a privilege they sometimes granted in exceptional cases. Not content with doing this only in Athens, <margin>c St. Jerome, *Concerning the writer on Quadratus*.</margin> <margin>d The location cited above.</margin> <margin>e Excerpts from Cassius Dio, Valesius edition, page 714.</margin> St. Jerome tells us that he was initiated into almost all the sacred rites of Greece. For this reason, Tertullian rightly calls him "the explorer of all curious and hidden mysteries," and the historian Cassius Dio tells us that he was infinitely curious and strangely addicted to all sorts of fortune-telling and magical arts.

VI. Hadrian stayed in Athens the entire winter. His busy and superstitious zeal was noticed there, which served as enough justification—without further orders—for active fanatics to hunt down and oppress the Christians. The persecution grew so intense and fierce that the Christians were forced

VII. It happened around this time that *Serenius Granianus*, the *Proconsul* of *Asia*, wrote letters to the Emperor. He represented to him the injustice of the common proceedings against Christians, explaining how improper it was that they should be put to death without any legal trial or specific crime charged against them, merely to satisfy the unreasonable and riotous demands of the crowds. Because of this letter, and the apologies offered to him by the Christians, the sharpness of the Emperor’s fury was dulled, and care was taken to ensure that greater moderation was 
<margin>d Justin Martyr, ibid. Eusebius, Chapter 9, page 123.</margin>
used toward them. To this end, he sent the following rescript <note>a formal imperial ruling or decree</note> to *Fundanus*, the successor of *Granianus* in the proconsulship of *Asia*.

->ADRIAN the Emperor, to MINUCIUS FUNDANUS.<-

> I received the letters sent to me by the most excellent *Serenius Granianus*, your *predecessor*. I do not think this is a matter that should be passed over without proper inquiry; we must ensure that these men are not needlessly disturbed and that informants are not given the opportunity or encouragement to make fraudulent accusations. Therefore, if the subjects of our provinces are able to openly appear and present their indictments against the Christians so as to answer for them before a public tribunal, let them take that course. They must not deal through petitions and mere noise or public outcry. It is much more appropriate that if any accusation is brought, you should have the legal authority to investigate it. If anyone brings an indictment and proves that they have broken the laws, then you shall pass sentence against them according to the nature of the crime. But if it appears that the person brought the charge only out of spite and malice, take care to punish that man according to the seriousness of such a wicked intent.

<margin>e In Eusebius, Book 4, Chapter 26, page 148.</margin>
*Hadrian* sent these same rescripts to several others (as *Melito*, the Bishop of *Sardis*, who presented an apology to *Marcus Antoninus*, informs us).

VIII. What became of Saint Quadratus after *Hadrian's* departure from *Athens* is unknown, except for what the *Greeks* relate in their *Menæon* <note>a Greek Orthodox liturgical book containing the lives of saints arranged by their feast days</note>. They record that he was driven from his position at *Athens* by the violence of persecutors. After being attacked with stones and then tortured by fire and various other punishments, he finally received the crown of martyrdom under *Hadrian* (likely toward the end of his reign). Where he fled after leaving *Athens* and where he suffered martyrdom remains uncertain, unless it was at *Magnesia*, a city of *Ionia* in *Asia Minor*. The same *Menæon* tells us he preached the Gospel there just as he had in *Athens*, that his body was buried there, and that his remains were famous for the miracles performed at that site. This place is also notable for the death of *Themistocles*, the great commander and citizen of *Athens* who was also banished by his own fellow citizens. After his brave and honorable achievements, *Themistocles* ended his own life here with a fatal drink. As *Plutarch* tells us, his descendants were granted certain honors and privileges by the people of *Magnesia*, which his friend Themistocles the Athenian enjoyed in his own time.

I. Justin the Martyr was one of the most learned and earliest writers of the Eastern Church. He lived not long after the Apostles, as <gloss>a</gloss> **Eusebius** says of him, and was near to them <term>in time and virtue</term> <note>original Greek: χρόνῳ καὶ ἀρετῇ (chronō kai aretē)</note> according to <gloss>b</gloss> **Methodius**, Bishop of Tyre. This surely refers either to the Apostles in a broad sense—meaning their immediate successors—or probably not to the individuals themselves, but to the doctrine and writings of the Apostles by which he was instructed in the knowledge of Christianity.

He was <gloss>d</gloss> born at Neapolis, a noted city of Palestine within the province of Samaria.
