II. In his younger years, and probably before his conversion to Christianity, he traveled to foreign lands to complete his studies. He went particularly to **Egypt**, the great center for all the more mysterious and obscure parts of learning and religion, which was therefore constantly visited by all the more grave and wise philosophers among the heathens. He assures us himself that he was at **Alexandria**, where he tells us the account he received from the inhabitants regarding the <term>Seventy Translators</term> <note>The seventy-two Jewish scholars who, according to tradition, translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek (the Septuagint).</note>. He was shown the cells where they performed that famous and painstaking work, which his inquisitive curiosity as a philosopher—and the reports he had heard of it by living among the Jews—had likely induced him to inquire after. 

Among the several sects of philosophers, after he had examined all their forms, he settled among the **Platonists**. Their ideas were most agreeable to his natural way of thinking and no doubt prepared him for the acceptance of Christianity. He tells us himself that the principles of that philosophy, though not alike in all things, were not foreign or contrary to the doctrines of the Christian faith. But alas, he found no satisfaction for his mind in this or any other school until he reached a full persuasion of the truth and divinity of that religion which was so much despised by the wise and the learned, and so much opposed and trampled on by the powerful and great men of the world. 

He has given us a very large and detailed account of this, and of the manner of his conversion to the Christian religion, in his *Dialogue with Trypho*. I know this account is suspected by some to be only a <term>prosopopoeia</term> <note>original: "Prosopopoeia"; a rhetorical device where a speaker or writer communicates by speaking as another person or character.</note> to represent the grounds of his becoming a Christian in the **Platonic** style by way of a **Dialogue**, a method familiar to the philosophers of that sect. However, even if it is granted that a few circumstances might have been added to ensure the <term>proper style</term> <note>original: decorum</note> of the meeting, I see no reason (nor is anything offered to the contrary besides a mere guess) to question the foundation of the story, the summary of which is briefly this:

<margin>*Dialogue with Trypho*, page 218, etc.</margin>

III. Being from his youth driven by a curious philosophical spirit to research and inquire after truth, he first went to the **Stoics**. But not satisfied with his master, he left him and went to a **Peripatetic** <note>A follower of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> tutor. This man’s vile greed soon made Justin conclude that truth could not dwell with him. Accordingly, he turned to a **Pythagorean**, who required a preparatory knowledge of **Music**, **Astronomy**, and **Geometry**. Justin quickly deserted him as well, and last of all delivered himself to the schooling of an eminent **Platonist** who had lately come to reside at **Neapolis** <note>Modern-day Nablus; the name means "New City."</note>. He was greatly taken with his intellectual ideas and resolved for some time to give himself up to solitude and contemplation. 

Walking out into a solitary place by the seaside, he met a grave, ancient man of a dignified appearance, who began to speak with him. The dispute between them concerned the excellence of philosophy in general, and of Plato-

[Platon]ism in particular; which *Justin* asserted to be the only true way to happiness, and of knowing and seeing God. This the venerable person refutes at length, and at last comes to show him who were the most likely persons to set him on the right path. He tells him that long before his reputed philosophers, there were certain blessed and holy men, lovers of God and divinely inspired, called *Prophets*. These men foretold things which have since come to pass. They alone understood the truth and sincerely declared it to the world. Their books, which are still available today, would instruct a man in what most becomes a philosopher to know. The fulfillment of their predictions sufficiently proved their faithfulness and integrity, and the mighty miracles they performed placed the truth of what they said beyond all doubt. They magnified God, the great Creator of the world, and announced his Son *Christ* to the world. He concluded his discourse with this advice: *“But as for yourself, above all things pray that the Gates of Light may be opened to you; for these are not things discerned and understood by all, unless God and Christ grant a man the knowledge of them.”* When this discourse was ended, he immediately departed from him.

<margin>The same, page 225.</margin>
IV. The wise discourse of this venerable man made a deep impression upon the Martyr’s mind. It kindled a divine flame in his soul and created in him a sincere love for the *Prophets* and those excellent men who were friends of *Christ*. And now he began to seriously inquire into and examine the Christian religion, which he confesses he found to be "the only certain and profitable philosophy" <note>original: μόνην φιλοσοφίαν ἀσφαλῆ τε καὶ σύμφορον / monēn philosphian asphalē te kai symphoron</note>. He could not help but praise it for containing a certain majesty and awe, being admirably adapted to terrify and persuade those who were off the right path, and to bring the sweetest serenity and peace to the minds of those who practice it. 

Nor was it the least inducement to sway him when he beheld the innocence of the Christians' lives and the constancy of their deaths—seeing with what fearless and undaunted resolution they sought out torments and encountered death in its most terrifying forms. He gives this very account of it to the *Roman* Emperor.

<margin>a *Apology I* (actually II), page 50.</margin>
> "For my own part," says <gloss>a</gloss> he, "while I was still following the Platonic teachings, when I heard the Christians slandered and insulted, and yet saw them rushing fearlessly into death and facing all those things that are considered most terrifying and shocking to human nature, I concluded for myself that it was impossible for those men to live in vice or be driven by a love of lust and pleasure. For what man who is a slave to pleasure and lack of control—one who considers the eating of human flesh a delicacy <note>A common false accusation against early Christians was that they practiced cannibalism, often a misunderstanding of the Eucharist.</note>—could cheerfully welcome death? He would know that death must put an end to all his pleasures and delights. Instead, he would try by all means to prolong his life as long as possible, to trick his enemies, and to hide from the officials, rather than voluntarily betraying and offering himself for immediate execution?"

V. We cannot exactly fix the date of his conversion, yet I think we may make a very close guess. ª *Eusebius* tells us that at the time when *Hadrian* consecrated *Antinous*, *Justin* still adhered to the studies and religion of the Greeks. Now, regarding this, we should know that when *Hadrian* came to *Egypt*, he lost his beloved favorite <term>original: "catamite"; a younger male companion</term>, *Antinous*. He felt his death so deeply that he promoted him to the status of a deity. Consequently, in an ancient inscription at ᵇ *Rome*, he is styled "the companion of the gods in Egypt" <note>original: ΣΥΝΘΡΟΝΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΕΝ ΑΙΓΥΠΤΩ ΘΕΩΝ</note>. He built a city for him in the place where he died called *Antinoopolis*, erected a temple, and appointed priests and prophets to serve it. He instituted annual solemnities and, every five years, sacred games called the *Antinoeia* <note>original: Ἀντινόεια</note>, held not only in *Egypt* but in other regions. Because of this, an ᶜ inscription from not long after those times, set up by the Senate of *Smyrna*, mentions *Lerenius Septimius Heliodorus*, an "Antinoian winner" <note>original: ANTINOEA</note>, who was victorious in the sports at *Smyrna*. 

But to return to the point. It is very evident that *Hadrian* had not been in *Egypt* until about the time when *Servianus* (or *Severianus*) was *Consul* (as appears from the Emperor’s letters ᵈ to him). This consulship coincided with the year of Christ 132, the 16th year of the Emperor *Trajan's* <note>The author uses Trajan's years as a chronological marker, though Hadrian was the reigning Emperor in 132 AD.</note> reign. So this affair with *Antinous* must have happened either that year or, at most, the year before. Accordingly, around this time (as *Eusebius* suggests), *Justin* left the Greeks and came over to the Christians. Therefore, in his first apology presented not many years after to *Antoninus Pius*, *Hadrian’s* successor, he speaks ᵉ of *Antinous* as "one who has recently been" <note>original: τὸ νῦν γεγενημένον</note>—meaning he lived and was consecrated very recently—and of the *Jewish War* led by *Bar Kokhba* <note>original: Barchachab</note> as having only lately passed. We know this war occurred at the same time as the death and deification <term>apotheosis; the elevation of someone to divine status</term> of *Antinous*. It is clear to everyone that *Justin’s* phrase "what has recently happened" in both passages cannot be strictly limited to the exact time he presented that *Apology*; instead, as the phrase is sometimes used, it must be extended to cover what was done in recent years.

The wiser and more thoughtful among the *Gentiles* <term>Gentiles; non-Jewish people, specifically pagans in this context</term> were quite troubled by the loss of such a useful and eminent person, and they wondered what had caused such a sudden change. For their satisfaction and conversion, as well as for his own defense, he thought it best to write a specific discourse to them. In its very first words, he addresses them as follows: ᶠ "Do not think, O Greeks, that I have departed from the rites of your religion rashly and without any judgment or deliberation. For I could find nothing in it that was truly sacred or worthy of divine acceptance. The matters among you, as your poets have arranged them, are monuments to nothing but madness and lack of self-control. A man can no sooner apply himself for instruction to even the most learned among you without becoming entangled in a thousand difficulties and becoming the most confused person in the world." 

He then proceeds with a great deal of wit and eloquence to expose the folly and absurdity of the main foundations of the *Pagan Creed*, concluding his address with these exhortations: "Come here, O Greeks, and share in a most incomparable wisdom. # The Life of St. Justin the Martyr.

<page-num>145</page-num>
<sig>V</sig>

<margin>
a. Second Apology, page 70.
b. Against Heresies, Book 42, page 135.
c. Dialogues against the Marcionites, pages 3–4. Basel edition, 1674, quarto.

...about the beginning of the reign of *Antoninus Pius*, he settled his residence near the *Timothine Baths* on the *Viminal Mount* <note>One of the famous Seven Hills of Rome</note>, as recorded in the accounts of his martyrdom. Here, he worked diligently to defend and promote the cause of Christianity. He was particularly focused on refuting and suppressing the heresies that were then deeply troubling the Church, even writing a book <sup>a</sup> against all types of heresies. He especially opposed *Marcion*, who was the son of a Bishop and born in *Pontus*. Marcion had been excommunicated for seducing a young woman; consequently, he fled to *Rome*, where he spread many dangerous errors. Among these was the claim that there were two Gods: one who created the world, whom Marcion identified as the God of the *Old Testament* and the author of evil; and another more sovereign and supreme Being who created more excellent things. This second God was the Father of Christ, sent into the world to abolish the Law and the Prophets and to destroy the works of the other deity, whom he called the God of the *Jews*. Others—specifically <sup>b</sup> *Epiphanius* and a more ancient author <sup>c</sup> of the *Dialogues against the Marcionites* written under the name of *Origen* (though I strongly doubt it was *Origen* himself)—claim that Marcion established three different principles or beings: a <term>good principle <note>original: ἀρχὴ ἀγαθὴ</note></term> who was the Father of Christ and the God of the *Christians*; a <term>creating principle <note>original: ἀρχὴ δημιουργικὴ</note></term> who made the visible world and presided over the *Jews*; and an <term>evil principle <note>original: ἀρχὴ πονηρά</note></term>, who was the Devil and ruled over the *Gentiles*. *Justin* fought against Marcion both in person and in writing, specifically publishing a book he had composed against Marcion's destructive principles.

<margin>See Eusebius, Book 4, chapter 18, page 139.</margin>
VIII. Around the year 140 AD, Christians appear to have been treated more severely. Although Emperor *Antoninus* was a mild and excellent prince who, as far as we know, issued no new decrees against Christianity, the Christians were still treated harshly everywhere. They were generally slandered as a wicked and barbaric people and were persecuted under the specific decrees of former emperors and the general standing laws of the *Roman Empire*. To clear them of the insults cast upon them and to lessen the harsh treatments they endured, *Justin* published his *First Apology* around this time. (Although it is listed second in all modern editions, it was undoubtedly his first.) He presented it—as shown by the dedication—to Emperor *Antoninus Pius* and his two sons, *Verus* and *Lucius*, as well as to the Senate and through them to the entire Roman people. In this work, using great strength and clear reasoning, he defends Christians against the standard accusations of their enemies. He proves the divinity of the Christian faith and shows how unjust and unreasonable it was to prosecute them without proper evidence or legal process. He also informs the authorities about the innocent rituals and customs of Christian assemblies. Finally, he reminds the Emperor of the policy his predecessor, *Hadrian* <note>original: "Adrian"</note>, had taken in this matter. Hadrian had commanded that Christians should not be needlessly or unjustly harassed, but that their cases should be examined and decided in open courts. Justin even attached a copy of the *rescript* <term>original: "rescript"; an official legal response or decree issued by an emperor</term> which *Hadrian* had sent to *Minucius Fundanus* for that purpose.

<margin>* Orosius, History, Book 7, chapter 14, folio 305.</margin>

The Emperor, being of a naturally merciful and generous disposition, was moved partly by Justin’s *Apology* <note>original: "Apology"; here meaning a formal legal defense of a belief system</note> and partly by reports he had received from other parts of the Empire. He gave orders that Christians should henceforth be treated in a more gentle and legal manner. This is evident <margin>a. Indeed, you could do them no greater favor than to allow them to be accused so that they may choose to die rather than live for the sake of the God they worship. In this way, they come out the winners, being ready to sacrifice their lives rather than be persuaded to follow your commands.

In such times, they are much more secure and confident in their God. Meanwhile, you seem to ignore God throughout the crisis; you neglect the rites of other gods and the religion of that immortal Deity. Instead, you banish and persecute the Christians who do worship Him. Regarding these men, several provincial governors have previously written to my father of sacred memory <note>The Emperor Hadrian</note>. He replied to them that Christians should not be bothered in any way, unless it appeared they were plotting something against the Roman state. I myself have received many reports of this nature, to which I answered according to the spirit of my father’s decree. After all this, if anyone continues to cause them trouble merely because they are Christians, let the person accused be discharged—even if it is clear he is a Christian—and let the informer himself face the punishment.

->Published at *Ephesus* in the place of the *Common Assembly of Asia*.<-

XI. Not long after his first *Apology*, *Justin* seems to have returned to the Eastern regions. In addition to what he says in the *Acts* of his martyrdom—that he visited *Rome* twice—^b *Eusebius* explicitly states that he was in *Ephesus*. It was there that he had his famous debate with *Tryphon*, which clearly took place after he presented his first *Apology* to the Emperor. ^c It is quite likely that he traveled to *Ephesus* in the company of those who carried the Emperor’s decree to the *Assembly of Asia*, which was then meeting in that city. While there, he became acquainted with *Tryphon* the *Jew*. This *Tryphon* was probably the same man as Rabbi *Tarphon* <margin>the wealthy priest</margin> (as they commonly call him), the wealthy priest and teacher or colleague of *Rabbi Akiva*, who is frequently mentioned in Jewish writings. He was a man of great fame and standing who had fled his country ^d during the recent war, in which *Bar Kokhba* <note>original: "Barchochab"; leader of the Jewish rebellion against Rome, 132–136 AD</note> incited and led the *Jews* in a rebellion against the *Romans*. Since that time, he had lived in Greece, especially in *Corinth*, and had greatly expanded his knowledge through discussions with the philosophers of those countries. *Justin* engaged him in a two-day debate, providing an account of it in his *Dialogue* with that clever man. In this work, he admirably defends and proves the truth of the Christian religion, undermining the core arguments of the *Jewish* position and dismantling all their excuses and claims against Christianity. He also reveals their relentless hostility and malice. He notes that they were not content to simply reject Christianity themselves, but sent specific agents throughout the world to spread the claim that *Jesus* the *Galilean* was a deceiver and a fraud, and that his entire religion was nothing but a cheat and a sham. ^e He also mentions that in their public ^f synagogues, they formally cursed <note>original: "anathematized"; to formally denounce or excommunicate</note> all those who converted to Christianity. They hated them, as he tells us elsewhere, ^g with a deadly enmity, oppressing and murdering them whenever they had the power to do so. *Bar Kokhba*, their recent General, made Christians the primary targets of his harshest severity and revenge unless they would renounce and blaspheme Christ. The result of the conference was that the *Jew* admitted he was highly pleased with the discussion, professing that he found more in it than he had expected. He expressed a wish that he might enjoy such conversations more often, as they would greatly help in achieving a true understanding of the Scripture, and he asked for Justin's friendship regardless of where in the world he might be.

Whether he went back to **Rome** or to some other place is not known. That he eventually returned there is unquestionable, for the fact is evident even if the timing is uncertain. I will not venture to determine whether it was while **Antoninus Pius** was still alive or at the beginning of his successor’s reign. Upon his arrival, he had frequent contests with **Crescens** the philosopher, a man of some note in **Rome** at that time. He was a <term>Cynic</term> <note>original: Cynic; a member of a school of ancient Greek philosophy that prioritized virtue but often expressed it through a contempt for social conventions and a surly, "dog-like" demeanor.</note> and, according to the spirit of that sect, he was proud, conceited, surly, and ill-tempered. He was a philosopher in appearance, but a notorious slave to all vice and wickedness. <margin>b *Oration Against the Greeks*, page 160.</margin> **Tatian**, Justin’s student (who saw the man in **Rome** and both wondered at and despised him for his childish, trivial, and effeminate manners), gives him this character: he was a slanderer of all their gods, the very embodiment of superstition, an accuser of noble and heroic actions, a clever plotter of murders, a prompter of adultery, a pursuer of wealth even to the point of rage and madness, a teacher of the vilest sorts of lust, and the great driving force and instigator behind men being condemned to execution. <margin>c Ibid., page 157.</margin> **Tatian** tells us of him that while in **Rome**, he was miserably enslaved to sodomy and greed above all others. Although he pretended to despise death, he actually dreaded it; it was to this "greatest of evils" that he sought to betray **Justin** and **Tatian** because they freely rebuked the vicious and degenerate lives of such philosophical impostors.

This was Justin’s adversary—a "philosopher" and a "noise-maker" <note>original Greek: φιλόσοφος (philosophos, "lover of wisdom") & φιλόψοφος (philopsophos, "lover of applause/noise")</note> <margin>d *Apology I* (more accurately *II*), page 46.</margin> as Justin calls him. He was a lover of public praise, not of true wisdom and philosophy, and he used every base art of insinuation to slander the Christians and represent their religion in the most infamous light. But in all their disputes, the Martyr found him wretchedly ignorant of Christian affairs and strongly biased by malice and envy. Justin offered to prove this (if it were permitted) in a public debate with him before the Emperor and the Senate. He assured them that either Crescens had never considered Christian doctrines—which would make him worse than the lowliest uneducated people, who do not usually testify or pass judgment on matters they know nothing about—or if he had noticed them, it was plain that he either did not understand them or, if he did, he hid his knowledge and approval out of a base desire to please his listeners. He did this for fear of being considered a Christian, worrying that if he spoke his mind freely, he would suffer the same fate as **Socrates**. Crescens was far from following the excellent principle of that wise man: *that no man should be respected more than the truth.* This free and impartial criticism only further enraged the man, leading him to hasten and promote Justin’s ruin.

XIII. In the meantime, **Justin** presented his *Second Apology* to **Marcus Antoninus** (his colleague **Lucius Verus** was probably absent from the city at the time) and the Senate. It is evident from several passages in the *Apology* itself that it was not addressed to the Senate alone. Some believe this, as well as the former apology, was presented to **Antoninus Pius**, but there is certainly no just evidence for that; furthermore, **Eusebius** and other ancient writers expressly attribute it to **Marcus Aurelius**, his son and successor. If the inscription and beginning of the work (which are now lost) were still extant, they would quickly resolve the doubt. The occasion for it was this: <margin>e *Apology I*, page 42.</margin> a woman in **Rome** and her husband had lived in all kinds of decadence and debauchery. However, after she was converted to Christianity, she sought by every argument and persuasion to reclaim him from his loose and vicious lifestyle.

No sooner had he said this than he, along with a third person, was sentenced to the same fate. The severity of these events stirred **Justin’s** concern and care for the rest of his brothers. He answered the objections usually urged against them and asked for no more favor than this: that whatever judgment they reached, his *Apology* should be attached to it, so that the whole world might judge the Christians once they were truly acquainted with their case.

XIV. **Justin’s** activity and zeal for the cause of Christianity only sharpened the malice and rage of **Crescens** against him. He added that as for himself, he thought he was too lowly to say anything worthy of Christ's infinite deity; that this was the work of the prophets, who had many ages before foretold the coming of this Son of God into the world.

He continued to instruct his disciples, who gave the Prefect an account of where he lived and told him that Justin preached Christian doctrine to everyone who came to him. XVII. In this way, we have followed the Martyr through the various stages of his life and brought him to his final, fatal end. Now, let us observe him a bit more closely. He was a man of a pious mind and a very virtuous life, deeply sensitive to the honor of God and the great interests of religion. He was not arrogant, nor did he value himself because of his great abilities; instead, on every occasion, he entirely credited the glory of everything to divine grace and goodness. He possessed a true love for all people and a great concern for the well-being of souls, whose happiness he continually prayed for and promoted—even that of his fiercest enemies. From no one did he and his religion receive more bitter insults and opposition than from the *Jews*. Yet, he tells <margin>a</margin> *Trypho* that they heartily prayed for them and all other persecutors, asking that they might repent, stop blaspheming Christ, believe in him, and be saved from eternal vengeance at his glorious appearance. He noted <margin>b</margin> that although they were accustomed to solemnly curse Christians in their synagogues and join with anyone who would persecute them to death, the Christians returned no other answer than: "You are our brothers; we urge you to acknowledge and embrace the truth of God." And in his <margin>c</margin> *Apology* to the Emperor and the Senate, he concludes this way: "I have no more to say, except that we shall strive as much as we can and heartily pray that everyone in the world may be blessed with the knowledge and acceptance of the truth."

In pursuing this noble and generous goal, he feared no dangers but spoke with the greatest freedom and impartiality. He informs the <margin>d</margin> Emperors how much it was their duty to honor and value the truth. He explains that he did not come to smooth things over or flatter them, but to ask them to pass sentence according to the strictest rules of justice. He told them <margin>e</bold> that it was their responsibility—and entirely reasonable—that once they had heard the case, they should perform their duty as righteous judges. If they did not, they would eventually be found inexcusable before God. Furthermore, <margin>f</margin> he warned them beforehand that if they continued to punish and persecute such innocent people, it would be impossible for them to escape God's future judgment while they persisted in this evil and unjust course. In this matter, he did not show favoritism to anyone, nor was he scared by the dangers involved. Therefore, in his conversation with the *Jew* <note>the dialogue with Trypho</note>, he says <margin>g</margin> that his only concern was to speak the truth, not caring whom he might offend—even if they were to tear him to pieces right then and there. He neither feared nor favored his own countrymen, the *Samaritans*, whom he had accused in his *Apology* to the Emperor for being so bewitched and seduced by the deceptions of *Simon Magus*, whom they hailed as a supreme deity, above all authority and power.

<margin>
a Cod. CXXV. col. 304.
b Photius.
</margin>

XVIII. As for his natural talents, he was a man of sharp intellect, a quick and pleasant wit, and a judgment capable of weighing different perspectives and adapting them for the most useful purposes. All of these were greatly improved and perfected by the benefits of studying abroad. He had reached the very peak of both Christian and pagan <note>original: "Ethnic"</note> philosophy. According to <margin>a b</margin> *Photius*, he "had reached the very summit, overflowing with a wealth of history and learning" <note>original Greek: εἰς ἄκρον ἀνηγμένος, πολυμαθείᾳ τε καὶ ἱστοριῶν περιρρεόμενος πλούτῳ</note>...

<margin>
* Dialogue with Trypho, page 331.
a Against Celsus, Book 6, page 306.
b Christopher Sand, *Treatise on Ancient Church Writers*, History of the Church, Volume 1, Preface page 44.

He was well-versed in history and all types of learning. In one area, however, he seems to have fallen short—an area where the early Church Fathers were generally deficient: skill in **Hebrew** and other **Eastern languages**. This is evident (to omit other examples) by one instance: his derivation of the word *Satanas* <note>original: "Satanas" (Satan)</note>. He tells us that *Sata* in Hebrew and Syriac signifies an "apostate," and *Nas* means the same as the Hebrew *Sata*; from the combination of both arises the single word *Satanas*. This is a trifling conceit <note>original: "conceit" (fanciful idea)</note>, and less pardonable in someone who was born and lived among the **Samaritans** and the **Jews**. Anyone who has even a passing acquaintance with those languages knows it springs from the word *Satan* <note>original Hebrew: שטן</note>, meaning "an adversary." As **Origen** <margin>a</margin> long ago observed regarding this very instance, when this word is formed according to the **Greek** style—which usually adds "as" to the end of words borrowed from foreign languages—it becomes *Satanas*, an "adversary."

Therefore, a recent author <margin>b</margin> (who has scoured the writings of the ancients, and whose quotations show far more ostentation <note>original: "ostentation" (showiness)</note> than either judgment or accuracy) betrays his ignorance of those very Fathers with whom he pretends to be so well-acquainted. To prove that the *Questions and Answers to the Orthodox* <margin>c</margin> is not the genuine work of our **Justin**, he cites the odd and ridiculous interpretation of the word *Osanna* found there, which is rendered as "super-excellent magnificence" <note>original Greek: μεγαλωσύνη ὑπερκειμένη</note>. He argues that **Justin** himself, being a **Samaritan**, could not have been ignorant of the true meaning of that word. Yet Justin's unquestionable writings show such clear evidence of his lamentable lack of skill in that language. But the man must be excused, seeing that in this (as in many other things) he traded purely on trust, securely stealing the entire passage word-for-word from another author. He had so little skill that he could not distinguish between true and false, nor did he know when to follow his guides and when to leave them.

As for **Justin** himself, his ignorance in this matter is less surprising if we consider that his religion as a person born a Gentile, his early and almost exclusive interaction with the **Greeks**, and his constant study of the writings of the Gentile philosophers might well have made him a stranger to a language that had little to tempt a mere philosopher to learn it. His great abilities in all other parts of learning can be seen in his extant writings (to say nothing of those that are lost). As **Eusebius** <margin>d</margin> says of them, they are "memorials of a trained mind and one studiously devoted to divine things, full of every kind of benefit" <note>original Greek: πεπαιδευμένης διανοίας & περὶ τὰ θεῖα ἐσπουδακυῖας ὑπομνήματα, πάσης ὠφελείας ἔμπλεα</note>. They were all written either in defense of the **Christian Religion** against both **Jews** and **Gentiles**, or to overthrow the common religion and those profane and ridiculous rites of worship that then ruled the world, or to prescribe rules for the daily conduct of the Christian life. He managed all of these with admirable sharpness and skill.

Some books, however, have been falsely attributed to him, such as the *Explanation of the Faith*, *Questions and Answers to the Orthodox*, *Greek Questions to Christians*, and *Five Questions to the Greeks*. All of these are undoubtedly from a later age, composed after Christianity was fully established in the world and the **Arian** controversies <note>A series of 4th-century theological disputes regarding the nature of Christ's divinity.</note> had begun to disturb the Christian Church. Or, if any of them were originally his, they have been so miserably altered and defaced by later ages that it is almost impossible to distinguish the true parts from the false.

XIX. As for the *Epistle to Diognetus*, although it is questioned by some,

# The Life of Saint Justin the Martyr

Some people doubt its authenticity, yet it is quite capable of maintaining its title as Justin’s work, as no compelling reason has been argued against it. It is not improbable that this was the very same **Diognetus** who was the tutor to the Emperor **Marcus Aurelius**. As the Emperor himself confesses <margin>a Marcus Aurelius, *Meditations*, Book 1, chapter 6, page 1.</margin>, Diognetus persuaded him to study philosophy and gave him wise counsel and direction for that purpose. Being a person of high status and distinction, he is accordingly addressed by the Martyr as "most excellent Diognetus" <note>original Greek: κράτιστε Διόγνητε (*kratiste Diognete*)</note>. 

His temperament and way of life had made him incredibly curious (as is evident from the first part of that Epistle) to know specifically what the Christian religion was, what their manners and rites were, and what inspired them with such brave and noble courage that they could scorn the world and despise death. He wanted to know on what grounds they rejected the religion and disowned the deities of the **Gentiles** <note>original: "Gentiles" (non-Jewish pagans)</note>, and yet separated themselves from the **Jewish** discipline and way of worship. He also asked about that admirable love and friendship by which they were so closely joined together, and why this new institution appeared so late in the world. To all these inquiries (which were typical for a man of a philosophical mind), **Justin** returns a very detailed and rational explanation in this Epistle. Justin was likely the person he addressed, as he was the most famous champion of the Christian cause. However, what effect this letter had upon the philosopher is unknown. 

That this Epistle is not mentioned by **Eusebius** <margin>b *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 4, chapter 18, page 140.</margin> is not a valid objection, seeing as Eusebius himself confesses that there were many other books by Justin besides those he listed. The fact that the style is a bit more polished and philosophical than usual is even less of an objection; for who can wonder if a great scholar like Justin, writing to a person so eminent in learning and philosophy, endeavored to give his writing all the advantages of flowery and eloquent speech? It must be admitted that his ordinary style does not usually reach this level; for a judgment on this, let us look at the critique of **Photius** <margin>c From the location cited above.</margin>, a man well-qualified to judge such matters:

> *He did not study (he says) to enhance the natural beauty of philosophy with the deceptive polish of rhetorical arts. For this reason his discourses, though otherwise very weighty and powerful, and following a structure agreeable enough to art and science, do not have those sweet and enticing persuasions—those attractions and allurements—that usually prevail upon common listeners and draw them in.*

### XX.

The thing that may seem most to damage the reputation of this ancient and venerable man is that he is commonly said to be guilty of some unorthodox sentiments and opinions that disagree with the accepted doctrines of the Church. It is true that he holds some notions not supported by general acceptance or the consensus of the Church, especially in later ages. However, there are hardly any that were not also held by most of the Fathers in those early times. For the most part, these views are speculative and do not negatively influence a virtuous life. We shall note the most significant ones here. 

First, he is accused of having too much kindness and indulgence toward the more eminent Heathens, particularly toward **Socrates**, **Heraclitus**, and others like them. 

<margin>
"We have been taught that Christ is the first-born of God, and we have declared him to be the Word <note>original Greek: λόγον (*logon*)</note>, of whom every race of men partakes. And those who lived according to reason <note>original Greek: μετὰ λόγου (*meta logou*)</note> are Christians, even though they were thought to be atheists; such as, among the Greeks, Socrates and Heraclitus, and others like them." *Apology II*, page 83.
<br/>
d *Apology I*, page 48.
</margin>

Indeed, he seems to allow that they were, in some sense, Christians. Regarding Socrates specifically, <margin>d</margin> he affirms *that Christ was known to him in part*, and he repeats similar ideas more than once. The basis for all of this was his belief that such persons lived "according to reason" <note>original Greek: μετὰ λόγου βιῶν (*meta logou bion*)</note>. He believed the <term>Logos</term> <note>The "Word" or "Reason" of God, identified with Christ.</note> is naturally in every man and is made manifest to him.

<margin>
The Savior, shining upon rational and governing beings so that their minds may see their own desires, is the light of the intellectual world. I speak of the vision of rational souls in the darker world, etc. <note>original Greek: Ὁ Σωτὴρ ἐκλάμπων... Origen, *Commentary on John*, p. 25; see also p. 40.</note>
a <note>original: *Dial. cum Tryph.* (Dialogue with Trypho), p. 234. p. 285. D.</note>

...him, if he but governs himself according to it. For a clearer understanding of this, it may be helpful to briefly inquire into the sense in which the early Church Fathers, and especially our **Justin**, use this word *Logos* <note>original: λόγος (Logos), meaning both "Word" and "Reason." This term was central to both Greek philosophy and early Christian theology.</note>. 

Their understanding was plainly this: that Christ was the eternal *Logos* or Word of the Father, the sum and center of all reason and wisdom, just as the Sun is the fountain of light. They believed that from him, a *logos* or reason was naturally derived into every person, like a beam or emanation of light from that Sun. To this purpose, they usually cited the words of **Saint John**: *In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... that was the true light that lightens every man that comes into the world.* 

**Justin** says <gloss>a</gloss> that first, and before the production of any creatures, God begot of himself a "certain rational power" <note>original: δύναμιν τινὰ λογικὴν (*dynamin tina logikēn*)</note>. In Scripture, this power is sometimes styled the glory of God, the Son, Wisdom, an Angel, God, Lord, and Word. He is described by all these names according to both the administration of his Father’s will and his own voluntary generation. 

And elsewhere <gloss>b</gloss>, he writes: "We love and worship the Word of the unbegotten and inexpressible God, which Word became Man for our sakes, so that by sharing in our sufferings he might work out our cure." Hence, Christ is called <gloss>c</gloss> the "universal Word" <note>original: τοῦ παντὸς λόγος (*tou pantos logos*)</note>. With respect to him, human reason is styled the "seminal Word" <note>original: σπερματικὸς λόγος (*spermatikos logos*)</note> that is sown in our natures. It is "related to the seminal Word" <note>original: τοῦ σπερματικοῦ παρὰ λόγου Συγγενὲς (*tou spermatikou para logou syngenes*)</note> <gloss>d</gloss>, and is the "internal sowing of the implanted Word" <note>original: ἡ ἐνεστὶ ἐμφύτῳ τοῦ λόγου σπορὴ (*hē enesti emphyto tou logou sporē*)</note>. Justin distinguishes this from "the seed itself" <note>original: αὐτὸ τὸ σπέρμα (*auto to sperma*)</note>—the primary and original source—from which all participation and imitation proceed, according to the measure of grace given by it. 

This is what he means by the "seeds of truth" <note>original: σπέρματα ἀληθείας (*spermata alētheias*)</note>, which he tells us <gloss>e</gloss> seem to be in all people in the world. They are a derivation from Christ, who is the root, and a kind of participation in a divine nature from him. **Clement of Alexandria** traces the lineage this way: "The image of God," he says <gloss>f</gloss>, "is his Word (for the divine Word is the genuine offspring of the Mind, the original light of light), and the image of the Word is Man." The true mind that is in man—which is said to be made after the image and likeness of God—is conformed in its heart to the divine Word, and by that means partakes of the Word or Reason.

<margin>
For the reason in each rational being has the same relationship to the Word who was in the beginning with God—the Word who is God—as the Word-God has to God. For as the Father, being God-in-himself and the true God, is the archetype of the image, and the image [the Son] relates to the secondary image [humanity] (which is why humans are said to be "according to the image," rather than being the images themselves), so the Word itself relates to the reason in each person. For both function as a source: the Father of deity, and the Son of reason. <note>original Greek: Ὁ γὰρ ἐν ἑκάστῳ λόγος... Origen, *Commentary on John*, Vol 1, p. 47; Vol 2, edited by Huet.</note> 

For God is the God of all, and not simply "a god," just as the Word is the source of the reason within each rational being. The reason in each could not properly be named God in the same way as the primary Word. <note>original Greek: ἔστιν γὰρ ὁ ὅτι πᾶσι θεὸς... *Ibid.*, p. 40.</note>
</margin>

XXI. **Origen**, the student of **Clement**, follows exactly in his master’s footsteps. He tells us that just as God the Father is God-in-himself <note>original: αὐτόθεος (*autotheos*), the source of Deity</note> to the Son, so God the Son (the *Logos*, the Word, or the supreme and eternal Reason) is the fountain and original source that communicates reason to all rational beings. These beings, as such, are "images of the image" <note>original: εἰκόνες τοῦ εἰκόνος (*eikones tou eikonos*)</note>, meaning they are a kind of shadow of the Word, who is the "brightness of his Father’s glory and the express image of his person." 

He further adds that when *Logos* is used with the definite article (the Word), it refers to Christ; but without the article (a word or reason), it refers to that reason which is derived from him. In short, the situation is this: every person is naturally endowed with principles of reason and clear perceptions of good and evil, like a light kindled from...

...from him, who is the Word and Wisdom of the Father. Thus, one may be said to partake of Christ—the primitive and original Word—more or less according to how they improve their own reason. 

So it is that whatever wise and excellent things either philosophers or poets have spoken, says <margin>a *Apology I*, p. 46; see also p. 48 C.</margin> **Justin the Martyr**, it was <margin>b *Ibid.*, p. 48.</margin> "due to the seed of the Word <note>original Greek: διὰ τὸ ἔμφυτον παντὶ γένει ἀνθρώπων σπέρμα τοῦ λόγου; Justin argues that a "seed" of the divine Reason/Word is implanted in all of humanity.</note> implanted in all mankind." Thus, he says that **Socrates** exhorted the **Greeks** to the knowledge of the "Unknown God" by searching for the Word. 

To conclude this, he nowhere affirms that **Gentiles** <note>non-Jews/Pagans</note> might be saved without embracing Christianity. Nor does he claim that their knowledge was, by itself, sufficient for that end. In fact, no man proves more strongly than Justin that Reason and Natural Philosophy are insufficient for salvation. However, he believed that as far as they improved their Reason and internal "Word" for the great and excellent purposes of religion, they were to that extent Christians and akin to the eternal and original Word. He held that whatever was rightly dictated or reformed by <margin>Not only were these things refuted among the **Greeks** by the Word <note>original: *logos*</note> through **Socrates**, but also among the **Barbarians** <note>non-Greeks</note> by the Word itself taking shape and becoming man, and being called **Jesus Christ**. *Justin, Apology II, p. 56.*</margin> this inward Word—whether by **Socrates** among the **Greeks** or by others among the foreigners—was in effect done by Christ himself, *the Word made Flesh*.

### XXII. ANOTHER 
opinion with which he was charged is **Chiliasm** <note>original: *Chiliasm*; the belief in a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth (the Millennium).</note>, or <margin>e *Dialogue with Trypho*, pp. 306, 307; see also p. 369.</margin> the reign of a thousand years. This he expressly asserts: that after the resurrection of the dead is over, **Jerusalem** should be rebuilt, beautified, and enlarged. There, our Savior, along with all the holy Patriarchs, Prophets, Saints, and Martyrs, should visibly reign for a thousand years. 

He confesses, indeed, that there are many sincere and devout Christians who would not subscribe to this opinion, but he nonetheless affirms that there were many of the same mind as him. As indeed there <margin>d *Quoted in Irenaeus*, Book 5, ch. 33, p. 498; see *Eusebius*, Book 3, ch. 39, p. 112.
e *Location cited above & in Eusebius.*
f *Quoted in Eusebius*, Book 7, ch. 24, p. 270.
g *Quoted in Jerome's Commentary on Ezekiel*, ch. 36, Vol. 5, p. 507.

The first person to introduce this notion among the orthodox Christians of those early times seems to have been the aforementioned **Papias**. As <margin>m *Book 3, ch. 39, p. 112.*</margin> **Eusebius** tells us, Papias claimed it was an "Apostolic Tradition," though he misunderstood the Apostles' discourses and too lightly accepted in a literal sense what they meant in a mystical or hidden way. For though Papias was a good man, he was not of great depth of understanding and so was easily mistaken. Yet, as **Eusebius** observes, his mistake influenced several ecclesiastical figures, as the venerable antiquity of the man made the error seem more credible to them. 

Among those influenced were especially our **Saint Justin** and <margin>n *Caius quoted in Eusebius*, Book 3, ch. 28, p. 100; *Dionysius of Corinth, ibid.*, & Book 7, ch. 25, p. 273.</margin> **Irenaeus**, who held the belief in an innocent and harmless sense. It is true that **Cerinthus** and his followers, mixing this belief with **Jewish** dreams and fables and pretending divine revelations to support it, degraded it into something brutish and sensual. They placed the millennium in a state of eating, drinking, and all manner of bodily pleasures and delights. However, what use later heretics have made of this idea, and how much they have expanded upon it, is not my current business to investigate.

...instance of **Samuel** being summoned up by the enchantments of the **Pythoress** <note>original: "Pythonesse"; refers to the Witch of Endor who summoned the spirit of the prophet Samuel</note>. Nor does he assert it to be necessarily so, seeing he grants that by our hearty endeavors and prayers to God, our souls at the hour of their departure may escape the seizure of those evil powers. To this we may add what he seems ᵃ to maintain: that the souls of good men are not received into Heaven until the Resurrection. He believes that when they depart from the body, they remain ᵇ in a better place <note>original Greek: ἐν κρείττονί ποι χώρῳ (*en kreittoni poi chōrō*)</note>, where the soul, being gathered within itself, perpetually enjoys what it loved; but that the souls of the unrighteous and the wicked are thrust into a worse condition, where they await the judgment of the great day. He reckons ᶜ it among the errors of some so-called Christians (who denied the Resurrection) that they affirmed their souls were taken into Heaven immediately after death. 

In this view, Justin did not stand alone but had the almost unanimous support <note>original: "suffrage"</note> of the primitive writers voting with him: ᵈ **Irenaeus**, ᵉ **Tertullian**, ᶠ **Origen**, ᵍ **Hilary**, ʰ **Prudentius**, ⁱ **Ambrose**, ᵏ **Augustine**, ˡ **Anastasius Sinaita**, and indeed almost everyone else. There was a general agreement in this matter: that the souls of the righteous were not immediately moved into Heaven upon the dissolution of the body—that is, they were not yet admitted to a full and perfect enjoyment of the divine presence. Instead, they were assigned to certain secret and unknown resting places <note>original: "Repositories"</note> where they enjoyed a state of imperfect blessedness, waiting for its full completion at the general Resurrection. They described this intermediate state using the terms **Paradise** and **Abraham’s Bosom**, and some of them even believed it to be a subterranean region within the bowels of the Earth.

XXIV. We may observe a similar agreement among the ancients (though not quite as universally accepted) with our **Justin** regarding his opinion on ᵃ **Angels**. He believed that God, having committed to them the care and supervision of this sublunary <term>sublunary: the earthly world "under the moon," subject to change and decay</term> world, they abused the power entrusted to them. They mixed themselves with women in lustful and sensual embraces, fathering a race and posterity of **demons**. This assertion was not only hinted at by ᵇ **Philo** and ᶜ **Josephus**, but expressly owned by ᵈ **Papias**, ᵉ **Athenagoras**, ᶠ **Clement of Alexandria**, ᵍ **Tertullian**, ʰ **Cyprian**, ⁱ **Lactantius**, ᵏ **Sulpitius Severus**, ˡ **St. Ambrose**, and many others. 

What first gave birth to this opinion (which was easily embraced by those who held angels to be physical beings) was a misunderstanding of the passage: *the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair, and they took them to wife, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men, men of renown* <note>Genesis 6:2-4</note>. This mistake was further encouraged by the fact that many ancient copies of the **Septuagint** <term>Septuagint: the primary Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible used by the early Church</term> (as is evident from **Philo**, **St. Augustine**, and the King's ancient **Alexandrian Manuscript** which exists today) read "the **Angels** of God" instead of "the **Sons** of God." The Church Fathers, who generally understood no Hebrew, were unable to correct this. I also have no doubt that this error was further supported by the authority of the **Book of Enoch** (highly valued by many in those days), in which this story was related, as appears from the fragments of it still surviving.

<margin>
a *Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 319.

<margin>
b *Against Heresies*, book 3, ch. 17, p. 280.
</margin>

...within our *Martyr*, his magnifying the power of man's will, which is notoriously known to have been the current doctrine of the Fathers through all the first ages until the rise of the *Pelagian* controversies. However, they still generally acknowledge a special grace <note>original Greek: χάριν ἐξαίρετον (*charin exaireton*)</note>, a mighty assistance of divine grace to raise up and enable the soul for divine and spiritual things. *Justin* tells his adversary that it is in vain for a man to think he can rightly understand the mind of the ancient Prophets, unless he is assisted by a mighty grace derived from God <note>original Greek: μεγάλης Χάριτος τῆς παρὰ Θεοῦ (*megalēs Charitos tēs para Theou*)</note>. As well may the dry ground (says *Irenaeus*) produce fruit without rain to moisten it, as we who at first are like dried sticks, be fruitful toward a good life without voluntary showers from above—that is, as he adds, the bath <note>original: "laver"; referring to the washing of the soul or baptism</note> of the Spirit.

<margin>
The free will in us, arriving at the knowledge of the good, leaps and bounds over the boundaries, as the gymnasts say; yet it is not winged or raised up without special grace. The soul is lifted above those things that lie above it, putting aside everything better and building upon the Savior. Clement of Alexandria, *Miscellanies* <note>original: *Stromat.*</note>, book 5, p. 588. For it is not possible for a soul to be without free choice; nor does everything depend on our own opinion, such as the final result. For we are saved by grace, though not without good works. It is necessary to have a healthy mind, one that is unswerving in the pursuit of the good. For this we especially need divine grace, right teaching, pure disposition, and the Father drawing us to Himself. *Ibid.*, p. 547.
</margin>

*Clement of Alexandria* affirms expressly that just as there is a free choice in us, so not everything is placed in our own power; rather, we are saved by grace, though not without good works. He writes that to do what is good, we especially need the grace of God <note>original Greek: μάλιστα τῆς θείας χρῄζομεν χάριτος (*malista tēs theias chrēzomen charitos*)</note>, a right upbringing, an honest temperament of mind, and that the Father draws us to him. He also teaches that the free will <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐν ἡμῖν αὐτεξούσιον (*to en hēmin autexousion*)</note>—the powers of the will—are never able to give the soul wings for a proper flight toward Heaven without a mighty portion of grace to assist it.

<margin>
c Book 4, p. 181; see also *ibid.*, p. 227.
</margin>
<margin>
This will be the power of divine grace, which is more powerful than nature, having the free power of the will—called the *autexousion*—subject to itself. Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 21, p. 279.
</margin>

The mysteries of Christianity (as *Origen* discusses against *Celsus*) cannot be properly contemplated without a better inspiration <note>original: "afflatus"</note> and a more divine power; *for as no man knows the things of a man except the spirit of a man that is in him, so no man knows the things of God, but the Spirit of God.* It is all to no purpose (as he elsewhere observes) unless God by His grace enlightens the governing faculty of the soul <note>original Greek: φωτίζῃ τὸ ἡγεμονικόν (*phōtizē to hēgemonikon*)</note>. I add no more than the testimony of *Tertullian*, who asserts that there is a power of divine grace, stronger than nature, which holds the power of our Free Will in subjection.

It is so evident, then, that when the Fathers talk most highly of the free will <note>original Greek: αὐτεξούσιον (*autexousion*)</note> and the powers of nature, they never intended to exclude and banish the grace of God. Some other debatable or disallowed opinions may probably be found in this good man's writings, but these are mostly technical and philosophical. Indeed, having been brought up under so many different systems of philosophy and coming (as most of the early Fathers did) fresh out of the schools of *Plato*, it is less surprising if the ideas he had absorbed there stuck with him. He endeavored, as much as possible, to reconcile Platonic principles with the dictates of Christianity.

IRENAEUS may justly claim to follow immediately after the Martyr <note>Referring to St. Polycarp.</note>, "one who lived near the time of the Apostles" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἐγγὺς τῶν Ἀποστόλων γενόμενος — 'ho engys tōn Apostolōn genomenos'</note>, as <margin>a</margin> St. Basil styles him. This is expressed by <margin>b</margin> St. Jerome as him being a man of the Apostolic times. His origins are so obscure that there has been some dispute as to which part of the world he belonged, whether East or West; though there is no legitimate reason to doubt that he was a Greek. Since the Ancients did not specifically record the place of his birth, he is generally supposed to have been born at Smyrna or thereabouts. In his youth, he did not lack a noble education in the studies of philosophy and the humanities, which prepared him to be a useful instrument in the Church later on. 

His first training in the doctrine of Christianity was established under some of the most eminent <margin>c</margin> persons then in the Christian Church. St. Jerome identifies him as a student of Papias, Bishop of Hierapolis, who had himself conversed with <margin>d</margin> the Apostles and their followers. This Papias (as Irenaeus and others inform us) was one of St. John’s disciples. Although <margin>e</margin> Eusebius argues that this "John" was not the Apostle but rather a man surnamed "the Elder"—a conclusion he seems to draw from a passage by Papias himself—it is nonetheless evident that while Papias affirms he diligently gathered whatever records <note>original: "Memoirs"</note> he could find concerning the Apostles from those who had followed them, he nowhere denies that he himself <margin>f</margin> conversed with them. 

He was (as <margin>g</margin> Eusebius characterizes him) a man very learned, eloquent, and knowledgeable in the Scriptures. However, as Eusebius also adds elsewhere, he was "of a very small mind" <note>original Greek: σφόδρα σμικρὸς ὢν τὸν νοῦν — 'sphodra smikros ōn ton noun'</note>, possessing a very weak and undiscerning judgment. This was especially true regarding the more abstruse and mysterious parts of Christian doctrine, which easily led him and his followers into great errors and mistakes. He wrote five books entitled, <margin>h</margin> *Explanation of the Oracles of the Lord* <note>original Greek: Λογίων Κυριακῶν Ἐξήγησις — 'Logiōn Kyriakōn Exēgēsis'</note>. As Photius suggests and the <margin>i</margin> *Alexandrian Chronicle* expressly affirms, he died a martyr, being put to death at Pergamus during the persecution under Marcus Aurelius. He held such great reverence and regard for his teacher that he took a most exact and particular notice of whatever was memorable about him, even to the smallest details of his conversation. He preserved this memory fresh and lively until his dying day.

II. It is not known by whose hands he was consecrated to the ministries of religion, nor exactly when or for what reason he came into France <note>The author uses "France" to refer to the Roman province of Gaul.</note>. It is probable that he accompanied St. Polycarp on his journey to Rome regarding the Paschal <term>Paschal: relating to the date of Easter</term> controversy. There, through the persuasion of Polycarp and Anicetus, he may have been convinced to go to France (where great numbers of Greeks lived, especially around Marseille). At that time, France was beginning to be overrun with those destructive heresies which invaded and disturbed the Church, and he went so that he might be helpful and assist Pothinus, the aged Bishop of Lyons, in quelling and subduing them. This Pothinus—if we may believe Gregory, Bishop of Tours, who lived for some time in this city with his uncle Nicetius, the Bishop there—came from the East and had also been sent here by St. Polycarp to govern and supervise this Church. If it seems strange to anyone how St. Polycarp’s care extended so far as to send a bishop to such remote and distant parts of the world, it is not improbable to suppose that Lyons, being a city famous for commerce and trade, had merchants who traded with Smyrna. Having been converted by Polycarp, they might have asked him to send a grave and capable person with them to plant and spread the Christian Faith in their own country, which consequently became Pothinus's responsibility.

But a learned man <note>The author refers to Pierre de Marca (1594–1662), a French historian and archbishop.</note> will never be able to convince us that this must have been done by the authority and ratified by the decree of the Bishop of Rome, even though he offers three arguments to prove it. I must say these arguments are weak and inconclusive. They suggest that he intended to reconcile himself with the Court of Rome (whose favor he needed at the time he wrote that tract to be admitted to the Bishopric of St. Léger de Conserans <note>Saint-Lizier de Couserans</note>, to which he was nominated). His admission was being delayed by that Court, which was offended by his recent book *On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire* <note>original Latin: *De Concordia Sacerdotii & Imperii*</note>. These arguments are unsuited to the learning and judgment of such a great man.

But I return to Irenaeus. He came to Lyons, the metropolis of Celtic Gaul <note>original Latin: *Gallia Celtica*</note>, situated at the confluence of the two famous rivers, the Rhône and the Saône (or the ancient Arar). It was famous for, among other things, its temple and altars erected in honor of Augustus at the common expense of all France, where an annual ceremony was held by people from all parts of the country on the first of August. It was on this day that most of the martyrs suffered in the following persecution. These festival ceremonies were usually celebrated not only with great competitions in learning and eloquence, but with sports and shows, and especially with the bloody conflicts of gladiators, with barbaric practices, and the throwing of criminals to wild beasts in the amphitheater. In these events, the martyrs mentioned by Eusebius bore a

...this sad and miserable period. After arriving in Lyons, Irenaeus served for several years as a Presbyter <note>A "presbyter" is an elder or priest in the early church.</note> under the care and government of Pothinus, until a heavy storm broke over them. In AD 177, during the reign of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, a violent persecution against the Christians began. It broke out in all places but raged with particular intensity in France. The Churches of Lyons and Vienne gave an account of this in a letter to the churches of Asia and Phrygia. In it, they state that it was impossible for them to describe the brutal fierceness and cruelty of their enemies, or the severity of the torments the martyrs suffered. They were banished from their houses and forbidden even to show their faces; they were reproached, beaten, dragged from place to place, plundered, stoned, imprisoned, and treated with all the expressions of an ungovernable rage and fury, as the letter relates in great detail. The occasion for writing this account was a controversy recently raised in the Asian churches by Montanus <note>Montanus was the founder of Montanism, a movement that claimed to receive new, direct prophecies from the Holy Spirit.</note> and his followers concerning the "Prophetic Spirit" to which they laid claim. To resolve this, these churches thought it best to send their judgment and opinion on the case. They included the epistles that several of the martyrs had written from prison to those churches about that very matter, all of which they attached to their commentary about the martyrs' sufferings—a document undoubtedly penned by the hand of Irenaeus.

III. The martyrs did not only write to the Asian churches, but also to Eleutherus, the Bishop of Rome, regarding these controversies. There was a just occasion for this if (as is most probable) this very Eleutherus was infected with the errors of Montanus. Tertullian tells us that the Bishop of Rome at that time accepted and embraced the prophecies of Montanus and his two prophetesses, and on that account had given "Letters of Peace" to the churches of Asia and Phrygia, though he was later persuaded by a man named Praxeas to revoke them. By the way, it may be observed here that the "infallibility" of the Pope was either away from home or so fast asleep that the "envious man" <note>A biblical reference to the devil (Matthew 13:25) sowing weeds among the wheat.</note> could sow tares in the very Pontifical Chair itself. The historian Baronius argues that this Bishop was Anicetus, but in all likelihood, it was our Eleutherus. In his later commendation of the Montanists, he followed the example of his predecessors (no doubt Soter and Anicetus), who had originally disowned and rejected Montanus's prophecies; otherwise, it is hard to imagine why the martyrs would write to him so specifically about it. 

And whereas Baronius argues that Pope Eleutherus died long before Tertullian became a Montanist—because in his book *Against Heresies* he calls him "the blessed Eleutherus," as if that phrase meant "whose memory is blessed" <note>original Latin: *cujus memoria est in benedictione*</note>—nothing was actually more common than to give that title to eminent people while they were still alive. For example, Alexander of Jerusalem calls Clement of Alexandria (who carried his letter) "the blessed Clement" in his epistle to the Church of Antioch. Similarly, the clergy of the Church of Rome call St. Cyprian (who was then in hiding) "the blessed Pope Cyprian" in their letter to the people of Carthage. These martyrs, then, directed their epistle to this Eleutherus. In those times, martyrs were held in great honor and reverence, and their judgment in any weighty case was always received with high esteem and veneration. They sent these letters to Rome by Irenaeus, whom they persuaded to undertake the journey. They particularly recommended him to Eleutherus with a very honorable testimony, desiring the Bishop to receive him not only as their...

I know that <margin>a Note on Eusebius, pages 91 & 92.</margin> **Monsieur Valois** <note>Henri Valois (1603–1676) was a prominent French scholar and editor of early church histories.</note> does not agree that Irenaeus actually took this journey. After his return home, Irenaeus wrote letters to both Florinus and Blastus to convince them of the dangerous and novel ideas they had embraced.

### IV.

AND now the persecution at **Lyons** was carried on daily with even greater violence. Great numbers had already gone to Heaven through <margin>e Letter of the Churches of Lyons and Vienne, in Eusebius, chapter 1, page 159.</margin> infinite and inexpressible racks and torments. To crown it all, **Pothinus**, their venerable and aged Bishop—over ninety years old—was arrested so that he might be sent the same way. Age and illness had made him so weak and infirm that he was hardly able to crawl to his execution. Yet he possessed a vigorous and lively soul within a decaying and ruinous body; his great desire to give the ultimate testimony for his religion, and for Christ to triumph in his martyrdom, gave him new life and spirit. 

After being arrested by the officers, he was brought before the public tribunal. The city magistrates followed him, and the common people shouted so loudly and joyfully it was as if our Lord himself were being led to his execution. The Governor immediately asked him, "Who is the God of the Christians?" Knowing this to be a deceptive and sarcastic question, Pothinus returned no answer other than, "*If you were worthy, you would know.*" Instruction only takes root in a humble and obedient ear. Truth is usually lost when exposed to the wicked and the mocking; it is pointless to hold a candle for the blind who cannot see, or for those who shut their <margin>And I am deaf to ungodly words, whenever we despair of those who have already received the confirmation of the worse fate. Origen, *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, page 169. <note>original: "Κἀγὼ ἡ πρὸς τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς λόγους κώφωσις, ἐπὰν ἀπογινώσκωμεν ἢ ἤδη τὰ χείρονα λαχόντων ἐπικύρωσιν."</note></margin> eyes and refuse to see. There is a reverence due to the principles of religion that obliges us not to "cast pearls before swine," lest they trample them under their feet and turn again to tear us apart. 

At this, with no respect for his age or even for basic humanity, he was rudely dragged away and unmercifully beaten. Those nearby kicked him and struck him with their fists; those further away threw whatever they could find at him, using anything at hand as an instrument of their fury. Every man considered it a religious duty <note>original: "piacular," meaning an act required to appease the gods or expiate a sin</note> to do something to show his insolent scorn and rage against him. By this means, they thought they were avenging the honor of their gods. But their savage cruelty deemed it too much kindness to kill him all at once; they likely intended a second public ordeal for him. If so, Heaven frustrated their plans. For when he was picked up, having barely enough breath left to be considered alive, he was thrown into

### V.

THE Church of **Lyons** being thus deprived of its venerable guide, no one was better suited for the Bishop’s chair than **Irenaeus**, a person honored and admired by all. He succeeded to the position accordingly around the year 179 AD, during a troublesome and tumultuous time. But he was a wise and skillful pilot, steering the ship of the Church with prudent leadership. There was certainly enough need for both his courage and his conduct; for the Church at this time was not only assaulted by enemies from without, but also undermined and betrayed by heresies <note>Teachings or beliefs that contradict established religious dogma.</note> from within. He endured the attacks of the former with meekness and patience, while he endeavored to prevent the infection and poison of the latter through diligent and vigilant watchfulness—exposing their leaders, revealing their designs, and refuting and condemning their errors, so that *their folly was made manifest to all*.

<margin>a Strasbourg edition, 1601, quarto, page 2.</margin>
The author of the ancient *Synodicon* <note>A collection of decrees from church councils.</note> published by **Pappus** tells us of a provincial synod held at Lyons by Irenaeus. There, with the assistance and support of twelve other bishops, he condemned the heresies of **Valentinus**, **Marcion**, **Basilides**, and the rest of that anti-Christian crew. Where he obtained this information, I do not know, as it is not mentioned by any other ancient writers. However, the event itself is not improbable; Irenaeus's zeal against that sort of men drove him to oppose them both by word and writing, especially when it is remembered—as he himself informs us—that they had invaded his own province and come home to his very door. For having given us an account of **Marcus**, one of those **Gnostic** <term>Heresiarchs</term> <note>A leader of a heretical sect.</note>, and his followers—their filthy and immoral practices, and the ridiculous and senseless methods, magic, and hellish rites they used to ensnare and initiate their seduced converts—

<margin>b *Against Heresies*, book 1, chapter 9, page 72; see Jerome's *Epistle to Theodore*, page 196.</margin>
he tells us <sup>b</sup> that they had come into the countries surrounding him, all along the **Rhone**, where they generally prevailed over the "weaker sex" (which seems to have been observed as a core strategy by all founders of sects). They corrupted their minds and debauched their bodies; when these women's <note>original: "cauterized consciences"</note> seared consciences were later awakened, some made public confession of their crimes. Others, though they left the sect, were ashamed to return to the Church, while still others fell into a desperate and total <term>apostasy</term> <note>The abandonment or renunciation of a religious belief.</note>, giving up any pretense of faith.

<margin>c Preface to book 1, page 2.</margin>
Irenaeus had personally encountered some of these ringleaders and read the books of others. This gave him the opportunity (which many had urged him to undertake) to begin that elaborate work, ***Against Heresies***. In this work, he fully displayed their wild and fantastic principles and their brutal and abominable practices, taking infinite pains to refute them. Indeed, they were so prodigiously extravagant and so utterly irreconcilable to any principles of sober reason that, 

<margin>d Book 1, last chapter, page 139.</margin>
as he himself <sup>d</sup> observes, it was victory enough over them simply to discover and expose them.

<margin>e Book 3, chapter 3, page 233; and in Eusebius, book 5, chapter 6, page 171.</margin>
He composed this work during the time of **Eleutherus**, Bishop of **Rome**, as is evident from his catalogue <sup>e</sup> of the bishops of that See, which ends with Eleutherus, the twelfth successive bishop, who did *then* possess the office.

### VI.

AND indeed, it was high time for Irenaeus and the rest of the wise and holy bishops of those days to exert themselves, as *grievous wolves* had entered in and wreaked havoc on the flock. The field of the Church was miserably overrun with weeds <note>original: "tares"—likely darnel, a weed that looks like wheat until it matures.</note>, which did not only endanger the

<margin>
a *Stromata*, book 7, page 753.

...choking of religion within the Church, but also obstruct the planting and spreading of the faith among those who were outside of it. Nothing was more commonly used as an objection against the truth and divinity of the Christian religion than the fact that Christians were torn apart into so many schisms <note>Formal divisions or splits within a church.</note> and heresies. <sup>a</sup> **St. Clement of Alexandria** specifically addresses this objection, and some of his excellent reasoning is to this effect: 

The first thing (he says) they charge us with, and the reason they claim they cannot embrace the faith, is the variety of sects among us; they claim truth is delayed and neglected while some assert one thing and some another. To this he answers that there were various sects and parties both among the **Jews** and the philosophers of the **Gentiles**, and yet no one thought this a sufficient reason to stop studying philosophy or adhering to Jewish rites and discipline. He notes that our Lord had foretold that errors would spring up alongside the truth, like tares <note>Weeds that look like wheat when young.</note> growing up with the wheat; therefore, it was no surprise that it happened. 

He argues that we ought not to fail in our own duty just because others abandon theirs, but rather we should stick closer to those who remain constant in the profession of the truth. A mind diseased and disturbed by error and idolatry should no more be discouraged from joining an institution that will cure it—simply because of some differences and divisions within it—than a sick man would refuse to take any medicine because physicians have different opinions and do not all use the same prescriptions. 

The Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 11:19.</note> has told us *that there must be heresies, so that those who are approved may be recognized*; these are the people who sincerely embrace Christian doctrine, improve themselves, and persevere in faith and a holy life. If truth is difficult to discern, finding it will abundantly repay the trouble and the labor. A wise man would not refuse to eat fruit just because he must take a little effort to distinguish what is ripe and real from that which is only painted and counterfeit. Shall the traveler resolve not to go on his journey because there are many ways that cross and block the common road, rather than asking which is the plain King's Highway? Or shall the farmer refuse to till his ground because weeds grow together with the plants? 

We ought instead to use these differences as an argument and incentive to more accurately distinguish truth from falsehood, and reality from pretension. By escaping the snares that are plausibly laid, we may attain to the knowledge of that which is truly reality <note>original: εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν τῆς ὄντως οὔσης ἀληθείας (eis epignōsin tēs ontōs ousēs alētheias)</note>, which is not hard to find for those who sincerely seek it. But to return back to **Irenaeus**.

VII. HAVING passed through the times of the Emperor **Commodus**—the only credit of whose reign was that he created no great disturbance for the Christians, though he was otherwise a most debauched and corrupt prince in whom the vices of all his predecessors seemed to meet as if in one common sewer—**Eleutherus** died, and **Victor** succeeded him in the See <note>The office or jurisdiction of a bishop.</note> of **Rome**. Victor was a man furious and hot-headed, impatient of contradiction, who gave free rein to an impulsive and ungovernable passion. He revived the controversy about the celebration of **Easter** and imperiously tried to impose the Roman custom—of keeping it on the next Lord's day after the **Jewish Passover**—upon the churches of **Asia Minor** <note>original: Lesser Asia</note> and those who observed the contrary custom. Because they would not yield, he rashly thundered out an excommunication against them...

...them, not only attempting, but as $^a$ **Eusebius** explains it in the following words, actually banning them and declaring them cut off from the Communion of the Church. The **Asiatics** <note>Christians from the Roman province of Asia, modern-day Turkey.</note> paid little attention to the fierce threats from **Rome**. Under the leadership of **Polycrates**, Bishop of **Ephesus**, they stood their ground, justifying their practice of observing Easter on the fourteenth day after the appearance of the Moon <note>This was the 14th of the month of Nisan, the date of the Jewish Passover.</note>, no matter what day of the week it fell upon. They followed the rule of the **Jewish Passover**, and this was based on constant tradition and uninterrupted usage derived from **St. John** and **St. Philip** the Apostles, **St. Polycarp**, and several others down to that very day. All of this Polycrates told Pope **Victor**, but it achieved nothing (for what can satisfy a stubborn and emotional mind?) to prevent him from tearing the Church apart.

<margin>
