To settle this unhappy division $^b$ Synods <note>Formal councils of church leaders.</note> were called in several places. Besides one at **Rome**, there was one in **Palestine** under **Theophilus**, Bishop of **Caesarea Maritima**, and **Narcissus**, Bishop of **Jerusalem**; another in **Pontus** under **Palmas**; and many more in other places. All were willing to help extinguish the common fire of conflict. $^c$ They all wrote to **Victor**, strongly rebuking him and advising him instead to focus on what concerned the peace of the Church and the love and unity of Christians with one another. Among the rest, our **Irenaeus** (who, as **Eusebius** observes, truly lived up to his name <note>The name Irenaeus is derived from the Greek word *eirene*, meaning "peace."</note> in his peaceful and peacemaking character) convened a $^d$ Synod of the Churches of **France** <note>Then known as Gaul.</note> under his jurisdiction. There, with thirteen other bishops besides himself (according to the aforementioned $^e$ *Synodicon* <note>A collection of historical church decrees.</note>), he considered and decided on this matter. In their name, he wrote a Synodal Letter to Pope $^f$ **Victor**, in which he told him that they agreed with him on the core issue of the controversy <note>That Easter should be celebrated on a Sunday.</note>, but he also solemnly and seriously advised him to be careful about excommunicating entire churches for following the ancient customs passed down to them from their ancestors. He noted that there was as little agreement on the manner of the *Preparatory Fast* before **Easter** as there was on the day itself: some thought they should fast only one day (likely meaning the most solemn day of Holy Week), others two, others more, and some measured the time by a continuous fast of forty hours (whether in memory of Christ lying so long in the grave, or in imitation of His forty-day fast in the wilderness, I do not know). He argued that this variety was long-standing and had developed in various places while the governors of the Church took less care to enforce uniformity in these customs. Yet, they had still maintained a sincere and mutual love and peace toward one another. This was the practice of all Victor's own pious predecessors. Irenaeus reminded him of **Anicetus** and **Polycarp**, who, although they could not convince each other to abandon their different customs, nonetheless embraced one another, shared the Communion together, and parted in peace. He wrote letters to the same effect to several other bishops to calm the dispute so unfortunately started in the Church.

...against them in this place. The persecution, which in other regions selected only a few individuals to serve as examples, here targeted everyone equally and completed its destructive work. For as $^a$ **Gregory of Tours** and the ancient *Martyrologies* inform us, **Irenaeus**, having been prepared by various torments, was at length put to death. (The $^c$ **Greeks** say he was beheaded, which is likely enough.) Together with him, almost all the Christians of that vast, populous city were killed; their numbers were so great they could not be counted, and the streets of the city flowed with the blood of Christians. His body was taken up by **Zacharias**, his presbyter <note>term: A priest or elder within the early church hierarchy.</note>, and buried in a vault, laid between **Epipodius** and **Alexander**, who had suffered in the persecution under **Antoninus** <note>Emperor Antoninus Pius or Marcus Aurelius Antoninus; the latter's reign saw significant persecutions.</note>. It is not easy to assign a certain date to his martyrdom, which may with almost equal probability be referred to two different periods: either to the time of that bloody edict which **Severus** published against the Christians around the tenth year of his reign (AD 202), or to his expedition into **Britain** (AD 208), when he passed through **Lyons** and might have seen the executions carried out with his own eyes. Indeed, the vast numbers said to have suffered there agree well enough with the temper of that fierce and cruel Prince, who had previously developed a particular displeasure against the citizens of **Lyons**, and a worse one against the Christians there.

IX. He was a true lover of God and of the souls of men. To promote their happiness, he considered no dangers or difficulties too great. He did not hesitate to leave his own country to undertake such a troublesome and tedious journey. Instead of the refined and sophisticated culture of the **Eastern** nations, he chose to settle among a people of a wild and savage nature, whom he had to civilize before he could even win them over to religion. Nor was it the least of his troubles (as he $^d$ plainly suggests himself) that he was forced to learn the language of the country—a rugged and, as he calls it, "barbarous" dialect—before he could do any good for them. He cheerfully underwent all of this, and much more, so that he might serve the greatest interests of humanity. He knew that nothing usually hinders the progress of piety more than when minds are corrupted and debased by false and distorted notions and principles. He also recognized that nothing could expose the Christian religion to the scorn of wise and discerning men more than the wild schemes of those absurd and ridiculous opinions then being promoted. Therefore, he set himself with all imaginable industry to oppose them. He read through all their writings, considering and unravelling all their principles with incomparable patience and diligence. For this reason, he is deservedly described by $^e$ **Tertullian** as "the most inquisitive investigator of all doctrines" <note>original: *Omnium doctrinarum curiosissimus explorator*</note>. In successfully managing this task, he was greatly aided by his natural sharp-wittedness and the subtlety of his intellect, as well as those studies of philosophy and classical literature of which he had made himself a master in his younger days. Sufficient evidence of this appears in the writings he left behind. For besides his epistles, he wrote many volumes. (Though $^g$ the author who claims he composed an *Ecclesiastical History* which **Eusebius** used is mistaken, likely confusing it with his work *Against Heresies*.) These other works are all lost, except for his five books against heresies, originally titled *The Refutation and Overthrow of Knowledge Falsely So-Called* <note>original: *Ἔλεγχος & ἀνατροπὴ τῆς ψευδωνύμου γνώσεως*</note>, which is to say, of **Gnosti-**

It is not easily guessed what his specific style and phrasing were in these books, as the vast majority of the <margin>Cited in the place mentioned.</margin> original Greek is missing. (The theory held by some that they were originally written in Latin is not worth mentioning.) His style was likely simple and unaffected, common and ordinary, and perhaps influenced—as he himself seems to admit—by the local language of the region [Gaul] where he lived. Nor had he studied the arts of rhetoric, the ornaments of speech, or the sophisticated methods and <margin>a In the preface, as cited above.</margin> skills of persuasion, for which he modestly apologizes. Nevertheless, his writings are serious and well-thought-out, and (as far as his subject matter allowed) clear and easy to understand. Throughout them, he shows great zeal and a spirit ready for martyrdom. For martyrs (as <margin>b Erasmus, Preface to the Works of Irenaeus.</margin> *Erasmus* truly notes) have a certain serious, energetic, and vigorous way of writing that surpasses other men.

<margin>c Photius, *Bibliotheca*, Codex 120, column 301.</margin> X. As for the works themselves, **Photius** <note>A 9th-century scholar and Patriarch of Constantinople known for his vast library and reviews of ancient texts.</note> critiques them by saying that in some, the accuracy of truth in Church doctrines is corrupted with false and spurious reasonings <note>original Greek: *nothois logismois*</note>, which should be noted. In the books still surviving, there are some claims that will not withstand a strict and rigorous examination. He was led into it partly by the false assumption that our Lord must have reached a more mature age to deliver his teachings with greater authority. He was also influenced by a mistaken report (which he had picked up somewhere, perhaps from his teacher **Papias** <note>An early Christian author whose work now survives only in fragments; he was known for collecting oral traditions about the Apostles.</note>) that St. **John** and the other Apostles had taught this. Additionally, he wrote out of opposition to his adversaries, who argued that our Savior remained on earth only until the thirty-first year of his age. In the heat of this dispute, he was tempted to support his claim with any plausible evidence. In his haste to push his argument, he did not take the time to calmly consider the context and instead seized upon the Jews' question to Christ: "*You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?*" From this, in passing <note>original Latin: *in transitu*</note>, he took it for granted that the Jews had a reason for mentioning that age, and therefore Christ must have been close to it.

XI. His care to have his writings passed down pure and uncorrupted to posterity was great and admirable. > I charge you, whoever you are that shall transcribe this book, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by his glorious coming, when he shall judge the living and the dead, that you compare what you transcribe and diligently correct it against the copy from which you are transcribing; and you shall likewise transcribe this oath and attach it to your copy.

It would have been well for the ancient writers of the Church if their books had been treated with this much care and reverence. More of them would have been preserved for us; or at least the few that remain would have arrived in a more sound and unpolluted state. I. <image-desc>Decorative initial letter T featuring ornate foliate scrollwork within a square border.</image-desc>Although the ancients provide us with very few accounts concerning this venerable Bishop, it may perhaps not be unacceptable to the reader to gather what little information can be found. There is a mistake not worth refuting and scarcely deserving mention that identifies him as the same *Theophilus* of *Antioch* to whom *Saint Luke* dedicated his Gospel writings; the distance of time between them is far too great for this to be possible. Whether he was born at *Antioch* is uncertain, but wherever his birthplace, his parents were *Gentiles* <note>Non-Christians, specifically practitioners of traditional Greco-Roman religion.</note>, by whom he was raised in the common rites of the religion that then governed the world. They gave him all the accomplishments of a learned and liberal education, and he made vast improvements in his studies. As a result, he was thoroughly versed in the writings of all the great masters of learning and philosophy in the heathen world. This, combined with a quick and engaging wit (as appears from his disputes against the *Gentiles*), rendered him a man of significant reputation and account among them.

II. When or by what means he was converted to Christianity is impossible to determine specifically; only this much may be gathered from the discourses he left behind. Being a man of an inquiring nature and undoubtedly of a very honest mind, he dedicated himself to a more free and impartial search into the nature and state of things. He found that the account of things given by the religion he was then involved in was altogether unsatisfactory. He saw that the stories of their gods were absurd and frivolous, and some of them profane and impious, and that their rites of worship were trifling and ridiculous. He considered the various parts of the creation and the excellent providence that governed the world, in which he easily discerned the clear evidence of a wise and omnipotent Being. He realized that God had purposely arranged things in this way so that His grandeur and majesty might appear to everyone. Accordingly, he directs his friend to this method of conviction, as it was undoubtedly what he had found most successful and satisfactory for himself. <margin>*To Autolycus, Book 1, page 72.* <note>original: "Ad Autolyc. l.1. p. 72."</note></margin> He bids *him survey and consider the works of God: the shifting and changing of the seasons, the revolutions of the heavenly bodies, and the wisely established course of the elements. He points to the beautiful order and arrangement of nights and days, months and years; the pleasant and admirable variety of seeds, plants, and fruits; and the many generations of beasts, birds, reptiles, fish, and the inhabitants of the watery regions. He notes the prudent instinct...*

III. THERE was one thing which he himself seems to suggest <note>original: "intimate"</note> was a particular obstacle ᶜ to his full acceptance of Christian doctrine: the belief in the Resurrection. He had been educated in the schools of philosophy, where he was taught that once life is lost, there can be no return to it. It is likely he could not imagine how the scattered dust of men, after so many ages, could be collected and rebuilt into the same bodies. Indeed, there is hardly any principle of the Christian faith that generally met with more opposition from the wise and the learned, or which was more difficult for them to admit into their creed. When Saint *Paul* preached to the philosophers at *Athens*, while he told them of a judgment to come, they had no trouble accepting it, as it is a principle evident by natural reason <note>original: "natural light"</note>. But when he spoke of a future *Resurrection*, they rejected it with contempt and scorn: *and when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked; and the most grave and sober took time to consider of it; others said, "we will hear you again on this matter."* And *Synesius* himself, that great philosopher, even after being baptized into the Christian religion, when invited by *Theophilus* of *Alexandria* to become the Bishop of *Ptolemais*, would not agree ᵈ until he had publicly declared his disagreement with the doctrine of the Resurrection—at least regarding the common explanation of that article of faith. He looked upon it as "something sacred and unutterable" <note>original: "ἱερὸν τι καὶ ἀπόῤῥητον"</note>, as containing a kind of sacred and indescribable mystery, but he could not agree with the common and accepted opinions. He was likely willing to accept it if he might explain it according to the principles of philosophy and in the *Platonic* style. Yet I do not see why any who acknowledge a Being of infinite power should struggle to believe this article. As *Athenagoras* and others argue on this subject, it is just as easy for Omnipotence ᵉ to restore our scattered parts and combine them again into the same form as it was to create them out of nothing in the first place. # The Life of Saint THEOPHILUS.

By observing the persistent manifestations <note>original: "Phænomena"</note> of Divine Providence, he overcame this objection—especially after he had studied and embraced the holy volumes <note>original: "Volums"</note>, in which these things were so clearly declared and published. And so he became a Christian. Having been frustrated and let down by all other refuges, he sought sanctuary in the Church, which (as he himself expresses it <margin>* Book 2, pages 93, 94.</margin>) God has set in the world like an island in the midst of the sea. Into its safe and convenient harbors, the lovers of truth might fly, along with all those who desired to be saved and to escape the judgment and the <margin>∴ See Book 1, page 69.</margin> wrath to come. He was glad that he had arrived there, rejoicing that he bore the name of a Christian—a name dear to God <note>original: "Θεοφιλὲς ὄνομα" / "Theophiles onoma"</note>—no matter how much it was otherwise despised and scorned by an ignorant and wicked age.

<margin>
a Eusebius's Chronicle, in the same year.
b Annals, page 359.
</margin>
IV. Around the year 169 (though <margin>b</margin> Eutychius attributes it to the sixteenth year of Emperor Antoninus’s reign), or rather the year before, his predecessor Eros having died, he was made Bishop of **Antioch**. He is accounted by some as the sixth and by others as the seventh Bishop of that See. Neither of them is mistaken; both are true according to different methods of counting. Some reckon Saint Peter as the first, while others—viewing him as an Apostle acting in a larger and more universal <note>original: "Oecumenical"</note> sphere than a private Bishop—begin the count with Euodius as the first Bishop. 

Once Saint Theophilus was established in his position, he set himself to promote the true interest and happiness of men. Since goodness always delights to share and spread itself, he studied how to bring others over to the faith that he had embraced himself. Among the rest, he attempted to convince a person of importance: his great friend **Autolycus**. <margin>c Theophilus, Book 3, page 119.</margin> We have no account of who this Autolycus was, other than what is given to us by Theophilus himself. He was a learned and eloquent man, inquisitive in all the arts and sciences. He pursued the acquisition of knowledge with such tireless diligence that he would bury himself among books and steal hours for study from his necessary rest, spending whole nights in libraries and in conversing <margin>d Ibid. Book 2, page 80.</margin> with the writings <note>original: "monuments"</note> of the dead. At the same time, however, he was a pagan <note>original: "Gentile"</note>, infinitely zealous for his religion and unreasonably prejudiced against Christianity. He denounced it as the highest folly and madness, loading it with all the common charges and slanders <note>original: "calumnies"</note> which either the wit or malice of those times had invented to make it hateful. He had even argued bitterly with Theophilus in defense of his views. 

Despite this, Theophilus was not frightened away from trying to reach him. He treated him with all the freedom and candor <note>original: "ingenuity"</note> that was appropriate for a <margin>e Ibid. Book 1, page 70.</margin> friend and a philosopher. He told him that the problem lay within himself—that he did not discern and embrace the truth because his wickedness and impieties had corrupted his mind and darkened his understanding. He argued that men should not blame the sun for a lack of light when they themselves were blind and lacked the eyes to see it. He said that the rust and dirt must be wiped off from the mirror <note>original: "Glass"</note> before it could provide a true and clear representation of an object. Likewise, God would not reveal himself except to purified and prepared minds—those who, through innocence and a divine life, had become fit and ready to receive and welcome him. Then, he explained to him the nature of God and gave him an account of the origin of the world according to Christian doctrine. He refuted and mocked the ridiculous deities of the heathens and particularly answered those dark accusations usually laid upon the Christians. Finally, because Autolycus had mainly argued that the Christian faith was a late and modern invention <note>original: "lateness and novelty"</note>, he showed...

He showed extensively how much superior Christianity was in many ways regarding its antiquity <note>original: "Seniority"</note>—predating by many ages anything the pagan religion could claim. He urged him at every opportunity to embrace such an excellent religion, assuring him that the *people whom he invited* him to join were not at all as he had portrayed them. Instead, they lived under the guidance of modesty, sobriety, temperance, and chastity. They banished injustice and uprooted all vice and wickedness; they loved righteousness, lived under law and order, practiced a divine religion, acknowledged God, and served the truth. They lived under the preservation of grace and peace, directed by a sacred Word, taught by wisdom, rewarded by an immortal life, and governed by God himself. What the final outcome <note>original: "issue"</note> of these discourses was, we cannot say for certain, but we can probably hope they achieved the desired success. This is especially likely since we find *Autolycus*, after the first conference, a little more favorable to the cause, setting aside his initial displeasure against *Theophilus* and asking him for a further account of his religion. Certainly, if wisdom, eloquence, strength of reason, and a prudent management of the controversy were able to do it, Theophilus could not have failed to reclaim the man from his error and idolatry.

<margin>
a Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 24, page 146.
b In the Greek excerpts of Theodotus, found in Clement of Alexandria, page 808 D.
</margin>
V. Nor was he more anxious to win others to the faith than he was to keep those who had already embraced it from being infected and corrupted by error. For this reason, he continually stood on his guard, faithfully warning of the approach of heresy and vigorously opposing it. Despite the care and vigilance of the good and pious men of those days (as *Eusebius* observes), envious men crept in and sowed weeds <note>original: "Tares"</note> among the pure Apostolic doctrine. Consequently, the pastors of the Church were forced to rise up everywhere to drive away these "wild beasts" from Christ's sheepfold—partly by exhorting and warning the believers, and partly by entering the ring <note>original: "lists"</note> with the heretics themselves. Some debated and refuted them in person, while others accurately exposed and disproved their opinions through the books they wrote against them. Among these, we are told, was our *Theophilus*, who struggled against these heretics. He specifically wrote against **Marcion**, who claimed there were two deities and that only the soul (being the divine and better part), and not the body, was capable of the happiness of the next world—and even then, this was granted to none but his followers, along with many other impious and foolish <note>original: "fond"</note> opinions. He wrote another book against **Hermogenes**, a man better skilled in painting than in drawing up systems <note>original: "Schemes"</note> of new theology <note>original: "Divinity"</note>. Hermogenes abandoned the Church and fled to the **Stoics**; influenced by their principles, he maintained that matter was eternal and that God created all things out of it, asserting moreover that all evil proceeded from matter. Furthermore, as *Clement of Alexandria* informs us, he claimed that our Lord’s body was lodged in the sun, ridiculously interpreting the scripture passage: *In them has he set a tabernacle for the sun.* Nor did our *Theophilus* neglect the weak and younger members of his charge. He had not only medicine for the sick and solid food <note>original: "strong meat"</note> for the mature, but "milk for infants" and those who were yet unskilled in the word of righteousness. He composed many introductory <note>original: "Catechetic"</note> discourses that contained the first basic principles of the faith.

</margin>

<sup>b</sup> *From Jerome, "On Illustrious Men" regarding Melito.*

I. <image-desc>Decorative square woodcut initial "S" with leafy floral patterns.</image-desc>ST. MELITO was born in Asia Minor, and probably at Sardis, the capital of Lydia. This was a great and ancient city and the seat of the Lydian kings; it was one of the Seven Churches to which St. John wrote epistles, and in which he notes some who dared to own and stand up for God and religion during the great degeneracy that had come upon it. He was a man of admirable talents <note>original: "parts"</note>, enriched with the equipment of all useful learning, acute and eloquent, but especially well-versed in the paths of divine knowledge, having made deep inquiries into all the more uncommon areas and theories of Christian doctrine. Because of his singular excellence and usefulness, he was chosen Bishop of Sardis. Although we cannot exactly define the time of his appointment—if I were to speculate—I would guess it was about the latter end of the reign of Antoninus Pius, or the beginning of his successors. He fulfilled all the roles of an excellent governor and guide of souls, whose well-being he was careful to advance both by word and writing.

So that he might attend to this with less worry and distraction, he not only remained unmarried <note>original: "kept himself within the compass of a single life"</note>, but was more than ordinarily exemplary for his chastity and sobriety, his self-denial, and his contempt for the world. On this account, he is styled by Polycrates, Bishop of Ephesus, as an "eunuch"—that is, in our Savior's explanation, one of those *who make themselves eunuchs for the Kingdom of Heaven’s sake*; those who, for the service of religion and the hope of a better life, are content to deny themselves the comforts of a married state and to renounce even the lawful pleasures of this world. And God, who delights to multiply His grace upon pious and holy souls, crowned his other virtues with the gift of prophecy. Indeed, Tertullian tells us that he was regarded by the orthodox Christians as a prophet, and Polycrates says of him that he "conducted his whole life in the Holy Spirit" <note>original: "ἐν ἁγίῳ πνεύματι πάντα πολιτεύεσθαι"</note>, being in all things governed and directed by the inspiration and suggestion of the Holy Ghost. Accordingly, in the catalog of his writings, we find one titled *On the Conduct of Life and the Prophets* <note>original: "περὶ πολιτείας, καὶ προφητῶν"</note>, and another *Concerning Prophecy*.

<margin>
<sup>e</sup> *Eusebius's Chronicon, for the year 171 AD.*
<sup>f</sup> *Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, in the place cited above.*
</margin>
II. It was about the year 170 AD, and the tenth year of Marcus Antoninus (his brother Lucius Verus having died the year before of a stroke <note>original: "Apoplexy"</note> as he sat in his chariot), when the persecution grew intense against the Christians. Greedy and malicious men took occasion from the Imperial edicts lately published to oppress and spoil innocent Christians by all methods of cruelty and plunder <note>original: "rapine"</note>. Upon this, as others did, St. Melito especially presented an apology and humble petition on their behalf to...

to the Emperor, wherein among other things he thus addresses him:
> “If these things, Sir, are done by your order, let them be considered well done. For a righteous prince will never at any time command what is unjust; and we shall not think it a burden to undergo the sentence of such a death. This is the only request we ask: that you would please first to examine the case of these determined people yourself, and then impartially determine whether they deserve punishment and death, or safety and protection. But if this new edict and decree—which should not have been proclaimed even against the most savage enemies—did not come from your own knowledge and consent, we humbly pray, and with even greater urgency, that you would not allow us to be any longer exposed to this public robbery <note>original: "rapine"</note>.”

III. After this, he reminded him how much the Empire had prospered since the rise of Christianity, and that none but the worst of his predecessors had maintained an unrelenting malice against the Christians.
> “This new school of philosophy,” he says, “which we profess, previously flourished among the *Barbarians* (by which he probably means *the Jews*). Afterward, during the reign of your predecessor *Augustus*, it spread itself over the provinces of your empire, beginning as a favorable sign <note>original: "omen"</note> for it. Since that time, the majesty and greatness of the *Roman* Empire has greatly increased. You are the desired heir and successor to this empire, and shall remain so along with your son, especially as long as you protect that religion which began with *Augustus* and grew up together with the empire—a religion for which your predecessors, along with other rites of worship, had some degree of reverence and regard. That our religion was raised with the prosperity of the empire and was born for the public good is proven by this great argument: since the reign of *Augustus*, no significant disaster has occurred; on the contrary, all things have turned out glorious and successful according to everyone's desire. None but *Nero* and *Domitian*, incited by cruel and ill-minded men, have attempted to disgrace and slander our religion. From them sprang the common slanders concerning us, as the unthinking common people <note>original: "injudicious Vulgar"</note> greedily believe such reports without any strict examination. But your parents of pious memory corrected this ignorance and injustice by frequent official letters <term>rescripts</term>, rebuking those who made any new attempts to cause trouble in this matter. Among them was your grandfather *Hadrian*, who wrote to several others, including *Fundanus*, the Proconsul of *Asia*; and your father, at the time you were a colleague with him in the empire, wrote to several cities (particularly to *Larissa*, *Thessalonica*, *Athens*, and all the cities of *Greece*) that they should not create any new disturbance regarding this affair. And as for yourself, who hold the same opinion of us as they did—and a much better one, more becoming of a good man and a philosopher—we are confident that you will grant all our petitions and requests.”

This was an address managed with great prudence and noble boldness <note>original: "ingenuous freedom"</note>, and by aligning with other defenses <note>original: "Apologies"</note> presented around the same time, it contributed significantly to the general peace and prosperity of Christians.

# The Life of St. MELITO.

<margin>a Melito himself, in Eusebius, Book 4, Chapter 26, page 147.</margin>
<margin>b In Eusebius, Book 5, Chapter 24, page 191.</margin>
<margin>c In Eusebius, as cited above, page 147.</margin>
During the time that Servilius Paulus was Proconsul of Asia, Sagaris, the Bishop of Laodicea, had suffered martyrdom in the recent persecution. At that time, the controversy regarding the Easter celebrations <note>original: "Paschal solemnity"</note> was intensively debated in that Church. Some, who were likely foreigners, urged that the festival be observed according to the Roman custom—celebrating it on the Lord’s Day (Sunday)—contrary to the tradition of those Churches in Asia, who had always kept it on the fourteenth day of the moon <note>This refers to the "Quartodeciman" practice of following the Jewish calendar for Passover, regardless of the day of the week.</note>, according to the Jewish manner. To quiet this contention, Melito immediately wrote two books *Concerning the Passover* <note>original: "peri tou Pascha"</note>, in which he undoubtedly treated at length the celebration of Easter according to the tradition of the Asian Churches. Therefore, Polycrates, in his letter to Pope Victor, specifically includes Sagaris and Melito among the chief champions of this cause. This book on Easter by St. Melito was also mentioned by Clement of Alexandria in a treatise on the same subject, in which he admits that he was moved to undertake his own work by the discourse Melito had published.

V. How tireless is true goodness and a love for souls! How willing it is to endure any difficulties if another’s happiness might be advanced. Melito's brother, Onesimus, had requested that he point out those passages of the Old Testament that primarily served to confirm the Christian religion, and to let him know how many of those books were admitted into the holy Canon. To thoroughly satisfy both his brother and himself in this matter, Melito took a journey specifically to the East—that is, I suppose, to Jerusalem—where he was most likely to receive a full and satisfying answer. Having informed himself there, he gave his brother an account of it upon his return. The letter itself, being short and containing such authentic evidence of which books of the Old Testament were received by the ancient Church, is included below.

->Melito *to his brother* Onesimus, *greeting.*<-

*Because of your great love for and delight in the Holy Scriptures, you have often requested me to collect those passages from the Law and the Prophets that relate to our Savior and the various parts of our Christian Faith. You also wished to be accurately informed about the books of the Old Testament—how many there are and in what order they were written. I have endeavored to comply with your desires in this matter. I recognize your great zeal and care concerning the Faith, and how much you desire to be instructed in matters of religion; especially, out of your love for God, I know how infinitely you prefer these things above all others, being concerned for your eternal salvation. For this purpose, I traveled to the East, and having arrived at the place where these things were done and published, and having accurately informed myself of the books of the Old Testament, I have sent you the following account:*

*The five books of Moses: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy. Joshua* <note>original: "Jesus or Joshua"</note> *the son of Nun; Judges, Ruth; the four books of Kings* <note>In the ancient numbering, the "four books of Kings" include what we now call 1 and 2 Samuel and 1 and 2 Kings.</note>. *Two books of Chronicles. The Psalms of David. The Proverbs of Solomon (also called Wisdom); Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, Job. The Prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, the twelve [minor] Prophets in one book. Daniel, Ezekiel, Ezra. From all of these, I have made collections, which I have organized into six books.*

VI. In this catalog, we may observe that the Book of *Esther* is omitted. It is also left out by <margin>b</margin> *St. Athanasius*, <margin>c</margin> *Gregory Nazianzen*, and <margin>d</margin> *Leontius* in their lists of the books of the holy Canon. The reason for this is uncertain, unless (as <margin>e</margin> *Sixtus Senensis* reasonably conjectures) it was not viewed in those times as having the same unquestionable credit and authority as the rest; the apocryphal additions at the end of it caused the entire book to be called into question. Nor is there any specific mention made of *Nehemiah*, likely because it was anciently included within the Book of *Ezra* <note>original: "Esdras"</note>. Furthermore, we see that by the title *Wisdom*, he does not mean the *Apocryphal Book* called the *Wisdom of Solomon* (as <margin>f</margin> *Bellarmine* and most Roman Catholic writers confidently assert), but rather Solomon’s *Proverbs*. <margin>g</margin> *Eusebius* expressly tells us that not only *Hegesippus* but also *Irenaeus* and all the ancient writers were accustomed to call the *Proverbs of Solomon* by the name of *Wisdom*, or *all-virtuous Wisdom* <note>original: "πανάρετον Σοφίαν" (panareton Sophian)</note>, meaning a wisdom containing a system of all kinds of virtues. Indeed, that *Melito* could mean no other book in this passage is proven beyond all doubt by the words of his letter restored by *Valesius*—*Solomon's Proverbs, which is also called Wisdom* <note>original: "Σολόμωνος παροιμίαι, ἢ καὶ Σοφία" (Solomonos paroimiai, e kai Sophia)</note>—according to the quotation by *Nicephorus* and the evidence of all the best and most ancient manuscripts.

<margin>
h Polycrates' Epistle in Eusebius, p. 191.
i In Jerome, *On Writers*, in Melito.
k "Among which were also found the writings of Melito, such as 'Concerning God being embodied'." Theodoret, *Question 20 on Genesis*, Vol. I. page 21.
l "Concerning him [Jesus Christ] Solomon also spoke, as if in his own person: 'The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works'."
</margin>
VII. At last, this good man—worn out by endless toil and labor, and weary of the anxieties of a troublesome world—retreated to the place of rest. The time and manner of his death are unknown; we only find <margin>h</margin> that he died and lies buried at *Sardis*, waiting for *the visitation from heaven* <note>original: "τὴν ἐξ οὐρανῶν ἐπισκοπήν" (ten ex ouranon episkopen)</note>, when our Lord shall come and raise him from the dead. Aside from his mental piety and the strict innocence of his life, he was a man of great talent and learning. He possessed *an elegant and oratorical genius* <note>original: "elegans & declamatorium ingenium"</note>, as <margin>i</margin> *Tertullian* said of him—a sharp, elegant wit, able to describe things with their most appropriate emphasis. He wrote books on almost every kind of subject: divine, moral, and philosophical. These were monuments of no less industry than learning, though they have all been long since lost, except for a few fragments. I know there are those who suspect him of having held views that were less than Orthodox regarding some of the great principles of religion. I confess this seems to me a most uncharitable and unjust reflection upon such a holy and good man, especially since the suspicion is based merely on the titles of some of his books, as none of the books themselves survive. A fair explanation of those titles could be given to satisfy any sober and impartial person. Only two titles could be liable to objection. One is *Concerning God in a Body* <note>original: "Περὶ ἐνσωμάτου Θεου" (Peri ensomatou Theou)</note>. This should be understood as concerning God, not as a *Physical Being* by nature (as <margin>k</margin> *Theodoret*, and apparently *Origen*, understood it), but as *God Incarnate* (as *Tertullian* would express it), or *concerning God clothed with a body* <note>original: "de Deo corpore induto"</note>, as *Rufinus* anciently translated it—referring to the *Word made flesh*. The other title is *Concerning the Creation* (though most copies read *Faith*) *and the Generation of Christ*. Even if we admit the title was *Creation*, he undoubtedly alluded to the words of *Solomon*: "The Lord possessed," or <margin>l</margin> *created me* <note>original: "ἔκτισε" (ektise)</note>, "in the beginning of his way." It is evident that before the rise of the *Arian Controversies*, the *Fathers*...

I. <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter "T" containing a seated scholar figure surrounded by floral and leaf scrollwork.</image-desc>THE silence of ancient history regarding the country and family of this excellent person has led to a variety of conjectures concerning his origins <note>original: "original"</note>. Some believe him to have been born to *Jewish* parents of high social standing and quality. For <sup>a</sup> *Clement of Alexandria*, listing his tutors, tells us that one (whom he names last) was from *Palestine*, a *Hebrew* of very ancient lineage. Clement then adds that after he had hunted this teacher out with infinite diligence and curiosity in *Egypt*, where he lay in obscurity, he placed himself under his discipline and instruction. This person is plainly assumed by <sup>b</sup> *Eusebius* to have been our *Pantaenus*. While there is no cause to doubt that Clement intended Pantaenus in the latter part of that statement, the first part is ambiguous. It is not clear whether the latter sentence is necessarily connected to the former, or if Clement intended only to indicate the last master he sought out, as distinct from those he had named before. I am inclined to think the latter, because whoever carefully considers *Clement’s* phrasing <note>original: "period"</note> will find that by his *Hebrew* or *Palestinian* master, he refers to one of the two he heard in the *East*, whereas *Pantaenus* was his master in *Egypt*, whom he both found and heard there. <sup>c</sup> Others argue he was born in *Sicily*, because *Clement* in the following words styles him "a truly Sicilian bee." Whether there might be something proverbial in that expression regarding *Sicily*, I will not investigate now. However, it is certain that the inhabitants of that island were generally *Greeks* and that many eminent philosophers were born or lived there—most notably the famous *Porphyry*, who had retired there for some years and wrote his hostile <note>original: "virulent"</note> books against the Christians. Let this remain as his country for now unless a more probable theory is offered; otherwise, we might say that, being descended from Sicilian ancestors, he was born at *Alexandria*, the place of his education.

II. HIS younger years were enriched with all learned and philosophical studies under the best masters that *Alexandria* could provide (for I assume his education took place there), which was at that time a famous center <note>original: "staple place"</note> of learning. Just as *Egypt* had in all ages been famous for the finest branches

branches of literature and the more uncommon speculations of theology—especially in *Alexandria*, where there were professors in all the arts and sciences and public schools of instruction. These were greatly aided by that noble library established there by *Ptolemy Philadelphus* and so highly celebrated by the ancient writers. In later times, there was a fixed and settled succession of philosophers in the *Platonic School*, begun by *Ammonius Saccas* and continued by *Photinus* <note>original: "Photinus"; likely referring to Plotinus, the famous Neoplatonist</note>, *Origen*, and their successors for several ages.

<sup>a</sup> *Ammianus Marcellinus* tells us that in his time, though the city was not as famous as it had been formerly, it still maintained its reputation to a high degree. He noted that all the liberal arts <note>original: "ingenuous Arts"</note>, methods of profound learning, and celebrated professors of all kinds flourished here. He added that it was enough to recommend a physician to public notice simply if he had studied at *Alexandria*. Indeed, many ages after him, *Benjamin the Jew* <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century traveler</note> during his time there found nearly twenty different schools of *Aristotelians* (the only men who then held the academic chairs), to which men flocked from all parts of the world to learn the Peripatetic philosophy.

III. AMONG all the sects of philosophy, he principally applied himself <sup>b</sup> to the *Stoics*, with whose notions and rules of life he was most enamored. This is no wonder, seeing (as *St. Jerome* observes) that their doctrines <sup>c</sup> <note>original: "dogmata"</note> in many things come closest to the teachings of Christianity. Indeed they do, especially regarding the moral and practical parts of their principles. They held that nothing was good except what was just and pious, and nothing evil except what was vicious and dishonest. They believed that a bad man could never be happy, nor a good man miserable, for the good man was always free, noble, and dear to Heaven. They taught that the deity was perpetually concerned with human affairs and that there was a wise and powerful providence that particularly oversaw the happiness of mankind and was ready to assist men in all lawful and virtuous undertakings. Therefore, they believed this God was above all things to be admired, adored, worshipped, prayed to, acknowledged, obeyed, and praised. They argued that it is the most fitting and reasonable thing in the world that we should universally submit to His will and <term>to embrace with all our souls everything that happens</term> <note>original Greek: ἀσπάζεσθαι ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς τὰ συμβαίνοντα</note>, cheerfully accepting all the outcomes and determinations of His providence. They held that we ought not to think it enough to be happy alone, but that it is our duty <term>to love from the heart</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ καρδίας φιλεῖν</term>—to relieve and help others, to advise and assist them, and to contribute what is in our power to their welfare and safety. This was to be done not just once or twice, but throughout one's whole life, and without bias or small-minded designs for applause or personal advantage. They believed that nothing should be as dear to a man as honesty and virtue, and that this is the first thing he should look at: whether the thing he is about to do is good or bad, and whether it is the act of a good or a wicked man. If the act were excellent and virtuous, they believed he ought not to let any loss, damage, torment, or death itself deter him from it. Anyone who reads the writings of *Seneca*, *Antoninus* <note>The Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus</note>, *Epictetus*, *Arrian*, and others will find these and many more principles claiming a very close kinship with the main rules of life prescribed in the Christian faith. It is no wonder, then, that *Pantaenus* was in love with such noble and manly principles. He liked them so well that he always retained the title of the *Stoic Philosopher*, and for the most part, he maintained his profession of that sect even after being admitted to eminent offices and employments in the Christian Church.

IV. I have not found exactly who instructed him in the principles of the Christian religion. ᵃ *Photius* tells us that he was a student of those who had seen the Apostles, though I cannot agree with his additional claim that Pantaenus had personally heard some of the Apostles themselves; the great length of time between their era and his makes this nearly impossible. But whoever his tutors were, he made such vast progress in his learning that his singular excellence quickly recommended him for a position of great trust and honor in the Church: Master of the <term>Catechetic School</term> <note>This was a prestigious institution in Alexandria focused on providing both foundational Christian instruction and advanced theological education.</note> at *Alexandria*. In that city, there were not only academies and schools of secular literature <note>original: "Humane Literature"</note>, but also an ecclesiastical school for training people in divine knowledge and the first principles of Christianity. According to ᵇ *Eusebius*, this was an "ancient custom" <note>original: "ἐξ ἀρχαίου ἔθους" (*ex archaiou ethous*)</note> dating back to the very time of St. Mark (as ᶜ *St. Jerome* says), the first planter of Christianity and Bishop of that place. From Mark’s time, there had been a constant succession of *Catechists* in that school, which *Eusebius* tells us continued into his own day and was managed by men famous for their eloquence and study of divine matters. The fame and glory of *Pantaenus* made him the most obvious choice for this position at that time, and he succeeded to it accordingly. As ᵈ *Eusebius* suggests, this occurred around the beginning of the reign of Emperor *Commodus*, when *Julian* became the Bishop of *Alexandria*; for around that time, he says, Pantaenus became the governor of the "School of the Faithful" there. While others before him had managed the school in a more private or restricted manner, he made the school more open and public, freely teaching everyone who approached him. He continued in this employment without interruption throughout the ten-year term of Bishop *Julian*, until, under Julian’s successor, he was sent on a long and dangerous journey for the following reason.

V. *ALEXANDRIA* was "the most populous of all cities" <note>original: "πολυανθρωποτάτη πασῶν πόλις" (*polyanthropotatē pasōn polis*)</note> (as the orator ᵉ Dio Chrysostom styles it), one of the most frequented cities in the world. It saw a constant influx not only of neighboring nations but of people from the most remote and distant countries: *Ethiopians*, *Arabians*, *Bactrians*, *Scythians*, *Persians*, and even *Indians* themselves. It happened that some *Indian* ambassadors (though it is uncertain if they were sent for this specific purpose) entreated ᶠ *Demetrius*, then Bishop of *Alexandria*, to send a worthy and excellent person with them to preach the Faith in those countries. No one appeared as well-qualified for this mission as *Pantaenus*, a grave man and a great philosopher, uniquely equipped with both divine and secular learning. *Demetrius* persuaded him to undertake this embassy. Although Pantaenus surely realized that he was leaving a pleasant and delightful country—a place where he was loved and honored by everyone with genuine respect—and that he was venturing on a journey where he must expect to encounter dangers, hardships, and the greatest difficulties and opposition, all these concerns were easily overcome by his insatiable desire to spread the Christian religion even to the remotest corners of the world. For there were many evangelical preachers even at that time (as ᵍ *Eusebius* adds on this occasion) who, inflamed with a divine and holy zeal in imitation of the Apostles, were willing to travel throughout the world to enlarge the boundaries of Christianity and build people up in the most holy faith. Exactly which "India" this was to which *Pantaenus*—and after him *Frumentius* (for it is highly probable they both went to the same country)—was sent, is not easy

...it is difficult to determine. There are some people, and they are men of no small reputation, who believe it was not *Oriental* but *African India*, which borders *Ethiopia*, or is rather a part of it. These *Indians* were a colony and settlement originally from the *East*. For ᵃ *Eusebius* tells us that in the early ages, the *Ethiopians* left the regions around the *Indus* River and settled near *Egypt*. This is why ᵇ *Philostratus* specifically calls the *Ethiopians* a colony of *Indians*, and ᶜ elsewhere he calls them an "Indian race" <note>original: "γένος Ἰνδῶν" (*genos Indōn*)</note>. The capital city <term>metropolis</term> of this country was *Axum*, where *Frumentius* was later said to be ordained Bishop by *Athanasius*. This is an opinion that I confess I am very inclined to accept, and I would agree with it without hesitation, if ᵈ *Eusebius* did not specifically state that *Pantaenus* preached the Gospel to the *Eastern* nations and traveled as far as *India* itself. I cannot imagine how such a passage could apply to *African India* and the countries that lie directly *south* of *Egypt*. For this reason, we have placed it in the *East* elsewhere. Nor is there any need to send them as far as *India beyond the Ganges*; there are places in *Asia* closer at hand, specifically parts of *Arabia* that anciently went by that name, which is why the *Persian* Gulf is sometimes called the *Indian* Sea. But let the judicious reader decide as he or she pleases in this matter.

Regarding the customs and institutions of the Brahmans, see among others: Alexander Polyhistor, *On Indian Matters*, in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book 3, page 451. Strabo, *Geography*, book 15, page 712. Bardesanes the Syrian, *On Fate*, in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 6, chapter 10, page 275. Plutarch, *Life of Alexander*, page 701. VI. Having arrived in *India*, he set himself to plant the Christian faith in those regions, specifically speaking with the ᵉ *Brahmans* <note>original: "Brackmans"</note>, who were the sages and philosophers of those countries. Their principles and way of life seemed to make them more naturally inclined to accept *Christianity*. As soon as their children were born, they committed them to nurses and then to guardians as they aged, who instructed them in principles suited to their abilities and progress. They were educated with the greatest imaginable severity of discipline and were not allowed even to speak, spit, or cough while their masters were teaching them; this lasted until they were thirty-seven years old. They were extremely strict and moderate in their diet; they ate no meat and drank no wine or strong liquor. They fed only on wild acorns and such roots as nature provided, quenching their thirst at the nearest spring or river, and were equally sparing in all other lawful pleasures and delights. They worshiped no images but sincerely adored God, to whom they prayed constantly. Instead of following the custom of other *Eastern* nations by turning toward the *East*, they devoutly lifted their eyes to Heaven. While seeking closeness with God, they took special care to keep themselves from being defiled by any vice or wickedness, spending a large part of both day and night in hymns and prayers to God. They considered themselves the most free and victorious of people, having hardened their bodies against all external hardships and subdued all irregular passions and desires in their minds. They despised gold and silver as things that could neither quench their thirst, satisfy their hunger, heal their wounds, nor cure their illnesses. They saw that such metals served no real or necessary natural purpose, but only fueled vice, luxury, trouble, and anxiety, leaving the mind in a state of constant tension <note>original: "Racks and Tenters" — instruments used for stretching cloth or as torture devices, here used metaphorically for mental strain</note>. They did not consider the minor occurrences of this world to be either good or evil. They frequently spoke about death, which they maintained was a "birth into" <note>original: "γένεσις εἰς" (*genesis eis*)</note>...

# The Life of S. PANTÆNUS.

<margin>a Palladius, *On the Brahmans*, page 52.</margin>
<note>original: "ὄντως βίος" (*ontōs bios*)</note> — a "true life," or a being born into a real and happy life. In preparation for this, they made use of the present time only as a state of preparation for a better life. In short, they seemed in most things to agree with the *Stoics*, whom they considered above all other sects to be <note>original: "λογίους Φιλοσόφους" (*logious Philosophous*)</note> the most excellent philosophers. For this reason, they could not help but be somewhat more acceptable to *Pantaenus*, who had so thoroughly absorbed all the wise and rational principles of that school.

VII. We are not told specifically what success he had in these regions. Certainly, his preaching could not have failed to have a considerable effect, especially among people who were so well-qualified to receive it by the rules of their order and their way of life. This was also a place where *Christianity* had been planted long before, though it was now overgrown with weeds and rubbish for lack of proper care and cultivation. 
<margin>b Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 5, chapter 10, page 175; Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, regarding Pantaenus.</margin>
For he met several people^b who still held the knowledge of *Christ*, which had been preached there long ago by *St. Bartholomew* the Apostle (as we have shown elsewhere in his biography). No small evidence of this was his finding of *St. Matthew’s* Gospel written in *Hebrew*, which *St. Bartholomew* had left when he was there. *Pantaenus* (as *St. Jerome* informs us, though I wonder if it is anything more than his own guess) brought it back with him to *Alexandria*, where he undoubtedly kept it as a priceless treasure. Just as our philosopher succeeded in the labors of *St. Bartholomew* in these *Indian* settlements, another person later succeeded in his. To make the story more complete, I believe the reader will find it relevant if I include an account of that here. 
<margin>c Socrates Scholasticus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 1, chapter 19, page 50; Sozomen, book 2, chapter 24, page 477; Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 1, chapter 23, page 54.</margin>
^c *Aedesius* and *Frumentius*, two young men from *Tyre*, accompanied *Meropius* the philosopher into *India*. There they were captured by the natives and presented to the King of the country. Pleased with their appearance and their skills, the King made one of them his butler and the other (*Frumentius*) his record-keeper—or, as *Sozomen* claims, his treasurer and <term>Major-domo</term> <note>original: "Major-domo"; a chief steward or head of a royal household</note>, putting him in charge of managing the palace. Because of their great diligence and faithfulness, the King granted them their freedom upon his death. They then decided to return to their own country, but were persuaded by the Queen to stay and oversee affairs during the minority of her son. They did so, with the main responsibility of government falling to *Frumentius*. Assisted by some *Christian* merchants who traded there, he built an oratory <note>a small chapel or place for prayer</note> where they gathered to worship God according to *Christian* rites, and he instructed several of the natives who joined their assembly. When the young King came of age, *Frumentius* resigned his position and asked permission to return home. This was granted with some difficulty, and they departed immediately. *Aedesius* went to *Tyre*, while *Frumentius* went to *Alexandria*. There, he gave *Athanasius*, the Bishop of that city, an account of the entire matter, showing him how much hope there was that the *Indians* would convert to the faith of *Christ*. He also begged him to send a Bishop and some clergy to them, so as not to neglect such a good opportunity for their salvation. *Athanasius*, having consulted with his clergy, persuaded *Frumentius* to accept the office himself, assuring him that he had no one better suited for it than *Frumentius* himself. This was done accordingly, and after being made a Bishop, *Frumentius* returned to *India*. There he preached the *Christian* faith, built many churches, and, assisted by divine grace, performed countless miracles, healing...

# The Life of S. PANTÆNUS.

...both the souls and bodies of many people at the same time. Rufinus claims to have received an account of all this directly from the mouth of Aedesius, who was then a Presbyter <note>term: a leader or priest in the early church</note> of the Church of Tyre. But it is time to look back again to Pantaenus.

<margin>
a As mentioned above.
b In the place already cited.
c From Eusebius, book 6, chapter 19, page 221.
</margin>

VIII. Having returned to Alexandria, he resumed his office as a teacher of the faith. I gather this partly from Eusebius, who mentions it again right after his expedition to India and adds that "he led at the last" <note>original: τελευταῖος ἡγεῖται (*teleutaios hēgeitai*)</note>—meaning that when he drew near to the end of his life, he governed the School of Alexandria. This is also supported by St. Jerome, who says expressly that he taught during the reigns of the emperors Septimius Severus and Caracalla, though his first period of leadership was under Commodus. He died during the time of Antoninus Caracalla, who began his reign in the year 211, though the exact date and manner of his death have been lost to history. His memory is preserved in the *Roman Calendar* on the seventh of July. 

Certainly, a just tribute of honor is due to his memory for his admirable zeal and piety, his tireless effort and industry, and his exquisite abilities. Eusebius truly describes him as "a man most famous for his learning" <note>original: τῆς ἀπὸ παιδείας ἀνὴρ ἐπιδοξότατος (*tēs apo paideias anēr epidoxotatos*)</note>. Even Origen, who lived closer to his time and was one of his successors, commends him for his great usefulness and ability in both philosophical speculations and theological studies; in the former, he was able to engage with philosophers, and in the latter, he could refute heretics and deceivers. In his school, as Eusebius tells us, he displayed the treasures of sacred doctrines through both speech and writing. However, St. Jerome says he taught more by word of mouth <note>original: *viva voce*</note> than through books. Jerome mentions only his commentaries on the Holy Scriptures, and of those, not even the smallest fragment remains today.

# The Life of Saint Clement <note>original: "S. Clemens"</note> of Alexandria.

*His succeeding Pantænus in the Catechetical <note>original: "Catechetic"</note> School. His being made a Priest <note>original: "Presbyter"</note> of Alexandria. The publication of his Stromata and when it occurred. The lawfulness of fleeing in times of persecution. His journey into the East and the tracts he wrote there. His travel from Jerusalem to Antioch and his return to Alexandria. His death. The tributes <note>original: "Elogia"</note> given to him by the ancients. His admirable learning and his writings. His Hypotyposes: Photius’s account of them and how they were corrupted by the Arians <note>original: "Arrians"</note>. His books that are still extant and the orderly progression of them. The design of his Stromata. His style of writing in that and his other books. A short defense <note>original: "Apology"</note> for some careless <note>original: "unwary"</note> assertions in his writings. A list of his works.*

<margin>a Epiphanius, Heresies 32, p. 96.</margin>
<margin>b Stromata, book 1, p. 274. and in Eusebius, book 5, ch. 11, p. 176.</margin>
<margin>c Book 6, ch. 13, p. 215.</margin>
I. <image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'T' set within a square ornamental border. The design depicts two figures standing amidst thick, swirling foliage and vines.</image-desc> TITUS Flavius Clement was, probably, born at Athens. For when ᵃ Epiphanius tells us that some affirmed him to be an Alexandrian and others an Athenian, he might well be both; the first being the place of his birth, while the other was his constant residence and employment. Nor can I imagine any other reason why the title of "Athenian" should be given to him. This conjecture is further supported by the course and progress of his studies: the foundations were laid in Greece, improved in the East, and perfected in Egypt. Indeed, his incomparable abilities in all branches of science make it more probable that his early years began in that great school of arts and learning. But he did not stay there; his insatiable thirst for knowledge made him travel through almost all parts of the world and converse with the learned of all nations. He did this so that he might furnish himself with whatever knowledge was useful and excellent, especially a thorough acquaintance with the mysteries of Christian doctrine. He tells us ᵇ of those lively and powerful discourses which he had the happiness to hear from blessed and truly worthy and memorable people. These teachers preferred that sincere and excellent doctrine which they had received directly from the holy Apostles Peter, James, John, and Paul, like children receiving it from the hands of their parents. By God’s blessing, they had lived down to his time, sowing those ancient and Apostolic seeds of truth. This is a passage which I have no doubt ᶜ Eusebius intended to highlight when he says that Clement, speaking concerning himself in the first book of his *Stromata*, affirms himself to have been of the next succession after the Apostles.

<margin>d Cited above.</margin>
<margin>e To the year 185, no. 4.</margin>
<margin>f Valesius's Annotations in Eusebius, p. 95.</margin>
II. Of these venerable men to whose instruction <note>original: "tuition"</note> he committed himself, he has given ᵈ us some account, though it is somewhat obscure. The first ᵉ was Ionicus, a Coele-Syrian <note>original: "Cælo-Syrian"</note>, whom he heard in Greece, and whom Baronius conjectures to have been Caius or Dionysius, the Bishop of Corinth. A second was an Egyptian, under whose discipline he studied in that part of Italy called *Magna Graecia* <note>original: "Magna Græcia," meaning "Great Greece"</note> and since known as Calabria. From there he traveled into the East, where the first of his masters was an Assyrian, supposed by some to have been Bardesanes and by others Tatian, the student of Justin Martyr. The next was originally a Jew of a very ancient lineage, whom he heard in Palestine. Baronius believes this was Theophilus, the Bishop of Caesarea (though there is no evidence among the ancients for his Hebrew descent); others ᶠ more probably believe it was Theodotus. This is why the excerpts from his *Hypotyposes* still in existence are titled, "From the eastern teachings of Theodotus" <note>original: "ἐκ τῶν Θεοδότου ἀνατολικῆς διδασκαλίας"</note>—

# The Life of Saint Clement of Alexandria.

The last of the masters whom he met with—who was, as he says of him, "indeed the first in power and virtue" <note>original: "δυνάμει δ' ἄρα πρῶτος"</note>—was one whom he inquisitively sought out and found in *Egypt*. In this person’s instruction he fully rested and sought no further. This person is generally supposed to have been *Pantaenus*, whom *Clement* elsewhere ᵃ expressly affirms to have been his master, and whom in the aforementioned *Epitome* he styles ᵇ *our Pantaenus*.

III. But though he put himself under the discipline of so many different masters, it was not out of any vain, inconsistent lightness or fantastic curiosity, but to research truth with an honest and inquisitive mind. He loved what was manly and generous wherever he encountered it. Therefore, he tells us ᶜ that he did not simply approve of all philosophy, but rather that of which *Socrates* speaks in *Plato* concerning their mysterious rites:

->—"Many are the wand-bearers, but few are the true mystics" <note>original: "ναρθηκοφόροι μὲ πολλοί· βάκχοι δέ τε παῦροι"</note>;<-

<margin>
d Diogenes Laertius, introduction to the *Lives of the Philosophers*, page 14.
e Aristotle, *Ethics*, book 1, chapter 4, page 3, volume 2.
f Laertius, same location as above.
g *Stromata*, book 1, page 288.
h Henry Dodwell, *Introduction to the Apology for Dr. Stearne’s book on Obstinacy*, page 115.
</margin>
...intimating, as he expresses it in the style of the Scripture, that *many are called, but few are chosen* <note>original: "elect"</note>, or few make the right choice. "And such," adds *Socrates*, "and such only, in my opinion, are those who embrace the true philosophy." Of which sort, says *Clement*, "through my whole life I have to my power approved myself, desiring and endeavoring by all means to become of that number." For this purpose, he never tied himself to any particular school <note>original: "institution"</note> of philosophy, but took up the *Elective Sect* <note>original: "αἵρεσις ἐκλεκτική"</note>, whose members did not oblige themselves to the dictates and sentiments of any one philosopher, but freely made choice of the most excellent principles from all of them. This sect (as the historian of philosophy ᵈ informs us) was begun by *Potamon*, also an *Alexandrian*, who selected what he judged best from every sect of philosophy. He gave himself the liberty to impartially inquire into the nature of things and what the true standard and measure of truth was. He considered that no man knows everything; that some things are obvious to one person but overlooked or neglected by another; that there are wholesome herbs and flowers in every field; and that if a thing is well said, it does not matter who says it. He believed that reason is to be submitted to before authority, and though a fair regard is due to the opinions and principles of our friends, yet it is "a sacred duty to prefer the truth" <note>original: "ὅσιον προτιμᾶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν"</note> (as ᵉ *Aristotle* himself confesses) and more reasonable to honor and esteem it. And thus he gathered a *system* of noble principles, like so many flowers from several gardens, professing ᶠ this to be the great end of all his inquiries: "a life perfected according to every virtue" <note>original: "ζωὴν κατὰ πᾶσαν ἀρετὴν τελείαν"</note>. Our divine philosopher belonged to this incomparable order. "I espoused not," says he ᵍ, "this or that philosophy—not the Stoic, nor the Platonic, nor the Epicurean, nor that of Aristotle—but whatever any of these sects had said that was fit and just, that taught righteousness with a divine and religious knowledge; all that being selected, I call philosophy" <note>original: "τοῦτο σύμπαν τὸ ἐκλεκτικόν"</note>. Although it cannot be denied that of any sect, he came nearest to the *Stoics*, as appears from his habit of speaking in paradoxes and his affected use of new words—two things peculiar to the men of that school, as a very learned and ingenious person ʰ has observed.

IV. After *Pantænus* died, Clement succeeded him in the *Catechetical School* <note>original: "Schola Κατηχήσεων"</note> at *Alexandria*. Without question, he had taught in it long before that, and probably during *Pantænus's* absence in *India*, supplying his place until his return and succeeding him after his death; for the ancient writers * are all agreed that he was *Pantænus's* successor. Here he taught with great industry and faithfulness, and with no less success; some of the most eminent men of those times, such as *Origen*, *Alexander* (Bishop of *Jerusalem*), and others, were educated under him. And now (as ^a he himself confesses) he found his philosophy and pagan learning <note>original: "Gentile-Learning"</note> very useful to him. For just as the husbandman first waters the soil and then casts in the seed, so the notions he derived out of the writings of the pagans served first to water and soften "its earthy nature" <note>original: "τὸ γεῶδες αὐτῆς"</note>—the gross and terrestrial parts of the soul—so that the spiritual seed might be better cast in and take vital root in the minds of men. Besides the office of a catechist, he was made a *Presbyter* <note>A priest or elder</note> of the Church of *Alexandria*, at least by the beginning of the reign of Emperor *Severus*; for *Eusebius* takes notice of him in that capacity in the year 195. About which time, prompted by his own zeal and compelled by the hardships <note>original: "iniquity"</note> of the times, he set himself to vindicate the cause of Christianity against both heathens and heretics. He did this at large with singular learning and skill in his book called *Stromata* <note>literally "Miscellanies" or "Patchwork"</note>, published around this time; for in drawing up a chronological ^b account of events, he ends his computation with the death of the Emperor *Commodus*. From this it is evident, as ^c *Eusebius* observes, that he compiled that volume during the reign of *Severus*, who succeeded him.

<margin>
d *Stromata*, book 4, page 504.
e Eusebius, book 6, chapter 14, page 214. Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*.
</margin>

V. The persecution under *Severus* raged in all provinces of the Empire, and particularly at *Alexandria*. This made many of the Christians willing to withdraw for the time, and *Clement* was probably among them. We therefore find him particularly discussing ^d the lawfulness of retreating in a time of persecution. He argues that although we may not cowardly decline a danger or death when it is necessary for the sake of religion, yet in other cases we are to follow the direction of our Savior: *when they persecute you in one city, flee to another* (Matthew 10:23). To not obey in such a case, he argues, is to be bold and rash, and to unwarrantably plunge ourselves into danger. He suggests that if it is a great sin against God to destroy a man, who is His image, then that man makes himself guilty of the crime if he offers himself up to the public tribunal. He says a man does little better when he might decline the persecution but instead rashly exposes himself to be apprehended, thereby conspiring, as much as is in his power, with the wickedness of his persecutors. Furthermore, if he irritates and provokes them, he is unquestionably the cause of his own ruin, like a man who needlessly rouses and enrages a wild beast to fall upon him. I do not doubt that he took this opportunity to visit the Eastern parts where he had studied in his younger days. We find him about this time at *Jerusalem* with *Alexander*, who was shortly thereafter the Bishop of that place. There seems to have been a peculiar intimacy between them, so much so that Saint *Clement* dedicated ^e his book to him, called *The Ecclesiastical Canon*, "or against those who Judaize" <note>original: "ἢ πρὸς τοὺς Ἰουδαΐζοντας"</note>. During his stay here, he preached constantly and declined no labor, even in that evil time, and with...

We may see his success through a fragment of a letter written by *Alexander*, who was then in prison and sent by our *Saint Clement* to *Antioch*. We insert it here: <margin>* From Eusebius, book 6, chapter 11, page 212.</margin> *Alexander, a servant of God and a prisoner of Jesus Christ, to the blessed Church at Antioch: greetings in the Lord. Our Lord has made the chains of my imprisonment light and easy for me during this time, as I learned that Asclepiades—a man wonderfully qualified by his prominence in the faith—has by divine Providence become the Bishop of your holy Church in Antioch.* He concludes: *These letters, worthy brothers, I have sent to you by Clement, the blessed Presbyter—a virtuous and proven man whom you already know and shall come to know even better. Having been here with us according to the good will and providence of God, he has greatly strengthened and expanded the Church of Christ.* 

By this letter, we may note in passing an error made by <margin>∴ In the *Chronicle* for the year AD 212.</margin> ∴ *Eusebius*, who dates the arrival of *Asclepiades* to the See of *Antioch* in the first year of the Emperor *Caracalla* (AD 212). However, we see here that it happened while *Alexander* was still in prison under the Emperor *Severus*, which Eusebius himself dates to AD 205. Clement then traveled from *Jerusalem* to *Antioch*, where we can be certain he worked with the same effort, zeal, and industry. Afterward, he returned to *Alexandria* to resume his duties. History is silent regarding how long he remained there or the manner of his death. 

It is certain that he lived for a considerable time after the death of *Pantænus*, who died during the reign of *Caracalla*. When Clement wrote his work *Stromata* <note>original: "Stromata" — meaning 'Miscellanies' or 'Patchwork'</note>, he mentioned that he did so to "store up things for his old age"—a clear sign that he was not yet very old at the time. I will add only what *Alexander* of *Jerusalem* <margin>ᵃ From Eusebius, book 6, chapter 14, page 216.</margin> ᵃ says in a letter to *Origen*. After telling him that their friendship (which began under their predecessors) should remain sacred and inviolable, and grow even stronger and more fervent, he adds:

"For we recognize as our fathers those blessed saints who have gone 
"before us, and whom we shall join after a short time; I mean *Pantænus*, 
"the truly happy, my master; and the holy *Clement*, my master, who 
"was a great help and benefit to me."

VI. To praise this excellent man, after the great things already said of him by the ancient writers, would be like holding a candle to the sun. Let us hear the character they give him: *The holy and blessed Clement, a very virtuous and proven man,* as we have seen from the testimony of *Alexander*, Bishop of *Jerusalem*, who knew him best. Indeed, his zeal, piety, modesty, and humility could not help but make him dear to everyone. 

Regarding his learning, Saint *Jerome* <margin>ᵇ Letter to Magnus, Oration, page 327.</margin> ᵇ judged him the most learned of all the ancients. *A man wonderfully learned and skilled, who searched the very depths of all the learning of the Greeks with an accuracy that perhaps few before him ever achieved,* says <margin>ᶜ *Against Julian*, book 7, page 231, Volume 6. See also book 6, page 205.</margin> ᶜ Saint *Cyril* of *Alexandria*. He was a holy man (says <margin>ᵈ *The Compendium of Heretical Fables* <note>original: "Hæret. Fabul."</note>, book 1, chapter 6, page 197.</margin> ᵈ *Theodoret*) "who surpassed everyone in his vast experience" <note>original: "πολυπειρίᾳ ἁπάντας ἀπολιπὼν"</note>, and one who, for his immense and wide-ranging learning, was incomparably superior to all other men. 

Nor was he less precise in matters of theology than in secular learning—an "incomparable master of Christian philosophy," as <margin>ᵉ *Ecclesiastical History* <note>original: "H. Eccl."</note>, book 6, chapter 13, page 215.</margin> ᵉ *Eusebius* calls him. This is proven by his many books, which *Eusebius* tells us are filled with a great variety of useful knowledge. Saint *Jerome* <margin>ᶠ *On Illustrious Men* <note>original: "De Script. in Clem."</note> and in the Letter to Magnus cited above.</margin> ᶠ adds that this knowledge was drawn from both the Holy Scriptures and secular learning. In his work, there is nothing unlearned, nothing that is not pulled from the very center and core of philosophy. These two authors have preserved the titles of his books, though most of the works themselves have been lost. Among the most memorable was the *Hypotyposes* <note>meaning 'Outlines' or 'Sketches'</note> or *Books*...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Saint Clement of Alexandria, specifically examining the contents and controversies surrounding his written works, including the lost *Hypotyposes* and his three famous surviving treatises.</meta>

of the *Institution* <note>original: "Hypotyposes"</note>, so often cited by *Eusebius*, which contained brief and precise explanations of many passages of Holy Scripture. In this work, ᵃ *Photius* tells us there were many wild and irreverent opinions, such as: that matter was eternal; that "Ideas" <note>Platonic forms or archetypes</note> were introduced by certain decrees; that there is a transmigration of souls; that there were many worlds before *Adam*; that the Son is among the number of created beings; and that the Word was not really *made flesh*, but only appeared to be so. He lists many more *monstrous blasphemies* <note>original Greek: βλάσφημοι τερατολογίαι (*blasphēmoi teratologiai*)</note>. But at the same time, Photius suggests that these things were probably inserted by someone else's hand; ᵇ *Rufinus* expressly assures us that heretics had corrupted *Clement's* writings. Certainly, had these books been infected with these profane and poisonous doctrines in *Eusebius's* time, we can hardly think but that he would have given us at least some indirect hint of it. And it is significant, as *Photius* observes, that these things are not supported by his other books—indeed, many of them are plainly contradicted by them.

### VII.
<margin>
c See Eusebius, Book 6, chapter 13, page 214.
d *Stromata*, Book 1, page 278; Book 4, page 476.
e Book 7, page 766.
f Photius, in the place cited above, column 288.
