The books still in existence (besides the little tract titled *Who is the Rich Man that Shall Be Saved?* <note>original Greek: Τίς ὁ σωζόμενος πλούσιος (*Tis ho sōzomenos plousios*)</note>, which was published recently) are chiefly three, which seem to have been written in a very wise and excellent order: the *Exhortation to the Greeks* <note>original Greek: Λόγος Προτρεπτικός (*Logos Protreptikos*)</note>, the *Instructor* <note>original Latin: *Pædagogus*</note>, and the *Miscellanies* <note>original Greek: *Stromata*</note>. In the first, he very rationally refutes the follies and impieties of the *pagan religion* and strongly persuades men to embrace Christianity. In the second, he tutors and instructs new converts; by the most admirable rules and moving suggestions, he prepares and forms them for a holy and truly Christian life. In the third, he administers *solid food to those who are mature* <note>A reference to Hebrews 5:14</note>, providing a clearer explanation of Christian doctrine and a more detailed refutation of both *pagan* and heretical opinions. This work admits the disciple—after his first purification and initiation—into a more immediate acquaintance with the sacred mysteries of religion.

His *Miscellanies* ᶜ are nothing but various discourses composed out of the Holy Scriptures and the books of the pagans, explaining and (as the occasion arises) refuting the opinions of the *Greeks* and *Barbarians* <note>meaning non-Greeks</note>, the sentiments of philosophers, and the notions of heretics. He inserts a variety of stories and treasures gathered from all sorts of learning. As he himself tells us ᵈ, he titled them *Stromata* (that is, a variegated tapestry of discourses), which ᵉ he compares not to a manicured garden where the trees and plants are arranged according to the strictest rules of method and order, but to a thick, shady mountain where trees of all sorts—the *cypress* and the *plane tree*, the *laurel* and the *ivy*, the *apple*, the *olive*, and the *fig tree*—grow together in a natural, unorganized way. 

In the first two of his books (as ᶠ *Photius* observes), his style is flowery but balanced by a well-proportioned gravity and a pleasing variety of learning. In the latter, he neither intended the ornaments of eloquence, nor would the nature of his project allow it, as he truly ᵍ apologizes for himself. His main care ʰ was to express things so that he might be understood; beyond this, he neither studied nor desired eloquence. If in these books of his there be some few things here and there—as ⁱ *Photius* affirms—that are *not soundly* <note>original Greek: οὐχ ὑγιῶς (*ouch hygiōs*)</note> or cautiously expressed, they are not like those in the *Institution*, but are capable of a fair and kind interpretation. They are not significantly harmful to either the doctrine or practice of religion, and are the kind of errors generally found in the writers...

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut drop-cap 'Q'. Inside the circular frame of the letter is a seated figure, likely a philosopher or classical figure, surrounded by stylized foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>QUINTUS Septimius Florens *Tertullian* was born at *Carthage*, the capital of *Africa* (as the ancients affirm and as he himself suggests by calling it his homeland). Carthage was famous above all others for its antiquity, sovereignty, and power; for several centuries, it even contended for glory and superiority with *Rome* itself. He was called *Septimius* because he descended from the *Septimian clan* <note>original: Gens Septimia</note>, a tribe of great importance among the *Romans*. This family was first royal, then common <note>original: Plebeian</note>, and finally reached the rank of consul and nobleman <note>original: Patrician</note>. The name *Florens* came from a particular branch of that house. The name *Quintus* (a common title among the *Romans*) was likely given because he was the fifth child of his parents. Finally, *Tertullian* is a derivative of *Tertullus*, likely taken from his immediate father. 

His father was a soldier, a *centurion* serving under the *Proconsul of Africa* (and is therefore called a "Proconsular Centurion" <note>original: Centurio Proconsularis</note> by St. *Jerome* and others), not a man of proconsular rank himself, as some claim. He was a pagan <note>original: Gentile</note>, and Tertullian was also raised in that religion, as he himself admits. He was educated in all the accomplishments that the learning of either the *Greeks* or *Romans* could provide. He seems to have left no path of study untraced, having intimately conversed with poets, historians, and orators. He did not merely look upon but entered into the secrets of philosophy and mathematics. He was also knowledgeable in medicine and the wonders of nature. 

As *Eusebius* notes, he was a man famous for many things, but especially for being admirably skilled in *Roman* laws. However, those who would conclude from this that he was a professional lawyer—and the same person as the one whose excerpts <note>original: Excerpta</note> are still found in the *Pandects* <note>term: a large collection of Roman legal writings</note>—are guilty of a notorious mistake. The name of that lawyer was *Tertylianus*. Furthermore, there is a clear difference in their style and language. Even if we suppose, as others do, that this *Tertylian* was one of *Papinian’s* students during the reign of *Alexander Severus*, he would have lived at least thirty years after the church father's conversion to Christianity. The error undoubtedly arose from the similarity of the names and the reputation of his skill.

<margin>* *Concerning the Mantle* <note>original: De Pallio</note>, chapter 5, page 118.</margin>
II. What his particular way of life was before he converted to the Christian religion is uncertain. Those who believe him to have been an advocate <note>term: a lawyer who pleads cases in court</note> who publicly argued cases do so because, after his conversion, he says of himself that he "owed nothing to the *Forum* <note>original: Forum; the public square where legal and political business was conducted</note>, took up no place on the *Rostra* <note>original: Rostra; the public speaker's platform</note>, made no noise among the benches, did not toss about the laws, nor shout out legal cases." However, one might just as easily conclude he had been a soldier, because he adds in the same passage that he "owed nothing to the military camp," along with other professions mentioned there. That he was married is certain, though I cannot positively determine whether this was before or after he embraced the Christian faith—it was likely before. However, according to his own strict principles, he lived with his wife for a great part of his life in a state of continence <note>term: voluntary sexual abstinence within marriage</note>, living with her as if she were his sister and encouraging her to remain a widow if he died and to live with the utmost strictness, as appears in his two books written to her on that subject.

<margin>

III. We may imagine his conversion to Christianity happened not long after the beginning of the reign of Emperor *Severus*, and a little before the end of the second century. Being a man of an inquisitive and sharp mind, he had observed the powerful and triumphant effect of the Christian faith over the minds and lives of men. He noted its great antiquity, the admirable consistency and truth of the prophecies recorded in the Christians' books, and the frequent testimonies that the pagan deities themselves gave to its truth and divinity. He also observed the common confessions of their *demons* <note>original: Daemones</note> when they were forced to leave the people they possessed at the command of a Christian. He shows ª at length (at least as we can probably guess) that these were the main reasons for his conversion. At the very beginning of the following *century* <note>original: Seculum</note>, while *Severus* was away making war against the *Parthians*, the magistrates in *Rome* and the governors of the provinces began to treat the Christians harshly. they viewed them as infamous persons and, especially, as traitors to the Empire. Among these officials, the most prominent person, I have no doubt, was *Plautianus*. He was a man in great favor with the Emperor; his daughter was married to *Antoninus* (the Emperor's eldest son), and *Severus* had made him the Prefect of *Rome* upon leaving for the *East*. We read of him ᵇ that, during the Emperor's absence, he put to death a vast number of both the nobility and the common people. We cannot doubt that the Christians were among them, and likely made up the largest share of the victims. This cruelty was so notorious that ᶜ *Severus*, upon his return, was forced to apologize for himself, claiming he had no part in it. Indeed, in the first part of his reign, *Severus* was very kind and favorable to the Christians (as *Tertullian* informs ᵈ us). This was because he had been cured of a dangerous illness by a Christian named *Proculus*, who anointed him with oil; *Severus* kept Proculus at court with him for the rest of his life. His kindness did not end there; for even when he knew that several men and women of the *Senatorial Order* were Christians, he was so far from persecuting them that he gave them an honorable testimony and restrained the common people when they were raging against the Christians. I suppose this happened at his return from the *Parthian Expedition*, when he found both governors and people engaged in such a hot and severe persecution of the Christians.

IV. The barbarous and cruel treatment that Christians generally faced moved Tertullian to defend and advocate for their cause against the malice and cruelty of their enemies. For this purpose, he published and distributed his *Apology*, dedicating it to the magistrates of the Roman Empire, and especially the Senate at Rome. (Though I must admit, I see no convincing evidence that he went to Rome himself to personally present it to the Senate.) In this work, using incomparable learning and eloquence, and with all possible evidence and strength of reason, he defends their cause. He complains about the unfairness and injustice of their enemies and their legal methods. Specifically, he demonstrates the emptiness and falsehood of the crimes commonly charged against Christians. He argues for their meekness and innocence, their temperance and sobriety, their piety toward God, and their obedience to their Prince—showing the reasonableness of their principles and the holiness of their lives beyond any just objection. This *Apology* undoubtedly contributed to cooling and calming the feverish passions <note>original: "Calentures"; a term for tropical fevers, used here metaphorically to describe the heat of persecution</note> of the time, especially upon the return of Emperor Severus. Indeed, it does not appear in that entire discourse that the Emperor had given any particular support to those harsh treatments; on the contrary, Tertullian expressly calls <gloss>*</gloss> him the *most constant Prince*. Not long after this, Tertullian found work closer to home. Scapula, the Governor and Proconsul of Africa—who was probably the same person as Scapula Tertullus, a provincial governor mentioned in a legal response from Emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus <gloss>a)</gloss>—was treating the Christians in much the same way that Plautianus <note>Fulvius Plautianus was a powerful and often ruthless commander of the Praetorian Guard under Severus.</note> had done at Rome. Tertullian therefore addressed him in a refined and passionate discourse, representing the honesty and simplicity of Christians, their sincere prayers, and their efforts for the prosperity of the Empire. He also pointed out specific instances of hardship that Divine Providence had recently inflicted upon the Empire, which could not reasonably be thought to have been sent for any other reason than to avenge the innocent blood that had been shed. He laid before Scapula the mercy and indulgence of former Princes and Governors, and even of the current Emperor himself, who was a great friend to Christians. This is clear evidence that this book was written at this time, before Severus broke out into open violence against them.

V. The Christians now enjoyed a little rest; but alas, it was only like the breaks between fits of a fever. Once over, the violent outbreak <note>term: paroxysm</note> returned with even fiercer intensity. In the year of Christ 202, the tenth year of Severus's reign <gloss>b</gloss>, the persecution was revived and was now carried out by the direct command of the Emperor. For Severus, during his journey through Palestine, forbade <gloss>c</gloss> anyone under the heaviest penalties from becoming Jews; and he issued the same orders concerning Christians. The general excuse was likely the prohibition of the *Heteriae* <note>term: illegal secret societies or political clubs</note>, or unlawful associations (which we have described elsewhere). The jurist Ulpian mentions such a legal decree <gloss>d</gloss> where Severus forbade these illegal groups, commanding that those frequenting them be accused before the Prefect of the City—a category into which they usually lumped the Christians. I have no doubt, however, that there were also specific edicts issued against them, as the historian Spartianus plainly states. The common people, who could hardly be restrained before, now had the reins thrown upon their necks. Spurred on by the Imperial orders, they rushed to carry them out, so that churches everywhere <gloss>e</gloss> were filled with martyrdoms and the blood of the saints. Weeks <note>This likely refers to the chronicler Judas, mentioned by the historian Eusebius, who calculated the "seventy weeks" of Daniel's prophecy to end at this time.</note> up to this year, broke off his calculations, assuming that the long-expected coming of **Antichrist** was now at hand. According to the historian, the minds of many were so exceedingly shaken and disturbed by the current persecution. Tertullian, seeking to speak a word in season, took advantage of the opportunity and wrote to the martyrs in prison to comfort them in their sufferings and exhort them to constancy and final perseverance. Around the same time, and for the same reason, he published his *Discourse concerning Patience*, in which he elegantly describes the benefits and praises of that **virtue**. In this work, he especially urges patience based on the example of God and our blessed Savior, and he speaks more favorably here than he did in his later writings about retreating during a time of persecution.

He was no less watchful to defend and preserve the Church from error and heresy, writing his *Prescription against Heretics*. (It is evident this was written around this time from several passages, especially where he mentions the time of persecution, the location of the **tribunal**, the character of the judge, the bringing out of lions <note>referring to Christians being thrown to beasts in the arena</note>, and similar details.) In this work, he lists and examines the various heresies that had infested the Church up to that time, censuring and refuting their absurd opinions and promising <margin>\* *On the Prescription of Heretics*, chapter 45, page 219.</margin> a more distinct and particular refutation of them later. He followed through on this promise in his discourses against the **Jews**, against **Hermogenes**, the **Valentinians**, **Marcion**, **Praxeas**, and several others of their converts and disciples. He also wrote against some of the **Montanists** <note>A rigorist Christian movement named after its founder, Montanus</note> themselves, writing a specific tract concerning **Baptism**—discussing the use of water in it and its necessity for salvation—against **Quintilla**, a woman of great note and prominence among the followers of Montanus, despite whatever value he later seemed to place upon that sect.

VI. Around the 15th year of the reign of **Severus** (207 AD), he published his book *On the Cloak* <note>original: De Pallio</note> on this occasion: he had recently stopped wearing the Gown <note>the *toga*, the standard garment of Roman citizens</note> and had put on the Cloak <note>the *pallium*, the traditional dress of philosophers</note>, which was the usual habit of philosophers and of those Christians who entered into a more disciplined or ascetic state of life, as we have shown in the life of **Justin Martyr**. Because of this, he was mocked by the people of **Carthage** for his perceived flightiness and vanity, as he had so impulsively skipped "from the Gown to the Cloak" <note>original: à Toga ad Pallium</note>; they satirically criticized his inconstancy in turning from one way of life to another. To defend himself, he wrote this discourse, in which he employs the sharpness of a sarcastic wit and all the power of his **African** eloquence. He turns the case back upon his accusers, showing the antiquity, simplicity, ease, and gravity of this habit, and sharply rebukes the luxury and extravagance that had overrun all ranks and orders of men.

The fact that this occurred around this time, and not when he first converted to Christianity, is judiciously noted and argued by **Baronius** <margin><sup>a</sup> *Year 197, numbers 3 and following.*</margin> and more fully proved by the learned **Salmasius** in his notes on that book. Indeed, the circumstances mentioned by <margin><sup>b</sup> *On the Cloak*, chapter 2, page 114.</margin> **Tertullian** do not fit any other time well. For instance, he mentions "the triple strength of the present Empire" <note>original: præsentis Imperii triplex virtus</note>, which can only reasonably refer to **Severus** and his two sons, **Antoninus** <note>better known as Caracalla</note> and **Geta**; in several ancient inscriptions, they are listed together under the title of **AUGUSTI** and **Emperors**. He also mentions the current happiness, security, expansion, and peace of the **Roman State**, which these three powers of the Empire had made like a well-cultivated field, "having uprooted every poisonous weed of hostility" <note>original: eradicato omni aconito hostilitatis</note> and se-

...opposition being rooted up, with a great deal more to the same purpose. This evidently refers both to his conquest of **Pescennius Niger**, who usurped the Empire and whom he overthrew and killed at **Cyzicus** <note>An ancient city in what is now Turkey</note> in the East, and to his victory the previous year (as <sup>a</sup> **Eusebius** records it) over **Clodius Albinus** and his party, whom he subdued and slew at **Lyon** in France. For achieving this—"the greatest honor and ornament of his Empire" <note>original: *maximum ejus Imperii Decus*</note>, as the historian styles it—where he conquered the natives and secured his conquests by the famous **Picts' Wall** <note>Also known as Hadrian's Wall or the Antonine Wall, built to separate Roman Britain from the tribes to the north</note> which he built, he rendered the state of the Roman Empire peaceful and quiet.

At the same time, we may suppose that **Tertullian** was made a Presbyter <note>an elder or priest</note> of **Carthage**, and that this was the particular occasion for altering his clothing and assuming the philosophic *pallium* <note>a simple cloak worn by scholars and ascetics, signaling a life dedicated to study and discipline</note>. The clergy of those times were generally those who undertook an ascetic course of life, which is undoubtedly why the cloak is called by Tertullian in his own terminology <sup>b</sup> "the priestly habit" <note>original: *Sacerdos Suggestus*</note>. Accordingly, <sup>c</sup> **Eusebius** takes notice of him this very year as becoming famous in the account and esteem of all Christian churches.

<margin>
d *The Soldier's Crown, chapter 1, page 100.*
</margin>
VII. Before **Severus** left Rome for his British expedition, the *Decennalia* <note>a Roman festival celebrating the tenth anniversary of an emperor's reign</note> of **Antoninus Caracalla** were celebrated. Besides many magnificent sports and shows and a largesse <note>a gift of money</note> bestowed upon the people, the Emperor gave a donative <note>a bonus given to soldiers on special occasions</note> to the soldiers. Everyone who received it was required to come up to the tribunal wearing a **laurel crown** upon his head. Among the rest, there was one <sup>d</sup> **Christian** soldier who brought his crown along with him in his hand. When he was asked the reason why he did not wear it on his head like the others, he answered that he could not, because he was a Christian. 

A council of war was immediately called, and the man was accused before the general. He was stripped of his military ornaments—his cloak, shoes, and sword—and unmercifully beaten until he was covered in his own blood. He was then cast into prison, where he awaited martyrdom and a better "donative" and reward from Christ. 

The rest of the Christians, who were fellow soldiers in the same army, took offense at his overly precise strictness. Was this not needlessly betraying their liberty and sacrificing the general peace and quiet of all Christians to one man's private whim? Did it not give the common enemy a just reason to attack them? Where did the laws of their religion forbid such an innocent compliance? In fact, did they not rather command us to prudently avoid danger by withdrawing from it? What was this but a stubborn and intentional distinctness, as if he were the only Christian? 

**Tertullian**, whose mighty zeal drove him to be a patron of whatever had the appearance of strictness and severity, immediately set himself to defend the act. He wrote his book *The Soldier's Crown* <note>original: *De Corona Militis*</note>, in which he praises the act as a heroic piece of zeal and Christian magnanimity. He argues it was not only justifiable but honorable, not only lawful but just and necessary, strengthening his claim with several arguments and attempting to dismantle the most plausible objections made against it. This military act, and Tertullian’s vindication of it, happened (as we have dated it) in the year **208 AD** (the 16th year of Severus's reign), while others refer it to the year **199 AD** (the 7th year of Severus's reign), when the Emperor, by decree of the Senate, named his elder son **Antoninus** as Emperor and his younger son **Geta** as Caesar. In testimony of this, he entertained the people with various shows and ceremonies, and be-

# The Life of TERTULLIAN.

...bestowed a gift <note>original: "Donative"</note> upon the soldiers. If the reader prefers this period of time, I will not argue with him, as it is something I myself, upon second thought, do not think improbable.

VIII. But let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall. **Tertullian**, who had until now stood firm and correct in the communion of the Catholic Church, began now—around the middle of his life, says <margin>ª *Jerome, On Illustrious Men, in the entry for Tertullian*</margin> ª **Saint Jerome** (which I am inclined to understand as his age as a Christian, rather than the total span of his life)—to lean toward the errors of the **Montanists**. Before we give an account of this, it may be helpful to inquire a little into the founder and the principles of that sect. <margin>ᵇ *Ancient writers in Eusebius, Book 5, chapter 16, page 180 etc.; Apollonius in the same work, chapter 18, page 184; Epiphanius, Heresies, 48, page 175; Tertullian, On the Prescription of Heretics, chapter 52, page 223.*</margin> ᵇ **Montanus** was born at **Ardaba**, a small village in **Mysia** on the borders of **Phrygia** <note>regions in modern-day western Turkey</note>, where toward the end of the reign of **Antoninus Pius**, but especially in the reign of his successor, he began to show himself. Pride and an immoderate ambition betrayed the man into the snare and condemnation of the Devil. Through this breach, Satan entered and took possession of the man. Acted upon by the influence of an evil spirit, he was prone to fall suddenly into enthusiastic fits and ecstatic raptures. While he was in them, in a furious and frantic manner, he poured out wild and unheard-of things, prophesying about what was to come in a style and manner that had not been used in the Church until then.

He did not lack converts <note>original: "Proselytes"</note> who came over to his party. At first, only a few of his countrymen, the **Phrygians** (from whom his sect derived the title **Cataphrygians** <note>literally "those from Phrygia"</note>), were drawn into the snare. He instructed them in the arts of slander, teaching them to reproach the entire Christian Church for refusing to accept and honor his false prophetic spirit. On the other hand, the same spirit pronounced those people blessed who joined themselves to this new prophet, swelling them with great hopes and promises of what would happen to them, while sometimes also gently correcting and condemning them. 

Among the rest of his disciples, two women were especially remarkable: **Prisca** and **Maximilla**. Having first corrupted them, he shared his demon <note>original: "Dæmon"</note> with them, by which they were immediately enabled to utter the most frantic, incoherent, and extravagant discourses. The truth is, he seemed to arrange his scheme with all imaginable craft and subtlety. In the great and foundational principles of religion, he agreed with the Catholics and embraced the Holy Scriptures entirely. He pretended that he must receive the gifts of Divine Grace extraordinarily conferred upon him, which he claimed were more immediately from the Holy Spirit. He made a singular show of some uncommon rigors and severities in religion. He gave laws for more strict and solemn fasts, which were to be observed more frequently than those among the Orthodox. He taught that divorces were lawful and forbade all second marriages. He called **Pepuza** and **Tymium**, two small towns of Phrygia, "**Jerusalem**," so that he might more plausibly invite simple and unwary converts to flock there. And because he knew no surer way to obligate such people as would be useful to him than by proposals of profit and advantage, he used all methods of extorting money from his deluded followers, especially under the concept of gifts and offerings. For this purpose, he appointed collectors to receive the offerings that were brought in, with which he maintained lower-level officers and paid salaries to those who spread his doctrines throughout the world. Such were the arts and such were the principles of the sect first started by **Montanus**; I am not concerned at present to inquire into what additions were made by his followers in later ages.

## IX.

<margin>
\* *As cited above; see Nicephorus, book 4, chapter 12, page 298.*
a *Eusebius, Church History, Book 6, chapter 20, page 222; Book 2, chapter 25, page 67; Jerome, On Illustrious Men, entry for Caius.*
b *Tertullian, On Fasting, chapter 1, page 544.*
</margin>

Drawn by the smooth and seemingly attractive claims of this sect, **Tertullian** began to lean in that direction. **Saint Jerome** tells us that the specific reason for his departure \* was the envy and insults he faced from the clergy of the Church of **Rome**. Those who imagine that he sought the bishopric <note>original: "See"</note> of **Carthage** after the death of **Agrippinus**, only to be opposed and rejected by the Roman clergy, and that he resented this insult so much that he left the Catholic Church, are speaking without evidence. They fail to consider the man's disciplined nature and his well-known contempt for worldly status. 

It is more likely that, because he was known for his extreme and overly rigorous lifestyle, some of the Roman clergy accused him of following **Montanus**. He may have even been warned to recant or disown those principles. His stubborn and resolute personality would not allow this; consequently, he—along with **Proclus** and the rest of the **Cataphrygian** <note>another name for the Montanists, after their region of origin</note> party—was excommunicated by the Bishop of Rome. A debate had recently been held in Rome between **Caius**, an early orthodox theologian, and **Proclus**, a leader of the Montanists. **Eusebius**—who read the account of the debate published by Caius—tells us ª that Proclus lost the debate. As a result, he and all followers of that sect were excommunicated; Tertullian himself strongly suggests ᵇ that he was among them.

Tertullian, being a man of a stern and unyielding character who could tolerate no compromise that seemed to weaken religious discipline, could not endure this. Dismissing the judgment and censures of the Church, he broke away and joined the followers of **Montanus**, whose claimed self-denial <note>original: "austerities"</note> seemed most suited to his own temperament and the way he lived his life. While it is certain he looked only at the outward appearances and claims of the sect—failing to see the corrupt motives driving it from within—it is reasonable and charitable to believe he never fully grasped their principles in their most extreme forms. 

If he occasionally seems to acknowledge Montanus as the **Paraclete** <note>the Comforter or Holy Spirit</note> who was to come into the world, he likely did not mean something different from the Holy Spirit given to the Apostles. Rather, he probably meant a powerful and extraordinary aid from the Holy Ghost given to Montanus, whom he believed God had sent to explain the Gospel more perfectly. He thought Montanus was sent to enforce the rules of Christian living that Christ had delivered on earth but which had not been fully detailed because the people of that time were not ready to receive them. To this end, he believed Montanus was granted miraculous powers and a spirit of prophecy (which was not unusual even then) and that Montanus’s two prophetesses were moved by the same spirit. 

An honest mind could easily be deceived by such clever and believable claims. It is clear that for a long time, Montanus maintained a reputation for great piety, zeal, and holiness before his true nature was revealed. Tertullian likely received his information about him not from the man himself, but from Proclus or others in the party, who could easily mislead him with false information. Regardless, nothing is more evident than that he looked

<margin>a *On Fasting, as cited above.*</margin>

Tertullian looked upon these new Prophets as introducing no innovations into the principles of Christianity. He believed that **Montanus** preached no other God, asserted nothing to the prejudice of our blessed Savior, nor subverted any rule of Faith or Hope, but only introduced greater severities than other men. He believed that Montanus was not the author, but the restorer of Discipline, and only reduced things to that ancient strictness from which he supposed they had degenerated—especially in the cases of celibacy, single marriages, and such like, as he <sup>b</sup> more than once particularly tells us. This is not to say that the followers of Montanus (as is usual with the later generations of every sect) did not assert many things which their leader himself never imagined. Yet, without distinction, these claims are blamed on him; and **Tertullian** too, because he was a supporter of the party, was drawn into the guilt and made liable for many of the later additions—the *Hay* and *Stubble* <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 3:12, meaning worthless or temporary additions to a foundation.</note> which the successors of that sect built upon it.

## X.

BUT however it was, he resented his excommunication and was highly offended at the looseness and remissness of the Discipline among the Catholics. With great sharpness, he persecuted them under the name of **Psychici**, or **Animal persons** <note>original: "Psychici"; a term used by Montanists to describe those they considered merely "natural" or "soulish," lacking the higher spiritual gifts</note>, as those who took too much liberty in their manners and practices of devotion. He styled his own party **Spirituales**, or **Spiritual persons**, whom he thought were more immediately guided by the Spirit, more plentifully endowed with its gifts, and engaged in a more divine and spiritual life. Against these "Animal persons," he immediately published a tract titled *On Fasting* <note>original: "De Jejuniis"</note>, wherein he defends the **Montanists** in their observation of fasts, their abstinence from meat, and their practice of eating only dried foods. He also defends their "Stationary days" <note>Days of fasting and prayer, usually ending at 3:00 PM or sunset</note> and their habit of keeping them until the very evening, while the Orthodox broke their fasts around three o'clock in the afternoon. In all these respects, he made many sharp and severe criticisms of them.

Indeed, the devotions of those times were vigorous and fervent, their customs strict and punctual, and their ecclesiastical discipline generally very rigid and extreme, seldom admitting persons who had fallen into sin after Baptism to Penance and the Communion of the Church.

But this was looked upon by moderate and sober men as making the gate too narrow, and as something that could not help but discourage converts from entering the faith.

<margin>c *Tertullian, "On Modesty," chapter 1, page 555.*</margin>
Accordingly, discipline began to be relaxed in several places. In particular, the Bishop of Rome <sup>b</sup> had lately published a constitution wherein he admitted persons guilty of adultery and fornication (and probably other crimes) to a place among the Penitents. Against this, **Tertullian** storms. He praises the severity of the ancient Discipline and writes his book *On Modesty* <note>original: "De Pudicitia"</note>, wherein he considers and disputes the case, aggravates the greatness of those offenses, and challenges the arguments that pleaded for forgiveness and indulgence. And if, in mentioning this decree, the Bishop of Rome is styled **Bishop of Bishops** <note>original: "Episcopus Episcoporum"</note>, the champions of that Church, before they try to take advantage of the title, should do well to prove it was intended as a formal part of the decree. It is infinitely more probable that it was mentioned by Tertullian as a sarcasm—intended by him as an ironical reflection and a sharp upbraiding of the pride and ambition of the Bishops of that Church, who took too much upon themselves and began (as appears from Pope **Victor's** conduct toward the **Asian** Churches in the case of **Easter**) to domineer over their brothers and usurp an insolent authority over the whole Christian Church. And that this was his meaning, I am abundantly satisfied from

Cyprian used the phrase in this exact sense in the famous Synod at Carthage. > "As for ourselves (the Bishops then in the Synod), none of them made himself a 'Bishop of Bishops,' <note>A title implying supreme authority over other bishops, which Cyprian rejected.</note> nor did anyone by tyrannical threats force his colleagues into a necessity of compliance. Since every bishop, according to the power and liberty granted to him, had his own proper jurisdiction, he could no more be judged by another than he himself could judge others."

XI. Whether he was ever reconciled to the Catholic communion remains unclear. It is certain that, for the main part, he eventually left the **Cataphrygians** <note>Another name for the Montanists, derived from Phrygia, where the movement began.</note> and kept his own separate meetings at Carthage. His church was still remaining until Saint Augustine's time, by whose labors the last remains of his followers, called **Tertullianists**, were dispersed and completely disappeared. How long he lived after his departure from the Church is not known. Saint Jerome says that he lived to a very advanced <note>original: "decrepit"</note> age, but the ancient writers do not tell us whether he died during the reign of **Alexander Severus** or before, nor whether he died a natural or violent death. He seems, indeed, to have possessed a passionate desire to lay down his life for the Faith; however, had he been a Martyr, some mention would undoubtedly have been made of it in the records of the Church.

<margin>d Cited in the same place as above.</margin>
<margin>e Letter to Magnus the Orator, page 328, Volume 2.</margin>
<margin>f *Commonitory* against Heresies, chapter 24, pages 59, 60.</margin>
XII. He was a man of sharp and acute wit, though perhaps his temperament was a bit too biting and satirical. Saint Jerome characterizes him as having a "sharp and vehement spirit," <note>original: "acris & vehementis ingenii"</note>—someone who did not know how to treat an opponent without salt and sharpness. He was of a stiff and rugged disposition, a rigid critic <note>original: "Censor"</note>, prone to anger, and impatient with opposition. He was a strict observer of rituals and discipline, and a zealous defender of the highest rigors and most precise severities of religion. His learning was admirable; while many others excelled, he had no superiors and few equals in the age he lived in. "Who is more learned, who more acute than Tertullian?" <note>original: "Tertulliano quid eruditius, quid acutius?"</note> says Saint Jerome, who adds that his *Apology* and his book *Against the Gentiles* drew upon all the treasures of human learning. **Vincent of Lérins** gives him this notable tribute <note>original: "Elogium"</note>:
> "He is justly (he says) to be esteemed the prince among the writers of the Latin Church. For who was more learned? Who was more well-versed in both divine and human studies? With a remarkable breadth and capacity of mind, he gathered all of philosophy and its various schools, all the authors and promoters of heresies with all their rituals and principles, and the entire scope of history and every kind of study within the compass of his own breast. He was a man of such quick and weighty intellect that there was almost nothing he set himself against which he did not either pierce through with his sharp wit or strike down with the strength and solidity of his arguments. Who can sufficiently praise his discourses, which are so packed with layers of reasoning that those they cannot persuade, they are ready to force into agreement? He has almost as many insights as he has words, and no more sentences than he has victories over those with whom he deals."

XIII. As for his books, though time has destroyed many, a great number still remain; some of them were written after his withdrawal from

<margin>a Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book 5, chapter 1, page 459.</margin>
<margin>b *On Baptism*, chapter 15, page 230; *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 6, page 104.</margin>
from the Church. His style is, for the most part, abrupt and haughty, and its character <note>original: "face"</note> is full of ancient wrinkles. Regarding this, ^a *Lactantius* long ago gave this judgment: although Tertullian was skilled in all areas of learning, his style was rugged, difficult, and very obscure. Indeed, reading him requires a very attentive, diligent, sharp, and perceptive understanding; yet his writing is lofty and powerful <note>original: "masculine"</note>, and it carries a kind of majestic eloquence that provides a pleasant satisfaction to the judicious and inquisitive reader. It is deeply influenced <note>original: "tinctured"</note> by the *African* dialect and owes much of its complexity and obscurity to his deep study of the writings of the *Greeks*. He made their forms and idioms so much his own that they naturally flowed from his pen. Just how great a master he was of that language is plain, as he ^b tells us himself that he wrote a book concerning *Baptism*, and some others, in *Greek*. This practice could not help but greatly degrade and infect his native style, rendering it less smooth, elegant, and delightful. We see a similar effect in *Ammianus Marcellinus*, who, being a native *Greek*, wrote his *Roman History* in *Latin* in a style that was rough, unpleasant, and nearly barbaric. Furthermore, what was already obscure and uneven became infinitely worse through the ignorance of succeeding ages. Later scribes changed what they did not understand and crowded in fake <note>original: "spurious"</note> words in place of those that were proper and natural, until they made his work look like something quite different than what it was when it first left the author's hand.

XIV. HIS errors and unsound opinions are frequently noted by *Saint Augustine* and other ancient writers (not to mention later critics <note>original: "Censors"</note>), and the editor *Pamelius* <note>Jacobus Pamelius (1536–1587), a Flemish theologian who edited Tertullian's works.</note> has reduced his *Paradoxes* to thirty-one, which he prefixed to the editions of Tertullian's works along with *Explanations* and *Antidotes*. We previously noted his error in believing *Montanus* was the *Paraclete* <note>The Holy Spirit, often referred to as the Comforter or Advocate.</note>; as for other matters relating to that sect, they are mostly issues of order and discipline rather than fundamental articles and points of faith. It cannot be denied that he held some unjustifiable notions, which he shared with other writers of those times, as well as some more peculiar to himself. However, he lived in an age when the Christian faith was still young <note>original: "green"</note> and tender—when the Church had not yet publicly and solemnly defined its beliefs through explicit articles and precise <note>original: "nice"</note> propositions. In those days, the philosophy of the schools was dominant, and men often moved directly from the *Stoa* <note>The Stoic school of philosophy.</note> and the *Academy* <note>The Platonic school of philosophy.</note> to the Church. At that time, a greater latitude of opinion was allowed, and good men were infinitely more concerned with piety and a virtuous life than with modes of speech or expressing every concept so critically and exactly that it could withstand a severe and hostile examination.

# The Life of ORIGEN.

*What things contributed to his development. His great fondness for Platonic principles. Saint Jerome's moderate criticism of him. His repentance for his rash propositions. A list of his writings, and those currently remaining.*

---

<margin>Born in the mountains. Suidas, under the entry "Origen," p. 330, Vol. 2.</margin>
<margin>$\textsuperscript{a}$ Halloix, notes on his defense of Origen, chapter 1, p. 1.</margin>
<margin>$\textsuperscript{b}$ Vossius, On Idolatry, book 2, chapter 10, p. 182.</margin>
I. ORIGEN, also called *Adamantius* <note>meaning "diamond-like" or "invincible"</note>—either because of the tireless nature of his mind and the strength of reason with which he built his arguments, or his firmness and constancy in religion despite all attacks against it—was born in *Alexandria*, the famous capital city of *Egypt*. Unless we assume that during a specific riot or persecution against the Christians in that city, his parents fled for safety to the mountainous parts nearby, where his mother gave birth to him, and for that reason he was called *Origenes*, as if he were "born in the mountains" <note>original: ἐν τῷ ὄρει γεννηθείς</note> (which most believe to be the origin of his name). Whether that is the correct derivation of the word, or if there was another specific reason for the name, let the reader decide. 

However, I believe the reader will find this a much more probable and reasonable theory than the one suggested by one author $\textsuperscript{a}$, who assumes he was named this because he was born of holy parents—since the saints in Scripture are sometimes metaphorically called "mountains." That is the first and last time, I believe, anyone ever made that suggestion. A learned man $\textsuperscript{b}$ instead assumes (and believes there is no doubt about it) that he was named after *Orus*, an Egyptian word and the title for *Apollo* or the Sun—no doubt derived from the Hebrew word for light or fire <note>original: אור</note>—which was one of their primary gods. From this came *Orus*, the name of an Egyptian king, as it has been for many others. Thus, just as the name "Diogenes" comes "from Zeus" <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ Διὸς</note> (meaning one born of Jupiter), so *Origenes* is derived "from Orus" <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ Ὤρου</note>, meaning one descended from *Or* or *Orus*, a deity solemnly worshipped in Alexandria. This theory might have been accepted if there weren't one major problem: we can hardly imagine that a man as good and as strict a Christian as Origen's father would give his child a name for which he was indebted to a pagan deity. He would see that deity worshipped daily with the most foolish <note>original: "sottish"</note> idolatry; it is unlikely he would let his son permanently carry the memory of pagan idolatry in his name—something they specifically and solemnly renounced in their baptism. But to return to the story.

<margin>$\textsuperscript{c}$ Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 6, chapter 2, p. 202.</margin>
<margin>$\textsuperscript{d}$ Under the entry "Origen," p. 385, Vol. 2.</margin>
<margin>$\textsuperscript{e}$ Eusebius, the same, p. 202.</margin>
II. He was born around the year 186 AD, being seventeen years old at the time of his father's death, who suffered martyrdom in 202 AD, the tenth year of the Emperor Severus's reign. His father was *Leonides*, whom *Suidas* $\textsuperscript{d}$ and some others (without any evidence from ancient writers that I know of) claim was a bishop. He was certainly a good man and a martyr for the faith. In his younger years, Origen was raised under the tutorship of his own father, who taught him all the basics of the humanities <note>original: "humane literature"</note>. Along with this, his father took special care to instill the principles of religion, seasoning his early years with knowledge of divine things. Like a second *Timothy*, *from a child he knew the holy Scriptures* and was thoroughly trained and instructed in them. Nor was his father more diligent in giving instructions than Origen was capable of receiving them. Part of his daily task was to learn and repeat some...

<summary>This page introduces the life of Origen, debating the etymological origins of his name and describing his early religious and secular education under his father, Leonides.</summary>
<keywords>Origen, Adamantius, Alexandria, Leonides, etymology, Christian education, martyrdom, Severus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the account of Origen's early education under his father Leonides and transitions to his formal schooling under Clement of Alexandria and Ammonius Saccas.</meta>

<page-num>216.</page-num>
->**The Life of ORIGEN.**<-

[...continued from previous page] some parts of the Holy Scriptures, which he readily completed. But not satisfied with the mere reading or recital of them, he began to inquire more closely into their deeper meaning, often pestering his father with questions about what this or that passage of Scripture meant. The good man, though seemingly reproving his busy eagerness and advising him to be content with the plain, obvious sense and not to ask questions beyond his years, nonetheless rejoiced in his heart. He sincerely thanked God for making him the father of such a child. The prudent man had much trouble keeping his overflowing love and joy from showing before others; but in private, he gave it vent, frequently going into the chamber where the youth lay asleep and reverently kissing his bare breast—the treasury of an early piety and a divine spirit. He reflected on how happy he was to have such an excellent son. It is such a great comfort and invaluable blessing to pious parents to see their children setting out early in the way of righteousness, absorbing religion almost with their mother’s milk.

<margin>a *Hierocles, book 1, On Providence and Fate, as cited in Photius, Code 214, column 549, and Code 251, column 1381.*</margin>
<margin>b *In Eusebius, same work, chapter 19, page 220. See also Theodoret, Sermon 6, On Providence, page 96.*</margin>
<margin>c *See Theodoret, in the place cited.*</margin>
<margin>d *In the place cited.*</margin>
<margin>e *Annals, page 332, Pocock edition. See also Selden’s notes on Eutychius, Section 23, page 147.*</margin>

### III.
Having finished his education at home, he was sent to perfect his studies under the instruction of *Clement of Alexandria*, then the head of the Catechetical School <note>A famous center of Christian learning in Alexandria</note> in *Alexandria*. There, matching the sharpness of his intellect with great industry, he made vast improvements in all sorts of learning. From Clement, he moved on to *Ammonius*, who had then newly established a *Platonic* school at *Alexandria*. Ammonius had reconciled <sup>a</sup> those long-standing feuds and differences that had existed between the schools of *Plato* and *Aristotle*, which had persisted among their disciples until his time. This he did (says my author) "out of a divine transport for the truth of Philosophy" <note>original: ἐνθυσιάσας πρὸς τὸ τῆς φιλοσοφίας ἀληθινὸν</note>, despising the petty opinions and argumentative bickering of spiteful men, and offering a more free and generous kind of philosophy to his listeners. Among these students was our *Origen*, as *Porphyry* <sup>b</sup> (among others) testifies, who saw *Origen* when Porphyry himself was only a youth. 

This *Ammonius* was called *Saccas* (from his carrying sacks of corn on his back, being a porter by trade before he took up the study of philosophy) <sup>c</sup>. He was one of the most learned and eloquent men of those times, a great philosopher, and the leader of the Platonic sect. Above all, he was a Christian, born and raised among them, as <sup>d</sup> *Porphyry* himself is forced to admit. However, when Porphyry tells us that Ammonius later, upon more mature consideration and entering into philosophy, renounced Christianity and embraced paganism and the state religion of the Empire, he is not to be believed. He is guilty of as obvious a falsehood (as *Eusebius* observes) as when he claims that *Origen* was born and raised a *Gentile* and then converted to Christianity. Nothing was more evident than that *Origen* was born of Christian parents, and that *Ammonius* retained his Christian and divine philosophy until the very last minute of his life—a fact to which the books he left behind were standing evidence. 

Indeed, <sup>e</sup> *Eutychius*, the Patriarch of *Alexandria* (if he refers to the same man), seems to give some support to *Porphyry's* report. He further adds that *Ammonius* was one of the twenty bishops whom *Heraclas*, then Bishop of *Alexandria*, appointed over the Egyptian churches, but that he deserted his religion. As soon as *Heraclas* heard of this, he convened a synod of bishops and went to the city where *Ammonius* was bishop. After thoroughly examining and discussing the matter, he brought him back...

to the truth. Whether he found this among the records of that church, or took it from tradition and report, is uncertain, as the matter is not mentioned by any other writer. But however it was, it is plain that Ammonius was a man of incomparable intellect and learning. Hierocles himself calls him <term>taught of God</term> <note>original Greek: *theodidaktos*</note>, and when Plotinus, the great Platonist, had found him out, he told his friend in a kind of triumph that this was the man whom he had been seeking. Under him, Origen made himself a perfect master of Platonist ideas, being daily conversant in the writings of Plato, Numenius, Cronius, Apollophanes, Longinus, Moderatus, Nicomachus, and the most principal among the Pythagoreans, as also of Chaeremon and Cornutus, the Stoics. From these (as Porphyry accurately enough observes) he learned that allegorical and mystical way of interpretation which he introduced into Christian doctrine.

IV. Besides our Adamantius <note>A nickname for Origen meaning "Man of Steel" or "Unconquerable," referring to his tireless work ethic and firm character.</note>, there was another Origen, his contemporary, a Gentile philosopher who is honorably mentioned by Longinus, Porphyry, Hierocles, Eunapius, Proclus, and others. He was a person of such learning and accurate judgment that, when he came one day into Plotinus’s school, that grave philosopher felt bashful and would have yielded his place. When Origen entreated Plotinus to go on with his lecture, Plotinus answered with a compliment: that a man could have little mind to speak in a place where he was to discourse to those who understood things as well as himself. After a very short discourse, he ended the meeting. I am well aware that most learned men have carelessly confused this person with our Origen. Because of this, Holstenius wonders why Eunapius would make Origen a schoolfellow of Porphyry, who was much younger than he. Porphyry says indeed that he knew Origen when he himself was very young, and this was probably not at Alexandria but at Tyre, where Porphyry was born and where Origen resided for a long time. So, his wonder would have ceased had he considered what is plain enough: that Eunapius meant this other Origen, Porphyry's fellow-student, who studied not under Ammonius at Alexandria, but under Plotinus at Rome. Indeed, if nothing else, this would be enough to distinguish them: the account given of Origen and what he wrote by Longinus, by Porphyry in the *Life of Plotinus*, and by others, does not in any way agree with our Christian writer.

<margin>
l *Eusebius, in the same work, chapter 2, p. 201.*
m *The same, chapter 2, p. 202.*
</margin>
V. The persecution under Emperor Severus in the tenth year of his reign was now growing hot at Alexandria. Laetus the Governor was daily adding fuel to the flames. Among the great numbers of martyrs, Leonides, Origen’s father, was first imprisoned and then beheaded; his estate was confiscated and seized for the public treasury. During his father's imprisonment, Origen began to display a most impatient desire for martyrdom, from which scarcely any entreaties or considerations could restrain him. He knew the deplorable state in which his father was likely to leave his wife and children, and he knew this must have a sad influence upon his father’s mind. Therefore, in letters, he passionately exhorted Leonides to persevere unto martyrdom, adding this clause among the rest: *Take heed, Sir, that for our sakes you do not change your mind.* He would have gone not only to prison but to the very execution block with his father if Divine Providence had not intervened. His mother, perceiving his resolutions, treated him with all the charms and endearments of an affectionate mother. She appealed to him with prayers and tears, entreating him that if not for his own sake, then at least for hers and for his nearest relatives, he would spare himself.

When all this failed to discourage him—especially after his father's arrest—she was forced to resort to a small trick: she hid all his clothes so that simple shame would keep him confined to the house. The historian notes this as a powerful example of youthful drive and maturity, and a most sincere devotion to the true religion.

<margin>a Eusebius, the same place, page 203.</margin>
<margin>b Letter in Eusebius, the same place, chapter 19, page 221.</margin>

VI. After his father’s death and the seizure of the family estate <note>original: "Estate seized for the Emperours use"</note> for the Emperor’s use, Origen and his family were reduced to great hardship. But the providence of God—who takes special care of widows and orphans, and particularly the families of those who suffer for Him—provided a way for their relief. A wealthy and noble matron of Alexandria, pitying his desperate situation, generously contributed to his needs. She did the same for others and, among them, supported a man named Paul of Antioch. Paul was a leader of the heretics in Alexandria who had so cleverly manipulated the lady that she had adopted him as her son. 

Although Origen depended entirely on her charity for his survival, he refused to associate with this favorite. He would not even join him in prayer, even though a vast number of people—not just heretics, but orthodox Christians as well—flocked to Paul daily, captivated by his eloquent speeches. From his childhood, Origen had religiously followed the rules and traditions of the Church and hated (as he himself put it) all heretical doctrines. I do not know if this noble lady withdrew her charity because of this, or if he simply thought it was more consistent with Christian principles to live by his own labor rather than depend entirely on another’s generosity. However, having completed his studies in secular subjects <note>original: "Foreign Learning"</note>, the foundations of which he had laid under his father’s instruction, he now began to work for himself. He opened a school for the liberal arts <note>original: "learned Arts"</note>, where, in addition to helping others, he earned a decent living. Even though he was still just a youth, serious and learned men, philosophers, and even the greatest masters of heresy did not think it beneath them to attend his lectures. Origen impartially weighed and examined their opinions, as he tells us himself. Many of these students <note>original: "Auditors"</note> eventually became his converts—and even martyrs for the faith, as we shall soon see.

<margin>d Ibid., page 205.</margin>
<margin>e Ibid., chapter 4, page 266.</margin>

VII. By this time, his reputation had brought him to public attention. He was considered fit, though only eighteen years old, to be appointed Master of the <term>Catechetic School</term> <note>An influential school in Alexandria for instructing new converts and scholars in Christian theology.</note> at Alexandria. It is uncertain whether he served as a colleague to his teacher Clement, or as his successor upon Clement's resignation. The latter seems more likely, because Eusebius reports that Demetrius, the Bishop of Alexandria, entrusted the instruction of the catechumens <note>Students training for baptism.</note> to him alone—unless we understand this as a private school separate from the official Catechetic School until Clement's death, whom the ancients generally say he succeeded. 

Students crowded his classes daily in such great numbers that he found his various responsibilities were clashing. Consequently, he stopped teaching the secular arts and sciences and devoted himself entirely to instructing his disciples in the basics of Christianity. Once established in this office, he worked with immense diligence and equal success. He not only strengthened those who were already Christians, but also converted a great number of pagan <note>original: "Gentile"</note> philosophers to the faith. These men embraced Christianity so sincerely that they were ready to seal their testimony with their own blood. The most notable of these was Plutarch, whom Origen accompanied to his martyrdom,

<summary>Following his father's martyrdom and the loss of the family wealth, the teenage Origen supported his family by teaching liberal arts before being appointed head of the prestigious Catechetic School of Alexandria at age eighteen.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the biography of Origen, detailing the martyrdom of his students and his own narrow escapes from the mob, as well as his controversial decision to castrate himself for the sake of his ministry and personal purity.</meta>

<page-num>219</page-num>

<margin>a The same place, page 204.</margin>
<margin>b Heresies 64, page 227.</margin>
Origen was nearly killed by the people for being the reason for his conversion; *Serenus*, who was burned for his religion; *Heraclides* and *Heron*, who were both beheaded—the one while still only a <term>Catechumen</term> <note>A person receiving basic instruction in the Christian faith before baptism.</note>, the other a beginner; next came a second *Serenus*, who, after enduring infinite torments, lost his head and gained a martyr's crown. Even the "weaker sex" <note>A common historical reference to women.</note> claimed a share in this glory: one *Herais*, a student and pupil of Origen, being (as he himself expresses it) "baptized by fire" <note>original: τὸ βάπτισμα τὸ διὰ πυρὸς λαβοῦσα</note>, left this world and mounted up to heaven in those flames. Nor was Origen so completely consumed by the care of his school that he failed to perform duties of piety and humanity toward others, especially the martyrs and those condemned to die. For *Aquila*, the successor of *Laetus* in the government of Alexandria, wishing to do something remarkable at the start of his term, renewed the persecution. It was so severe that everyone looked out for their own safety and stayed hidden; consequently, when the martyrs were in prison, or led to trial or execution, there was no one to comfort them or care for them. Origen boldly took this duty upon himself, attending the martyrs to the very place of execution, embracing and saluting them as they were led along. This continued until the enraged multitude pelted him with showers of stones, and a hundred times his life was in danger, had not divine Providence immediately intervened to rescue him. At last, they resolved to find him, with great crowds surrounding his house. Because he had a vast number of students, they brought a guard of soldiers with them who hunted him from house to house, so that no place could offer him a quiet refuge. During this period, some learned men believe (quite probably, in my opinion) that the event reported by *Epiphanius* occurred: that Origen was dragged up and down the city, reviled, reproached, and treated with insolent scorn and fury. Once, having shaved his head in the manner of the *Egyptian* priests, they set him upon the steps of the Temple of *Serapis*, commanding him to hand out palm branches (as the priests used to do) to those who went up to perform their sacred rituals. Taking the branches with a ready and fearless mind, he cried out aloud, "Come here and take the branch—not of an idol-temple, but of Christ!" This display of courage, I suppose, did nothing to calm their rage against him.

<margin>c As above, page 228.</margin>
<margin>d To Pammachius regarding the Errors of Origen, Volume 2, page 192.</margin>
<margin>e Eusebius, the same place, chapter 8, page 209.</margin>
<margin>f Apology 2, page 71.</margin>
VIII. Around this time, he made that famous attempt upon himself—so much commended by some, but condemned by others—by making himself a <term>eunuch</term>. As it appears from *Epiphanius*, some of the ancients believed this was done through medical applications which weakened the natural powers and tendencies of nature; however, others, and *Saint Jerome* explicitly, say it was done with a knife. But regardless of how it was done, he did it partly out of a mistaken interpretation of our Savior's meaning when He says, *there are some who make themselves eunuchs for the Kingdom of Heaven's sake*, which Origen felt he must understand literally. Partly, he did it out of a desire to remove all suspicion of lust or lack of self-control, which the non-Christians might be quick to accuse him of when they saw him admitting not only men, but women, into his teaching. Furthermore, by this act, he secured himself against any temptations toward indecent or improper relationships. We have shown at length in another place how strict and severe the chastity of those early Christian times was; it was so great that *Justin Martyr* tells us of a young man of Alexandria who, to convince the non-Christians of the falsehood of that malicious...

<margin><sup>a</sup> See Commentary on Matthew, p. 368 and pp. 370–371, Huet edition. <note>original: Vid. Comment. in Matt. p. 368. & p. 370. 371. Edit. Huet.</note></margin>
...malicious charge of sexual immorality <note>original: incontinency</note> and promiscuous behavior, which was often leveled against the Christians, Origen presented a petition to Felix, the Governor <note>original: President</note> of Alexandria. He requested permission for physicians to make him a eunuch. The Governor refused this, as it was prohibited by the laws of the Roman Empire, just as it was later forbidden by several provisions and canons of the Church. Although Origen tried to hide this act from some of his friends, the news quickly spread. Demetrius, the Bishop, who at the time admired it as a heroic act of temperance and an instance of a great and daring mind, later used it against him, bringing it up as an inexcusable charge with every possible exaggeration. I will add nothing more concerning this except that whatever Origen might have done in the vigor of his youth and through the intensity of his devout zeal, in his more mature and level-headed years he changed his mind. He condemned <sup>a</sup> such attempts, soberly interpreting that passage of our Savior which he had previously so fatally misunderstood. <note>Origen took Matthew 19:12 literally: "and there be eunuchs, which have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven's sake."</note>

<margin><sup>b</sup> Eusebius, Book 6, chapter 14, p. 216. <note>original: Euseb. lib. 6. 14 p. 216.</note></margin>
<margin><sup>c</sup> Ibid. chapter 15, p. 217.</margin>
<margin><sup>d</sup> Apology against Rufinus, Volume 2, p. 201. <note>original: Apolog. adv. Ruffin. Tom. 2. p. 201.</note></margin>
IX. After Emperor Severus, that violent enemy of Christians, died in AD 211, Origen <sup>b</sup> had a great desire to see the Church of Rome, so respected for its antiquity and renown. Accordingly, he traveled there while Pope Zephyrinus served as Bishop of that See. He did not stay long, but returned to Alexandria and to his accustomed role as a teacher <note>original: Catechetic office</note>, as Demetrius earnestly urged him to resume it. However, he found the workload <sup>c</sup> increasing so much that it completely took up his time, leaving him no leisure for retirement, contemplation, or the study of the Scriptures, because students crowded around him from morning to night. To help, he recruited Heraclas—who had been his own student and was well-versed in both divine and secular <note>original: humane</note> studies—to be his partner. They divided the work between them: the younger and more uninstructed <term>Catechumens</term> <note>People receiving basic instruction in the Christian faith before baptism.</note> were assigned to Heraclas, while the more mature and long-standing students were reserved for Origen's own instruction. He then gave himself over to a closer and more accurate study of the Holy Scriptures. To ensure his success in this, he set himself to learn the Hebrew language—the true key to unlocking the door. (As Saint Jerome <sup>d</sup> likely suggests, Origen was assisted in this by Huillus, the Jewish Patriarch of that time, at least regarding the Rabbinic interpretation of the Scripture.) This was a subject little understood in those times and in that place. For Origen, who was then in the prime of his age and at the peak of more pleasant and delightful studies, it was no doubt very difficult and uneasy. But nothing is too hard for industrious diligence and a willing mind.

<margin><sup>e</sup> Eusebius, ibid. chapter 18, p. 218. <note>original: Eus. ib. c. 18. p. 218.</note></margin>
X. These labors did not interrupt his activity in his other duties. Whenever he noticed <sup>e</sup> any of his students possessed particularly sharp and quick minds, he first instructed them in geometry, arithmetic, and other preparatory subjects. He then led them through a course of philosophy, explaining the principles of each sect and the books of the ancients, and sometimes writing commentaries on them himself. As a result, even the non-Christians <note>original: Gentiles</note> praised him as an eminent philosopher. He often encouraged the less educated members of his audience to study the liberal arts, assuring them that these subjects would contribute significantly to a right understanding of the Holy Scriptures. Many flocked to him to test his famous skill and learning; others came to be instructed in the precepts of both philosophy...

# The Life of ORIGEN.

<margin>* Eusebius, in the same place; Jerome, *On Illustrious Men* regarding Ambrosius; Suidas, under the entry "Origen" <note>original: Ὡριγ.</note>; Epiphanius, where mentioned above, page 228.</margin>
<margin>a Letter found in Suidas, where mentioned above, page 390; see Jerome, Letter to Marcella, page 129, Volume 1.</margin>
<margin>b Jerome, *On Illustrious Men* regarding Ambrosius.</margin>
Origen’s teaching drew many listeners from both the schools of philosophy and the various branches of Christianity. Great numbers of heretics were among his audience, some of whom he converted from their errors. Among these was *Ambrosius*, a man of high nobility and wealth in *Alexandria*. Ambrosius had been led astray by the errors of *Marcion* and *Valentinus* <note>Marcion and Valentinus were leaders of Gnostic sects that the early Church regarded as heretical for their divergent views on the nature of God and Christ.</note>, but after being convinced by *Origen's* discourses, he renounced his former heresies and returned to the Catholic <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the universal or orthodox teachings of the early Church.</note> doctrine of the Church. From then on, he became Origen's intimate friend, great patron, and benefactor. He was a man of refined and elegant abilities and was continually encouraging *Origen* to explain and interpret various parts of the Scripture. As *Origen* himself tells us (a), Ambrosius would not let a single supper time pass without discussions on these topics, nor did he allow their walks or recreations to happen without them. A large part of the night, in addition to their morning studies, was spent on these pious exercises. Their meals and their rest were introduced with continual lectures, and both night and day, where prayer ended, reading began; just as after reading, they returned again to prayer. Indeed, this *Ambrose* was a pious and good man, and though he was a person of great status, he did not think it beneath him to take on the office of a *Deacon* in the Church. He even underwent great hardships and sufferings, becoming an eminent *Confessor* for the faith. There is only one stain (b) that I know of upon his memory: when he died wealthy, he did not remember his dear and old friend Origen in his will. Origen’s humble and poor condition could have well used a legacy, and his hard work and friendship certainly deserved such a gift.

<margin>c Eusebius, in the same place, chapter 19, page 221.</margin>
XI. Around this time, a messenger (c) arrived from the Governor of *Arabia* with letters to *Demetrius* the Bishop and to the Prefect of *Egypt*. He requested that *Origen* be sent with all speed to teach Christian doctrine to him; so great had the fame of this remarkable man become in foreign nations. Accordingly, Origen went to *Arabia*, and having completed his mission, he returned to *Alexandria*. Not long after his return, the Emperor *Caracalla* brought his army into those regions, intending to attack that city severely. To avoid the Emperor's rage and cruelty, *Origen* thought it best to withdraw. Knowing of no place in *Egypt* that could offer him safety, he retired to *Palestine* and settled in *Caesarea*. When his excellent abilities were noticed there, the local bishops requested him—even though he was then only a <term>layman</term> <note>original: Laic; a member of the church who is not ordained as a priest or member of the clergy.</note>—to expound the Scriptures to the people publicly in the church and in their own presence. News of this was quickly carried back to *Alexandria* and was deeply resented by *Demetrius*. He wrote letters debating the matter with *Theoctistus*, Bishop of *Caesarea*, and *Alexander* of *Jerusalem*, claiming such a thing was unheard of in the Christian Church. In their answer, they reminded him that this was not an unusual practice and provided him with specific examples. None of this satisfied *Demetrius*, who commanded *Origen* by letter to return and sent *Deacons* specifically to urge him to do so. Consequently, Origen returned and applied himself to his usual duties.

<margin>d In the same place, chapter 21, page 223; see excerpt from John of Antioch, page 835.</margin>
XII. *ALEXANDER SEVERUS*, the current Emperor, had come to *Antioch* to prepare for his expedition against the *Persians*. He was accompanied by his mother *Mammæa*, a wise, prudent, and (says *Eusebius* [d]) most pious and religious Princess. She had a great influence on her son, whom she engaged in a very strict and constant administration of justice.

# The Life of ORIGEN.

Justice and the affairs of the Empire occupied his time, so that he might have no leisure to be corrupted by vice and luxury. Indeed, he was a Prince of matchless virtues. Historians represent him as mild and gentle, compassionate and charitable, sober and temperate, just and impartial, devout and pious—one advanced to the Empire for the recovery and happiness of mankind. He was no enemy to Christians, whom he not only did not persecute, but favored at every opportunity. In his private *Oratory* <note>A private chapel or place of prayer.</note>, he kept among other *Heroes* the images of *Abraham* and of *Christ*. He was once even minded to have built a temple to Christ and publicly admitted him into the number of the gods. He highly admired some precepts of the Christian religion, and from their discipline, he learned some rites which he made use of in the government of the Empire.

<margin>* Eusebius, in the place cited before.</margin>
But to return to *Mammea*: being a *Syrian* by birth, she could not be unacquainted with the affairs of both *Jews* and *Christians*. Having heard of the great fame of *Origen*, she was very desirous to see him and hear him discourse concerning religion, so that she might know why the whole world held him in such veneration. For this purpose, she sent for him, ordering a military guard to conduct him to *Antioch*. He stayed there for a considerable time, and having fully explained the doctrines of our religion and given her many demonstrations of the Christian faith—to the great honor of God and religion—he was dismissed and permitted to return to his old duties at *Alexandria*.

<margin>b Ibid, chapter 23, page 224.</margin>
XIII. From this point forward, he set about writing *Commentaries* on the Holy Scripture at the urging of his dear friend *Ambrosius*. Ambrosius did not only earnestly press him to do it but furnished him with all the conveniences necessary for the task. He provided for Origen's maintenance and allowed him seven <term>Notaries</term> <note>original: "Notaries"; these were stenographers or shorthand writers who recorded spoken words in real-time.</note> (and more as the occasion required) to attend to him, who by turns might record what he dictated to them. He also provided as many *transcribers*, besides young women employed for that purpose, who made fair copies of what the others had hastily taken down. These *notaries* were very common among both the Greeks and *Romans*, making use of certain peculiar notes and signs for either secret writing or shorthand. Through the dexterity of their art, they were able to capture not only words but entire sentences. The origin of this art is ascribed by some to Tiro, *Cicero's* servant; by others to Aquila, servant to *Maecenas*; and by others to Ennius. They say it was polished and enlarged afterward, first by Tiro, then by Aquila and others. It may be that in its first rough form it was much more ancient, and was improved and perfected by degrees, with every new addition claiming the original invention, until it arrived at such accuracy and perfection that (as appears from what <margin>c Martial, Book 14, Epigram 208. d Ausonius, Epigram 36.</margin> *Martial* says on the matter, and *Ausonius* <gloss>d</gloss> reports of his *secretary* <note>original: "Amanuensis"</note>) they were able not only to keep pace with but often to outrun the speaker. 

There is no doubt that they were in frequent use in the Primitive Church, being chiefly employed to write the *Acts* of the Martyrs. For this purpose, they used to frequent the prisons and be present at all trials and examinations. If the proceedings were done "behind the veil" <note>original: "intra Velum"</note> within the "private court chamber" <note>original: "Secretarium"</note>, they used bribes to procure copies of the examinations and answers from the *Proconsul's* register. From there, they followed the martyrs to the place of execution to record <note>original: "remarque"</note> their sayings and their sufferings. <margin>e Tertullian, On the Crown, chapter 13, page 109. f Saint Cyprian, Letter 37, page 51.</margin> This was done in the earliest ages, as is evident from *Tertullian's* mention of the "Church Records" <note>original: "Fasti Ecclesiae"</note> and from what <gloss>f</gloss> *St. Cyprian* says in his letter...

So it is that the origin of this institution is, with some probability, traced back to the time of *Saint Clement*, Bishop of *Rome*. I note all of this because it gives us a reasonable explanation for how the answers and speeches of the martyrs, the arguments and discourses of synods and councils, and the extemporaneous <term>homilies</term> <note>Sermons or religious discourses intended for spiritual edification.</note> of the Fathers came to be transmitted so entirely and perfectly to us.
