This is an intolerable mistake, not only disagreeing with *Eusebius's* account, but plainly inconsistent with the course of *Origen’s* life. Indeed, *Epiphanius* alleges no better authority than "as the story goes" <note>original: ὡς ὁ λόγος ἔχει</note>, having picked up the story from some common tradition and report. 

His industry and diligence in these studies was incredible, as few parts of the Bible escaped his narrow and critical research. In this he attained such admirable accuracy and perfection that <margin>I say this one thing: that I could wish, even with the envy attached to his name, to also have his knowledge of the Scriptures, disregarding the images and shadows of ghosts—whose nature is said to be to terrify children and chatter in dark corners. <note>original: *Hoc unum dico, quod vellem cum invidia nominis ejus habere etiam scientiam Scripturarum, floccipendens imagines umbrasque larvarum: quarum natura esse dicitur, terrere parvulos, & in angulis garrire tenebrosis.*</note> Jerome, Preface to *Questions on Genesis*, Volume 3, page 201.</margin> *Saint Jerome* himself (who was not always very polite to him) confesses that he would be content to bear the load of envy that was cast upon Origen's name, if only he also had his skill and knowledge in the Scriptures. This is a passage which <margin>Invectives II against Jerome, among the works of Jerome, Volume 4, page 225.</margin> *Ruffinus* later turned against him quite sharply.

XIV. But a stop was put to this work for the present by some affairs of the Church, which called him into *Achaia* <note>A province of the Roman Empire, roughly corresponding to modern-day Greece.</note>, which was then disturbed by various heresies that overran those churches. It was undoubtedly during this time that he stayed for a while at *Athens*, where (as <margin>As cited above, page 227.</margin> *Epiphanius* tells us) he frequented the schools of the philosophers and conversed with the sages of that place. On his journey to *Achaia*, he went through <margin>Eusebius, in the place cited; Jerome, *On Illustrious Men* regarding Alexander.</margin> *Palestine* and took *Caesarea* in his way. There, presenting his letters of recommendation from *Demetrius*, he was ordained a <term>Presbyter</term> <note>A priest or elder. In the early church, this was a significant step in clerical rank.</note> by *Alexander* of *Jerusalem* and *Theoctistus*, Bishop of *Caesarea*. This was not done through any underhanded arts or the ambitious procurement of *Origen* himself, but was entirely the act of those two excellent men. They designed by this means to furnish him with a greater authority for managing his mission and to render him more useful to the affairs of the Church. However, the action was deeply resented by *Demetrius*, as—

This was seen as an insult to his jurisdiction and a contempt of his authority. Now the wind has turned into a blustering gale, and nothing but excommunications <note>original: "anathema’s"</note> are thundered out against him from Alexandria. Demetrius had for some time held a secret grudge against him, and he took this occasion to attack him. The truth is, he envied the honor and reputation which Origen’s learning and virtue had earned him in the thoughts and words of all men. Lacking an opportunity until now to vent his jealousy, he finally found one. Accordingly, he charged Origen with everything that spite and malice could invent. He publicly accused him of making himself a eunuch (a fact he had previously admired in him) and severely criticized the bishops who had ordained him. Indeed, he stirred up such a storm that he caused Origen to be condemned ᵃ in two separate <note>original: "several"</note> synods. One, composed of bishops and priests <note>original: "Presbyters"</note>, decreed that he should be banished from Alexandria and not permitted either to live or teach there. The other, under Demetrius and some Egyptian bishops, pronounced him to be stripped of his priesthood; even his greatest supporters were forced to sign the decree. ᵇ Saint Jerome adds that the majority of the Christian world consented to this condemnation and that Rome itself convened a synod against him. This was not for heresy or innovations in doctrine, but merely out of envy, as they were unable to bear the glory and renown of his learning and eloquence. It was said that while he taught, others were looked upon as mute and dumb, just as the stars disappear in the presence of the sun. And yet all this conflict <note>original: "combustion"</note> vanished like smoke, for Origen still retained his priesthood, continued publicly preaching in the church, and was honorably received wherever he went by the wiser and more moderate members of the Church.

XV. Exhausted by the annoying attacks of his enemies, he resolved to leave Alexandria, where the sentence of the synods would not allow him to remain much longer. He first resigned the leadership of his Catechetical School <note>A school for religious instruction for new converts.</note> entirely to his colleague, Heraclas ᶜ. This Heraclas was born a Gentile and was the brother of Plutarch, who (as we noted before) suffered martyrdom for the faith. Heraclas had been Origen’s student and was converted and built up in the faith by him. He was first taken on as Origen’s assistant <note>original: "Usher"</note> or partner in the catechetical office, then became his successor, and finally became the Bishop of Alexandria. He was a man of tireless diligence and led a strict life; he was learned and eloquent, a great master of philosophy and the humanities, but especially skilled in theology <note>original: "divine Studies"</note>. He retained his philosopher’s robe even after he was made a priest <note>original: "Presbyter"</note> of Alexandria, and he never ceased to industriously read and study the writings of the Gentiles. Indeed, he arrived at such singular fame and reputation that Julius Africanus, one of the most learned men of those times, came ᵈ specifically to Alexandria to see and hear him. It is no wonder, therefore, if Origen entrusted this great care and responsibility to him, as Heraclas’s personal merit and his specific obligation as Origen's student seemed to earn it. Before his departure (for those who claim it happened during the time of Decius are speaking without evidence, as Origen was not in Alexandria then), an incident occurred which, if true, hastened his flight with more shame and sorrow than all the malice of his bitterest enemies could create. We are told ᵉ that some Gentiles, who were his mortal enemies, seized him and forced him into a terrible dilemma: either he must allow his body to be sexually abused by an African man <note>The original text uses "Blackmoor," a historical term for a person of African descent; the passage describes a threat of forced sexual assault intended to humiliate Origen.</note> or offer a sacrifice to an idol. Of the two, he chose to sacrifice, though it was more their act than his, as they forced frankin-

XVI. YEAR 233. *Origen* left *Alexandria* and, directing his course for *Palestine*, went to his good friend and patron *Theoctistus*, Bishop of *Cæsarea*, and from there to *Jerusalem* to greet *Alexander*, its Bishop, and to visit the venerable antiquities of that place. And here *Epiphanius*, continuing the previous story, tells us that being greatly urged to preach, Origen stood up in the congregation. Having pronounced those words of the penitent *David*, *But unto the wicked God says, what have you to do to declare my statutes, or that you should take my covenant in your mouth?* <note>Psalm 50:16.</note> he could go no further. He shut the book, laid it down, and sat down, bursting into sighs and tears, with the whole congregation joining him in that mournful scene. To carry on the mood and make the story more complete, later ages presented us with a ᵈ *Discourse* under his name called *Origen’s Complaint*, in which he passionately resents and laments his fall as a desperate wound to himself, a grief to good men, and an inconceivable dishonor to God and religion. And it is a pity, if the story is true, that

# The Life of ORIGEN.

if this *Lamentation* <note>The "Lament of Origen" is a spurious work in which Origen allegedly mourns a temporary lapse into paganism; most scholars consider it a later forgery.</note> were not genuine. But as it stands, its strongest support is that it is designed to satisfy a pious fancy and a tender emotion, for there is nothing in it otherwise worthy of this great man. I fear it was first written by its author to cast a slight upon Origen and to lend credibility to the reports raised against him. 

From Jerusalem, he returned shortly thereafter to Caesarea, where (as he had previously done in Alexandria) he established <margin>a *Ibid* [Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*], book 6, chapter 30, page 229.</margin> a school for both divine and secular <note>original: "humane"</note> learning. His great reputation quickly brought him scholars from all parts—not only from the surrounding country but even from the remotest provinces. Among the most notable were Gregory, later called *Thaumaturgus* <note>Meaning "the Miracle-Worker."</note>, and his brother Athenodorus. These two left the study of the Law, being more delighted with philosophy and the arts, and committed themselves to Origen's guidance and tutelage. He first instructed them in philosophy and then trained them in a more accurate knowledge of the Christian faith. They remained under his discipline for five years. When they were sufficiently enriched with the knowledge of religion, they returned to Pontus, their own country, where they both became bishops and proved to be eminent lights and governors of the Church. 

During his residence at Caesarea, a firm intimacy and bond <margin>b *Ibid*., chapter 27, page 228.</margin> of friendship was established between Origen and Firmilian, the Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. Firmilian had such a great affection for Origen that he would sometimes persuade him to come to that province to build up the churches in those parts; at other times, he himself would go to Judea to visit Origen and stay for a considerable time to improve himself through his company and conversation. This Firmilian was a gentleman of Cappadocia who later became the Bishop of Caesarea in that country. He was a person of great reputation and note who kept in contact with most of the eminent men of those times. There were few significant affairs of the Church in which he was not involved, either by his presence or his advice. There were great contests between him and Stephen, the Bishop of Rome, concerning the baptism of heretics, in which he took the side of Cyprian <note>Cyprian of Carthage argued that baptisms performed by heretics were invalid, a view Firmilian supported.</note>. He was twice at Antioch to examine the case of Paul of Samosata, the Bishop of that Church. While traveling to a third synod assembled there for that purpose, he died at Tarsus along the way. Nor was Origen admired and sought after only by foreigners and the young men who had been his students, but also by the grave and wise at home. Both Alexander and Theoctistus, though they were senior bishops, did not disdain to essentially become his disciples, committing to his sole care the authority of interpreting the Holy Scriptures and everything concerning Church doctrine.

XVII. It was now about the year 235 when Maximinus the Thracian <note>Emperor Maximinus Thrax (r. 235–238).</note> succeeded to the Empire. He was a fierce and ill-natured man, and, given his upbringing, brutish and cruel. He hated whatever <margin>c *Ibid*., chapter 28.</margin> had relation to his predecessor <note>Alexander Severus, who was relatively tolerant toward Christians.</note>, and because the Christians had found some favorable treatment in his predecessor's household, Maximinus began his persecution with them. He especially targeted the bishops as the chief pillars and promoters of their religion, whom he commanded to be put to death everywhere. To <margin>"Now, as if being sent, carrying the cross with Jesus, as a priest..." <note>original: "Νῦν ὥσπερ πεμπόμενοι αἱ- ρων τ' σταυρὸν τῷ Ἰησῷ, ἱερεῖ"</note></margin> contribute toward the comfort of Christians in this evil time, Origen wrote his book *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, which he jointly dedicated to <margin>"Ambrose; and following him, speaking before governors and kings; so that he himself, traveling with you, may give you both speech and wisdom; and to you, his fellow-soldier Protoctetus; and to those bearing witness with you, who fill up what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ (may it not be so with us!) at the handing over of God." <note>original: "Ἀμβρόσιε· κ' ἀκολουθῶν αὐτῷ, φράζον πὶς πρὸ ἡγεμόνας κ' βασιλεῖς · ἵνα αὐτός σοι συμπορευθεὶς, αὐτός σοι δῷ κ' στόμα κ' σοφίαν · καὶ σοὶ τῷ συναγωνιστῇ αὐτῷ Πρωτόκτητε · κ' Συμμαρτυροῦσιν ὑμῖν, τοῖς ἀναπληροῦσι τὰ ὑστερήματα τῶν παθημάτων τοῦ Χριστοῦ, (μὴ ἡμῶν γένοιθ) ἐπὶ τῇ παραδώσει τοῦ Θεοῦ." Origen, *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, page 200.</note></margin>

As for *Origen* himself, he is said to have taken sanctuary in the house of *Juliana*, a wealthy and charitable lady who courteously hosted him and provided him with useful books. These included the version of the Old Testament by *Symmachus*<sup>a</sup> and his commentaries in defense of the *Ebionites* <note>A Jewish-Christian sect that followed Jewish law and often used a modified version of Matthew’s Gospel.</note>, which were particularly aimed against *St. Matthew’s* Gospel—books which *Juliana* had inherited.

XVIII. While he enjoyed the fortunate opportunity of this retirement, he applied himself more directly to a project he had long planned: collecting and comparing the various editions and versions of the Old Testament with the original text. He completed this in three separate parts<sup>b</sup>: the *Tetrapla*, the *Hexapla*, and the *Octapla*. In the first (which, though considered a distinct part, was actually made last), there were four translations set side-by-side: those of *Aquila*, *Symmachus*, the *Septuagint*, and *Theodotion*. These made up the *Tetrapla* <note>Literally "four-fold."</note>. In the second, these four versions were arranged in the same order, with two other columns placed before them. First was the *Hebrew* text in its own letters; then, in the next adjoining column, the same *Hebrew* text in *Greek* characters, so that those who were unfamiliar with the Hebrew alphabet might still be able to read the original language. Next followed the various versions of *Aquila*, *Symmachus*, the *Septuagint*, and *Theodotion*. These constituted the *Hexapla* <note>Literally "six-fold."</note>. In this work, the *Septuagint* was placed after the versions of *Aquila* and *Symmachus*, which led some unobservant people to think it had been written after the first two. However, it was placed in the middle (as *Epiphanius* informs us<sup>c</sup>) only as a standard by which the quality and accuracy of the others were to be tested and judged. 

In the third part, which made up the *Octapla* <note>Literally "eight-fold."</note>, were all the columns from the previous version, arranged in the same manner, but with two more versions added at the end. One was called the *Fifth Edition*, found by a student at *Jerusalem* in a large jar <note>original: "Hogshead"</note> at *Jericho* during the time of the Emperor *Caracalla*. The other was called the *Sixth Edition*, found by one of *Origen’s* scholars at *Nicopolis* near *Actium* during the reign of *Alexander Severus*. All of these in the *Octapla* were arranged in several columns in this order: in the first column was the original *Hebrew* in its native characters; in the next, the *Hebrew* in *Greek* letters; in the third, the translation of *Aquila*; then that of *Symmachus*; next the *Septuagint*; in the sixth, that of *Theodotion*; and in the last two, the version from *Jericho* and the one from *Nicopolis*. Indeed, it is clear from what<sup>d</sup> *St. Jerome* tells us that these last two were not complete and entire translations, but contained only some parts of the Old Testament, especially the Prophetic books. Whether we may conclude from this that the *Hexapla* and the *Octapla* were actually one and the same work, only receiving a different title based on the sections that had these last two versions attached, I will not say. Besides these, there was a *Seventh Edition*; but as this applied only to the Book of *Psalms*, it did not change the title of the whole work. The structure and order of this excellent invention will be better understood by the reader through the following scheme, modeled after a sample of the *Hexapla* still existing in Cardinal *Barberini’s* very ancient manuscript of the Minor Prophets, regarding these words: *When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my Son out of Egypt.*

To make the work more complete and useful, he distinguished additions and missing parts with specific marks. Whenever something had been added by the Septuagint <note>The standard Greek translation of the Old Testament used by the early Church.</note> that was not present in the original Hebrew text, he placed an *obelus* <note>A symbol (÷) used in ancient scholarship to mark text as doubtful or added.</note> before it. Where something was missing from the Greek but present in the *Hebrew*, he inserted the words with an *asterisk* <note>A symbol (※) used to mark text restored from the original source.</note> to distinguish them from the rest of the *Septuagint* translation.

Where various readings <note>original: "Lections"</note> were confirmed by the majority of translations, he added a note called a *lemniscus* <note>a symbol indicating a variety of readings</note>; where only two of them agreed, he used an *hypolemniscus*. In this way, he upheld the truth without being unfair to any version. It was a work of immense labor and wonderful usefulness, which the ancients specifically called the *Opus Ecclesiae* <note>original: "Work of the Church"</note>. Because of this, St. Jerome ᵃ calls him "that immortal genius" <note>original: "Immortale illud ingenium"</note>. Indeed, if he had done nothing else, this alone would have been enough to make his name eternal and memorable to future generations. It would have been a great blessing if it had been preserved; I can only attribute its loss to the sheer effort, expense, and difficulty involved in copying such a massive work. However, a portion of it—specifically the *Septuagint*—was later extracted and published more accurately by Eusebius and Pamphilus, correcting the errors that had crept into it during previous copying. This was a long-term project and was not finished by Origen all at once; it began in Caesarea and was completed in Tyre, as Epiphanius plainly indicates.

XIX. From Caesarea, Origen seems to have taken a second journey to Athens, though I do not know for what reason. During his stay there, we find him finishing his commentaries ᵇ on Ezekiel and beginning his exposition of the *Canticles* <note>the Song of Solomon</note>. He completed five books of that work there and finished the rest upon his return to Caesarea. Some believe he took the opportunity of this journey to go to Nicomedia to visit his friend Ambrosius, who was living there at the time with his wife and children. While he continued here (which was not for long), he wrote a reply to a letter he had recently received from Julius Africanus regarding the History of Susanna <note>a story often included with the Book of Daniel in early Bibles</note>. Africanus argued with short but very powerful points that the story was a fictional and fake account. Origen took up the case and defended the story as authentic and genuine, but he did so with arguments that show the sharpness of his mind more than the strength of his case. They clearly demonstrate how much even the most learned and capable men struggle when they try to defend a weak position that lacks the truth to support itself. Around this time, it happened that Beryllus ᶜ, the Bishop of Bostra in Arabia, fell into absurd and dangerous errors. He claimed that our Lord, before his incarnation, had no distinct existence and no personal deity, but only a divinity derived from the Father. The local bishops met to discuss this but could not convince him to change his mind. Consequently, Origen’s help was requested. He went there and debated with Beryllus in both private meetings and public synods. Origen’s greatest challenge was simply understanding what the man meant. Once he had figured it out, he pressured him so effectively with logical reasoning and proofs that Beryllus was forced to give up his position, take back his errors, and return to the path of truth. After this was done, Origen left and returned to Palestine. Beryllus ᵈ, behaving like a true convert, wrote several letters thanking Origen for his kind efforts in convincing him, "kissing the hand" that brought him back to the faith.

There was a similarity of temperament and *intellect* <note>original: "genius"</note> between these two persons. *Celsus* was a man of intelligence and talent, and had all the advantages that learning, philosophy, and eloquence could provide. However, he was a severe and incurable enemy of the Christian religion, against which he wrote a book titled *The True Word* <note>original: "Ἀληθὴς λόγος"</note>. In this work, he attacked Christianity with every art of insinuation, witty reflection, and bitter insult, using all the plausible reasoning that a man of talent and malice could muster. To this, *Origen* provided a full and solid answer in eight books. Because Origen had the better cause, he managed it with such strength of reason, clarity of argument, and convincing evidence of truth that, even if there were no other evidence of this great man’s abilities, this book alone would be enough to prove them. It was likely written around the beginning of the reign of the Emperor *Philip*, with whom *Origen* seems to have had some acquaintance.

Philip ᵃ wrote one letter to Origen and another to the Empress. Based on this and some other minor probabilities, *Eusebius* first, and then the general consensus of ecclesiastical writers, have claimed that this Emperor was a Christian—the first of the Imperial line to be so. We have shown elsewhere the futility of this mistake and the source from which it sprang. Nor is the matter improved by those who say that *Philip* was privately baptized by *Fabian*, the Bishop of *Rome*, and thus his Christian profession was known only to Christians but concealed from the *Gentiles*. This is merely a conjecture and a *mere assertion* <note>original: "gratis dictum"</note> without any authority to confirm it; it may be rejected with the same ease and justice with which it is forced upon us.

Such an event would have made a louder noise in the world and would have had more and better witnesses to attest to it than an obscure and uncertain report—the only authority that *Eusebius*, who gave the first hint of it, offers on this matter.

# The Life of ORIGEN.

They maintained the truth in their hearts. They carried a book around with them which they claimed had been dropped directly down from Heaven; they believed that whoever received it and believed in it would receive forgiveness for their sins, though this was a different kind of pardon than the one our Lord *Jesus* bestowed upon his followers. However, the extent to which *Origen* was involved in opposing this absurd and senseless group <note>original: "generation"</note> is unknown to me. The best part of it is that this sect, like a blazing comet, though its influence was harmful and diseased <note>original: "malignant and pestilential"</note>, suddenly appeared and just as suddenly vanished.

<margin>a In the same place, chapter 39, page 234.</margin>
XXII. After the Emperor *Philip* was killed by his soldiers, *Decius* managed, with the help of the army, to take the throne. He was a deadly enemy to the *Church* ᵃ, and during his short reign, more martyrs—especially prominent and distinguished men—were executed than under those who governed the Empire ten times longer than he did. In *Palestine*, *Alexander*, the aged and venerable Bishop of *Jerusalem*, was thrown into prison. After long and harsh treatment, and after making a glorious confession <term>A formal statement of Christian faith made by a "Confessor" under the threat of torture or death.</term> of the Christian faith before the public tribunal, he died. This *Alexander* (whom we have 
<margin>b In the same place, chapter 11, page 212.</margin>
often mentioned) had first been a bishop in *Cappadocia* ᵇ. There, out of a pious desire, he had decided to go on a pilgrimage to *Jerusalem* to visit the holy and ancient sites of that place. He was particularly encouraged to do this by a divine revelation suggesting to him that it was God’s will for him to assist the bishop of that city. It happened at this time that *Narcissus*, the Bishop of *Jerusalem*, had returned to his see <term>The jurisdiction or official seat of a bishop.</term> some years earlier (which he had left many years before), but he had become unable to properly manage his duties because of his extreme age and frailty (being 116 years old). As *Alexander* approached *Jerusalem*, the people were warned by a vision and a voice from heaven to go out of the city and receive the man whom Heaven had chosen to be their bishop. They did so, and finding *Alexander*, they welcomed and introduced him with all possible kindness and respect. At the urgent request of the people, and with the consent of all the neighboring bishops, he was forced to become a colleague with *Narcissus* in the government of that church. I believe this is the first clear example we find in the history of the early Church of two bishops serving at once (and by mutual consent) in one see. But the case was justified by an extraordinary authority. # The Life of ORIGEN.

With all his schemes and tactics, the Emperor singled him out above all others of that time to make him the object of his greatest rage and fury. Origen was cast into the depths of a loathsome and miserable dungeon, weighed down with irons and a chain around his neck. His feet were set in the stocks, with his legs painfully stretched four holes apart for many days together. He was threatened with execution by fire and tested with every torture that a merciless enemy could devise. Given his advanced age and a body already broken by so many burdens and labors, this was an incredibly heavy weight to bear. Yet he endured everything with noble patience and was ready to submit to the final fatal blow of execution. However, the Judge—wishing to intensify his misery as much as possible—ordered the tormentors to torture him in such a way that they would not kill him.

XXIII. Human councils and resolutions, no matter how active and violent, are still subject to the One who is higher than the highest and can overrule them; for there are powers higher than they. <note>original: "yet he that is higher then the highest can over-rule them, and there be that are higher then they." This is a reference to Ecclesiastes 5:8.</note> His enemies had so far only tested him with preliminary cruelties, saving him for a more formal execution. But God, to whom belongs the escape from death, thwarted their malice and provided a way for him to escape. This was likely brought about by the death of the Emperor *Decius*, who was killed after reigning for two and a half years.

# The Life of ORIGEN.

<margin>
a Eusebius, Book 6, Chapter 3, p. 205.
b Gregory of Neocaesarea, Panegyric Oration on Origen, p. 205.
c Eusebius, ibid., p. 206.
</margin>

...if we take a brief look back at him, we shall find that he was an extraordinary person. His life was truly strict and philosophical ᵃ, serving as an admirable example of discipline and virtue. As his teachings were, so were his manners; his life was the very image of his mind. That wise and good man whom he used to describe in his lectures to his students (as one of the most eminent of them ᵇ assures us) he had first formed and modeled in the example of his own life. 

He held the glory of God and the well-being of souls in the highest regard. He studied every possible way to promote their happiness, considering no task too difficult, humble, or lowly if it served that purpose. He was modest, humble, chaste, and temperate. His abstinence and sobriety were so exemplary that for many years he lived on almost nothing. He abstained from wine and everything except what was absolutely necessary to sustain life, until his extreme fasting almost ruined his health ᶜ and threatened to weaken his constitution beyond recovery. 

His contempt for worldly things was singular. He literally followed our Lord's command to his disciples: not to have *two coats*, to provide *no sandals*, and not to be anxiously worried about tomorrow. Many people, out of respect for his tireless diligence, wanted to share their own resources to help with his needs, but he refused. Rather than being a needless burden to anyone, he sold his library, agreeing with the buyer to receive four *oboli* <note>An *obolus* was a small Greek coin; four *oboli* was a tiny amount, roughly five pence at the time of this writing.</note> a day for his maintenance. 

His diligence in studying, preaching, writing, traveling, and refuting Pagans and heretics—as well as settling divisions and differences within the Church—was tireless. Because of this, the ancients gave him the titles of *Adamantius* <note>original: "Adamantius," meaning "unbreakable" or "man of steel."</note> and *Chalcenterus* <note>original: "Chalcenterus," meaning "bowels of brass," a nickname for someone with an iron-like capacity for work.</note>. It was believed that nothing but a constitution made of brass and iron could have endured such infinite labors. He spent part of the day fasting and the rest in other religious duties and employments. He devoted the night to the study of the Scripture, reserving only a very small portion for sleep, which he usually took on the bare ground rather than in a bed. 

This lifestyle admirably trained and increased his patience. He further improved it through other hardships: fasting, enduring cold and nakedness, studying while standing, and going barefoot for many years. He never reduced these rigors and hardships, despite all the advice and persuasion of his friends who were troubled by his excessive severity. Through this lifestyle, however, he won people over and converted many of the Pagan <note>original: "Gentile"</note> philosophers—men famous for their learning—not only to admire him but to imitate him.

d Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, regarding Origen.

</margin>

XXV. When we view him in terms of his natural talents and acquired abilities, we see he had a quick, sharp understanding, a strong and faithful memory, an acute judgment, and a ready way of speaking. All of these were polished and perfected by a massive amount of learning and all the intellectual improvements that *Rome* or *Greece* could provide. He was incomparably skilled (as St. Jerome ᵈ and Suidas ᵉ observe) in both Pagan and Christian learning: *Logic*, *Geometry*, *Arithmetic*, *Music*, *Philosophy*, *Rhetoric*, and the various opinions of all the philosophical sects. He always provided his listeners with insights far above common observation. The force and sharpness of his mind were so great (says Vincent of Lérins ᶠ), and so profound, quick, and elegant, that no one could come near him. His stock of all kinds of learning was so vast that there were few corners of divine philosophy, and perhaps none of human philosophy,

There was no subject he had not thoroughly investigated. When the Greeks could lead him no further, he conquered the language and learning of the **Jews** with unparalleled industry. No better description of his character is needed than that given by <margin>Found in Eusebius, Book 6, Chapter 19, p. 220.</margin> <margin>Lucas Holstenius, *On the Life and Writings of Porphyry*, Chapter 6, p. 27.</margin> **Porphyry**, who knew him personally. (Although a certain learned man, based on a passage in **Eusebius**, mistakenly claims Porphyry was Origen's student, this is surely an error.) Porphyry, though an enemy of Christianity, granted that Origen was held in very high esteem in those times. He noted that Origen had earned more than ordinary glory and renown from the greatest masters Christianity then had in the world, and that under the discipline of **Ammonius**, he attained an admirable skill in learning and philosophy. 

The evidence of this skill (as Porphyry observes) was found in the books and writings Origen left behind. These were remarkable not only for their subject matter but for their sheer quantity. <margin>As cited above, p. 256; see also Rufinus, *Apology for Origen*, within the Works of Jerome, Vol. 4, p. 197.</margin> **Epiphanius** tells us it was commonly reported that Origen wrote six thousand volumes. Since the greatest part of these were likely letters and single homilies <note>short sermons or lectures</note>, this number is not unbelievable. It should not have given **Rufinus** and **St. Jerome** cause to argue so much about it—Jerome flatly denied that he had ever read that many, or that Origen had ever written them. <margin>In the place cited.</margin> **Vincentius** affirms that no man ever wrote as much as Origen did, and that it was impossible to even find all his books, let alone read them. 

For this reason, antiquity rightly gave him the title of <term>The Composer</term> <note>original: "Syntacticus"</note>, as his innumerable discourses on all sorts of subjects made that title appropriate. His books were categorized by many ancient writers into specific classes: *Scholia* (short notes on difficult passages), *Homilies*, and *Tomes* (as the ancients divided them); or *Exegetica* and *Syntagmata*, as some modern writers classify them. Although the greatest part of these works perished long ago through the carelessness or ill will of later generations, a very large portion still remains. 

His phrasing and way of writing is clear, unaffected, fluent, and rich. <margin>Assessment of Origen's Works.</margin> **Erasmus** gives high praise <note>original: "encomium"</note> to it, preferring it over most other writers of the Church. He notes that Origen’s style is not inflated and lofty like that of **St. Hilary**, which flies above the reach of ordinary readers; nor is it set off with flashy and forced ornaments like that of **St. Jerome**. It does not overflow with rhetorical flourishes and witty sentences like **St. Ambrose**, nor is it over-seasoned with sharp and satirical reflections and obscured by outdated terms like **Tertullian**. It is not excessively precise in its structure like **St. Gregory**, nor does it wander into large digressions or use rhythmic rhyming words like **St. Augustine**. Instead, Erasmus describes it as always brisk, lively, easy, and natural. 

However, when Erasmus commends Origen for being concise and brief, he likely forgot himself or was mistaken—which is unsurprising, as he probably judged Origen by translations rather than the original Greek. For while Origen's style is generally plain and clear, it is also expansive and lush, flowing with an abundance of words that could often be spared. Because of this, some of his critical adversaries charged him with "multiplying an infinite crowd of words" <margin>Epiphanius, *Letter to John of Jerusalem*, within the works of Jerome, Vol. 2, p. 158.</margin> <note>original Latin: "infinita verba multiplicare"</note>. They claimed that <margin>Eustathius of Antioch, *Dissertation on the Witch of Endor against Origen*, within the *Sacred Critics*, Vol. 8, columns 441, 453.</margin> "he filled the world with a vast abundance of useless empty talk" <note>original Greek: "kenologia perittois apeiroplethei to kosmo"</note> which he poured out immeasurably, and that "he repeated himself with much nonsense" <note>original Greek: "phlyaria polle tautologein"</note>, exceedingly trifling with vain...

For although he used many words, he was always recognized as eloquent. XXVI. But alas, that which has cast clouds and darkness upon all his glory, and buried much of his fame in disgrace and reproach, is the dangerous and unsound doctrines and principles scattered throughout his writings. Because of these, almost every age—without any respect for his talents, learning, piety, or the judgment of the wisest and best people of his own time—has mercilessly pronounced him a heretic. They have called his sentiments and speculations rash, absurd, harmful, blasphemous, and indeed, every other bad name. The alarm began long ago and was pursued with great outcry and intensity, especially by **Methodius**, Bishop of Olympus; **Eustathius** of Antioch; **Apollinaris**; **Theophilus** of Alexandria; and **Epiphanius**. This outcry continued loudly in later ages, so much so that even mentioning his name is considered disgusting in the Greek Church today. I had once resolved to consider the main ideas and principles for which Origen is so heavily accused by the ancients. However, I set aside that task when I found that the hard work of the learned **Monsieur Huet** in his *Origeniana* <note>original: *Origeniana*; a major scholarly work by Pierre-Daniel Huet, published in 1668, analyzing Origen's life and thought.</note> had left no room for anyone else to follow him. He has discussed and examined this matter so fully, clearly, and impartially, and with such an infinite variety of reading, that I refer the learned and capable reader to him. For those who cannot or will not take the trouble to read his large and excellent discourses, <margin>Published in London, 1661, in quarto.</margin> they may consult a more accessible source: the ingenious author of the *Letter of Resolution concerning Origen and the Chief of his Opinions*. There they will find his most objectionable tenets <note>original: *dogmata*</note> listed, along with the apologies and defenses that a sincere lover of Origen might be expected to make on his behalf. These pleas are presented with all the advantages that wit, reason, and eloquence could provide.

XXVII. Nor were there lacking in the past those who stood up to plead and defend his cause, especially **Pamphilus the Martyr** and **Eusebius**, who published an *Apology* in six books on his behalf. The first five of these were written by Pamphilus with Eusebius's assistance while they were in prison; the last was finished and added by Eusebius after Pamphilus's martyrdom. Besides these, $^a$ **Photius** tells us there were many other famous men in those times who wrote defenses for him. He gives us a specific account $^b$ of one—though without a name—where in five books the author endeavors to justify Origen as sound and orthodox. This author cites **Dionysius**, **Demetrius**, and **Clement**, all of **Alexandria**, and several others to give evidence for him. The majority of these defenses perished long ago; otherwise, Origen's cause might perhaps appear in a better light. As it stands, we now have nothing but his ideas dressed up and explained by his self-professed enemies, and many things are attributed to him that he never actually claimed but were instead invented by his so-called followers. For my own part, I shall only note some general remarks from the ancient writers which may be argued to soften the rigor and severity of the sentence usually passed against him. First, many things were said and written by him not as positive and established doctrine, but **for the sake of intellectual exercise** <note>original: γυμνασίας χάριν (gymnasias charin)</note>, says the $^e$ author of his defense in Photius; by way of practice and experimentation.

his own position; and this he himself was accustomed to plead at every turn. He would beg the reader’s pardon and declare that he proposed these things not as established doctrines, but as disputable problems, with the goal of searching for and finding the truth. **Pamphilus** assures us of this, and **St. Jerome** himself cannot help but admit it. Even if we had the testimony of neither man, there is enough evidence for this purpose in his books still in existence to place it beyond any fair objection. 

Thus, when discussing the union of the two natures in the person of our blessed Savior, he affirms it to be a mystery that no created understanding can sufficiently explain. Concerning this, he says, "Not from any rashness of ours, but only as the order of discussion requires, we shall briefly speak rather of what our faith contains than what human reason is accustomed to assert, producing our own conjectures rather than any plain and absolute affirmations." He expresses himself to the same purpose at every opportunity. This is not even to mention that he wrote many things in the heat of a dispute, which his calmer and more thoughtful reflections might have corrected. 

So the author of the *Apology* in **Photius** pleads that whatever he said wrongly regarding the doctrine of the **Trinity** proceeded merely from a forceful opposition to the **Sabellians** <note>The Sabellians were followers of a 3rd-century heresy that taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons, but merely different "modes" or masks of a single person.</note>, who confused the number and difference of the divine persons, and whose sect was one of the most widespread heresies of that time. His attempt to refute them led him to argue for a greater difference and distinction between the persons of the Trinity than the rules of faith strictly allowed. 

*Secondly*, those books of his that reveal the most unsound and unjustifiable notions were written privately. He had no intention of making them public; they were meant as secrets shared among friends, not as doctrines to disturb the Church. He freely acknowledged this in his letter to **Fabian**, Bishop of Rome, and blamed his friend **Ambrosius** "because he made public those things that were meant to be kept secret" <note>original: *quod secretò edita in publicum protulerit*</note>, intending them to go no further than the hearts or hands of his dearest friends. A greater freedom and latitude is always allowed when debating things among friends, and those secrets should not be disclosed, nor should the public be made judges of the innocent liberty taken within a person's private walls. 

*Thirdly*, the controversial opinions he maintains are often those that were not yet the established and Catholic doctrines of the Church. They had not been defined by Church Synods nor debated by theologians, but were either philosophical ideas or speculations that had not been considered before. He himself carefully distinguishes these at every turn from those propositions that were accepted by the common and current consent and approval of the Christian Church. I am certain that he establishes it as a fundamental rule in the very beginning of that book containing his most dangerous assertions: that those Church doctrines must be preserved which had been delivered in succession from the Apostles and were then received, and that nothing was to be accepted as truth that differed in any way from the tradition of the Church.

He notes that at the request of his brothers in the faith, he had written several Epistles, but that the "apostles and emissaries of the Devil" had filled them with weeds and tares <note>A biblical reference to the Parable of the Tares (Matthew 13:24-30), meaning the insertion of false or corrupting ideas.</note>, removing some things and adding others. The author of the *Apology* mentioned in **Photius** tells us that **Origen** himself complained of this during his lifetime. Indeed, he does so in his letter to the people of Alexandria, where he sharply resents the charge of blasphemy that had been attributed to him and his doctrine—of which he was never guilty. He writes that it was no wonder if his teachings were corrupted, when even the great **St. Paul** could not escape such treatment. He tells them of a prominent heretic who, having taken a copy of a debate he had held with **Origen**, later removed and added whatever he pleased, changing it into something else entirely while carrying it around and boasting of it. When some friends in Palestine sent this version to **Origen** while he was in Athens, he returned a true and authentic copy to them. He informs them that he had met with the same foul play in other places, such as Ephesus and Antioch, as he recounts in detail. If they dared to do this while he was still alive and able to defend himself (as he did), what might we think they would do after his death, when there was no one to challenge them? On this basis, most of those assertions where **Origen** is made to contradict himself must be dismissed. As **Rufinus** rightly argues, it is highly improbable that so prudent and learned a person—someone far from being a fool or a madman—should write things so contrary and repugnant to one another, not only in different books but within the very same volume.

XXIX. I might further observe his constant zeal against heretics: his opposing and refuting them wherever he went, both in speech and writing; his being sent for by foreign countries to convince those who argued against the faith; his profession of hating all heretical doctrines; and his refusal to even take part in prayer with **Paul the Heretic** of Antioch, even though his entire livelihood depended on it. It also deserves to be considered that **Athanasius**—who, during the heat of the Arian controversies <note>A major 4th-century theological dispute over the nature of Jesus Christ's divinity.</note>, was perhaps the most diligent in searching out heretical persons and opinions, and the most accurate in examining and refuting the very doctrines now blamed on **Origen**—never once charged him with heresy. On the contrary, **Athanasius** specifically quotes him to prove our Lord's co-eternity and co-essentiality <note>The doctrine that Jesus is of the same substance and eternal nature as God the Father.</note> with the Father, exactly according to the decisions of the Council of Nicaea. He dismisses him with the honorable description of *thaumasios kai philoponōtatos* <note>original: θαυμασὸς & φιλοπονώτατος</note>, meaning "the most admirable and infinitely industrious person." Nor is there any unorthodox opinion of his, that I know of, mentioned in all of **Athanasius's** works, except for the one concerning the duration of future torments, and even that is only mentioned indirectly. From this, I am inclined to conclude either that **Origen's** writings were not then so notoriously full of errors, or that this great man and zealous defender of the Church's doctrine (who, as Bishop of Alexandria, could not have been ignorant of what **Origen** taught or wrote, and indeed assures us he had read his books) did not believe those dangerous ideas in the texts represented **Origen's** true views. Indeed, he says expressly that the things **Origen** wrote for the sake of controversy and debate are not to be looked upon as his own definitive words and...

And if, as some would have it, they were his own sentiments, we ought rather to deal compassionately with so learned a man, who has conveyed such a vast treasury of learning to us. Whatever faults there are in his writings, those orthodox and useful things which they contain are more than sufficient to outweigh them."

XXX. This and a great deal more is, and may be, pleaded in **Origen's** defense. And yet, after all, it must be confessed that he was guilty of great mistakes and rash propositions, which the largest charity cannot excuse. He had a natural warmth and fervor of mind, a comprehensive wit, an insatiable thirst for knowledge, and a desire to understand the most abstruse and mysterious speculations of theology. This led him to give himself unbounded liberty in inquiring into and discussing the nature of things. He wrote much and dictated quickly, and was engaged in an infinite variety of business, which seldom gave him leisure to review and correct his writings, or to let them pass the scrutiny of second and more mature thoughts. He was well-versed in the writings of the pagans and was intensely concerned with making the doctrines of Christianity seem as similar as possible to their best and most beloved notions. And certainly, what **Marcellus**, Bishop of **Ancyra**, long ago objected against him is unquestionably true (notwithstanding what **Eusebius** said to soften it): that coming fresh out of the schools of philosophy, and having been accurately trained for a long time in the principles and books of **Plato**, he applied himself to divine things before he was sufficiently prepared to receive them. He began writing about them while secular learning still held the primary place in his mind, and so he unwarily mingled philosophic notions with Christian principles further than the core of the Christian faith would allow. And I do not doubt that whoever compares his and the **Platonic** principles would find that most of the <term>κυρίαι δόξαι <note>original: "kyriai doxai", meaning principal doctrines or authoritative tenets</note></term> he is charged with—his master-notions—were brought out of the school of **Plato**, as the aforementioned **Huetius** has specifically observed in many instances. **St. Jerome** himself (whom the trends of that time made a severe enemy to **Origen**) could not help but have some tenderness for him, even in the very tract where he passes

I. <image-desc>Decorative drop-cap letter S with floral and scroll-work motifs.</image-desc> So great and general is the silence of the early Church regarding the life of this holy martyr—especially the former part of his life—that I would pass over him entirely if his later years did not provide us with several memorable passages concerning him. His country, parents, education, and way of life are all unknown; it is also unknown whether he was born and raised as a pagan <note>original: "Gentile"</note> or a Christian. No doubt he was trained with the advantages of a liberal and noble education, living in places that provided such opportunities and in times when only men of known talent and eminence in both learning and piety were promoted to the government of the Church. During this era, high levels of art and learning were not only commendable but necessary: both to nourish and preserve the flock of God, to resist and convince opponents, and to defend Christianity against the attacks of both secret and open enemies. For just as the Christian Church never lacked declared adversaries from the outside who endeavored by both sword and pen to stifle its growth, it also faced pretended friends from within who disturbed its peace and tore at its very core through schisms and heresies; these were never more prevalent than in those times and parts of the world where this good man lived.

</margin> says of him) guided the holy vessel of that church through storms, tempests, and the many waves that crashed against it. Indeed, in the beginning of his leadership over that church, he did not face much trouble from the Roman powers—the old enemies of Christianity—but a fierce storm blew from another direction.
<margin>

<margin>The same source, chapter 27, page 670 <note>Refers to a historical account of the Roman-Persian wars</note></margin>
His conquests struck such dread into all regions that the terror of them reached even *Italy* and startled the people in *Rome* itself. He severely oppressed the people of *Antioch*; it is not difficult to imagine what kind of treatment the Christians there must have received under such a merciless and arrogant enemy, who was never favorable to them at any time. But it was not long before God lifted this burden from their necks. For Emperor *Gordian*, having raised a powerful army, marched into the *East*. After clearing the territories as he advanced, he arrived in *Syria* and went directly to *Antioch*. There, he completely defeated the *Persian* army, recovered *Antioch* and the conquered cities, and captured several significant strongholds belonging to *Sapor*, whom he forced to retreat back to his own country. Gordian gave an account of all these events in a letter to the Senate, who joyfully received the news and decreed a triumph in his honor upon his return to *Rome*.

III. The Church of *Antioch* being thus restored to its former peace, *Babylas* oversaw his duties with great diligence and faithfulness. He instructed, nurtured, and governed his flock, preparing both young and old to endure the severest trials that their religion might expose them to, as if he had specifically foreseen the dark and gloomy persecution that was soon to overtake them. 

<margin>ª Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 6, chapter 39, page 234.</margin>
<margin>ᵇ Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Life of Gregory Thaumaturgus*, page 999, Volume 2.</margin>
<margin>ᶜ Cyprian, *Epistle 7*, page 16.</margin>
Having quietly lived through the reign of *Philip* <note>Philip the Arab, reigned 244–249 AD</note>—who was so far from causing any trouble for the Christians that he is generally, though likely without evidence, thought to have been a Christian himself—he entered the turbulent and stormy times of *Decius*. Decius was unexpectedly promoted and essentially forced into the role of Emperor. He was a man whose character might have been considered among the better princes had he not permanently stained his memory with his excessive violence toward the Christians. 

The primary cause of this violence, according to most writers following the suggestion of *Eusebius* ª, was his hatred for his predecessor, *Philip*. Since Philip was considered a Christian (in their view), Decius resolved to punish the Christians out of spite and malice toward him. However, the account given by *Gregory of Nyssa* ᵇ seems much more likely: it was the widespread and triumphant dominance of the Christian faith. Christianity had spread everywhere, taking root in every corner and filling not only the cities but also the rural villages. Pagan temples were abandoned while churches were crowded; altars were toppled and sacrifices were cast aside. 

This enormous growth of Christianity and the great decline of paganism provoked *Decius* to take notice. He was frustrated to see the religion of the Empire being trampled upon and the worship of the gods everywhere slighted and neglected—opposed and undermined by a new and rising sect of Christians that multiplied daily. This made him resolve to use all possible force to restrain and control this expanding group. He attempted through methods of cruelty to weary Christians into abandoning their faith and to bring the people back to the religion of their ancestors. Consequently, he issued edicts to the provincial governors, strictly ordering them to act with total severity against Christians and to spare no form of torture unless they returned to the obedience and worship of the pagan gods. 

Although I do not doubt that this was the primary cause that triggered their enemies' rage and malice, *Cyprian* ᶜ—like a man of great piety and humility—looks for a cause closer to home. He honestly admits that their own sins had opened the floodgates for God's displeasure to break in upon them, while

# The Life of Saint Babylas.

Pride, self-seeking, schism, and factionalism reigned so much among them—even among the martyrs themselves, who should have been a good example to others—that they cast off the order and discipline of the Church. Being swollen with such vain and immoderate pride, it was time for God to send them a "thorn in the flesh" <note>A biblical reference to a source of suffering or trial intended to humble someone</note> to cure it.

<margin>* Chrysostom, *Book on Saint Babylas*, Volume 6, page 658 and throughout. Philostorgius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 7, chapter 8, page 94. Suidas, under the word "Babylas." Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 10, chapter 28, page 63.</margin>

IV. The provincial governors, eager enough to act on their own in such a matter, made even more haste when they were not only encouraged but threatened by imperial edicts. Thus, the persecution was carried out in all parts with a swift and heavy hand. We shall speak more elsewhere concerning its severity; at present, it is enough to note that it swept away many of the most eminent bishops of the Church, including **Fabian**, Bishop of **Rome**, **Alexander**, Bishop of **Jerusalem**, and several others.

It was not long before it reached **Saint Babylas’s** door. For **Decius**, probably around the middle of his reign or some time before his **Thracian** expedition (in which he lost his life), came into **Syria** and then to **Antioch** to manage his affairs regarding the **Persian War**. I admit his arrival in these parts is not mentioned in the **Roman** histories; this is no surprise, as the accounts of his life were either not written by the authors of the *Augustan History* <note>original: *Historiæ Augustæ Scriptores*</note>, or if they were, they have long since perished, and few of his deeds are noted by the historians who remain. However, the event is clearly enough acknowledged by ecclesiastical writers.

While he stayed here, either out of curiosity or a plan to find some more plausible excuse to attack them, he insisted on going into the Christian congregation when the public assembly had met together. **Babylas** would by no means allow this. Standing in the church porch with undaunted courage and resolution, he opposed him, telling him that, as much as lay in his power, he would never allow a wolf to break into Christ's sheepfold. The Emperor did not push the matter further at the time, either being unwilling to provoke the rage and fury of the people, or planning to achieve his goal another way. 

There are some writers, including **Nicephorus** (with whom the *Menaion* and *Menologies* <note>Liturgical books used in the Eastern Orthodox Church containing lives of the saints</note> of the **Greek Church** exactly agree), who attribute this passage not to **Decius**, but to **Numerianus** (whom **Suidas's** translator incorrectly calls **Marianus**), who reigned at least thirty years later. This is a mistake without any basis or truth to support it, as there was no **Babylas** serving as Bishop of **Antioch** at that time; all agree that he suffered under the Decian persecution.

<margin>a For the year 253, number 126. See Symeon Metaphrastes in *The Martyrdom of Saint Isidore*, in Surius, February 5th, page 48.</margin>

And it is not improbable, as **Baronius** ᵃ conjectures, that the mistake might have first arisen because there was a man named **Numerius** under **Decius**. He was one of the generals of the army and a violent persecutor of the Christians. It is likely that the first people to misreport the story confused him with **Numerianus** and applied to the latter what actually concerned the Emperor under whom he served.

This was probably either the son of some minor prince in those parts who entered into a league with him while he was at **Antioch**, or some young prince of **Persia**, given as a pledge to ensure the peace between those two crowns. No sooner had the Emperor received him than he inhumanely butchered him, either to gratify his own cruelty or by pretending some fraud in the articles of the treaty. 

The author of the <margin>b</margin> *Alexandrian Chronicle* <note>A 7th-century Byzantine world chronicle</note> tells us—and cites **Leontius**, Bishop of **Antioch**, as his source—that **Philip** (in the Greek text, "the Junior" <note>original: ὁ Ἰουνίωρ</note> is added, likely a mistake for "the Julius" <note>original: ὁ Ἰούλιος</note>, the surname of that Emperor, and not "Junior," the Younger, as the translator renders it and elsewhere corrects as "the Elder" <note>original: Πρεσβύτερος</note>) was Governor of a province during the reign of **Gordian**. **Gordian** had committed the care of his young son to him, whom he slew after the father's death to usurp the Empire. 

The author claims that despite being a Christian, Saint **Babylas** would not admit him or his wife into the Church because he was guilty of murder. He suggests that **Decius** later put Saint **Babylas** to death because of this affront offered to such great persons, and not merely because he was a Christian himself. This is a strange medley of true and false information, as it is indeed the custom of that author to confuse times, events, and people. However, it is most evident from **Chrysostom** that it was the same Emperor who murdered this young prince and put Saint **Babylas** to death, who could be no other than **Decius**. With hands still reeking with the blood of the innocent, he would have irreverently rushed into the holy place of the Christian sanctuary, where only pure hands are lifted up to Heaven.

VI. **DECIUS**, although he <margin>c</margin> hid his anger for the time being and went away, inwardly resented the affront. Having returned to the palace, he sent for **Babylas**. After sharply reprimanding him for his boldness and the insolence of his actions, he commanded him to offer sacrifice to the gods, assuring him that this was the only way to atone for his crime, avoid punishment, and earn honor and renown. 

The Martyr answered all his inquiries with a generous confidence; he despised the Emperor's offers and defied his threats. He told him that regarding the offense he was charged with, he was obliged as a Pastor to do whatever benefited his flock. As for the command to sacrifice, he was resolved never to abandon the service of the true God to sacrifice to devils and those who falsely usurped the name and honor of deities. 

Finding his resolutions firm and inflexible, the Emperor <margin>d</margin> ordered that chains and fetters be clapped upon him. He was sent to prison, where he endured many severe hardships and sufferings. Yet he rejoiced in his bonds and was more troubled by the misery awaiting the man who sent him there than by the weight of his own chains or the sharpness of those torments

VII. There is some slight difference in the accounts of the ancient writers regarding the manner of his martyrdom. <margin>a</margin> **Eusebius** and some others state that after a famous confession of faith, he died in prison; while <margin>b</margin> **Chrysostom** (whom I am more inclined to believe in this matter, as he was better able to know the traditions and examine the records of that church) and **Suidas** affirm that, being bound, he was led out of prison to undergo his martyrdom. The former plainly implies and the latter positively states that he was beheaded. Once the fatal sentence was passed, as he was led to execution, he began his song of triumph: *Return to your rest, O my soul, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with me.* <note>Psalm 116:7</note> Along with him were led three youths, who were brothers. The *Roman Martyrology* <margin>*</margin> tells us their names were **Urbanus**, **Prilidianus**, and **Epolonius**. He had carefully instructed them in the faith and had trained them for such a severe trial. The Emperor, hoping to overcome them due to their young age, had taken them from their tutor and treated them with all kinds of hardship and cruelty, thinking these methods most likely to make an impression on weak and fearful minds. 

But perceiving them to be immovably determined not to offer sacrifices to idols, he commanded that they also be beheaded. Upon arriving at the place of execution, **Babylas** placed the children first, giving them the priority of martyrdom, lest the sight of his own bloody fate might weaken their resolve and cause them to abandon their post. As the officer was beheading them, he cried aloud, *Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me;* <note>Isaiah 8:18; Hebrews 2:13</note> and after that, he laid his own neck upon the block. He had already <margin>c</margin> given orders to his friends, to whom he had entrusted the care of his body, that his chains and fetters should be buried in the same grave with him. He wanted them to remain there as banners <note>original: "Ensigns"</note> of honor and badges of his suffering, and as evidence of how much he considered those things that seem most shameful among men to be, for Christ’s sake, most splendid and honorable. In this, he imitated the great **Saint Paul**, who took pleasure in bonds, chains, imprisonments, and reproaches, professing to rejoice and glory in nothing so much as in his sufferings and in the cross of Christ. Accordingly, his chains were buried with him in the grave, where **Chrysostom** assures us they remained in his own time.

<margin>a. Chrysostom, ibid., page 671. Sozomen, book 6, chapter 19, page 625. Nicephorus, book 10, chapter 28, page 61.</margin>

VIII. We are not told where his body was first buried; but wherever it was, it rested there until the reign of **Constantius**, when it was given a more magnificent burial. This event led to one of the most remarkable occurrences that church history has passed down to us. <margin>a</margin> There was a place in the suburbs of **Antioch** called **Daphne**, a place that seemed naturally designed to be a supreme setting for pleasure and delight. It was a beautiful grove, densely planted with cypress and other trees which provided all kinds of fruits and flowers according to the season. It was furnished with an infinite variety of shady walks where the trees, joining their leafy tops, blocked the sun from annoying or scorching those below. It was watered by many crystal fountains and pleasant streams; the air was cool and mild, and the wind playing through the branches of the trees added a natural harmony and a delightful murmur. It was the usual setting for the amorous and lustful fantasies of the poets, and indeed, it was so great a temptation to in-

IX. It seems the Devil did not like having him as such a close neighbor, as his presence struck the demon dumb, so that from then on, not a single syllable of an oracle was delivered. At first, this silence was ᵃ viewed merely as the result of neglect—that the sullen demon would not answer because he did not receive his usual tribute of sacrifices, incense, and other ritual honors. However, it was later discovered to be caused by the proximity of *Saint Babylas's* ashes, which led to their second removal on the following occasion. After Julian succeeded Constantius as Emperor, he came to Antioch for his expedition into Persia. Being excessively consumed by superstition, he immediately went to Apollo's Temple to consult ᵇ the Oracle about the success of the war and other important affairs of the Empire, offering the finest sacrifices and making very rich and costly presents. But alas, it was all in vain; his prayers, gifts, and sacrifices achieved nothing. The demon gave him to understand that the "dead" kept him from speaking, and that until the place was cleared of the corpse <note>original: "Corps"</note> that lay nearby, he could provide no answers through the Oracle. Julian quickly understood his meaning; although many dead bodies had been buried there, he suspected it was *Babylas's* remains that were specifically being targeted, and therefore he commanded the Christians to remove them from the site. The Christians then assembled in massive numbers—people of all ages and sexes—and, placing the coffin upon an open chariot, brought it into the city in a solemn triumph. They sang psalms of joy the entire way, and at the end of every verse, they added this sharp, stinging line: *Shamed be all those who worship carved images.* <note>Psalm 97:7</note>

Such miserable fates had overtaken some of his predecessors at the height of their actions against the Christians, and he had recently seen sad examples of it very close to home. His uncle, Julian, Governor <note>original: *Præfect*</note> of the East—an arrogant mocker and an apostate who ridiculed Christians—had broken into the great church at Antioch and treated their communion vessels <note>original: *Plate*</note> with the greatest irreverence and contempt, throwing them upon the ground, kicking them, and sitting upon them. After finally carrying them away into the Emperor's treasury <note>original: *Exchequer*</note>, he was immediately seized with a repulsive disease (which I am not willing to describe) which, within a few days, despite all the skills of medicine, put an end to his miserable life. And Felix the Treasurer, a man of the same spirit and temperament and involved with him in the same plan, fell down suddenly upon the top of the steps while coming up to the Palace and burst open. Ammianus Marcellinus himself <note>A pagan Roman historian known for his relatively objective accounts.</note> confessed that he died of a sudden hemorrhage <note>original: *Flux of blood*</note>. There were others who, about that time, came to wretched and untimely ends, but these two only are specifically noted by Chrysostom. These were examples which probably placed Julian under a sense of awe and restraint.

XI. But *evil men grow worse and worse*. Julian, however much he was awed for the moment, soon found a vent for his rage which all his philosophy could not stop. Annoyed to see the Christians pay such solemn reverence to the Martyr, and especially stung by the hymns which the Christians sang, the very next day he gave orders—against the advice of his Privy Council—to Sallust the Prefect to persecute the Christians. Many were accordingly arrested and thrown into prison. Among the rest, one Theodore, a young man, was seized in the streets and put upon the rack. His flesh was torn off with iron pincers, and he was scourged and beaten. When no tortures could shake his constancy or even move his patience, he was at length dismissed. Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus, a monk and historian.</note> later met this Theodore and asked him whether he felt any pain in the midst of his torments. He replied that at first he felt a little, but then someone in the shape of a young man stood by him, who gently wiped off the sweat...

XII. HEAVEN showed that it was not well pleased with the Emperor’s actions. Immediately, the Temple of *Apollo* in *Daphne* caught fire, which in a few hours burned the famous image of the god and reduced the temple—excepting only the walls and pillars—to ashes. The Christians attributed this to divine vengeance, while the *Gentiles* <note>meaning: pagans or non-Christians</note> blamed it on the malice of the Christians. Although the priests and guards of the temple were tortured on the rack to force them to say so, they could not be brought to claim anything more than that it was set on fire by a light from heaven.

This great fire is mentioned not only by Christian writers, but also by <margin>a. Ammianus Marcellinus, *History*, Book 22, page 1629.</margin> *Ammianus Marcellinus* and by <margin>b. In the place cited above.</margin> *Julian* himself. It is discussed especially by *Libanius* the Orator, who, in a speech specifically made to the people, elegantly mourns its unhappy fate. Saint *Chrysostom* <note>John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople and a famous preacher.</note> challenges this speech and makes witty and eloquent remarks about it.

If the reader asks what became of *Babylas's* <note>original: "Babylas his"</note> remains after all this noise and bustle, they were entombed within the city in a church dedicated to his name and memory. In later ages, <margin>c. See Bollandus, *Acta Sanctorum*, January 24, page 580.</margin> they are said to have been moved <note>term: translated (the formal religious term for moving a saint's remains from one location to another)</note> by certain Christian princes—likely during their wars in the Holy Land—to *Cremona* in *Italy*. There, those who are curious about such things may investigate how often the remains have been honorably placed, and with how much pomp and ceremonial veneration they are still kept.

THASCIUS Caecilius Cyprian was born at Carthage in the latter part of the previous century <note>original: "Sæculum"</note>, though the particular year cannot be determined with certainty. Who or what his parents were is unknown. Cardinal Baronius (not to mention others) claims he was descended from a wealthy and honorable family, and was himself one of the leading members of the Senatorial Order; he bases this on the authority of Gregory of Nazianzus <note>original: "Nazianzen"</note>, who indeed affirms it. However, Gregory surely forgot that just a few lines earlier he had dismissed as a mythical error the confusion of our Cyprian with another man of the same name, to whom Gregory’s description unquestionably applied. For besides our Cyprian of Carthage, there was another born at Antioch—a person of great learning and prominence who traveled through Greece, Phrygia, Egypt, India, Chaldea, and many other places. This other Cyprian was famous for the study and arts of magic, through which he sought to win the affections of Justina, a noble Christian virgin at Antioch. Through her prayers and efforts, he was converted and baptized, serving first as a sacristan <note>original: "Sexton"</note> and then as a deacon of that church. He was endowed with miraculous powers and afterwards consecrated as Bishop of that church (though I must admit I do not find his name in the catalog of the bishops of that See drawn up by Nicephorus of Constantinople).

The history of all this was largely described in three books of verse written by the noble Empress *Eudocia*; the excerpts <note>original: *excerpta*</note> of which are still extant in ^a *Photius*. This account *Simeon Metaphrastes*, *Nicephorus*, and the later *Greeks* unhesitatingly attribute to Saint *Cyprian* of *Carthage*; indeed, some of them even claim he suffered martyrdom under the *Decian* Persecution. Though the mistake is more pardonable because not only *Prudentius*, but Gregory of Nazianzus <note>original: *Nazianzen*</note> had long before clearly confused these two eminent persons. Finding several passages in the life of the *Antiochian Cyprian* very similar to the other, they attributed the rest of the story to him as well, just as two people who look alike are often mistaken for one another. To prove that our *Cyprian* was not the one described by *Nazianzus* would be a pointless and unnecessary attempt; the accounts concerning them are so vastly different regarding their country, education, manner of life, episcopal duties, and the time, place, and companions of their deaths, that it is plainly impossible to reconcile them. But enough of this.

II. SAINT CYPRIAN’S education was liberal <note>original: "ingenuous"; meaning noble or befitting a free-born person</note> ^b, polished by study and the liberal arts, though he mainly devoted himself to the study of oratory and eloquence. In these fields, he made such vast improvements that he taught rhetoric at *Carthage* ^c publicly and with great applause. During all this time, he lived in great pomp and plenty, in honor and power; his clothing was magnificent and his staff of servants was stately. He never went abroad (as he himself tells us ^d) without being thronged by a crowd of clients and followers. He passed the far greatest part of his life among the errors of paganism <note>original: "the Gentile Religion"</note>, and was nearly an old man when he was rescued from the enslavement of long-held customs, the darkness of idolatry, and the errors and vices of his past life, as he himself ^e suggests in his epistle to *Donatus*. He was converted to Christianity by the arguments and persistence of *Caecilius* ^f, a priest <note>original: "Presbyter"</note> of *Carthage*, a person whom he ever after loved as a friend and revered as a father. There was such a mutual affection between them that *Cyprian*, in honor of him, assumed the name of *Caecilius*; and the latter, at his death, made Cyprian his executor and committed his wife and children to his sole care and guardianship. While still a student of the faith <note>original: "Catechumen"</note> ^g, he gave early examples of a great and generous piety. He practiced a strict and severe temperance and sobriety, considering it one of the best preparations for receiving the truth to subdue and trample down all irregular appetites and inclinations. He sold his estate, or at least the greatest part of it, and distributed the proceeds among the poor in their need. In doing so, he triumphed over the love of the world while practicing that great duty of mercy and charity, which God values above all the ritual devotions in the world. Thus, by the speedy progress of his piety (says his friend and deacon, Pontius), he became almost a perfect Christian before he had even learned the rules of Christianity.

<margin>h Epistle 1, pages 2, 3.</margin>

### IV.
The beginning of his care and leadership was calm and peaceable, but he had not been in office long before a storm overtook him. For what reason I do not know, he was publicly outlawed <note>original: proscribed</note> ᵉ by the name of *Caecilius Cyprian, Bishop of the Christians*, and every man was commanded not to hide or conceal his property. Not satisfied with this, the crowds frequently called out for him to be thrown to the lions. Being warned by a divine sign and a command from God (as he pleads for himself ᶠ), and lest by his resolute defiance of the public sentence he should provoke his enemies ᵍ to attack the whole Church more severely, he thought it best to withdraw himself for the time. He hoped that their malice would cool and die away, and the fire would go out once the fuel that kindled it was removed. During this retreat, though absent in person, he was present in spirit, making up for his absence through letters (of which he wrote no fewer than thirty-eight), pious advice, serious warnings, frequent corrections, earnest encouragements, and especially by hearty prayers to Heaven for the welfare and prosperity of the Church. The matter that caused him the greatest trouble was the case of the *lapsed* <note>The "lapsed" (lapsi) were Christians who had renounced their faith or performed pagan sacrifices to avoid persecution and later sought readmission to the Church.</note>, whom some priests <note>original: Presbyters</note>, without the knowledge and consent of the Bishop, hastily readmitted to the communion of the Church on very easy terms. Cyprian, a firm defender of church discipline and the rights of his office, would not tolerate this; through several letters, he not only complained about it but also worked to correct it,
