V. This laxity in discipline and the easy admission of penitents gave Novatus, one of the priests <note>original: "Presbyters"</note> of Carthage, an opportunity to break away and draw a faction after him. He denied any place in the peace and communion of the Church to the lapsed, even if they were penitent. This was not because they absolutely excluded the mercy and pardon of God—for they left such people to the judgment of the divine tribunal—but they maintained that the Church had no power to absolve those who had once lapsed after baptism and to receive them back into communion. 

After he had sufficiently embroiled the Church at home (where he was in danger of being excommunicated by Cyprian for his scandalous, irregular, and unpeaceable practices), Novatus traveled to Rome with some of his party. There, by pretending to have uncommon sanctity and severity, and with the help of some confessors lately delivered from prison, he seduced Novatianus—a man who is almost constantly confused with Novatus by the Greek Fathers. Novatianus was a priest of the Roman Church with an insolent and ambitious temper who had already attempted to seize the bishop’s chair <note>original: "that Chair"; referring to the papacy or bishopric of Rome</note> for himself. Through secret arts and uncanonical means, the party arranged for him to be consecrated as a bishop. They then set him up against Cornelius, who had recently been ordained Bishop of Rome. 

They specifically charged Cornelius with holding communion with Trophimus and others of the <term>Thurificati</term> <note>original: "Thurificati"; those who had escaped death by offering incense to Roman idols</note> who had performed sacrifices during the late persecution. Although this was a plausible accusation, it was a false allegation; Trophimus and his party were not taken back in until they had given satisfaction to the Church through great humility ᵇ and public penance. Even then, Trophimus was not allowed to serve in any role other than as a layperson.

Being disappointed in their designs, they now openly showed their true colors and separated from the Church. They charged the Church with laxness and licentiousness for admitting scandalous offenders. By way of distinction, they called themselves the <term>Cathari</term> <note>original: "Cathari"; from the Greek for "The Pure"</note>, the pure and undefiled party, who kept themselves from all society with the lapsed or those who communicated with them. Consequently, they were opposed on all sides by individuals, condemned by public synods, and denounced by the common vote of the Church. This opposition was probably not so much because of their different opinions regarding the pardon of sin and ecclesiastical penance—where they were not at a very great distance from the doctrine and practice of the early ages of the Church—but rather for their insolent and domineering temper. They were hated for their proud and surly behavior, their rigorous and imperious way of imposing their methods on other churches, and for taking it upon themselves, by their own private authority, to judge and condemn those who did not join or who opposed them. Most importantly, they were condemned for boldly stripping the governors of the Church of the great power lodged in them to forgive crimes upon repentance, which seems to have been the very soul and spirit of the Novatian sect.

<meta>This page continues the biography of Saint Cyprian, describing the extreme tortures faced by the martyrs during the Decian persecution and Cyprian's eventual return to Carthage to address Church divisions and the treatment of the "lapsed" Christians.</meta>

### The Life of St. Cyprian

The instruments of torment were often used on one man all at once, so that there were more tortures than there were limbs and members of his body. They were spoiled and plundered, chained and imprisoned, thrown to wild beasts, and burned at the stake. When the persecutors had exhausted all their old methods of execution, they studied to find more, for "an ingenious cruelty devises new punishments," <note>original: "excogitat novas pænas ingenioſa crudelitas"</note> as he complains. Nor did they only vary the torments, but repeated them; where one ended, another began. They tortured them without any hope of dying and added this cruelty to all the rest: they stopped them on their journey to heaven. Many who were desperately desirous of death were tortured in such a way that they might not die; they were purposely kept upon the rack so that they might die piece by piece, ensuring their pains were lingering and their sensation of them was without any break. They gave them no intervals or times of respite, unless any of them happened to escape their hands and expire in the midst of the torments.

All of this only served to make their faith and patience more illustrious and make them long for heaven even more earnestly. They tired out their tormentors and overcame the sharpest engines of execution; they smiled at the busy officers who were poking into their wounds. Even when their flesh was weary, their faith was unconquerable. The multitude watched these heavenly conflicts with admiration and stood astonished to hear the servants of Christ—in the midst of all this and with an unshaken mind—making a free and bold confession of him. They were destitute of any external help but armed with a divine power, defending themselves with the shield of faith.

<margin>
a To Cornelius, Letter 41, page 55.
b To Antonian, Letter 52, page 67.
</margin>

VII. St. Cyprian had remained in his retirement for two full years when the persecution eased somewhat due to the death of the Emperor Decius. He returned to Carthage in the year 251 AD, where he set himself to reform disorders and to settle the differences that disturbed his Church. For this purpose, he convened a synod <term>synod: a council of church leaders convened to decide on points of doctrine or discipline</term> of his neighboring bishops to consult about the case of the **lapsed** <note>original: "lapſed"; Christians who had renounced their faith or performed pagan sacrifices under the threat of death or torture</note>. 

As soon as they had met, messengers arrived with letters from Novatian, announcing his ordination to the See of Rome <term>See of Rome: the jurisdiction and office of the Bishop of Rome (the Pope)</term> and bringing an accusation and charge against Cornelius. However, as soon as these men appeared, they were disowned and rejected from communion, especially after Pompeius and Stephanus arrived from Rome and brought a true account and report of the case. The synod, therefore, advised and charged them to stop their turbulent and schismatic proceedings and not to tear the Church apart by spreading a harmful faction. They told them that their best and safest course of action was to show themselves to be true Christians by returning to the peace of the Church. 

As for the lapsed, having discussed their case according to the rules of the Holy Scripture, the synod concluded upon this wise and moderate solution: that they should not be denied all hope of peace and communion, lest—viewing themselves as being in a desperate case—they should fall back into a total apostasy from the faith. Yet, the censures of the Church should not be so relaxed as to rashly admit them to communion. Instead, each case would be examined, taking into account the will of the offenders and the severity of particular cases. Their time of penance would be accordingly prolonged, and divine mercy would be sought through acts of great sorrow and repentance. Their meaning was that the lapsed, being of several types, should be treated according to the nature of their crimes. The **Libellatici** <term>Libellatici: Christians who had not actually sacrificed to idols but had purchased "libels" (certificates) from Roman officials to falsely state they had complied with the law</term>, who had only purchased certificates of security and dismissal from the heathen magistrate to excuse them from performing sacrifices in times of persecution, should

This synodical decision was immediately sent to Rome and ratified by Cornelius and a council of sixty bishops, along with more than sixty priests <term>original: "Presbyters"</term> and deacons. The decree was examined, agreed upon, and published by the bishops in their various provinces. VIII. The next year, on May 15, 252 AD, another council began at Carthage about this matter. In this council, they followed the same course they had taken before, though they were more inclined toward moderate advice because they were frequently warned by divine revelations of an approaching persecution. Therefore, they did not think it wise or reasonable that men should be left vulnerable and unarmed in the day of battle. Instead, they believed they should be able to defend themselves with the shield of Christ’s body and blood. For how could they ever hope to persuade them to shed their own blood for Christ’s cause if they denied them the benefit of his blood? How could it be expected that they would be ready to drink from the cup of martyrdom if the Church barred them from the privilege of drinking from the cup of Christ? 

While peace and tranquility smiled upon the Church, they extended the time of penance and did not allow the *Sacrificati* to be readmitted except at the hour of death. But now that the enemy was breaking in upon them and Christians needed to be prepared and encouraged for suffering, encouragement had to be given to those who, by the sincerity of their repentance, had shown themselves ready to resist even to the point of death <note>original: "resist unto blood"</note> and to fight earnestly for the Faith. They did this not to favor the lazy, but to motivate the diligent; the Church’s peace was granted not for ease and comfort, but for conflict and struggle. And if anyone used this mercy for worse purposes, they only cheated themselves, and such people were left to the judgment of God <note>original: "divine Tribunal"</note>.

<margin>c Ibid. page 82.</margin>
At this synod, a man named Privatus appeared. Having been condemned for heresy and other crimes some years prior by a council of ninety bishops, he asked for his case to be heard again, but he was rejected by the synod. Thereupon, gathering a party of the "lapsed" <note>Christians who had renounced their faith during persecution</note> or the schismatics, he ordained one Fortunatus as bishop at Carthage, claiming that no fewer than twenty-five bishops were present at the consecration. But once the obvious lies and vanity of their claims were discovered, they left the city and fled to Rome.

...messenger knocking as he went along at every door. The streets were filled with the bodies of the dead, which seemed to plead for the help of the living and to demand it as a right by the laws of nature and humanity—a service that they themselves might shortly stand in need of. But alas, it was all in vain; everyone trembled, fled, and shifted for themselves, deserting their dearest friends and nearest relations. None considered what might be their own case, nor how reasonable it was that they should do for another what they would want another to do for them; and if any stayed behind, it was only to loot the dead. 

In this calamitous and tragic scene, St. *Cyprian* called the Christians together and instructed them in the duties of mercy and charity. Drawing from the precepts and examples of the Holy Scripture, he showed them what a mighty influence these virtues have to gain God's favor. He argued that it was no wonder if their charity extended only to their own party; the way to be perfect, and to be Christians indeed, was to do something *more than heathens and tax collectors—to overcome evil with good*, and, in imitation of divine kindness, to *love our enemies*. According to our Lord’s advice, they were to pray for the happiness of those who persecuted them. He reminded them that God constantly makes His sun rise and His rain fall upon seeds and plants, not only for the benefit of His own children, but for all other men. Therefore, they should act as became the nobility of their spiritual rebirth and imitate the example of such a Father, since they professed themselves to be His children. 

Persuaded by this and much more that he discussed to the same effect—enough to convince even the *Gentiles* <note>original: "Gentiles"; here referring to the non-Christian pagan population of the Roman Empire</note> themselves—they immediately organized their help according to each person's rank and ability. Those who, because of poverty, could contribute nothing financially, did what was significantly more: they personally labored in the common calamity, providing assistance far beyond all other contributions. Indeed, everyone was ambitious to serve under the leadership of such a commander, and in a service where they might so eminently prove themselves to God the Father, to Christ the Judge of all, and in the meantime, to so pious and good a bishop. Through this large and abundant charity, great benefit resulted not only to those who were *of the household of Faith*, but universally to everyone. And so that he might not be lacking to anyone, he wrote at this time his excellent discourse concerning *Mortality*, in which he so eloquently teaches a Christian to triumph over the fear of death and shows how little reason there is to mourn excessively for those friends and relations who are taken from us.

X. This horrible pestilence, together with the wars which had recently and were even then overrunning the Empire, were generally blamed on the Christian religion by the *Gentiles*. They claimed that the gods were implacably angry with the world because of it. To defend the faith from this common objection, *Cyprian* addressed a discourse to *Demetrian* the *Proconsul*.

...especially by *Fidus*, an *African* Bishop, who argued that Baptism should not be administered on the third or fourth day, but—as with Circumcision under the *Jewish* law—it should be deferred until the eighth day. Saint *Cyprian*, in a Synod of sixty-six Bishops, determined this question, deciding that it was not necessary to defer it for so long, nor should the grace and mercy of God be denied to anyone as soon as they are born into the world. It was their universal decision and resolution that no one should be prohibited from baptism and the grace of God; and while this rule was to be observed toward all people, it was to be applied even more so toward infants and newborn children.

<margin>b *Epistle 68, page 112 and following.*</margin>
Not long after this, another Council was held by *Cyprian* (at the urgent request of the Bishops of *Spain*) to consult concerning the case of *Basilides*, Bishop of *Asturica*, and *Martial* of *Emerita* in *Spain*. These men had lapsed into the most horrible idolatry during the late Persecution, yet they still retained their positions in the Church. The Synod resolved that they had fallen from their Episcopal Order and even the lowest degree of the ministry; upon their repentance, they were to be restored to no more than the status of laypeople <note>original: "Laics" – members of the church who are not clergy</note> in the Communion of the Church.

XI. In this Synod, or another called not long after, the famous contest about rebaptizing those who had been baptized by heretics received its first official approval. The issue had been debated some time before in the *East* due to the *Montanists* and *Novatians*; from there, the controversy spread to *Numidia*. The Bishops there brought it before *Cyprian* and the Council at *Carthage*, who determined that rebaptism was necessary. *Cyprian* assured them in the Synodic Epistle on this matter that this was no new decision, but had been decreed by his predecessors and constantly practiced among them.

<margin>c *Epistle 69, page 117.*</margin>
<margin>d *Epistle 72, page 121.*</margin>
Among others to whom they sent their decrees, the Synod specifically wrote to *Stephen*, the Bishop of *Rome*. *Stephen* had so strongly supported the opposite opinion that he had even excommunicated the Synod at *Iconium* for making a similar determination. The Carthaginian Synod informed him of the decision they had passed and the reasons for it, which they hoped he would also agree with. However, they did not authoritatively <note>original: "magisterially"</note> impose it upon him, as every Bishop has his own authority within the jurisdiction of his own Church, for which he must give an account to God. Pope *Stephen* (who was supported by a large part of the Church) did not like their proceedings. Consequently, a more general Council was summoned, where no fewer than eighty-seven Bishops from all parts of the *African* Churches met together. They unanimously ratified the former decision; their names and individual votes are preserved in the Acts of that Council.

<margin>e *Found in Cyprian, page 282, and Councils, Volume 1, column 786, latest edition.*</margin>
But these numbers did not make the cause any better received <note>original: "resented"</note> at *Rome*. Indeed, the controversy rose to such a height between these two good men that *Stephen* used very rude and unchristian language toward *Cyprian*, calling him a *false Christ*, a *false Apostle*, a *deceitful worker*, and other such names. On the other hand, *Cyprian* treated *Stephen* with more than ordinary sharpness and severity, charging him with pride, irrelevance, and self-contradiction, as well as ignorance, indiscretion, childishness, and obstinacy. He used expressions that were far removed from the reverence and regard which Saint *Stephen's* successors claim for themselves today.

This serves as a significant example of how passion and prejudice can drive even wise and good men far beyond the true merits of a cause, and beyond what the laws of kindness and charity should allow. I will note nothing more concerning this matter, except that Cyprian and his party expressly disowned *Anabaptism* <note>The practice of "re-baptizing" those already baptized; Cyprian argued he wasn't re-baptizing, but performing the only valid baptism.</note>, or rebaptization. They freely confessed that there was only one Baptism; they argued that those who came over from heretical churches (where they had received their supposed baptism) were not being rebaptized, but truly baptized for the first time. They believed their former baptism was, by that very fact <note>original: "ipso facto"</note>, null and invalid, and they were only then receiving what they had not lawfully possessed before.

XII. It was now the year 257 when Aspasius Paternus, the Proconsul of Africa, summoned Cyprian to appear before him. He told Cyprian that he had lately received orders from the Emperors (Valerian and Gallienus) commanding that all who followed a foreign religion must worship the gods according to the Roman rites, and he desired to know Cyprian's decision. Cyprian answered, "I am a Christian and a Bishop. I acknowledge no other gods but the one only true God, who made Heaven and Earth, and all that is within them. This is the God whom we Christians serve, to whom we pray day and night, for ourselves, for all men, and for the happiness and prosperity of the Emperors." 

"And is this, then, your firm resolution?" asked the Proconsul. 

"That resolution," replied the Martyr, "which is founded in God, cannot be altered." 

The Proconsul then told him that he was also required to search out the priests <note>original: "Presbyters"</note> as well as the bishops, demanding that Cyprian identify them. To this, Cyprian gave no other answer than that, according to their own Roman laws, they were not bound to be informants. The Proconsul then informed him that he was commanded to prohibit all private assemblies and to proceed with the penalty of death against any who attended them. To this, the good man told him that his best course was to do as he was commanded. Finding it was in vain to negotiate with him, the Proconsul commanded Cyprian to be banished. Accordingly, he was transported to Curubis <note>A town in modern-day Tunisia.</note>, a small city standing on a peninsula in the Libyan Sea, not far from Pentapolis. It was a pleasant and delightful place where he was treated with kindness and courtesy, was frequently visited by his fellow Christians, and was provided with all the necessities he required.

<margin>In the place already cited.</margin>
XIII. But the greatest comfort in this retirement was the divine and heavenly visions with which God was pleased to honor him. By one of these, on the very first day of his arrival, he was specifically forewarned of his approaching martyrdom. Pontius the Deacon, who accompanied him in his banishment, gives us this account from the Martyr’s own mouth: 

As he was going to rest, there appeared to him a young man of extraordinary height who seemed to lead him to the *Praetorium* <term>Praetorium: The headquarters or judgment hall of a Roman governor.</term> and present him to the Proconsul, who was then sitting on the bench. When the Proconsul looked at Cyprian, he began to write something in a book. The young man, looking over the official's shoulder, read it; but not daring to speak, he signaled what it was through signs. Extending one of his hands fully, he made a cross-stroke over it with the other—a gesture by which Cyprian immediately guessed the manner of his death <note>The cross-stroke signified beheading by the sword.</note>. 

Thereupon, he urgently begged the Proconsul for just one day's delay to settle his affairs. Partly by the pleasantness of the judge’s facial expression, and partly by the signs the young man made regarding what the Proconsul was noting in his book, Cyprian immediately understood that his request was granted. And it happened exactly as predicted, both regarding the time and the...

XIV. How active and diligent he was to use his opportunities to the best advantage is evident from the several letters he wrote during his confinement. He especially wrote to the martyrs in prison, whose spirits he refreshed with proper consolations, urging them to persevere until they won the crown of martyrdom. While he was here, news was brought to him<sup>a</sup> of the daily increase of the persecution. The Emperor Valerian had sent an official decree <note>original: "Rescript"</note> to the Senate, ordering that bishops, presbyters, and deacons should be put to death without delay; that senators and men of rank and quality should lose their honors and positions, forfeit their estates, and if they still continued as Christians, be beheaded; and that matrons <note>Married women of high social standing.</note>, having had their goods confiscated, should be banished. He also heard that Xystus <note>Pope Sixtus II</note> and Quartus had already suffered in the cemetery where their solemn assemblies were held, and that the city governors carried on the persecution with all their power, robbing and killing everyone they could find. This sad and uncomfortable news<sup>b</sup> gave the good man a clear reason to expect and prepare for his own fate, which he waited for and wished for every day. 

Indeed, some people of the highest rank—his ancient friends—came to him and persuaded him to withdraw for the time being, offering to provide a secure place for his retreat. But the desire for that heavenly crown which he kept in his sight had set him above the world, making him deaf to their kind offers and pleas. It is true that when news was brought that officers were coming to take him to Utica to suffer there, he stepped aside on the advice of his friends. He was unwilling to suffer anywhere but at Carthage, in the sight of the people where he had so long and so successfully preached the Christian faith. He desired to seal the truth of that faith with his blood. It was very fitting and appropriate that a bishop should suffer for our Lord in the place where he had governed his Church, and by that notable confession of faith, build up and encourage the flock committed to him. This is what he told the people under his care in the last letter<sup>c</sup> he ever wrote. As for the people themselves, he advised them to maintain peace and unity, not to cause trouble for one another, and not to offer themselves up to the Gentiles <note>The Roman pagan authorities.</note>; but if anyone was apprehended, they should stand firm and freely confess their faith as God enabled them.

<margin>
d Pontius, as cited above, page 15. Acts of the Passion, as cited above, pages 16, 18, 19, 24.

XV. When Galerius Maximus, the new Proconsul <note>A provincial governor in the Roman Empire.</note>, returned to Carthage<sup>d</sup>, Cyprian (who had resolved only to conceal himself until that time) came home and took up residence in his own gardens. Officers were immediately sent to arrest him. They placed him in a chariot and carried him to the place where the Proconsul had retired for his health. The Proconsul commanded that he be kept until the next day. This was done in the house of one of the officers who guarded him. The people, alarmed by the news of his return and arrest, flocked to the doors and watched there all night. The next morning, September 14, AD 258 <note>original: "Septemb. XIV. Ann. Chr. CCLVIII"</note>, he was led to the Proconsul's palace. Since the governor had not yet come out, Cyprian was taken aside to a private place where he rested on a seat. By chance, the seat was covered with a linen cloth, so that (as my author says) even in the hour of his passion <note>His suffering and death.</note>, he might enjoy some part of episcopal honor <note>Linen was associated with the status and ceremonial seating of a bishop.</note>. XVI. Sentence being passed, he was led away from the tribunal with a strong guard of soldiers. Infinite numbers of people crowded after him, with the Christians weeping, mourning, and crying out, “Let us also be beheaded with him!” The place of execution was Sextus’s Field, a large circuit of ground where the trees (of which the place was full) were loaded with people who had climbed them to behold the spectacle. The martyr immediately began to strip himself, first taking off his cloak, which he folded up and laid at his feet; then falling down upon his knees, he recommended his soul to God in prayer. After this, he took off his dalmatic <note>A long-sleeved tunic worn by clergy.</note>, or under-coat, which he delivered to the deacons, and so standing in nothing but a linen vestment, he awaited the executioner. Indeed, elsewhere <margin>a Year 1 of the 259th Olympiad, Indiction 4, in the 2nd year of Valerian.</margin> he places Saint Cyprian's martyrdom in the second year of the Emperor Valerian’s reign, which (as appears by the list of Consuls) should actually be the fifth year—that is, the year of Christ 258. Pontius was a true lover of him and followed him to the very end; he declared that he did not rejoice so much at the glory and triumph of his master as he mourned that he himself was left behind.

XVII. Saint **CYPRIAN**, though starting late, ran quickly in the Christian race. He had a soul inflamed with a mighty love and zeal for God, whose honor he studied to promote in every way. He was a wise and prudent governor, a great defender of the Church’s rights, a resolute patron and protector of the Truth, and a faithful and vigilant overseer of his flock. He was powerful and diligent in preaching, prudent in <margin><note>original: "Quæcunque bona in multis libris tuis intulisti, nescius ipsum te nobis designasti: es enim omnibus in tractatu major, in sermone facundior, in consilio sapientior, in patientia simplicior, in operibus largior, in abstinentia sanctior, in obsequio humilior, & in actu bono innocentior."</note> Whatever good qualities you have discussed in your many books, you have unknowingly described yourself to us: for you are greater than all others in your treatises, more eloquent in speech, wiser in counsel, more sincere in patience, more generous in your works, holier in your self-denial, humbler in obedience, and more innocent in every good action. Letter from Nemesianus and others, Martyrs, to Cyprian, p. 157.</margin> his determinations, moderate in his advice, grave and stern in his warnings, moving and affectionate in his persuasions, and kind to those who were sorry for their sins, yet unyielding to the stubborn and rebellious. He took infinite pains to win back the lapsed <note>original: "lapsed"—Christians who had renounced their faith during persecution but later sought to return to the church.</note> and to restore them to the Church through <margin>c See the Letter to Cornelius, Epistle 55, page 85.</margin> methods of penance and proper humility. He invited them kindly and treated them tenderly; if their intentions were honest and their desires sincere, he would not strictly judge their crimes by overly precise standards. He was so inclined toward pity and compassion that he feared he might be sinning himself by being too quick to forgive the sins of others. He valued the welfare of souls above his own life, remaining constant in his religious profession, from which neither hope nor fear could pull him away. We noted at the beginning of his life how strictly chaste and self-controlled he was, even when he first became a Christian. His humility was clearly seen in how he turned down the honor of the Episcopal Order <term>Episcopal Order: The rank or office of a bishop.</term> and desired that it might be given to a more deserving person. When some divisive and troublemaking people slandered him, claiming he was overstepping his authority because he restricted their wild and lawless behavior, he defended his humility at length in <margin>d Epistle 69, page 116.</margin> a letter to Pupianus, who had made himself the leader of the party opposing him. He was so modest that in all major transactions concerning the Church, he always consulted both his colleagues and his congregation. <margin>e To the Presbyters and Deacons, Epistle 5, page 14.</margin> He assured us that from the very start of his time as Bishop, he determined not to decide anything by his own private authority without the advice of the clergy and the consent of the people. <margin>f Pontius the Deacon, in the Life of Cyprian, page 12.</margin> His behavior was composed and sober, and his face was grave yet cheerful—neither showing a frowning sternness nor excessive mirth, but an even balance of both. It was hard to say whether he deserved more to be loved or feared, but he equally deserved both. He was the same in his clothing—sober and moderate, keeping a proper distance from both sloppiness and luxury. His appearance showed that he was neither swollen with pride and vanity nor affected by a stingy and miserable spirit. But the virtue that crowned all others was his admirable and exemplary charity; he was of a kind and compassionate nature...

Upon his first embracing the Christian religion, he sold his estate (which was not mean or insignificant) and gave almost all of it to the poor, allowing no considerations to restrain him. His hand, tongue, and heart were open on <margin>* To the Bishops of Numidia, Epistle 60, page 97.</margin> all occasions. We find him at one time not only earnestly pressing others to contribute toward the redemption of Christians taken captive by the Barbarians, but sending a collection of many thousands of crowns himself. <margin>a Pontius, as cited above.</margin> Nor was this a single act done once in his life, but his ordinary practice; his doors were open to all who came, and the widow never returned empty-handed from him. To any who were blind, he would be their guide to direct them; to those who were lame, he was ready to lend his assistance to support them; if any were oppressed by power, he was at hand to rescue and protect them. These things, he used to say, ought to be done by those who desired to render themselves truly acceptable and dear to God.

XVIII. His natural talents seem to have been ready and acute enough, though how far he improved them through secular and *pagan learning* <note>original: "Gentile Learning"</note> is unknown. He seems to have laid no deep foundations in the study of philosophy, as few or no traces of it are to be seen in any of his writings. His main excellence was eloquence, as rhetoric was his profession before his conversion to Christianity. In this he reached such a high level that *Erasmus*, a competent judge of these matters, does not hesitate to <margin>b Preface to Cyprian, among the Epistles of Erasmus, book 28, Epistle 6, column 1616.</margin> affirm that among all the ecclesiastical writers, he is the only *African writer* who attained the native purity of the Latin tongue. *Tertullian* is difficult and obscure; Saint *Augustine* is strangely complex and dry; but *Cyprian* <margin>c Epistle to Paulinus, page 104, Volume 1.</margin> (as Saint *Jerome* <note>original: "S. Hierom"</note> long ago truly judged) is smooth and sweet like a pure fountain. And *Lactantius* <margin>d On Justice, book 5, chapter 1, page 459.</margin> long before him passed this judgment: that *Cyprian* alone was the chief and famous writer, eminent for teaching oratory and writing books admirable in their kind. He noted that Cyprian had a fluid, copious, pleasant, and (which is the greatest grace of speech) <margin>->His blood rests in Libya, but his tongue prevails everywhere;
It alone survives the body, and alone it cannot die.
While Christ permits the human race to be and the world to thrive,
While any book remains, while the sacred cabinets of literature exist,
Every lover of Christ shall read you, Cyprian, and learn from you.
That Spirit of God, who flowed as the source into the Prophets,
Has watered you from the springs of eloquence, nurtured from heaven.
O style of speech whiter than snow! O new flavor!
Like ambrosial liquid, it softens the heart, bathes the palate,
Penetrates the seat of the soul, nourishes the mind, and flows through the limbs;

His mind was inflamed with piety, and his speech was answerable to his mind: he spoke elegantly, yet spoke of things more powerful than elegance; nor did he speak powerful things so much as live them. After his conversion to the Church, he made such quick and <margin>e At the year 250, number 11.</margin> vast progress in Christian theology that *Baronius* thinks it not improbable to suppose either that before his conversion he had been familiar with the books of Christians, or that he was miraculously instructed from above. <meta>This page continues the biography of Saint Cyprian, focusing on the reception of his writings, his reputation for divine guidance, and the eventual fate of the churches dedicated to his memory in Carthage.</meta>

...had it from the mouth of *Cyprian's* own *secretary* <note>original: "Amanuensis"</note> at *Rome*. And certainly, it speaks highly in praise of his judgment that he could drink so freely at that great man's fountain <note>This likely refers to Tertullian, whom Cyprian studied daily</note> and yet take in none of his strange and unusual opinions; he could pick the flowers and pass by the useless or harmful weeds. Just as a wise man is often far from being corrupted, he is actually more warned and confirmed in the truth by another man's errors and mistakes. As for his writings, *St. Jerome* <margin>a *Ibid. in Cypr.* Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*.</margin> passes over them with the comment that it was unnecessary to list them, as they were clearer and more obvious than the sun. Many of them are undoubtedly lost; the greatest part of what remains are *Letters* <note>original: "Epistles"</note>, and all of them are written in such a way that they admirably tend to promote the peace and order of the Church, and advance piety and a good life. A great number of tracts, either doubtful or clearly counterfeit, are attributed to him; some of them are very ancient and most of them useful. It was his good fortune above all other writers of the Church (says *Erasmus*) that <margin>b *As cited above.*</margin> nothing is attributed to him except what is scholarly, and what was the work of some significant author.

XIX. He was highly honored while he lived, not only by men—being consulted and appealed to in all weighty cases by foreign churches—but also by frequent visions and "divine favors" (as he was accustomed to call them), by which he was immediately warned and directed in all important affairs and emergencies of the Church. After his death, his memory was held in great veneration. The people of *Carthage* <margin>c *Victor Vitensis, History of the Vandal Persecution, book 1.*</margin> built two prominent churches to honor him: one at the place of his martyrdom, and the other on the *Mappalian* way, where he was buried. The former was called *Mensa Cypriani*, or *Cyprian's Table*, because there he had been offered up as a sacrifice acceptable to God. And here they held their yearly commemorations of him. Whether this was the church mentioned by *Procopius* <margin>d *On the Vandal War, book 1; see also Nicephorus, book 17, chapter 12.*</margin>, I cannot say; he informs us that the *Carthaginians*, above all people in the world, honored *St. Cyprian* by building a magnificent church to his memory outside the city walls near the seaside. Besides other expressions of honor shown to him, they kept a yearly festival which they called the *Cypriana*. This church *Huneric* <note>original: "Honoricus"</note>, King of the *Vandals*, later took from the *Catholics*—casting out the orthodox clergy with disgrace and contempt—and gave it to the *Arians* <note>original: "Arrians"</note>. Ninety-five years later, it was recovered by the Emperor *Justinian* under the command of *Belisarius*, who besieged and took *Carthage* and drove the *Vandals* out of all those regions.

His service as a judge in civil cases. His drying up a lake by his prayers, which had been the cause of a relentless quarrel between two brothers; and his restraining the flooding of the River Lycus. The accusation of Sabellianism <note>a heresy claiming the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three distinct persons, but only three modes of one person</note>. I.
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'G' featuring leafy ornamentation and a small shield in the center containing the letter 'S.'.</image-desc>GREGORY, originally called *Theodorus*, was born at <margin>a Gregory of Nyssa, *Life of Gregory the Wonder-worker*, page 969, Volume 2.</margin> *Neocaesarea*, the capital city of *Cappadocia*, located on the River *Lycus*. His parents were pagans <note>original: "Gentiles"</note>, but were distinguished by their high social standing and wealth. He had a brother named *Athenodorus*, who was his fellow student and later his colleague as a bishop in his own country, and at least one sister, who was married to a judge under the Governor of *Palestine*. His father <margin>b Gregory the Wonder-worker, *Speech of Praise to Origen*, page 182.</margin> was a devout follower of his religion, in which he took care to educate Gregory, along with the knowledge of the pagan <note>original: "Gentile"</note> world. When he was fourteen years old, his father died. After this, he felt more freedom to investigate various subjects. As his reasoning became more sharp and mature, aided by his advancing education, he more clearly recognized the folly and vanity of the religion in which he had been raised. This soon dampened his enthusiasm for paganism and turned his interests toward Christianity. But though he had lost his father, his mother <margin>c The same, page 184.</margin> took care to complete his upbringing, placing him and his brother under masters of rhetoric and eloquence.

# The Life of Saint GREGORY the Wonder-worker <note>original: "Thaumaturgus"</note>.

<margin>a Same source as above <note>original: *Ibid.*</note> p. 171.</margin>
By one of his teachers, who was appointed to teach him the Latin tongue as a necessary part of a noble and refined education, he was persuaded to study Roman Law. The teacher argued that this would be a great advantage to him in whatever way he might use his rhetorical studies later. Since the man himself was a significant lawyer, he read lectures to Gregory with great accuracy and diligence. Gregory attended these sessions faithfully, though more to satisfy the teacher's whim than out of any love for the studies or a desire to master them. This, however, sufficiently demonstrates his industry; those laws (as he himself observes <margin>a</margin>) were vast and varied, and could not be learned without great trouble and difficulty. What increased the labor above all else was that they were all written in Latin, a language (as he confesses) that was indeed great and admirable, suited to the majesty of the Empire, but which he found difficult enough to become even competently proficient in.

<margin>b In the place mentioned above <note>original: *ubi supr.*</note> p. 972.</margin>
II. HAVING laid the foundations of his first and most necessary studies at home, he planned to further improve himself through foreign travel. He likely went first to Alexandria, which had grown more than usually famous because of the Platonic School recently established there. Indeed, I am not certain of the precise timing of this period of his life, but I know I cannot be far off the mark; Gregory of Nyssa <margin>b</margin> assures us that he came there in his youth. Through the intensity of his studies, but especially through the admirable sobriety and strictness of his life, he visibly put to shame the debaucheries of his fellow students, who were of a more wanton and immoral character. They immediately began planning revenge, conspiring with a common prostitute to insult and shame him. Accordingly, dressed in provocative clothing, she came to him one day while he was engaged in a serious and grave discussion with some learned and close friends. She impudently charged him with having been overly familiar with her, describing what she chose to claim had been said or had passed between them. She further accused him of cheating her out of the payment for their lewd encounters. The company, who knew him to be a person of a completely different character, were outraged at the boldness and impudence of the woman. Meanwhile, Gregory, regardless of the insult, said nothing in his defense. He calmly asked a friend to give her the money she demanded so that their discussions would no longer be interrupted. But see how ready Heaven is to defend the cause of injured innocence! The money was no sooner paid into her hand than, as if possessed by a furious demon <note>original: *Dæmon*</note>, she fell into fits of the most wild and extravagant madness. She roared with a horrific noise, threw herself upon the ground, pulled and tore at her hair, distorted her eyes, and foamed at the mouth. She could not be freed from the brutal treatment of the merciless demon until Gregory, whom she had wronged, had forgiven her and prayed to Heaven on her behalf.

<margin>c *Ecclesiastical History* <note>original: *H. Eccl.*</note> Book 4, Chapter 27, p. 244.</margin>
<margin>d *In the Life of Proaeresius* <note>original: *In vit. Proæ-ref.*</note> p. 117.</margin>
III. DEPARTING from Alexandria, he came back—as we may probably suppose—through Greece, and stayed a while at Athens, where Socrates <margin>c</margin> tells us he studied. From there he returned to his own country, applying himself to his old study of the Law. He now had a great opportunity to improve this by going to Berytus <note>modern-day Beirut</note>, a city of Phoenicia and a famous university for the profession of Roman Law. For this reason, Eunapius <margin>d</margin> says of Anatolius that it was no wonder he was incomparably skilled in the laws, having been born at Berytus, the "Mother of those Studies." Here...

# The Life of St. GREGORY the Wonder-worker <note>original: "Thaumaturgus"</note>.

<margin>
a Panegyric to Origen, p. 186.
b The same author, in the same place, p. 188.
c Gregory of Nyssa, in the same place, p. 974.
d Life of Origen, Preface to the Works of Origen.
e Ecclesiastical History, book 5, chapter 20, p. 369.

He came to this region upon a specific occasion <gloss>a Panegyric to Origen, p. 186</gloss>. The Governor <note>original: "President"</note> of Palestine had taken his brother-in-law, an eminent lawyer, with him to be his assistant judge <note>original: "Assessor"</note> and advisor in governing the affairs of that province. Not long after, the lawyer sent for his wife, requesting that Gregory also come along with her. All things conspired to make him willing to undertake this journey: the chance to please his sister with his company, the persuasion of his friends, the convenience of residing at Beirut <note>original: "Berytus"</note> to study law, and the advantage of government transport <note>original: "public carriages"</note> sent to fetch his sister and her retinue to those parts. Whether he actually studied at Beirut cannot be concluded from any account he himself gives; in fact, he suggests the contrary <gloss>b Panegyric to Origen, p. 188</gloss>, though St. Jerome and others explicitly claim he did. 

If he did study there, he did not stay long, quickly growing weary of legal studies after being tempted by the more pleasant and charming contemplations of philosophy. The fame of Origen soon reached him. Origen had at that time opened a school at Caesarea in Palestine, and Gregory had no doubt heard his renown celebrated in Alexandria. Gregory immediately went to him. There, he accidentally met <gloss>c Gregory of Nyssa, p. 974</gloss> Firmilian, a gentleman from Cappadocia <note>modern-day Turkey</note> and later Bishop of Caesarea in that country. Finding an extraordinary connection in their personalities and studies, they entered into a bond of friendship and joined Origen's school together, along with Gregory's brother, Athenodorus. 

In this matter <gloss>d Preface to the Works of Origen</gloss>, the mistake of Erasmus must be forgiven, for he believed our Gregory and "Theodorus" were two distinct students of Origen, when it is well known they were two names for the same person. He is more easily excused because Nicephorus Callistus <gloss>e Ecclesiastical History, book 5, chapter 20, p. 369</gloss>, writing long before him, had also claimed there was another Theodorus who was a student of Origen at Caesarea at the same time, who supposedly became an eminent bishop in Palestine. However, there is a total silence on this from all other writers, and not even a hint of it appears in Eusebius, from whom Nicephorus derives his accounts. It is clear that out of two different names, he mistakenly created two different people.

<margin>
f Panegyric, p. 197, etc.
g In the same place, p. 178, 181.
h In the same place, p. 218, etc.
</margin>

IV. He was glad to have come under such a fortunate education, as Origen led him through the entire scope of philosophy using the most appropriate and easy methods. St. Gregory himself has given <gloss>f Panegyric, p. 197, etc.</gloss> large and detailed accounts of the many stages by which Origen brought him through the various parts of discipline—Logic, Physics, Mathematics, Ethics, and Metaphysics—and how he introduced him into the mysteries of Theology. It is not necessary to dwell on those details here. 

Above all, Origen endeavored to settle him in the full belief and persuasion of the Christian religion, of which Gregory already had some insight. He sought to ground him in the knowledge of the Holy Scriptures as the best system of true wisdom and philosophy. Gregory remained Origen's disciple for five years until he was recalled to his own country. When it was time to take his leave, he delivered a speech <note>original: "Oration"</note> before his master and a large audience. In this speech, he gave Origen his deserved praise and specifically thanked God <gloss>g In the same place, p. 178, 181</gloss> for the happy advantages of his instructions. He also gave thanks to his protective and guardian angel, who had watched over him since his birth and had especially guided him to such a good master. He eloquently mourned <gloss>h In the same place, p. 218, etc.</gloss> his departure from that school, describing it as a kind of banishment from Paradise, like being turned out of his father's house like the Prodigal Son, or being carried captive into Babylon as the Jews were. He concluded that...

# The Life of St. GREGORY the Wonder-worker <note>original: "Thaumaturgus"</note>.

...of all things upon earth, nothing could give so great an ease and consolation to his mind as if his kind and benign Angel would bring him back to that place again.

<margin>
a Found in *Origen's Philocalia*, chapter 13, page 41.
</margin>
V. He had no sooner returned to Neocaesarea but Origen followed him with a letter <margin>a</margin>, commending his excellent talents, which were able to make him either a distinguished lawyer among the Romans or a great philosopher among the Greeks. However, Origen especially persuaded him to use those talents for the sake of Christianity and the practice of piety and virtue. For this purpose, he explains that he instructed Gregory mainly in those sciences and branches of philosophy which might serve as an introduction to the Christian religion. He acquainted him with those aspects of geometry and astronomy which might be useful for understanding and explaining the Holy Scriptures. He argued that these subjects were as useful a preparation for the knowledge of Christian doctrine as geometry, music, grammar, rhetoric, and astronomy are prerequisites for the study of philosophy. He advised him above all things to read the Scripture, and to do so with the most profound and diligent attention. He warned him not to rashly adopt notions of divine things or to speak of them without serious forethought; he urged him not only to *seek* but to *knock*, and to pray with faith and fervency. Origen noted that it is in vain to think the door should be opened where prayer has not been sent beforehand to unlock it.

<margin>b Gregory of Nyssa, in the same place, page 975.</margin>
At his return <margin>b</margin>, all eyes were upon him. The people expected that in public meetings he would show himself and let them reap some fruit from all his studies. He was universally sought after and urged to do so, especially by the wise and great men of the city, who entreated him to reside among them and to reform and direct the manners of the people through his excellent precepts and rules for living. But the modest young man, knowing how unfit they generally were to receive the dictates of true philosophy, and fearing that a large following and public applause might unknowingly trap him into pride and vanity, resisted all these requests. He withdrew himself into the wilderness, where he devoted himself to solitude and contemplation. There, he conversed with God and his own mind, delighting his thoughts with the pleasant study of nature and the curious and admirable works of the great Creator <note>original: "Artificer"</note> of the world.

VI. Neocaesarea was a large and populous place, but it was miserably overgrown with superstition and idolatry. It seemed to be the place where "Satan's seat" was, and where Christianity had as yet scarcely made an entrance. This was a cause of great grief and resentment to all good men, who heartily wished that religion and the fear of God were planted in that place.

<margin>c Gregory of Nyssa, in the same place, page 976.</margin>
Phaedimus, the Bishop of Amasea (a neighboring city in that province) and a man endowed with a prophetic spirit, had set his eye upon our young philosopher <margin>c</margin>. He saw that Gregory's mature talents and piety far outweighed his youth, making him a fit person to be a "Guide of Souls" in his own birthplace, where his local ties would make the work more meaningful to him. When Gregory received notice of this, he moved his quarters. Whenever he was sought after, he fled from one desert or solitary shelter to another. Despite all his skill and industry, the good Bishop could not catch him; the one was no more earnest to find him than the other was vigilant to avoid him. Phaedimus, at last despairing of meeting him, resolved to go ahead with his design anyway. Being moved "by a certain divine impulse" <note>original: "ὁρμῇ τινι θειοτέρᾳ" (hormē tini theiotera)</note>, he resorted to this pious stratagem—the likes of which...

<summary>Upon returning home, Gregory rejects public fame to live as a hermit, but Bishop Phaedimus of Amasea identifies him as the ideal person to bring Christianity to the pagan city of Neocaesarea.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the biography of Gregory of Neocaesarea (Gregory Thaumaturgus), describing his unique consecration while he was away and his arrival in a predominantly pagan city where he receives a divine vision of a creed.</meta>

# The Life of St. GREGORY the Wonder-worker <note>original: "Thaumaturgus"</note>.

...confident (and probably not to be found elsewhere in the ancient records of the Church) that despite Gregory's absence—who was at that time at least a three days' journey away—the bishop made his address and prayer to God. Having declared that both himself and Gregory were at that moment equally seen by God as if they were present, instead of the traditional laying on of hands, he directed a discourse to St. Gregory. In this way, he set him apart for God and appointed him Bishop of that place. God, who guides the hearts of men, inclined Gregory to accept the responsibility—no matter how reluctant he had been before—and he likely received a more formal and solemn consecration later.

<margin>a The same author as cited above, page 977.</margin>

VII. The province he entered was difficult; the city and surrounding areas were entirely devoted to the worship of idols <note>original: "Demons"</note> and enslaved to the practice of diabolical rites. There were no more than seventeen Christians in those parts, so he had to found a church before he could even govern it. Additionally, and this was no small inconvenience, various heresies had spread across those countries. Though Gregory was well-educated in the humanities, he was at that time entirely inexperienced in theological studies and the mysteries of religion. As a remedy for this, he is said to have received immediate assistance from Heaven. While he was deeply considering these things one night and debating matters of faith in his own mind, he had a vision. Two majestic and venerable persons—whom he understood to be St. John the Evangelist and the blessed Virgin Mary—appeared in his chamber and discussed the points of faith he had been debating with himself. After they departed, he immediately wrote down that canon <term>canon: a rule or law of the Church</term> and rule of faith which they had declared. He made this the standard of his doctrine for the rest of his life and left it as a priceless legacy and trust <note>original: *depositum*</note> to his successors. We shall insert the substance of it here, alongside the original Greek <note>The following is an English translation of the original Greek text provided in the source document.</note>:

One God, the Father of the living Word, of the subsisting Wisdom and Power, and of His eternal Image: the perfect Begetter of the Perfect, the Father of the only-begotten Son. One Lord, alone from the Alone, God from God, the exact representation <note>original: χαρακτῆρ (character)</note> and image of the Godhead, the active Word, the wisdom encompassing the constitution of the universe, and the power that created the whole world; the true Son of the true Father, Invisible of the Invisible, Incorruptible of the Incorruptible, Immortal of the Immortal, and Eternal of the Eternal. VIII. Being thus incomparably equipped, he began to apply himself more directly to the charge committed to him. He was greatly aided in his success by a power of working miracles—a gift much discussed among the ancient writers—which was bestowed upon him. <margin>a The same author as cited above, p. 980.</margin> While he was returning home from the wilderness, he was caught in a storm as night fell. He and his companions turned aside to seek shelter in a *pagan* <note>original: "Gentile"</note> temple, famous for its oracles and divinations, where they spent the night in prayer and hymns to God. Early in the morning, the *pagan* priest arrived to perform the customary devotions to the *demons* <note>In this context, the author refers to the pagan gods or spirits as demons.</note> of the place. It seems the spirits had told the priest that they must leave the temple from now on because of the man who had stayed there. The priest performed his ritual purifications <note>original: "lustrations"</note> and offered his sacrifices, but all in vain; the *demons* were deaf to all his pleas and prayers. At this, he burst into a fit of rage, shouting against the holy man and threatening to complain about him to the magistrates and the Emperor. 

But when the priest saw that Gregory bravely disregarded his threats and possessed the power to command *demons* to enter or leave at his will, his fury turned to wonder. He begged the Bishop, as further proof of the divine authority attending him, to bring the *demons* back into the temple once more. To satisfy him, it is said that Gregory tore off a piece of paper and wrote these words upon it: *Gregory to Satan: enter.* As soon as this note <note>original: "Schedule"</note> was placed upon the altar and the usual incense and offerings were made, the *demons* appeared again just as they used to. This clearly convinced the priest that Gregory held an authority superior to all infernal powers, and he decided to follow him. However, being uncertain about some parts of Christian doctrine, he was only fully converted after he saw St. *Gregory* confirm his teachings with another obvious miracle. Following this, the priest freely left his home, friends, and family to dedicate himself to the instructions of Gregory's divine wisdom and philosophy.

VII. THE province he entered was a difficult one. The city and surrounding areas were entirely devoted to the worship of *demons* <note>In this context, "demons" refers to the pagan gods or spirits worshipped in the region.</note> and enslaved to the practice of diabolical rites. There were no more than seventeen Christians in those parts, so he had to establish a church before he could lead it. Not the least of his hindrances was that various heresies had already spread over those countries. Furthermore, although he was well-equipped with a foundation in secular education <note>original: "humane Learning," referring to the liberal arts and classical studies</note>, he was entirely inexperienced in theological studies and the mysteries of religion. As a remedy for this, he is said to have received direct help from Heaven. One night, while he was deeply contemplating these matters and debating points of faith in his own mind, he had a vision. Two majestic and venerable figures (whom he recognized as Saint *John the Evangelist* and the *Blessed Virgin*) appeared in the chamber where he was and discussed those very points of faith he had been debating. After they departed, he immediately wrote down that *canon* <note>A "canon" is a rule or standard, here referring to a formal statement of religious belief.</note> and rule of faith which they had declared. He ever after made this the standard of his doctrine and left it as a priceless legacy and *sacred trust* <note>original: "depositum"</note> to his successors. We shall insert the substance of it here, together with the original Greek; since it is very difficult to translate exactly into our language, the learned reader may translate it for himself if he does not like my version.

X. It was no small weight on the good man’s joy to think of the profane and idolatrous place where his lot had fallen, and he realized he must lose no time. Accordingly, that very day<sup>a</sup> he began preaching, and with such success that before nightfall he had converted a small congregation <note>original: "little Church"</note>. Early the next morning, the doors were crowded. People of all ranks, ages, and suffering from various infirmities and diseases flocked to him. He performed two cures at once, healing both soul and body: instructing their minds, proving their errors, and reforming their behavior. He did this with ease because, at the same time, he was strengthening the weak, curing the sick, healing the diseased, and driving demons out of the possessed. People greedily embraced the religion he taught as they beheld such clear demonstrations of its power and divinity before their eyes, hearing nothing reported except what was verified by the evidence of their own senses. Having thus gathered a large congregation, his next care was to build a church where they might assemble for the public ceremonies of religion. Through the cheerful contributions of some and the hard labor of others, the building was both begun and finished in a short time. The foundations of it seem to have been laid upon a firmer basis than other buildings, seeing it survived not only the earthquakes frequent in those parts, but also the violent storm of Diocletian’s reign <note>referring to the Diocletianic Persecution, c. 303–313 AD</note>, when the Emperor commanded Christian churches in all places to be demolished. It was still standing in the time of Gregory of Nyssa <note>original: "Gregory Nyssen"</note>, who further tells us that when a terrible earthquake recently happened in that place—which destroyed and ruined almost all the buildings, both public and private—this church alone remained entire, and not even a single stone was shaken to the ground.

They entreated him to intercede with his God (whom they believed to be a more powerful and superior Being) on their behalf, that He would restrain that violent disease that raged among them. He did so, and the pestilence subsided, and the destroying angel took his leave. The result was that the people generally deserted their temples, oracles, sacrifices, and the idolatrous rites of their religion, and took sanctuary in Christianity as the most secure refuge and the best way to persuade Heaven to protect them.

XII. His known prudence, and the reputation of his mighty and (as my author <sup>a</sup> calls them) *Apostolic* miracles, advanced him into so much favor and veneration with the people that they looked upon whatever he said or did as the effect of a divine power. Even in secular legal cases, where the matter was at all complex and difficult, it was usually brought to him; his sentence was accounted more just and impartial, more firm and valid, than any other decision whatsoever. 

It happened that two brothers were at law over a lake, which both claimed as belonging to that part of the inheritance their father had left them. The arbitration <note>original: "Umpirage"</note> of the case was left to him. Using all the persuasive arts of suggestion, he first endeavored to reconcile them and peacefully resolve the difference between them. But his pains proved fruitless and ineffectual; the young men stormed and resolved each to maintain his right by force of arms. A day was set when they were to try their titles by all the power which the tenants of each side could bring into the field. To prevent this, the holy Bishop went the night before to the place, where he continued all night in exercises of devotion. By his prayers to Heaven, he procured the lake to be turned into a parcel of dry and solid ground, thereby removing the bone of contention <term>the source of a dispute</term> that was between them; the remains of which lake were shown many ages after. 

Thus <sup>b</sup> also he is said to have miraculously restrained the violence of the River Lycus. This river, coming down from the mountains of Armenia in a swift, rapid torrent and swollen by the tributary flow of other rivers, fell down into a flat, open plain <note>original: "plain Champain Countrey"</note>. He went along with them to the place and made his address to Him who has set a boundary for the waters so that they may not pass over, nor turn again to cover the earth. She taught them in their youth and supervised their education, having been a student and listener of our *Saint Gregory* in her younger years. <margin>* In the same place, p. 999 <note>original Latin: "Ibid."</note></margin>
XIV. In this faithful and successful management of his office, he quietly continued until about the year 250 AD. At that time, the Emperor *Decius* <gloss>*</gloss> (disturbed to see the Christian religion gaining so much ground over declining paganism) published very severe edicts against the Christians. He commanded the governors of provinces to execute these laws strictly and rigorously, on pain of death. In this persecution, the regions of *Pontus* and *Cappadocia* suffered as much as, if not more than, the rest of the empire. All other business seemed to stop; the persecution of Christians became the primary topic of all public councils and the main concern of magistrates. This hostility did not manifest itself merely in threats and harsh words, but in the creation of methods of cruelty and instruments of torture. The mere thought of these is terrifying and shocking to human nature. There were swords and axes, fire, wild beasts, stakes, and machines to stretch and pull apart the limbs. There were iron chairs made red-hot and wooden frames set upright, where the bodies of the victims were hung and scraped with iron nails that tore off their flesh. Innumerable other cruelties were daily invented, as every high-ranking official was careful that another should not seem more fierce and cruel than himself. Some acted as informers, others as witnesses; some searched every private corner, while others captured those who tried to flee. Some who hungered for their neighbors' estates took the opportunity to accuse and persecute them for being Christians. This resulted in general confusion and terror. Everyone was afraid of even their closest relatives: fathers did not look out for the safety of their children, and children ignored their duty to their parents. The pagan <note>original: "Gentile"</note> son betrayed his Christian father, and the infidel father accused his son for embracing Christianity. Even brothers considered it a deed of piety to violate the laws of nature for the sake of religion, condemning their own brothers because they were Christians. Because of this, the woods became full of refugees and the cities were emptied. Yet, as soon as houses were cleared of their owners, they were turned into common jails, as the public prisons could not hold the multitudes of Christians sent to them. You could not go into the markets or common gathering places without seeing some people being arrested, others led to trial or execution, and some weeping while others laughed and rejoiced at the common misery. No regard was shown for age, sex, virtue, or merit. Just like a city being stormed by a proud and powerful conqueror, everything was exposed without mercy to the rage and brutality of a barbaric and inhuman enemy.

<margin><sup>b</sup> In the same place, p. 1001 <note>original Latin: "Ibid."</note></margin>
XV. Saint GREGORY, seeing the sad and disastrous state of the times, and having seriously considered <sup>b</sup> the frailty and weakness <note>original: "imbecillity"</note> of human nature, realized how few (especially among his new converts) would be able to endure those fierce conflicts. He knew that the cause of religion would involve them in such trials. He wisely advised his church to avoid the full force of the current storm for a time. He told them it was better to save their lives by fleeing than to risk falling away from the faith by staying to face those furious trials. To show them that this was permissible and that doing so would not harm their spiritual well-being, he decided to lead by example. He was the first to retreat from danger, withdrawing to a desert mountain. He was accompanied only by the pagan priest whom he had converted and who served him in...

<summary>This page describes the brutal persecution of Christians under Emperor Decius around 250 AD and Saint Gregory's decision to lead his congregation into hiding to preserve their faith and lives.</summary>
<keywords>Emperor Decius, persecution of Christians, Pontus, Cappadocia, torture, social breakdown, religious exile, Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the biography of Saint Gregory the Wonder-worker, recounting his escape from Roman persecutors through divine intervention and his subsequent efforts to reorganize the church in Neocæsarea after the persecution ended.</meta>

-># The Life of Saint GREGORY the Wonder-worker <note>original: "Thaumaturgus"</note><-

...in the capacity of a deacon. It was high time for him to withdraw, as the enemy primarily targeted him as the leader of the Christian group <note>original: "head of the Party"</note>, laying every possible snare to capture him. Having been informed where he was hiding, they went in large numbers to hunt him down. Some surrounded the base of the mountain to prevent his escape, while others climbed up and searched every spot until they were very close to him. Encouraging his deacon to have firm confidence in divine protection, Gregory immediately began to pray. Following his example, the deacon did the same, with eyes and hands lifted up to heaven. 

Meanwhile, the persecutors pried into every corner, examining every bush and shrub, every crevice of rock, and every nook and hole. Finding nothing, they returned to their companions at the bottom, hoping that by then he might have fallen into their hands. When the informant described the exact spot where Gregory was hiding, the searchers insisted they saw nothing there but a couple of trees a short distance apart. Once the group had left, the informant stayed behind and went directly to the spot. Finding them at their prayers and concluding that their escape was the result of immediate divine protection—God having blinded the searchers' eyes so they could not see them—he fell at the bishop’s feet. He converted to Christianity and became a companion in Gregory’s solitude and dangers.

<margin>In the same place <note>original Latin: "Ibid."</note>, p. 1002.</margin>

XVI. Despairing now of finding the "shepherd," these "wolves" turned with even fiercer rage upon the "flock" left behind. This did not happen only there; they ran throughout all parts of the province, seizing men, women, and children who showed any reverence for the name of Christ. They dragged them to the city and threw them into prison, where they were certain to be faced with various tortures. 

*Saint Gregory*, meanwhile, remained in his solitary retreat until God mercifully commanded the storm to pass and the tyranny of the persecution to end. He then left his quiet, secluded walks and returned to *Neocæsarea*. Visiting every part of his diocese, he established annual festivals and solemn ceremonies in every location to honor the memory of the martyrs who had suffered in the recent persecution. This was a significant example of his wisdom and prudence. Not only did he honor the memory of the martyrs, but he also used these events to encourage people to embrace religion more readily. They saw that the faith allowed them some joy and freedom amidst the strict demands <note>original: "severe Yokes"</note> it placed upon them. He had observed how pagan idolatry gained an advantage by allowing its followers liberty—or rather, excessive indulgence <note>original: "licentiousness"</note>—during their religious ceremonies. He reasonably assumed it would be a strong encouragement for some to abandon their superstitions and convert to Christianity if they were allowed to rejoice and enjoy a bit more innocent freedom than usual. He felt this was best done at the commemorations of the martyrs, though it cannot be denied that this custom later led to some negative consequences.

<margin>
a History <note>original Latin: "Hist."</note>, book 7, chapter 22, folio 311.
b Trebellius Pollio, in the *Life of Gallienus* <note>original Latin: "in vit. Gallien."</note>, chapters 4–5, pages 717, 718. See <note>original Latin: "vid."</note> Zosimus, *History*, book 1, page 352 and chapter 359; and Trebellius Pollio, in the *Life of Claudius*, chapter 8, page 806.
</margin>

XVII. During the reign of the Emperor *Gallienus*, around the year 260 AD (and for several years prior), God was determined to punish the world. As *Orosius* <note>Likely Paulus Orosius, a 5th-century historian; the original text spells it "Osorius."</note> <sup>a</sup> accurately enough suggests, God was offended by the cruel treatment Christians received from the ruling powers. To that end, He not only allowed the Emperor *Valerian*—who was friendly at first but later became a bitter persecutor of Christians—to be betrayed into the hands of *Sapor*, the King of *Persia* (who treated him with extreme scorn and insolence), but also permitted the *northern* <sup>b</sup> nations, like...

--- Page 363 ---
<meta>This page continues the biography of Saint Gregory the Miracle-worker, moving from his survival of Roman persecution to the external threats of barbarian invasions and the internal threat of the Samosatenian heresy.</meta>

-># The Life of Saint GREGORY the Miracle-worker <note>original: "Thaumaturgus"</note><-

...like a mighty flood <note>original: "inundation"</note> breaking down the banks and overflowing most parts of the Roman Empire. The Germans made their way, some into Spain, while others crossed the Alps and traveled through Italy as far as Ravenna. The Alemanni plundered <note>original: "forraged"</note> France and invaded Italy; the Quadi and Sarmatians devastated Pannonia; the Parthians invaded Mesopotamia and Syria; and the Goths broke into Pontus, Asia, and parts of Greece. The outrages committed by these barbarian people were intolerable wherever they went, but especially toward the Christians. They plundered their goods, raped their wives and daughters, tortured them, and forced them to offer sacrifices and participate in idol-feasts. Many renegades even robbed their fellow Christians, and some, under the pretense of finding lost items, stole or kept their neighbors' property for their own use. 

In this general chaos, a nearby bishop wrote to Saint Gregory of Neocaesarea to ask for advice on how to handle this tragic state of affairs. Gregory sent back a "Canonical Epistle" (frequently cited and praised by ancient authors, and still in existence today) through a man named Euphrosynus to correct these irregularities and disorders. In this letter, he prescribes the various levels and orders of penitents <term>penitents: individuals undergoing public discipline to be readmitted to church fellowship</term>, but he especially rebukes and censures their excessive greed. He shows how unbecoming it is in itself, how unsuitable for Christians, and how offensive it is to God and all good men to covet and seize what belongs to someone else. He emphasizes how much more barbaric and inhuman it is in such a disastrous time to rob the oppressed and enrich themselves from the blood and ruin of their suffering brothers. 

Because some might argue they did not steal but only took what they happened to find, he informs them that they were bound by God's Law to return anything belonging to a neighbor—even an enemy—much more so to their brothers, who were suffering the same hardships. If anyone thought they were justified in keeping what they found because they had suffered great losses themselves, he tells them that this is to justify one sin with another; because the Goths had been enemies to them, they were becoming Goths and barbarians to others. Indeed, he tells us that many even joined with the barbarians to openly persecute, capture, and torment their brothers. In all these cases, he pronounces them unfit for the communion of the saints and forbids their readmission until they have made public and solemn satisfaction to the church through proper penance, according to the circumstances of the case.

<margin>Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 7, chapter 27, page 278. <note>original: "Euseb. H.E. l. 7. c. 27. p. 278."</note></margin>
XVIII. Not long after this, Paul of Samosata, the Bishop of Antioch, began to introduce very harmful <note>original: "pernicious"</note> doctrines concerning the person of our blessed Savior. To prevent this infection from spreading, the most prominent bishops and clergy from all those regions met frequently in a council <term>original: "Synod"</term> at Antioch. The leaders among them were Firmilian, Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, our Saint Gregory, and his brother Athenodorus (also a bishop in Pontus), along with several others. When the council had met and examined the matter, the clever heretic saw it was useless to argue. Therefore, disguising his errors as best he could, he confessed what could not be hidden and, through a fake repentance, saved his reputation for the time being and secured his continued position in that honorable office he held in the church. This council was held in the year of Christ 264, which Saint Gregory does not seem to have survived for long, dying either this year or, most likely, the following...
