...following year. <margin><sup>a</sup> Nicephorus Callistus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 6, chapter 17, p. 408.</margin> *Nicephorus* claims that he lived to a very great age, which he must have if (as he affirms) he died during the reign of *Diocletian*. <margin><sup>b</sup> *The Suda*, under the entry "Gregory," p. 628.</margin> *Suidas* <note>The *Suda*, a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>, by a much more enormous mistake, claims he died during the reign of *Julian the Apostate*. A little before his death, realizing his time was near, he sent <margin><sup>c</sup> Gregory of Nyssa, as cited above, p. 1006.</margin> messengers throughout the city and the surrounding area to make a strict inquiry into whether there were any who were still strangers to the Christian faith. When he was told there were only seventeen in all, he sighed and, lifting his eyes to heaven, appealed to God about how much it troubled him that he should leave any part of humanity's salvation incomplete. Yet, he added that it was a mercy demanding the most grateful acknowledgment <note>original: "resentment," which in this period meant "feeling" or "appreciation"</note> that, although he had found only seventeen Christians when he first arrived there, he would leave only seventeen idolaters to his successor. Having heartily prayed for the conversion of infidels and the growth and perfection of those already converted, he calmly and peacefully passed away <note>original: "resigned up his soul to God"</note>. He had first instructed his friends not to make any trouble over his funeral or secure a private or special burial place for him. Instead, just as he had lived as a pilgrim and foreigner in the world, claiming nothing for himself, so after death he might share the lot of a stranger and be buried in a common grave.

<margin>
<sup>d</sup> Saint Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 29, p. 359, Vol. 2.
<sup>e</sup> Saint Basil, *Letter to the Clergy of Neocaesarea*, Letter 63, p. 97.
</margin>
XIX. He was a man (says *Saint Basil*) of a prophetic and apostolic character, who in the whole course of his life demonstrated the height and discipline of a life lived according to the Gospel. In all his devotions, he showed the greatest reverence, never covering his head in prayer; he considered the Apostle Paul’s teaching most appropriate and sensible: *that every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head* <note>1 Corinthians 11:4</note>. He avoided all oaths, making *Yes* and *No* the usual standard of his communication. Out of regard for our Lord's warning, he never dared to call his brother a *Fool*. No anger, wrath, or bitterness ever came out of his mouth. He greatly hated slandering and reproaching others, seeing it as a quality opposite to a state of salvation. Envy and pride were strangers to his innocent and guileless soul. He never approached the holy Altar until he was first reconciled with his brother. He severely detested lies and falsehoods, and all cunning or artificial methods of slander, well knowing that every lie is the offspring of the Devil and that God will destroy all those who speak lies.

<margin>
<sup>f</sup> Saint Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, under the entry for "Theodore."
</margin>
XX. His writings are first mentioned in detail by *Saint Jerome*, who lists his *Eucharistical Panegyric* to *Origen*, his short and (as he calls it) very useful *Metaphrase* <term>metaphrase: a literal or word-for-word translation or summary</term> on *Ecclesiastes*, several Epistles (in which his *Canonical Epistle* undoubtedly held the first place), and his *Creed* or short exposition of Faith. Although not mentioned in some versions, this Creed is found in other editions of *Saint Jerome's Catalog*. All of these (with the exception of some of his letters) still exist and are probably everything he ever wrote. For though there are other works commonly attributed to him, there is no great reason or evidence to prove they are authentic, and even those who defend them are not very confident. It appears <margin><sup>g</sup> Saint Basil, *Letter to the Learned Men of the Church of Neocaesarea*, Letter 64, p. 101.</margin> from *Saint Basil* that some in the past suspected him of leaning toward *Sabellianism* <term>Sabellianism: the heresy that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three distinct persons but only one person</term>. Many critics shielded themselves under his authority because of an expression he used, affirming that the *Father* and *Son* are *two in the consideration of the mind, but one in person*. To this, *Saint Basil* offers a long defense, showing that it was spoken in the heat of a debate against *Aelian*, a Gentile...

<meta>This page concludes the biography of Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus, specifically defending his theological reputation against claims of heterodoxy and listing his known works.</meta>

...Gentile, not dogmatically, but in the heat of debate <note>original Greek: οὐ δογματικῶς, ἀλλ᾿ ἀγωνιστικῶς; "not dogmatically, but competitively," meaning in the context of an argument rather than a formal statement of faith</note>, not dogmatically as a point of doctrine, but in haste and in the fervor of disputation, when judgment and consideration are not at leisure to weigh everything by delicate scruples. His earnest desire to win over the Gentile made him less cautious and concerned about the exactness of his words, and he indulged somewhat in the perspectives of his adversary so that he might gain a better advantage over him regarding the greater and more important principles. This betrayed him into some incautious expressions, which the heretics of later times used for bad purposes and strained to a different sense than what was originally intended by the one who spoke them. <margin>Ibid. p. 99.</margin> As to the particular charge of the Sabellian error <note>Sabellianism was a heresy that claimed the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons but merely different "modes" or roles of one God.</note>, he was so far from it that it had been chiefly refuted and put to rest by the evidence of that very doctrine which Saint Gregory had preached, the memory of which was preserved fresh among them. <margin>Apology against Rufinus, Book 2, p. 219, Volume 2.</margin> However, nothing can be more true and modest than what Saint Jerome <note>original: Hierom</note> observes in such cases: that it is a great rashness and irreverence to immediately charge the ancient writers with heresy because of a few problematic expressions. It may be that they erred with a simple and honest mind, or wrote them in another sense, or the passages have been altered since by ignorant transcribers. Or perhaps they took less heed and care to deliver their minds with the utmost accuracy and exactness while men of perverse minds had not yet sown their weeds <note>original: "tares," a biblical reference to weeds sown among wheat</note>, nor disturbed the Church with the noise of their disputes, nor infected people's minds with their poisonous and corrupt opinions.

I. Saint Dionysius was in all probability born at Alexandria, where his parents ^a seem to have been people of considerable importance and status. His father, and possibly his ancestors, had held very honorable offices, and he himself lived for some time in great worldly prestige and power. He was born and raised a pagan <note>original: "Gentile"</note>, but I do not know the specific occasion of his conversion to Christianity, other than what we learn from a vision and voice that spoke to him, mentioned by ^b himself. Through a diligent reading of whatever books fell into his hands and an impartial examination of the things contained in them, he was first brought over to the Faith. Having completed his youthful studies, he placed himself under the instruction of the renowned ^c Origen, the great master in Alexandria at that time, who was famous for both philosophical and Christian lectures. After this, some say ^d he publicly taught rhetoric and eloquence. Indeed, a distinct vein of imagination <note>original: "Fansie"</note> and rhetoric seems to run through those fragments of his discourses which still

yet remain. But I can barely believe that the *Dionysius* mentioned by *Anastasius* and *Maximus*—who is said by them to have been a rhetorician before being made Bishop of *Alexandria*—is the same as our Dionysius. If for no other reason, he is said to have written *commentaries* <note>original: "Scholia"; brief explanatory notes on a text</note> on the works of *St. Denis* the *Areopagite*, which we are certain did not exist in the world until many years after his time. 

In AD 232 <note>original: "Ann. CCXXXII"</note>, *Demetrius*, the Bishop of *Alexandria*, died. *Heraclas*, one of *Origen's* students and his successor in the *Catechetical School*, took his place. Upon this promotion, *Dionysius*, then a priest <note>original: "Presbyter"</note> of that church, was advanced to head the school. In that role, he performed his duties with such care and diligence, and with such universal approval and satisfaction, that upon the death of *Heraclas* (who served for fifteen or sixteen years), no one was thought as fit to be his successor as *Dionysius*. Accordingly, he entered upon that seat <note>original: "See"; the jurisdiction or office of a bishop</note> <margin>a *Eusebius, Book 6, Chapter 35, page 232.*</margin> in AD 246 <note>original: "Ann. CCXLVI"</note>, though *Eusebius* in his *Chronicon* <note>A book of global history and timelines</note> places it two years later, in the fifth year of Emperor *Philip's* reign. This is explicitly contrary to his *History*, where he assigns the third year of that Emperor for the time of his consecration to that office.

II. THE first years of his service as bishop were calm and peaceful, until *Decius* succeeded to the Empire in AD 249. He turned everything into chaos and conflict <note>original: "hurry and combustion"</note>, persecuting the Christians with the greatest violence, of which the Church of *Alexandria* suffered a heavy share. Indeed, the persecution there had begun <margin>b *His letter to Fabian, in the same place, Chapter 41, page 236.*</margin> a year earlier, while Emperor *Philip* was still alive, due to this occasion: A certain pagan priest or poet led the way <note>original: "led the Dance"</note>, inciting the people of that place (who were naturally prone to superstition) to avenge the quarrel of their gods. Once the crowd was riled up, they ran with uncontrollable fury, considering cruelty toward Christians to be the only true act of piety toward their gods. 

Immediately, they seized *Metras*, an elderly man. When he refused to blaspheme his Savior, they beat him with clubs, poked him in the face and eyes with sharp reeds, and after leading him into the suburbs, stoned him. The next person they seized was a woman named *Quinta*, whom they carried to the temple. When she refused to worship the idol, she was dragged by her feet through the streets of the city over sharp flints, dashed against great stones, lashed with whips, and finally killed in the same manner. *Apollonia*, an elderly virgin, was captured; they knocked out all her teeth and threatened to burn her alive. Asking only for a brief moment of respite, she voluntarily and cheerfully leaped into the flames. <margin>c *See Bollandus regarding the lives of the Saints for February 9th.*</margin> It is incredible (though the case is evident from more instances than one) with what misguided <note>original: "fond"; here meaning foolish or overly superstitious</note> veneration the Church of *Rome* celebrates the memory of this martyr. They infinitely praise her for her noble birth, the eminent piety and virtues of her life, her chastity, humility, frequent fastings, and fervent prayers (though not a single syllable of all this is mentioned by any ancient writer). They even introduce a voice from heaven calling her the *Spouse of Christ* and telling her that God had granted her what she had asked. III. This was the state of affairs when Decius, having usurped the Empire and defeated and killed his master Philip, sent his edict to Alexandria, which gave new life to the persecutors' rage and cruelty. And now they fell upon the Christians afresh. Persons of all ages, social standings, and professions were accused, summoned, dragged, tortured, and executed with all imaginable severity. Dionysius particularly reckons up a multitude of these people, ᵃ along with the manner of their martyrdom and execution. Vast numbers ᵇ who fled for shelter to the woods and mountains met with a worse death abroad than that which they sought to avoid at home. They were famished with hunger and thirst, starved with cold, overrun with diseases, surprised by thieves, or worried by wild beasts. Many were taken by the Arabs and nomadic Saracens, who reduced them to a state of slavery more miserable than death itself. 

In this evil time, though many revolted from the faith, others maintained their station with a firm and unshaken courage. Several who until that moment had been strangers and enemies to the Christian religion suddenly came in and publicly professed themselves Christians, in open defiance of the immediate dangers that followed. One instance may suffice: a man who was thought to be a Christian and ready to renounce his religion was being led into the place of judgment. Ammon, Zeno, and the rest of the military guard standing at the door derided him as he was going in, gnashing their teeth at him and making such mocking, grotesque gestures <note>original: "mimic and antique gestures"</note> that all eyes were upon them. Then, behold, before anyone could lay a hand on them, they suddenly came into open court and unanimously professed themselves to be Christians. 

This accident strangely surprised and troubled the governors and the legal assistants <note>original: "Assessors"</note> on the bench. The condemned Christians were cheerful and courageous, ready to undergo their torments, while the judges themselves were amazed and trembled. Once sentence was passed upon them, the Christians went out of court in a kind of celebratory procession, rejoicing in the testimony they were to give for the faith, and that God would so gloriously triumph in their execution.

# The Life of Saint Dionysius of Alexandria

<margin>a See his letter to Domitius in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 7, Chapter 11, page 260. <note>original: "Vid. Epist. ejus ad Domit. ib. l. 7. c. 11. p. 260."</note></margin>
...the searcher <note>original: *frumentarius*; a military officer who acted as a secret police agent or tax collector.</note>, or military officer (whose role was to seize offenders and investigate seditious reports and practices against the State, a duty belonging specifically to judges and provincial governors), arrived to arrest him. The officer searched everywhere, ransacking every corner and looking in all the ways and places where he thought Dionysius might hide. However, in the meantime, he never searched Dionysius's own house, concluding that he would not dare to stay at home. Yet, Dionysius stayed there for four days, waiting for the officer's arrival. Finally, warned by God, he left his house with his servants and some of the brothers who attended him. But not long after, he fell into the hands of the soldiers. Having received his sentence, he was led by a guard under the command of a centurion and other officers to *Taposiris*, a small town between *Alexandria* and *Canopus*, likely to be beheaded there with less public outcry.

In the meantime, it happened that *Timotheus*, one of his friends who knew nothing of his arrest, came to the house where he had been. Finding it empty and a guard at the door, he fled in great shock and confusion. A countryman met him on the road and asked why he was in such a hurry. *Timotheus*, probably hoping to hear news of his friends, gave him a broken and incomplete account of what happened. The man was on his way to a wedding feast (which they used to celebrate all night) and, upon entering the house, told the guests what he had heard. Warmed with wine and high-spirited with mirth, they all rose and ran out of doors, shouting loudly as they approached the place where Dionysius was held. 

The guard, hearing such noise and confusion at that time of night, abandoned their prisoner and ran away. The crowd entered and found Dionysius in bed. The good man, supposing them to be thieves, reached for his clothes lying nearby to give to them. But they commanded him to get up immediately and go with them. Understanding now why they had come, he begged them to let him go and depart. At the very least, he asked them to be so kind as to finish the soldiers' work and behead him themselves. While he was passionately pleading with them, they forced him to rise. When he threw himself on the ground, they began to drag him out by his hands and feet, but they released him shortly after and likely returned to their drunken celebrations. Once this tragicomic scene was over, *Caius* and *Faustus*, *Peter* and *Paul*, presbyters <term>Presbyters: Elders or priests in the early church.</term> and his fellow prisoners, picked him up. Leaving the town, they set him upon a donkey and took him away <sup>a</sup> into a desolate and uncomfortable part of the Libyan desert. There, along with *Peter* and *Caius*, he remained hidden until the storm of persecution had passed.

<margin>b Ibid. Book 6, Chapter 40, page 238.</margin>
V. The persecution having largely subsided following the death of *Decius*, *Dionysius* emerged from his solitude and returned to *Alexandria*. There he found the affairs of his church incredibly tangled and disordered, especially because of the great number of people who had denied the faith and fallen into idolatry <note>These people were known as the *Lapsi*, or "the lapsed."</note> during the recent persecution. Among these were many wealthy and honorable people, including those in positions of authority and power. Some renounced their faith freely; others strayed so far from the bravery of a Christian spirit that when they were summoned to appear and sacrifice to the gods (as he tells us <sup>b</sup>), they trembled and looked as pale and ghostly as if they had come not to offer a sacrifice, but to be made into one themselves. This was to such an extent that even the pagans <note>original: "Gentiles"</note> mocked and despised them,

Most of these individuals, after his return, petitioned to be readmitted to the communion of the Church. The ecclesiastical discipline of those times did not easily allow this, especially after the *Novatian* principles began to prevail, which denied all communion to the lapsed <note>original: "lapsed"; Christians who had renounced their faith or performed pagan sacrifices under the pressure of Roman persecution.</note>, even if they expressed their sorrow through long and rigorous penance. We have already noted in the *Life of Saint Cyprian* the occasion upon which *Novatus* and his partner *Novatian* <note>The author likely refers to the Roman priest Novatian and the African priest Novatus, who were key figures in the rigorist movement that refused to forgive those who had faltered during persecution.</note> first started this rigorous and severe opinion, how eagerly *Cyprian* and the *African* bishops contended against it, how far it was condemned both there and at *Rome*, and in what cases and by what measures of penance the lapsed penitents were to be taken back in. *Saint Dionysius* was of the moderate party, in which he had the agreement of most of the *Eastern* bishops. As he pleads, this was the general judgment and practice of the holy martyrs, many of whom had, before their deaths, received the lapsed back into the Church upon their repentance and had themselves freely shared communion with them. He thought it was not reasonable that the martyrs' judgment should be despised, nor their practice controlled, nor the established order overturned. Indeed, he himself had always observed this course; therefore, at the beginning of the persecution, he had given orders to the priests <note>original: "Presbyters"</note> of the Church to restore peace and give the Eucharist to penitents, especially when they were in danger of death and had previously earnestly desired it. 

This was done accordingly, as appears from the memorable instance he mentions of *Serapion*, an elderly man. Having lapsed in the time of persecution, Serapion had often desired reconciliation, but in that confused time, he could not obtain it. However, he was suddenly overtaken by the summons of death. After lying speechless for three days, on the fourth day he regained just enough use of his tongue to tell his nephew, a boy who attended him, to go for one of the priests to give him absolution, without which he could not die. The priest was sick at that time, but pitying the man's case, he gave the boy a small portion of the consecrated Eucharist which he kept by him, telling him to moisten it and put it into the man’s mouth. As soon as this was done, the old man breathed out his soul with unspeakable comfort and satisfaction, knowing that he now died in communion with the Church.

<margin>b Same source, chapter 45, page 247. <note>original: "Ibid. c. 45. p. 247."</note></margin>
VI. Nor was his care in this matter confined to his single diocese; he wrote letters about this subject to most of the eminent bishops and governors of the Church. And so that he might leave nothing unattempted, he reached out to *Novatian* (or as he calls him, *Novatus*) himself, endeavoring by all mild and gentle methods to reduce him to the peace and order of the Church. His letter to him, being short and very moving <note>original: "pathetical"</note>, we shall include here:

->Dionysius to our brother Novatus, greetings:<-

> *Since you yourself confess that you were unwillingly drawn into this schism <note>A formal split or division within the Church.</note>, prove it by your willing and ready return to the Church. Indeed, in my mind, it is much more honorable. For in the one case, a man suffers only for his own soul, but in this case, he undergoes martyrdom for the whole Church of God. And if you shall now persuade and lead your brothers back to peace and concord, your...*

VII. No sooner had he finished with this matter than he was engaged in another controversy which involved and disturbed the whole Christian Church: I mean the dispute concerning the rebaptizing of those who had been baptized by heretics, which was so hotly disputed between **Saint Cyprian** and **Stephen**, Bishop of **Rome**. <sup>a</sup> **Dionysius**, together with **Firmilian**, Bishop of **Caesarea** in **Cappadocia**, and many others in the **East**, stood on **Cyprian’s** side, maintaining that they ought to be baptized again. However, he conducted himself with great temperance and moderation. He distinguished between apostates <note>People who had once belonged to the Church but left it.</note> who had received their baptism in the Catholic Church; these he did not rebaptize upon their return (as **Cyprian** also affirms) but only admitted them by the laying on of hands. This rule and practice, he tells us<sup>b</sup>, he had learned from his predecessor **Heraclas**. But as for pure heretics, who had received no baptism other than what had been conferred by heretical persons (which in reality was null and of no effect), he thought it proper for them to be entered into the Church by Catholic baptism. Besides this, he acted more as a mediator than a partisan, writing to Pope **Stephen** to urge moderation in the case, as he also did to **Sixtus**, Stephen's successor, and most other Bishops of that time. Indeed, that he was not stiff and rigorous in his views may appear from the instance he relates in his Epistle to Pope **Sixtus**<sup>c</sup>, wherein he begs his advice.

A certain man in his church, who was ranked among the faithful <note>The "faithful" (fideles) were baptized members in full communion, as opposed to "catechumens" who were still learning.</note> during both his and his predecessors' days, observed the form and manner of baptism as it was administered among the Orthodox. He came to **Dionysius** and tearfully bewailed his own case; falling at his feet, he confessed that the baptism he had received among the heretics was nothing like this, but was full of blasphemy and impiety. For this reason, he was infinitely troubled in his conscience and dared not lift up his eyes to Heaven, begging that he might partake of the true and sincere baptism, and the grace and acceptance that was conferred by it. **Dionysius** would not allow this, telling him that his long communion with the Church was equivalent to it. He argued that for one who had so often been present at the giving of thanks <note>The Eucharist or Thanksgiving service.</note>, had said *Amen* to the prayers of the congregation, had stood before the holy Table and taken the holy food into his hands, and had been for such a long time a partaker of the body and blood of our Lord **Jesus Christ**—having done this for so many years together—he dared not admit him to another baptism. He told the man to be of good cheer and, with a firm faith and a good conscience, to approach the Holy Sacrament. Notwithstanding all of this, the man’s mind was not quieted; he still drooped under his fears and scruples, dared not be present at the Lord’s Table, and could hardly be persuaded even to come to public prayers. What answer **Sixtus** returned to this case is uncertain, but it is evident from this that **Saint Dionysius** was no zealot for the opposing opinion. Though it must be admitted there was something unique in this case that did not occur in ordinary circumstances, he presumed that such a long communion with the Church and such a continued and open profession of the Orthodox faith was equivalent to <note>original: "tantamount"</note> being legally initiated and baptized into it.

<margin>

VIII. In these disputes, he lived through the short reign of **Gallus**, the successor to **Decius**. **Gallus** failed to take warning <sup>a</sup> from his predecessor's errors and stumbled over the same stone. Although he found the world at peace, he felt compelled to begin persecuting the Christians, even though their prayers to Heaven actually secured the peace and prosperity of the Empire. But this, alas, was merely a preliminary storm compared to what followed during the reign of **Valerian**. Our **Dionysius** <sup>b</sup> identified **Valerian** as the *Beast* in the *Book of Revelation*, *to whom was given a mouth speaking great things and blasphemies, and power was given unto him to continue forty and two months*. 

Initially, **Valerian** was exceptionally kind to Christians—more so than any previous Emperors, including those who were thought to be Christians themselves. His entire household was full of pious and good people, and his home was a kind of Church. However, this favorable climate was too mild to last long. Seduced and misled by a high-ranking magician of **Egypt**, **Valerian** was persuaded to abandon his kindness and persecute the Christians. The magician portrayed them as people who hindered the Emperor's success through "wicked and cursed charms." He used their power over **demons** <note>original: "Dæmons"; in the ancient world, these were often thought of as intermediary spirits, but Christians viewed them as evil spirits or fallen angels.</note> as a pretense, claiming they obstructed his magical arts and drove spirits away simply by speaking a word. He convinced the Emperor that the ready way to be happy was to enforce **pagan rites** <note>original: "Gentile Rites"</note>, maintain **purification rituals** <note>original: "Lustrations"</note>, and offer sacrifices or perform **divinations** <note>Predicting the future by inspecting the internal organs of animals or humans.</note> using the blood and entrails of men and beasts. Consequently, edicts were published everywhere against the Christians, leaving them unprotected against the public’s rage.

<margin>
<sup>c</sup> His letter to Germanus, in the same source, chapter 11, page 257. <note>original: "Ep. ejus ad Germ. ib. c. 11. p. 257."</note>
</margin>

IX. When these orders arrived in **Alexandria**, **Dionysius** <sup>c</sup>, accompanied by some of his clergy, went before **Aemilian** the Governor. At first, **Aemilian** did not directly forbid him from holding their solemn assemblies, but instead tried to persuade him to abandon that way of worship, assuming others would quickly follow his example. The answer **Dionysius** gave was short and modeled after the Apostles: *that we must obey God rather than men*. He openly assured the Governor that he would worship the true God and no one else, and that he would never abandon this resolution nor ever stop being a Christian. 

The Governor told them that he had informed them, both in person and in writing, of the Emperors' great mercy, which permitted them to be safe if they would only act in accordance with nature and worship the gods who protected the Empire. He expressed his hope that they would not be so ungrateful as to refuse. The Bishop replied that everyone worships those they believe to be gods; as for themselves, they worshipped and served the one God who is the Creator of the world and who granted the government to the Emperors, and to whom they offered daily prayers for the stability of their Empire. To this, the Governor responded that if he were a god, nothing stopped them from worshipping him alongside those who were truly gods, since they were commanded to worship [not one, but] gods, and specifically those whom everyone recognized as such. **Dionysius** answered, *“We cannot worship any other.”* 

“I see,” replied **Aemilian**, “that you are a group of foolish and ungrateful people who do not appreciate the favor of our Lords the Emperors. Therefore, you shall stay in this city no longer. You will be sent to **Cephro** in the region of **Libya**, for I have decided to banish you there according to the Emperor’s command. Neither you nor any of your sect will be allowed to hold meetings or visit your **cemeteries** <note>original: "Cæmeteria"; early Christians often met in cemeteries or at the tombs of martyrs, which were considered sacred and safe places for assembly.</note>.”

# The Life of St. Dionysius of Alexandria

> “...which if anyone dares to attempt, it shall be at his own peril, and he shall be punished according to his crime. Therefore, depart to the place assigned to you.”

<margin>* *History of the Church*, Book 6, chapter 10, page 402. <note>original: "Lib. 6. c. 10. p. 402." This likely refers to the work of Nicephorus mentioned below.</note></margin>

X. This sentence was quickly carried out. Dionysius, although he was sick at the time, was not granted even a single day’s rest to recover or prepare for his journey. Indeed, when he learned specifically where he was being exiled, he was somewhat troubled, knowing it to be a place lacking the company of good people and constantly exposed to raids by thieves and robbers. However, he felt more encouraged when told it was near a large and populous city; its proximity would provide him with people for conversation and opportunities for conversion. *Cephro* was the most rugged and wild region of the Libyan Desert, and *Coluthius* (which, as *Nicephorus* <note>original: *Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos*, a 14th-century Greek historian who compiled earlier church records</note> tells us, was the specific part of it intended for Dionysius) was likely the most miserable area of them all. 

He was sent there, and many Christians soon followed him, coming both from Alexandria and from other parts of Egypt. Upon his arrival, he was treated harshly and pelted with stones. However, before long, he not only refined their wild customs but also turned them away from idolatry and led them to embrace the Christian faith. As he found success, he moved from place to place, preaching throughout those wild and lonely regions, effectively turning the wilderness into a church. 

Neither the malice nor the threats of the Governor could prevent the Christians from gathering in Alexandria, even though their beloved Bishop had been snatched away from them. Meanwhile, *Aemilian* <note>The Roman prefect or governor of Egypt</note> proceeded with extreme severity against all who were brought before him. He executed many with refined cruelty, kept others for the rack and torture, loaded them with chains, and threw them into filthy and foul dungeons, forbidding any of their friends from visiting them. Yet, even at the height of these trials, God supported their spirits and inspired others to risk their lives to provide comfort and necessities to the prisoners. They did not hesitate, even at the risk of execution, to bury the bodies of the martyrs.

<margin><sup>a</sup> Eusebius, *History of the Church*, Book 7, chapter 13, page 262. <note>original: "Euseb. l. 7. c. 13. p. 262."</note></margin>

XI. I do not find exactly how long Dionysius remained in exile, but it was likely until Emperor *Valerian* was captured by the King of Persia in the year 259. At that time, *Valerian’s* son, *Gallienus*, began to rule alone. From his father’s misfortunes, *Gallienus* learned how to conduct himself toward the Christians. He observed that while his father favored the Christians, heaven smiled upon his plans and everything proceeded smoothly. However, once he began to treat them harshly, the tide turned, and divine vengeance pursued and overtook the empire. *Gallienus* concluded that nothing could be more prudent or reasonable than to halt the current fury and allow them to practice their religion safely. He did this through the following edict: <sup>a</sup>

# The Life of St. Dionysius of Alexandria

-> Emperor Caesar Publius Licinius GALLIENUS, *Pious, Fortunate, August*, to *Dionysius, Pinnas, Demetrius*, and the rest of the Bishops. <-

> WE have given orders that our generous favor shall be extended throughout the world, so that all places of worship shall be protected from force and violence. Therefore, you also may freely benefit from our official decree <term>rescript</term> <note>original: "Rescript"; a formal written reply from the Roman Emperor to a petition</note>, so that no man shall dare to harass or trouble you. This legal right, which you may now lawfully enjoy, has been granted by us for a long time. For this purpose, *Aurelius Cyrenius*, our High Steward <term>Procurator</term>, shall keep a copy of this edict which we have now granted.

He also sent a similar decree to other bishops, giving them free use of their *cemeteries* <note>original: "Cæmeteria"</note>—the places where they buried their dead and often assembled for their religious ceremonies, especially the memorials of the martyrs.

<margin>a Trebellius Pollio, *The Life of Aemilianus*, page 778, and *The Life of Gallienus*, chapter 4, page 715.</margin>
XII. Dionysius had barely settled back at home when he was alarmed by another event. This forced him once again to go into hiding, or at least to stay so secluded that he was unable to carry out his duties. <sup>a</sup> *Aemilianus* the Governor <term>Prefect</term>, driven partly by his own ambition and partly forced by an unhappy accident in which he was involved, claimed the title of Emperor. The Roman Army in Egypt joined him, partly out of dislike for Gallienus and partly out of affection for Aemilian, who was a sharp and active man. Immediately, he seized the storehouses, as that country was the common granary of the Empire. When Gallienus was informed of the news, he ordered his general *Theodotus* to march with an army into those parts. Theodotus besieged Alexandria and reduced the city to great extremity. For the citizens were not only vigorously attacked by the enemy from the outside, but also undermined <sup>b</sup> by internal parties and factions <margin>b Dionysius, *Letter to Hierax*, in Eusebius, Book 7, chapter 21, page 266.</margin>. The city was divided into two groups: one fighting for Gallienus and the other for Aemilian. As a result, there was no conversation or trade between them. Dionysius was compelled to handle all his private affairs and the public business of his church with his friends through letters. He noted that it was safer for a person to travel from the East to the West than to pass from one part of Alexandria to another, so barbaric and inhuman were the outrages committed there. The outcome was that Gallienus’s party succeeded in letting Theodotus and his army in. They captured the rebel leader and sent him to the Emperor, who had him strangled in prison.

XIII. How stormy and tempestuous is the state of this lower world! One wave of trouble constantly follows another. The persecution was followed by a civil war and a cruel famine; and no sooner was that over, but a terrible plague followed close behind it—one of the most dreadful and amazing judgments that God sends upon mankind. It overran the city and the country...

...country, sweeping away what the fury of the recent wars had left behind. The historian <margin>a *Zosimus, History, Book 1, p. 347.*</margin> says that in no other age had there been such a great destruction of mankind. This plague (which some say <margin>b *Pomponius Laetus in the Life of Gallus, p. 1235; Eutropius, Roman History, Book 9, p. 1924.*</margin> first originated in Ethiopia) began during the reigns of Gallus and Volusian. Ever since then, it has more or less spread across most parts of the Roman Empire, and it now maintained its deadly presence at Alexandria. There, with an impartial severity, it mowed down both pagans <note>original: "Gentiles"</note> and Christians alike. 

It turned the Easter <note>original: "Paschal"</note> festivities <margin>c *Dionysius, in the same work, chapter 22, p. 268.*</margin> into days of weeping and mourning. Every place was filled with dying groans and the sorrow of those mourning friends already dead or those about to depart. It was now as it had been during the great Egyptian plague of old—or perhaps even worse: *there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where there was not only one, but many dead.* 

In this sad and miserable time, the conduct of the Christians was vastly different from that of the heathens. Out of the abundance of their kindness and charity, and without any regard for their own health or lives, the Christians boldly ventured into the greatest dangers. They daily visited, assisted, and ministered to their sick and infected brothers, cheerfully taking their pains and diseases upon themselves and even dying with them. When many of those they cared for recovered and lived, the caregivers themselves died—as if, by a miraculous and unheard-of charity, they had willingly taken the diseases upon themselves and died to save others from death. Among those who did this were the most prominent members of both the clergy and the laity, who cheerfully embraced a death that deserved a title little less than that of martyrdom. They embraced the bodies of the dead, closed their eyes, laid them out, washed them, and dressed them in their funeral clothes <term>weeds</term>. They carried the bodies on their shoulders to their graves, and it was not long before others performed the same services for them. The pagans, on the contrary, abandoned all sense of humanity. When anyone began to fall sick, they immediately cast them out and fled from their dearest friends and relatives. They left them half-dead in the highways or threw them out as soon as they died, fearing the infection—which, despite all their care and diligence, they could not avoid.

XIV. Nor were these the only troubles the good man faced; he had conflicts of another nature that consumed his time and concern. Sabellius, a Libyan born at Ptolemais (a city of Pentapolis), had recently introduced <margin>d *Dionysius, Letter to Sixtus, in the same work, chapter 6, p. 252; Nicephorus, Book 6, chapter 26, p. 419.*</margin> dangerous notions and opinions regarding the doctrine of the Holy Trinity. He claimed that the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost were but one single existence—one person under three different names. He argued that in the time of the Old Testament, this person gave the Law as the Father; in the New Testament, he became man as the Son; and he afterwards descended upon the Apostles as the Holy Ghost. 

Dionysius, acting as a vigilant pastor of his flock, immediately challenged the man. However, while he handled the case with too much eagerness and fervor in his arguments, he "bent the stick" too far in the opposite direction. He asserted not only a distinction of persons <note>original: "ἑτερότητα τῶν ὑποστάσεων"</note> <margin>d</margin>, but a difference of essence <note>original: "οὐσίας διαφοράν"</note> <margin>e *Basil, Letter 41 to Magnus the Philosopher, p. 60.*</margin> and an inequality of power and glory. For this, he is severely criticized by St. Basil and some of the other ancient writers as one of those who opened the door to the Arian impieties <note>Arianism: the heresy that the Son was a created being, not co-equal with the Father</note> that later broke out in the world. Yet St. Basil could not help but give him credit, saying that it was not from any ill intention, but only an over-eager desire to oppose his adversary that led him into those...

XV. No sooner was this controversy settled than he was engaged in another. Nepos, an Egyptian Bishop who had recently died, had fallen into the error of the Millenarians <term>Millenarians: those who believe that Christ will establish a physical kingdom on Earth for a literal thousand years.</term>. Nepos was a man eminent for his constancy in the faith, his industry and skill in the Holy Scriptures, and the many psalms and hymns he had composed, which the brothers sang in their public meetings. He had published books to show that the promises made in the Scriptures to good men were to be understood "in a more Jewish manner" <note>original: *Ioudaikoteron*</note>—that is, literally. He taught that there was to be a thousand-year state upon Earth where they would enjoy sensual pleasures and delights. He endeavored to prove his assertions from certain passages in Saint John’s Revelation, titling his book *A Refutation of the Allegorists* <note>original: *Elenchos Allegoriston*</note>. 

This book was eagerly snatched up and read by many. It gained such a reputation that the Law and the Prophets, and even the writings of the Evangelists and Apostles, were neglected and thrown aside. The doctrine of this book was celebrated as containing "some great and hidden mystery" <note>original: *mega ti kai kekrymmenon mysterion*</note> that had been previously concealed from the world. The simple and unwary were taught to abandon all sublime and magnificent thoughts of our Lord’s glorious coming, the Resurrection, and the final judgment, and our conformity to Him in glory. Instead, they were taught to hope for a state in the Kingdom of God where they would be entertained with the small, trifling, fading, and transitory things that this world provides. 

Dionysius was then in the province of Arsenoite <note>The region around the Faiyum Oasis in Egypt.</note>, where this opinion had prevailed so far that it had drawn entire churches into schism and separation. He summoned the presbyters <note>original: "Presbyters"; elders or priests.</note> and teachers who preached in the country villages, as well as any of the people who wished to come, advising them to publicly examine this doctrine in their sermons. They immediately defended themselves using Nepos's book. At that point, Dionysius began to engage in debate with them directly. He stayed with them for three days together, from morning until night, weighing and discussing the doctrines contained in the book. During all this time, he admired their persistence and love for the truth, as well as their great quickness and readiness of understanding. The discussions on both sides were managed with such order, decency, modesty, and moderation as doubts were proposed and points were conceded. # The Life of Saint Dionysius of Alexandria

...with all imaginable scorn and arrogance, magnifying himself as far beyond them. The hymns that were ordinarily sung in honor of our Lord, he abolished as if they were recent and novel inventions. He was so far from restraining these claims that he highly encouraged them, listening to them himself not only with patience but with delight. 

Moreover, he was strongly suspected of sexual immorality, keeping <term>subintroduced women</term> <note>original: "Συνεισάκτους γυναῖκας" (Syneisaktoi gynaikes); these were women who lived in the houses of clergy under a vow of chastity, a practice often condemned because it led to scandal.</note> in his house, some of whom were of exquisite beauty, contrary to the canons of the Church and to the great scandal of religion. To avoid being reproached by those around him, he endeavored to corrupt his clergy by overlooking their vices and irregularities and bribing others with pensions. Those whom he could not win over with evil arts, he intimidated through his power and his great influence with the princes and high officials of those parts. Consequently, they were forced to mourn his behavior in private, as they did not dare to publish or declare it abroad.

XVII. To correct these outrages, most of the chief bishops of the East resolved to meet in a council at *Antioch*^a, to which they earnestly invited our **Dionysius**. But, alas, age and infirmities had rendered him incapable of such a journey and had given him a "writ of ease" <note>An official document releasing someone from a duty or position; here, a metaphor for his retirement due to old age.</note>, on which account he begged to be excused. But so that he might not be lacking in doing what he could, he sent letters in which he declared his judgment and opinion on those matters. In his epistle to the Church of *Antioch*, to show his displeasure regarding the matter, he not only refused to write to the man himself but did not even give him the civility of a greeting. 

In this council, the crafty fox hid his head, disguising his true sentiments and making excuses for his misconduct. By confessing and recanting what he was unable to hide, he managed to remain in his position for the time being. How he was later discovered and exposed, convicted, condemned, and deposed in another council in that city, and **Domnus** appointed in his place; how he refused to submit to the sentence of the council and for some time maintained his station through the power of **Zenobia** (a Queen in those parts and a convert to Judaism whose favor he had sought and obtained); and how at last, upon the bishops' appeal, he was turned out and the council's decree executed by the immediate order of the Emperor **Valerian**—all this is beyond the scope of my current task to investigate.

c Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, Book 69, page 311. <note>original: "Haeres. LXIX. p. 311."</note>
</margin>

XVIII. A little after this first council at *Antioch*, our **Saint Dionysius** died in the twelfth year of the reign of **Gallienus**^b, in the year **265 AD**. He had served as Bishop of *Alexandria* for seventeen years, dying probably in the same year and on the same day as **Saint Gregory the Miracle-Worker** <note>original: "S. Gregory Thaumaturgus"</note>. Their memories are accordingly celebrated on **September 17** in the *Calendar of the Roman Church*. His memory was preserved at *Alexandria* (as we learn from **Epiphanius**^c) by a church dedicated to him. However, his memory flourished much more in the unmatched virtues of his past life and those excellent writings he left behind him, which mainly consisted of a great number of letters. Indeed, it is probable that all his writings were of this nature, as his larger treatises were written in the form of epistles. If these were still extant today, instead of the little...

---

Our Lord is generally supposed to have been born on December 25, six days before the commencement of the Common Era <note>original: vulgar Æra</note>, in the 42nd year of the reign of Emperor Augustus <note>original: Ann. Augusti Imp. XLII</note>. 

Although, strictly speaking, the 42nd year of Augustus ended on November 27 (counting his reign from the time he entered the Triumvirate <term>a board of three officials in Ancient Rome</term>), the civil Roman year did not expire until the last day of December; therefore, his reign may be said to extend through that entire time. His 43rd year, by common reckoning, and the first year of the Common Era of our Lord, commenced on January 1, which was when the Romans began their year and the new Consuls took office.

It also includes a scholarly note on the specific dating of Christ's birth relative to the Roman calendar.</summary>

# A Chronological Table.

| Year of Christ <note>original: Ann. Chr.</note> | Roman Emperors. | Consuls. | Ecclesiastical Affairs. |

| 52 | Reign of Claudius, years 11 & 12 | P. Cornelius Sylla Faustus. L. Salvius Otho Titianus. | *St. Paul departs from Corinth, passes to Ephesus, then to Jerusalem, and returns back to Ephesus.* |
| 53 | years 12 & 13 | D. Junius Silanus. Q. Haterius Antoninus. | *He preaches and disputes daily in the School of Tyrannus, convinces the Jews, and converts great numbers to the Faith.* |
| 54 | years 13 & 14; Nero begins Oct. 13, year 1 | M. Afinius Marcellus. M. Acilius Aviola. | *St. Paul fights with "Beasts"—that is, men of evil and brutish manners—at Ephesus. He continues to preach there and in the surrounding areas.* |
| 55 | years 1 & 2 | Nero Claudius, Emperor <note>original: Imp.</note>. L. Antistius Vetus. | *St. Paul's departure from Ephesus. He passes through Macedonia and Greece, and gathers contributions for the Saints at Jerusalem.* |
| 56 | years 2 & 3 | Q. Volusius Saturninus. P. Cornelius Scipio. | *St. Paul comes to Jerusalem and is apprehended in the Temple and secured in the Castle. His imprisonment at Caesarea and arraignment before Felix, the Roman Governor.* |
| 57 | years 3 & 4 | Nero Claudius, Emperor, 2nd time <note>original: Imp. II.</note>. L. Calpurnius Piso. | *St. Paul is kept prisoner at Caesarea under Felix.* |
| 58 | years 4 & 5 | Nero Claudius, Emperor, 3rd time <note>original: Imp. III.</note>. M. Valerius Messala. | *St. Paul's arraignment before Festus. He is sent to Rome, where he arrives about the end of this year or the beginning of the following year. \** |
| 59 | years 5 & 6 | C. Vipsanius Poplicola (also known as <note>original: al.</note> Apronianus). C. Fonteius Capito. | *St. Paul's free imprisonment <note>house arrest</note> at Rome. He writes his Epistles to the Ephesians, Colossians, Philippians, to Timothy, and to Philemon.* |
| 60 | years 6 & 7 | Nero Claudius, Emperor, 4th time <note>original: Imp. IV.</note>. Cossus Cornelius Lentulus. | *About the latter end of this year, St. Paul is set at liberty, and before his departure from Italy, he writes his Epistle to the Hebrews.* |

---

\* The time of St. Paul's being sent to Rome depends upon Festus's arrival in Judea to succeed Felix. Though this cannot be precisely determined, it is plain that it must have been while Pallas (Felix's brother, by whose influence with the Emperor Felix had his life spared when accused by the Jews of bad management) was still in some favor with Nero. Pallas's influence was declining some time before, and he seems to have fallen completely upon the death of Agrippina (on whose interest he relied at Court), who was killed in the 5th year of Nero, AD 59. Pallas himself was poisoned in the 8th year of Nero, AD 62.

\* Some of the most learned chronologists of the *Roman Catholic Church* place the martyrdom of these two great Apostles two years later, specifically in AD 67 <note>original: Ann. Chr. * In the list <note>original: Catalogue</note> of the **Bishops of Rome** recorded by **Optatus** and **Saint Augustine**, **Anicetus** is placed before **Pius**. According to that account, Anicetus’s succession to that **See**, and consequently **Polycarp’s** arrival in Rome, must be placed fifteen years earlier. See the *Life of Saint Polycarp*, Number IV, page 115.

---

\* Although this seems the most appropriate period for the martyrdom of the *Theban Legion*—as that was when *Maximian* was sent against the rebels in *France*—the accounts of their martyrdom state that during their journey from the East, they came to *Rome* and were strengthened in the faith by *Marcellinus*, who was then Bishop. If that is true, they could not have suffered earlier than the year of Christ 296, when *Marcellinus* succeeded to that office <note>original: See</note>.
